FOREWORD 

This issue of the 18-monograph series on the Selective Service expe rience of World War II is No. 11 and entitled "Conscientious Objec tion." The basic law of the System gave recognition to the fundamental problem of honest conviction against war. So, for more than six years of operation, special attention was given to the selective process as it pertained to the mobilization of two distinct types of conscientious objectors who were militarily liable registrants: (1) those willing to perform military service only of a noncombatant nature and (2) those unwilling to perform any kind of military service whatsoever. Monograph No. 11 treats exhaustively of conscientious objection in World War II and provides, in addition, a historical background regarding it.

The monograph is of further significance from the standpoint of source and preparation. It was written by Lt. Col. Neal M. Wherry of the division in National Headquarters which was responsible for the conscientious objection program of Selective Service. As he prepared the book he maintained close consultation with Col. Lewis F. 

Kosch and Mr. Austin S. Imirie, chief and assistant chief, respectively, of that division and with Maj. James L. Montague and Mr. Victor A. 

Olsen likewise of the division. Dr. Mapheus Smith of the System's 

Records and Research Division and Mr. Kenneth H. McGill, assistant to the Director, did much of the final editing work. Acknowledgment must also be made of the clearance efforts of a committee composed as follows: 

Col. Daniel O. Omer, Chairman 

Col. Richard H. Eanes 

Col. Lewis F. Kosch.

Col. Percival S. Moses 

Col. Raymond T. Higgins 

Col. George A. Irvin 

Lt. Col. Arthur R. Boone

I 

CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION AND SELECTIVE SERVICE 

The philosophy of Selective Service, as embodied in its basic law of 1940, was that no militarily liable citizen had the right of exemption from service to the Nation in time of emergency, whatever his religious training or affiliation, and whatever his personal beliefs and opinions. 

The registrant of the System, regardless of his conscientious scruples against the employment of force or service in the armed forces, was classified and selected for whatever duty he could best perform and which would be of greatest benefit to his country. That was the process of selection as it operated for conscientious objection. 

Selective Service Approach to Conscientious Objection 

The treatment of conscientious objectors by Selective Service was a matter of importance to individual objectors and to the people with whom they were most closely associated their families, neighbors, members of religious congregations, members of civil rights organizations. It was of significance also to the rest of the Nation, consisting among others of men who volunteered for service in the armed forces as well as those who served after selection and induction. The relatives and friends of these men likewise had a particular interest in the System's approach to conscientious objection. 

If no consideration at all had been given to those objecting on the grounds of conscience, the result might have been considerable opposition to Selective Service operations and a lessening of national unity. 

On the other hand, if the treatment of individuals who claimed to have scruples against service had been liberal enough to allow them freedom of action, the other and vastly larger group of citizens, willing to make sacrifices, would have been antagonized to the point where unity would also have been impaired. 

In an attempt to avoid the harsh treatment of conscientious objectors, on the one hand, and their overly liberal treatment, on the other, the policy of the System, pursuant to legislation, was to require conscientious objectors to perform such service to the Nation as their beliefs would support. Although this was not entirely satisfactory either to pacifistic groups or the nationalistically-minded, it did lie 1

<< D 

CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION 

between the two extremes. The soundness of this approach was demonstrated in the contributions to the war effort and to the national welfare by the different classes of conscientious objectors, and by the fact that such contributions were made without lowering the morale of the armed forces or of other groups. 

Varieties of Conscientious Objectors 

Within the broad World War II definition of a conscientious objector as one who claimed religious or private convictions against employing force in war or who objected to performing military duty, there were a number of classes important to identify. For instance, there were general groups identifiable on the basis of the degree to which they would serve. The most extreme variety of conscientious objection involved opposition to any kind of service to the Nation in time of war. This was absolute or complete objection and it grew out of the individualistic or religious feeling either of a person or of a small isolated group.

A more limited type of conscientious objection was unwillingness to perform any duty which was connected with warlike activity or a military organization, even in time of peace. During World War II conscientious objectors of this type were sent to special public service camps to perform work of national importance under civilian direction. 

A third and still more limited kind of conscientious objection involved refusal to engage in combat activities but willingness to serve in the armed forces if unarmed, or to serve in the medical corps, or in any other noncombatant capacity. Conscientious objectors of these last two kinds were recognized in the Selective Service law and consequently by the System's classification process. They performed valuable service throughout the war.

Others more religious than conscientious in their objection would not serve in World War II for particular reasons of religion, though they were not usually opposed to all war as a matter of principle. 

There were likewise those whose religious feelings would allow them to accept service only in a war of defense, in employing force for restraining or policing purposes, or in a war which did not interfere with religious duties. Also somewhat different from the conscientious objector was the pacifist who would not serve unless convinced that arbitration for the settlement of international disputes had been tried and had failed to achieve peace. 

Conscientious objectors were also classifiable into general groups on the basis of religious views. Some objected entirely because of training and affiliation with religious groups, mainly the historic nonresistant or pacifist churches, which were opposed to violence and warfare. The grounds for opposition by others were individual re-

CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION AND SELECTIVE SERVICE » 3 

ligious convictions rather than the traditions of a sect to which they belonged. Still others based their objection on personal philosophies or other grounds not associated with religious beliefs or teachings. 

In practice it was often difficult to place an individual in any one of these classes. For instance, a man might have claimed adherence to the tenets of a "peace church" but not actually have been a member. 

Or a registrant could nominally have been a church member through having his name on the church roll, although for some time he had been nonattendant. Then, too, there were others who mixed humanitarian, intellectual, and political views with their professed religious beliefs, and there were also atheists and agnostics. 

Department of Justice Groupings 

Taking somewhat the same approach, a member of the Department of Justice, after handling the cases of over 10,000 men claiming conscientious objection during World War II, distinguished 12 classes as follows: 

1. The religious objector sincerely believes in a personal Creator whose immortal laws forbid the killing of human beings, particularly as set forth in the Commandment "Thou shalt not kill." He believes that war is contrary to the spirit and teachings of Christianity and in opposition to God's will, and he cannot participate, without subjecting his soul to eternal perdition. 

2. The moral or ethical objector considers war inconsistent with his moral philosophy and humanitarianism which is independent of religious beliefs, except as it may be predicated upon a belief in a brotherhood of man. That concept is not based on a belief in the fatherhood of God. His conscience is bound by a moral law, which enjoins him from having to do with so destructive and futile a force as war, which evidences a breakdown of reason by substituting force. 

In fact, most of this type of objector denies a belief in a deity except insofar as there may be a moral force in the universe. It is his view that mankind is sufficient to itself, that it owes no obligation to any power except humankind, and that it may achieve perfection in and of itself without the interposition of any deity or supernatural power. 

3. The economic objector, as a student of history, sees all wars as based upon the inequitable distribution of natural resources, complicated and supported by tariff barriers, immigration restrictions and nationalistic control of colonial markets and sees no hope of this war effecting a more equitable distribution of economic opportunity. 

4. The political objector sees war as a means of exploiting the masses for the few who are politically ambitious, or for the governments and deceiving the people. 

5. The philosophical objector, generally a student of metaphysics, possesses a personal philosophy which dominates his ways of life. 

6. The sociological objector whose objections are based upon a theory that war has no place in his own particular ordering of society. 

7. The internationalist objector would destroy or abolish all international boundaries and sovereignty, racial and trade lines, and consider the world one big family of peoples devoid of war.

8. The personal objector, who objects to this particular war, because he believes it to be a war of imperialism or that the Allied Nations have brought it on, or that it is not the type of war in which he can participate. 

9. The neurotic objector has a phobia of war's atrocities, a mental and physical fear and abhorrence of killing and maiming, and who therefore cannot participate in it. 

10. The naturalistic objector's objection is physiological, and based upon an abhorrence of blood. 

11. The "professional pacifist” objector would have "peace-in our time at any cost." He would tolerate nothing which would inconvenience his mode of living, but would aggressively limit the liberties of others. He wants to enjoy all the protections of the Government, but is unwilling to bear any of the responsibilities of citizenship in this respect. 

12. The Jehovah Witness objects to all man-made wars and Governments, but says he is not a conscientious objector to all wars, since he would fight and kill in defense of the Theocracy, his property and his brethren.¹ 

It should be understood, however, that these 12 classes were not equally common among conscientious objectors, a fact which will be developed later.

Conscientious Objection and Manpower Procurement In terms of numbers, the problem of the conscientious objector in World War II was extremely small. Statistically, therefore, the 

Selective Service policy toward conscientious objectors had a minor relationship to the over-all problem of military manpower procurement. Nor were conscientious objectors numerically important in any age group. The consideration given them did not affect the successful filling of induction calls for the armed forces except in a few counties in the United States where registrants of the so-called peace groups were heavily concentrated and their deferment left an insufficient number of men. In spite of this, no State encountered serious difficulty in meeting its calls on account of the System's conscientious objection approach.

Although conscientious objectors did not create a difficult problem in terms of the number involved, or of meeting the calls for induction into the armed forces, they did constitute an administrative difficulty. 

The practice of having Civilian Public Service Camps for objectors where they could fulfill their obligation without violating the dictates of conscience was one of the features of the System's administration. 

In view of the national unity which the program helped to create and maintain during the war, however, its administrative difficulties seemed justified. 

1 Unpublished report of the Assistant to the Attorney General, 1945, on file at National

CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION AND SELECTIVE SERVICE » 5 Public Approval of the Objector Program 

As already suggested, the Selective Service System from 1940 to 1947 sought to deal with conscientious objection not only in accordance with legislation, but also in a way that would result in the greatest possible agreement on the part of the whole country that the problem was handled in a "fair and just" manner. Although extreme groups were not completely satisfied, the System's policy apparently met with general approval. This was particularly noticeable for citizens whose primary basis of judgment was that the best policy was one which produced the greatest national unity and effort during the emergency. The armed forces likewise were appreciative of the efforts of Selective Service because the induction of objectors who were opposed to any military or naval service, would have created difficulties for them.

In judging the conscientious objector and the System's program for him, it should perhaps be kept in mind that most World War II objectors were members of religious denominations and that their opposition to warfare was an integral part of their doctrinal beliefs. 

It will be recalled that freedom of religious conscience has always been one of the Nation's cherished traditions. This motivated many of the early colonists to turn to America for new homes, and during the emergency of 1940-47 Freedom of Religion was espoused as one of the Four Freedoms for which democratic countries were fighting. 

At the end of World War I it was said that the conscientious objector "has been eulogized by well-meaning persons, who understood neither the conscientious objector himself nor the national interest in a time of war, and he has, on the other hand, been roundly abused and reviled by a large part of our citizenry as a coward and a slacker. 

Apparently, there is no compromise ground: he is diabolically black to his critics while to his defenders his raiment is as the snows." 2 

Perhaps World War II saw an advance over these extremes of attitude.

This Report on Conscientious Objection The purpose of the present monograph is to set forth in detail the record of Selective Service in dealing with conscientious objection during World War II. Preliminary to this there will be a review of the problem throughout American history, as well as the background of some of the outstanding religious groups who have recorded their opposition to war. The legislative history of the conscientious ob-

jection provisions of the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940 will be given, as well as a discussion of the general Selective Service Regulations on the classification of conscientious objectors and the special regulations for the administration of their camps. General statistics in the field will likewise be presented. Finally, a review will be made of the outstanding events which occurred in connection with conscientious objection during World War II, as well as a discussion of some recommendations for future operations of this kind.

II 

The experience of Selective Service from 1940 to 1947 again brought to the attention of the United States the fact that objection to war was not of modern origin. Recalled was the philosophy of nonviolence which was said to have had a long history in the Orient. Some pacifists quoted a Chinese proverb, "When a man fights, it shows that the fool has lost his argument"; they credited the statement to a Chinese philosopher that "weapons are instruments of ill omen." By way of precedent it was also pointed out that even Ulysses upon one occasion plowed up a beach, feigning madness when he did not want to go to war.

Religious Basis for Conscientious Objection Those who were opposed to performing combatant or any service in the armed forces of the United States under the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940 styled themselves, for the most part, conscientious objectors. Their objections were largely religious and usually stemmed from interpretations of the Mosaic law and the teachings of Jesus. Their forerunners, two thousand years ago, had trouble with the imperial Roman legions. Strangely enough, that difficulty had to do more with the First Commandment of the Decalog of Moses, "Thou shalt have no other gods before me," than with the Sixth, "Thou shalt not kill," which was stressed in the national emergency of 

World War II. 

The Christians and the Roman Empire An early formula for religion had been set by Alexander the Great. 

The peoples he conquered were permitted to continue worshipping their old gods, but with the addition of his Zeus. Very much the same policy was followed when Rome became mistress of the world. But since the Roman chief of state was also the religious head of the state religion (pontifex maximus), statues of the emperors were placed in houses of worship throughout the Roman world. The situation which this brought into existence for the Jews was as follows:

But in this respect the position of the Jews was peculiar. Their god, Jaweh or 

Jehovah was, as he had declared himself, a jealous god and would have no strange gods before him. He was conceived by the Jews to be the supreme ruler over all things and over all men. The Jews, therefore, could not place in their temples the statue of the deified Augustus without disobeying the explicit command of Jehovah. With their usual practical good sense, the Romans recognized the special difficulty of the Jews and made them an exception. But the Jews promptly ran into another difficulty. How could they render military service when the soldier's oath of allegiance involved the recognition of the emperor as the deified head of the state? Here again the Roman government acted with sense and generosity. The Jews were practically exempted from military service.¹

A little later, the circumstances were these: man. * * The position of the Christians compelled them to be in a measure un-Ro- * Civil and military duties were refused where they might have been accepted. Yet it was not a principle with the Church at large to proscribe this public service; and we know as a matter of fact that there were Christians in the Roman Army.²

On the other hand, the canons of the Church of Alexandria, probably in the second century, "absolutely forbade volunteering which was the foundation of the Roman Army, and authoritatively stated that 'it was not fitting for Christians to bear arms.'" ³ 

Christian Acceptance of "the Just War"

From the time of Constantine, however, Christianity generally accepted the theory of "the just war." But modern doctrinal justification of war dates from St. Thomas Aquinas, who interpreted Jesus' command to Peter to put up his sword as one addressed to him as a cleric rather than a representative of all Christians. Later, some of the smaller sects coming out of the Reformation of the Middle Ages developed well-defined opposition to warfare. It has been only in recent years that strong pacifistic tendencies have appeared among the larger denominations.

The Principal Pacifist Churches 

The largest churches which retained doctrines of conscientious objection in World War II were the Mennonite, Brethren, and Friends. Together with certain smaller denominations, such as the 

Christadelphian and Molokan, these three made up what were commonly known as the "pacifist churches" or "historic peace churches," and furnished well over half of all conscientious objectors. Other groups having a degree of pacifism in their doctrines included the

The Jehovah's Witnesses also contributed many conscientious objectors, but as a religious group were enough different to require separate consideration.

Among the churches commonly considered "nonpacifist," those furnishing the largest number of conscientious objectors were the Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, Congregational-Christian, Church of Christ, and Catholic, in that order. First, however, there will be presented historical sketches of the groups which were known to have expressed nonresistance viewpoints before 1940. 

The Mennonites 

The Mennonite Church was the largest of seventeen denominations grouped as "Mennonite bodies" by the United States Bureau of the Census in its 1936 report on the decennial Census of Religious Bodies.* 

This group included the Hutterites and the Amish people. In 1936, there were 913 churches in the United States with 114,337 members comprising the Mennonite bodies. The largest numbers of these members were located in Pennsylvania, Ohio, Indiana, Kansas, and Oklahoma.

The Mennonite Church was founded in Zurich, Switzerland, in 1525, by a group of Bible students known as the Swiss Brethren. They were commonly called Anabaptists because of their practice of adult, as opposed to infant, baptism. The name "Mennonite" came into use about 1550 and probably referred to followers of one Menno Simons, a prominent leader of the group. The first Mennonite confession of faith, adopted by the Swiss Brethren at Schlatten in 1527, said they must lay down "weapons of force, such as sword, armor and the like, together with all their use, whether for the protection of friends or against personal enemies."

In 1683, the first Mennonites came to America from Crefeld, Germany, on the ship Concord and settled at Germantown, now a part of Philadelphia. During the eighteenth century, many Swiss Mennonites migrated to Pennsylvania. In fact, practically all of the socalled Pennsylvania Dutch Mennonites were supposedly of Swiss descent. Mennonites spread northward and westward from Germantown into other counties of Pennsylvania, and southward to Virginia. 

Later they went into the Ohio Valley and still farther west. However, the largest Mennonite migration to the United States apparently was from Russia in 1870. This was probably brought about in the main by the Russian threat to their nonresistant way of life. 

U. S. Census Bureau, Religious Bodies, 1936 (Washington: 1941), II, pp. 1002-1081. 

Guy F. Hershberger, War, Peace and Nonresistance (Scottdale, Pa.: Herald Press, 1944), p. 73. • John Horsch, The Principle of Nonresistance as Held by the Mennonite Church (Scottdale, Pa.: Mennonite Publishing House, 1927), p. 20.

Position of the Mennonites, 1937 

Representatives of the Mennonite Church, assembled in general conference near Turner, Ore., on August 25 and 26, 1937, and representing 16 conferences, adopted among other resolutions the following one setting forth the position on military service of the Mennonite 

Church at that time:

OUR POSITION ON MILITARY SERVICE 

In the light of the above principles of Scripture we are constrained as followers of Christ to abstain from all forms of military service and all means of support of war, and must consider members who violate these principles as transgressors and out of the fellowship with the church. Specifically our position entails the following commitments: 

1. We can have no part in carnal warfare or conflict between nations, nor in strife between classes, groups, or individuals. We believe that this means that we cannot bear arms personally nor aid in any way those who do so, and that as a consequence we cannot accept service under the military arm of the Government, whether direct or indirect, combatant or noncombatant, which ultimately involves participation in any operation aiding or abetting war and thus causes us to be responsible for the destruction of the life, health, and property of our fellow men. 

2. On the same grounds consistency requires that we do not serve during wartime under civil organizations temporarily allied with the military in the prosecution of the war, such as the YMCA, the Red Cross, and similar organizations which, under military orders, become a part of the war system in effect, if not in method and spirit, however beneficial their peacetime activities may be. 

3. We can have no part in the financing of war operations through the purchase of war bonds in any form or through voluntary contributions to any of the organizations or activities falling under the category described immediately above, unless such contributions are used for civilian relief or similar purposes. 

4. We cannot knowingly participate in the manufacture of munitions and weapons of war either in peacetime or in wartime. 

5. We can have no part in military training in schools and colleges, or in any other form of peacetime preparation for service as part of the war system. 

6. We ought carefully to abstain from any agitation, propaganda or activity that tends to promote ill will or hatred among nations which leads to war, but rather endeavor to foster good will and respect for all nations, peoples, and races, being careful to observe a spirit of sincere neutrality when cases of war and conflict arise. 

7. We ought not to seek to make a profit out of war and wartime inflation, which would mean profiting from the shedding of the blood of our fellow men. 

If, however, during wartime, excess profits do come into our hands, such profits should be conscientiously devoted to charitable purposes, such as the bringing of relief to the needy, or the spreading of the gospel of peace and love, and should not be applied to our own material benefit. 

OUR WILLINGNESS TO RELIEVE DISTRESS 

According to the teaching and spirit of Christ and the Gospel we are to do good to all men. Hence we are willing at all times to aid in the relief of those who are in need, distress or suffering, regardless of the danger in which

we may be placed in bringing such relief, or of the cost which may be involved We are ready to render such service in time of war as well as in in the same. time of peace.

OUR ATTITUDE DURING WARTIME 

If our country becomes involved in war, we shall endeavor to continue to live a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty; avoid joining in the wartime hysteria of hatred, revenge, and retaliation; manifest a meek and submissive spirit, being obedient unto the laws and regulations of the Government in all things, except in such cases where obedience to the Government would cause us to violate the teachings of the Scriptures so that we could not maintain a clear conscience before God (Acts 5:29). We confess that our supreme allegiance is to God, and that we cannot violate this allegiance by any lesser loyalty, but rather must follow Christ in all things, no matter what it costs. We love and honor our country and desire to work constructively for its highest welfare as loyal and obedient citizens; at the same time we are constrained by the love of Christ to love the people of all lands and races and to do them good as opportunity affords rather than evil, and we believe that this duty is not abrogated by war. We realize that to take this position may mean misunderstanding and even contempt from our fellow men, as well as possible suffering, but we hope by the grace of God that we may be able to assume, as our forefathers did, the sacrifices and suffering which may attend the sincere practice of this way of life, without malice or ill will toward those who may differ with us.

If once again conscription should be established, we venture to express the hope that if service be required of us it may not be the military arm of the Government, and may be such that we can perform it without violating our conscience, and that we may thus be permitted to continue to enjoy that full liberty of religious faith and conscience which has been our privilege hitherto.' 

This basic position of the Mennonites with respect to resistance or violence did not change materially throughout World War II. 

The Brethren 

The "Church of the Brethren" was the official name of the largest and oldest church body of the four composed of people commonly called Brethren. In the early history of this church the members were called Tunkers, Dunkers, and Dunkards, and these names have persisted. The words were adapted from the German verb 'tunken” meaning "to dip" and referred to the form of baptism used. 

This church was founded by Alexander Mack and seven others at 

Schwarzenau, Germany, in 1708. The first Brethren came to America, settling in Germantown, Pa., in 1719. The greater part of the membership in this young church probably migrated from Europe. 

At any rate the fate of the Brethren who failed to come to America is not known. Those who came spread from Pennsylvania to New

The founders of the Church of the Brethren took the position that war was contrary to the life, spirit, and teachings of Jesus, and that it was wrong to fight. There follows an early statement regarding this belief taken from The History of Pennsylvania, published in 1798: 

They also hold it not becoming a follower of Jesus Christ to bear arms, or fight; because, say they, their true master has forbid his disciples to resist evil; and because he also told them not to swear at all, they will by no means take an oath; but adhere close to his advice, in the affirmation of "yea” and “nay."⁹ 

Brethren's Belief in the 1930's

The Brethren's historical position was summarized thus during the annual conference of 1932: 

One of the fundamental tenets of the Church of the Brethren since its origin in 1708 has been the acceptance of the New Testament as its rule of faith and practice. Our church fathers have consistently taught and declared in private life as well as in official pronouncements that Christianity and war are incompatible. They believed in, and taught the gospel of peace and good will. They founded their faith in the spirit and teachings of the Bible as exemplified in the life and teachings of the Prince of Peace.10 

In addition, the minutes of the annual conference of the Church of the Brethren in 1938 contained the following as part of a report from the committee on counsel for conscientious objectors:

The committee on counsel for conscientious objectors desires to make the following recommendations to the conference of 1938 on the positions that our people should take in the event of war: 

I. Types of service considered consistent with the historic position of the church: 

1. Constructive service under church or civilian direction, such as housing, road making, farming, forestry, hospitalization, and recreational work. 

2. Relief work under the church or civilian direction in and outside the war zone, or in neutral zones, either as a denomination or in cooperation with the Friends and the Mennonites.

II. Types of services considered not consistent with the historic position of the church: 

1. Chaplaincy in the Army or Navy. 

2. Red Cross service if this organization is definitely committed to render active service under military command in the event of war. 

3. Hospital service if under military command. 

4. YMCA work if under military command. 

5. Services of any kind within the ranks of the army, all of which are without question under direct military command.

III. Types of peace testimony to register our convictions and to avoid our participation in war-related activities:

In consequence their position during the national emergency of the 1940's was established well in advance of that circumstance. 

Religious Bodies, 1936, reported 1,381 churches in this group with a total membership of 188,290. Its members were the most numerous of the pacifist groups. Although individual churches were scattered throughout 35 States, the membership was concentrated for the most part in Pennsylvania, Virginia, Indiana, Ohio, and West Virginia. 

The Friends or Quakers

In its early days the church fathered by George Fox was called the "Religious Society of Friends" to which was frequently added "commonly called Quakers." This last name is said to have been applied to the members first by a justice in response to an address from them in which he was called upon to "tremble at the word of God."

During the period of Selective Service operations from 1940 to 

1947 there were four denominations using the name "Friends." The largest of these was the Society of Friends (Orthodox). This sect originated in England. The root doctrine of the Inner Light, or the speaking of God to the human soul, was the basic belief. Conscience was early distinguished as liable to err because of its human nature. 

However, it was the view of the Friends that when properly enlightened from above, conscience could be trusted implicitly as a guide to conduct.12

The first recorded visit of Quakers to America was that of two women who arrived in Massachusetts from the Barbados in 1656. 

They were immediately put under arrest, examined to see whether they were witches, and finally shipped back to the Barbados. Two days later, eight more arrived. These were forcibly returned to 

England. Severe laws were then enacted and heavy penalties provided for those who knowingly brought into the community that "cursed sect of heretics lately rised up in the world which are commonly called 'Quakers,' who take upon them to be immediately sent of God and infallibly assisted by the Spirit to speak and write blasphemous opinions, despising government." 18 " Church of the Brethren, Minutes of the Annual Conference on War and Peace, 19361940, (Elgin, Ill.: Brethren Publishing House, 1940) pp. 8-9. 

12 American Friends Service Committee, An Introduction to Friends Civilian Public 

Service (Philadelphia, Pa.: American Friends Service Committee, 1945), pp. 16–17. 

13 Religious Bodies, op. cit., p. 706.

CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION 

The Friends had trying experiences in Virginia and Connecticut, as in Massachusetts. Rhode Island received them more cordially. In 

New York, New Jersey, and Maryland they became numerous. The culmination of their influence was felt in Pennsylvania, under the charter given to the great Quaker leader, William Penn. 

Quaker Doctrine, 1937

The Quaker doctrine has always been recognized as including the specific belief in nonresistance. This was stated again in a letter to 

President Franklin D. Roosevelt, presented by a delegation of Friends on February 12, 1937. Anticipating a new Selective Service program this letter reads in part as follows:

For almost 300 years the Society of Friends has labored to do away with war by first doing away with the causes and occasions for it. It has endeavored in its own circle to remove the roots and seeds of war by forming an atmosphere of life that makes war unthinkable. * * Insofar as they are true to these principles, Friends will make heavy sacrifices to transmit their spirit of love and faith, but they cannot, as followers of Christ, endorse war methods or support them, or be themselves a voluntary part of a system engaged in making war.

We feel an obligation to make this conviction a matter of record with our Government now, in peacetime, not only in behalf of members of the Society of Friends, but for any others who, for religious or conscientious reasons would take a similar position." 14

According to Religious Bodies, 1936, there were at that time 717 churches in the Friends bodies, with a total of 93,697 members. 

The Christadelphians 

The followers of John Thomas, an English doctor who came to the United States in 1844, organized themselves into societies which were without a distinctive name until the Civil War. At that time members applied to the Government to be relieved from military duty in consequence of religious and conscientious scruples. In order that they might be identified they adopted the name "Christadelphian" or "Brothers of Christ." They have consistently maintained that their faith prohibited participation in the armed forces of any country, whether in times of peace or times of war. 

Under the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940 the Christa delphian Church as a whole was perhaps the most strict of the nonresistant groups. It took action to disfellowship all members who entered the military forces. On the other hand the group was not actively pacifistic. The Christadelphians did not work against the war; each one simply took his individual stand when called upon to participate. 

14 Peace A Positive Testimony, pp. 11-12.

>> 

15 A very definite stand was taken by this church regarding the employment of its membership in civilian work directly connected with the war effort.

When the Christadelphian Service Committee was appointed on October 16, 1938 it was given certain instructions in this regard: 

The committee shall urge the Brotherhood not to engage in any form of munition work, defined as follows: Any work or industry, which has as its special purpose the production, in manufacturing, or equipping of direct instruments of death; viz, guns, rifles, bullets, shells, bombs, and/or anything that is obviously and essentially for the destruction of human life and property in offensive or defensive warfare, and for no other good or useful purpose.15 

Religious Bodies, 1936, recorded 2,755 members in 109 local Christadelphian organizations, or ecclesia. Molokans

The most recent of these nonresistance groups to immigrate into the United States was the Molokans. Their church at the time of the 

1940-47 emergency was officially known as the "Russian Christian

Molokan Spiritual Jumpers." Research does not disclose any definite date or place for the origin of the Molokans. The Russian Encyclopedia states that the Molokan sect separated from the Dukhobors in the latter part of the eighteenth century. It also says that "the Molokans teach the evasion of those laws which in their opinion are contrary to the Holy Scriptures, as for instance the laws of military service and the taking of oaths." For this they suffered successive periods of persecution in Russia followed by periods of relief. Between 1903 and 1912 about 4,000 Molokans migrated to southern California. In 

1940, there were estimated to be about 10,000 of them in California, Arizona, and Oregon.

The Molokan Petition of 1940 

A signed petition from the Molokans, presented to the Director of Selective Service under date of September 23, 1940, is quoted in full: 

From our fathers we inherited a Christian religion, which shed much innocent blood, being compelled to submit to severe suffering; even bodily punishment and tortures were inflicted upon them. They were made prisoners in fortresses, monasteries, and mines worked by prisoners. They were exiled to Siberia and to the wild regions of Trans-Caucasia, etc. * * During this period of exile in 

Trans-Caucasia our religion was exempt from military service for 50 years, and upon the expiration of these 50 years the Russian Government inaugurated compulsory military service in Trans-Caucasia, and for a continuous period of about 5 years thereafter our fathers, without success, pleaded with that government for the exemption of our people from such service. Therefore, we, following in the footsteps of our ancestors and fulfilling their holy covenant, were compelled to leave our native country, our cultivated fields and all of our property earned and accumulated by hard labor. 

15 From a letter dated January 9, 1946, on file at the National Headquarters of Selective 

Service. 

737977°-50—vol. 1- -3

In the early part of this century, in search of peace, comfort and liberty, we immigrated into the United States. 

We found the United States a country of peace, comfort, and liberty, and we rejoice in America's prosperity; we are loyal to America and its government; we always pray for the Lord's blessing upon this land and its people. 

In the year of 1917, during the World War, we petitioned the President of the United States for exemption from military service, on religious basis only, and our petition was granted and we were fully exempt. 

We are a home-loving people, we are industrious and readily respond to a good cause.

We have lived in this country for over 30 years, we are industrious, and to the best of our ability we have contributed to the development of this country. 

We stand ready now, as we did in the last war, within our means, to contribute sums of money, through the Red Cross or other suitable agency, to give aid to the widows, orphans, and the injured.

Wherefore, in view of what we have hereinabove expressed, we respectfully petition Your Excellency, to give this matter your earnest consideration, and determine that our people, who are members of our religious denomination, are to be exempt from compulsory military service, as was ruled and ordered during the last World's War. For which we will be ever grateful.16

Seventh-Day Adventists 

The religious denomination known as the Seventh-Day Adventists had its rise about 100 years before World War II. The name was based upon two of the distinct beliefs held, namely, the observance of the Sabbath of the Scriptures and the imminent personal second advent of Christ.

Throughout their history Seventh-Day Adventists have been noncombatant. This position was declared during the Civil War and affirmed repeatedly throughout the succeeding years. The Adventist 

Church was peculiar among those of the conscientious objector groups of World War II in that it recognized civil government as ordained of God so that order, justice, and quiet might be maintained. The great majority of its members and adherents did not refuse to serve in the armed forces, but asked that their service be in such capacity as would not violate their conscientious obedience to their interpretation of the Scriptures regarding killing. This approach was set forth as follows in a statement of July 25, 1940: 

Seventh Day Adventists, as you know, are noncombatants.

We are not pacifists nor militarists nor conscientious objectors, but noncombatants.

A pacifist is one who does not believe in participation in war, and he believes in peace at any price. He is an internationalist instead of a nationalist. 

As to the antimilitarist, he does not believe in any military establishments whatever. He is opposed to wearing any uniform, saluting a flag, or making any appropriation for war of any kind. 

The conscientious objector does not believe in participation in war. He does not believe in bearing arms. He does not even believe in helping to administer 

10 From a letter on file at National Headquarters.

to the needy who are in the Army, the sick and the wounded, and does not want to have anything to do with war. 

But as to the noncombatant he merely believes that he should not take human life. But he is willing to cooperate with his Government in any capacity that he can, without having to violate his conscience in regard to taking a life. We are noncombatants."

The Adventist Approach, 1943 

Seventh-Day Adventists welcomed assignments to the medical departments. The church had done much to prepare its youth for such work. Because of this they styled themselves "conscientious cooperators." The following statement on the official position of the 

Seventh-Day Adventist Church was approved by its general conference committee at a meeting in Washington, D. C., October 11, 1943:

On the various battle fronts of earth Seventh-Day Adventist youth are present who do not participate in the fighting, who destroy no lives, who endeavor to cause no injury, but who have made no effort to avoid the fighting fronts. Their mission is to bind up, to bring relief to the helpless. They go into places of gravest danger on errands of mercy and healing. Instead of sword and steel, they carry the equipment of healing and salvation. They bear no arms. Their first concern is not their own safety. They place their lives in jeopardy, entirely without weapons of defense, trusting in the armor of Heaven. They minister to human suffering, human need, human welfare. Hundreds are serving as physicians; many as trained nurses; and thousands in other lines of medical service, having received preinduction training by officers of their church which has especially fitted them for this phase of service. 

The noncombatant position taken by Seventh-Day Adventists is thus based on deep religious conviction. It leads no man who sincerely holds it to attempt to evade the patriotic duty and responsibility which is both the obligation and the high privilege of every able-bodied citizen-cooperation for the common welfare of his country. It leads to neither moral nor physical cowardice. On the contrary, it engenders loyalty and courage. It holds men true to the steady performance of duty even to the jeopardy of life, inasmuch as that duty, both to fellow men and government, is seen to be duty to God. On this broad platform of twofold allegiance to God and to country-we encourage our members everywhere to hold true to their supreme loyalty to God while maintaining their devoted loyalty to their government and their fellow men." 

This church was credited by Religious Bodies, 1936, with 2,054 local organizations and 133,254 members in the United States. 

Assemblies of God

In the case of the Assemblies of God the statement was made that, "While they recognize human government and affirm unswerving loyalty to the United States, the Assemblies of God claim that as followers of the Prince of Peace they are constrained to declare that they could not conscientiously participate in war and armed resistance

which involved the actual destruction of human lives.19 This was based on article XVI of the bylaws of the general council of the church which was adopted when it was organized in 1914. 

Local churches were held to be independent entities, however, and this bylaw was therefore not necessarily binding upon them. Religious Bodies, 1936, listed 2,611 local units of this denomination with

Churches of Christ

Regarding the doctrine of the Churches of Christ, the 1936 Census of Religious Bodies stated "In general, the doctrine of nonresistance is advocated." 20 Yet it must be understood that this denomination had no national headquarters and that the local churches maintained strict congregational independence. The denomination was reported to have 3,815 local organizations and 309,551 members. 

Jehovah's Witnesses 

Out of the meeting of a few Christian persons in a little town in Pennsylvania about the year 1872 came the organization known in 1940 and following as Jehovah's Witnesses. Some 12 years later it was incorporated under the name of Zion's Watchtower Tract Society, but still later the name was changed to Watchtower Bible and Tract Society. At the time of World War I this group was commonly known as the International Bible Students Association.

Primarily Jehovah's Witnesses carried on their work from house to house. They used Bibles, books, booklets, magazines, pamphlets, tracts, and other documents. In following up on their work, Jehovah's 

Witnesses arranged to call on interested persons sometimes starting studies in their homes. These interested persons were often referred to as People of Good Will. 

All Jehovah's Witnesses who were felt to have made a careful study of the Lord's word were deemed qualified by their sect to teach and conduct studies of the Bible in homes. After having consecrated their lives to serve God they were considered by the group to be ordained ministers. They took their authority for a spiritual ordination from the Bible, Isaiah 61:1 and 2, and it was claimed that once so ordained they must of necessity do preaching work. 

World War II Position of Jehovah's Witnesses 

This church was not understood to teach nonresistance directly as a part of its doctrine nor to advise its members in the matter of claiming conscientious objection to warfare. Jehovah's Witnesses might or might not claim to be conscientious objectors in accordance with 

19 Religious Bodies, 1936, op. cit., p. 71. 

20 Ibid., p. 470.

» 

their own personal interpretations of the Scriptures. However, the church did maintain officially a position of "neutrality" in wars between nations and maintained that position during World War II. 

As a matter of fact, many members of this body who claimed before their local boards to be conscientious objectors to any service with the armed forces and stated in writing that they felt they should be assigned to work of national importance under civilian direction took somewhat the position of absolutists after such assignment and refused to perform any kind of duty. Their position was essentially one of "religious" objection rather than that of "conscientious" objection. 

They usually maintained that either military service or alternate civilian duty interfered with their church work and that they therefore could engage in neither.

The local congregations of Jehovah's Witnesses were called "companies." In most instances their assembly place was called a kingdom hall, which was for them what a church edifice was to other denominations. On September 1, 1943, there were reported to be 3,227 organized companies in the United States. Authentic membership figures were not available, but it was estimated at the time that there were approximately 75,000 members in this country. Statistics for the group were not included in Religious Bodies, 1936.

It must be remembered that almost all of the above denominations are rather recent in origin, and that therefore they are without a long and sustained history of conscientious objection or nonresistance. In certain instances their opposition to warfare prior to 1940 had not been tried by any period of emergency. In some cases they had not made a vigorous statement against military service; at least no such statement appeared in Religious Bodies, 1936.

For instance, it was said of the National Spiritualist Association that "they are opposed to war, to capital punishment, to restrictive medical laws, and to every form of tyranny, political or religious.” 22 

Regarding the Church of God (Salem, W. Va.) it was stated that “all carnal warfare, and the participation therein, is condemned." 23 With respect to the Church of God as Organized by Christ, it was said, "they teach * * * nonresistance." 24 The fact that the name "Church of God" was used by a number of different small religious groups in the United States made for confusion in interpreting the doctrinal position taken by them. These excerpts from doctrinal statements were taken from Religious Bodies, 1936, and it should be noted that they were prepared in each case from information furnished by an official of the church, and that in nearly all cases they were approved in the form given by such official. 

Conscientious Objectors in Nonpacifist Churches Although they did not take a clear stand against participation in warfare or military organizations, a number of prominent nonpacifist churches within the 10 years preceding World War II expressed sympathy for and a desire to protect minority members of their faiths who did have such objection. 11. ACTION OF THE EXECUTIVE BOARD OF THE UNITED LUTHERAN CHURCH IN AMERICA (1940) 

The executive board of the United Lutheran Church in America has been officially requested by the board of social missions and by the conference of synodical presidents, to define the position of the church with respect to the rights and duties of Christian citizens, particularly in the emergencies of war. 

The position of the United Lutheran Church in America, based upon the Scriptures and interpreted by its confessions, may be summarized as follows: 

1. It is the function of the Christian Church to proclaim the gospel of redemption and peace. 2. It is the duty of the Christian citizen to obey and support lawful government. Concerning such duty we hold—what is plainly taught by Scripture and stated in the church's confessions-that "lawful civil ordinances are good works of God * * * it is right for Christians to bear civil office, to sit as judges to engage in just wars, to serve as soldiers, to make legal contracts, to hold property, to make oath save only when commanded to sin, for then they ought to obey God rather than man." Augsburg Confession, article 

XVI. Romans 13: 1-7; I Peter 2: 13-17; Titus 3: 1; Matthew 22: 17-21; Acts 

5: 29. * * * 3. We hold that a justifiable war not only may be possible, but that the 

Christian citizen is in duty bound to bear arms and to offer his life if need be in defense of his country. 

4. We believe that the conscience of the individual, informed and inspired by the Word of God, is the final authority in determining conduct (Acts 5: 29). 

Conscientiousness is one of the essential virtues of good citizenship. Therefore, under this evangelical principle of freedom of conscience we recognize the individual right to conscientious objection to service in a war. Such recognition does not imply the church's approval of such conscientious objection but does 

Ibid., p. 315. 

Ibid., p. 315.

CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION 

proclaim its devotion and respect for the Scriptural principle of the supreme moral responsibility of the individual conscience. (Acts 5: 29). As the exponent and defender of Christian principle the church must respect and safeguard the Christian in his right to the honest exercise of that responsibility. The obvious difficulties involved, such as the abuse of the principle by hypocrites using conscience as a cloak for cowardice, do not excuse the church from its sacred obligation of defending the principle at stake. They do challenge the church to special care in judging the spirit and motives of those who may call upon the church for safeguarding in such a position. They also challenge all Christians to a heart-searching study of what the Word of God and the witness of the church teach concerning the duties of the Christian citizen to the State. We reiterate that duty to be loyal support and service to the Nation whose protection and benefits he enjoys." 

12. ACTION OF THE INTERNATIONAL CONVENTION OF THE DISCIPLES OF CHRIST (1939) 

As a free democratic fellowship, the Disciples of Christ recognize the right of individuals to follow their own consciences in matters of practical conduct. 

Inasmuch as convinced Christian pacifists constitute an unpopular and misunderstood minority, we reaffirm at this time our respect for them and their position, and pledge our assistance to any who may face persecution or privation because of their pacifist convictions.

In order that Christian pacifists among us may have an opportunity to record their convictions as to participation in war, we urge that provision be made for an early enrollment of all conscientious objectors within our fellowship. We also recommend that the department of social education and social action of the United Christian Missionary Society begin immediately to confer with the Friends and with other strongly peace-minded bodies of Christians with a view to determining now the types of constructive sacrificial service in which pacifists may engage."7

Summary 

The significance for World War II of the above list of 345 religious sects and organizations, as well as the many church statements in this chapter, was that the American conscientious objector who in the main based his objection upon religion, might occur in connection with any religious group. It is true that a registrant opposed to warfare and armed forces, one who conscientiously believed in nonviolence or nonresistance, was more likely to belong to a pacifist than a nonpacifist sect. Conscientious objection on a personal basis, however, was found in most of the religious organizations of the United States. 

What is more, some nonpacifist churches also went on record as feeling that objectors among their membership had a right to their views and that these convictions should be recognized and provided for in the basic law and the fundamental operations of a Selective Service program. They did not, as did most pacifist sects, take a stand for all of their members against participation in war and the manufacture of weapons, but rather they left it up to the individual who, if in opposition, would have church support in his right to such belief. 

Interestingly enough some pacifist organizations, most of them minor from the standpoint of membership, seemed to take a similar approach. 

However, the conscientious objection provisions of the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940, made possible extensive recognition and consideration by the Federal Government of the principles set forth by both nonpacifist and pacifist churches with respect to individual or group violation of conscience on the grounds of religion. 

Thus the human right of religious freedom even during a national emergency came to maturity in democratic America along with the Nation's general interest in the individual rights of all citizens.

III CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION IN AMERICAN HISTORY 

In dealing with conscientious objection during World War II, Selective Service gave considerable recognition to the backgrounds of the problem. These backgrounds showed that most conscientious objectors based their opposition to war upon religious scruples and were members of pacifist churches. The history of nonviolence or nonresistance precepts in such churches was of long standing. It is therefore important in discussing the System's work from 1940 to 1947 to review the American antecedents of objection to warfare and to the armed forces. This experience of the Nation may be said to fall into three general periods: the Colonial and the Revolutionary 

Wars, the Civil War and World War I. 

Early Objection a Local or State Problem 

The handling of conscientious objectors to military and naval service has been a governmental problem in this country ever since the settlement of nonresistant sects during early colonial times. At first it was an issue of local Government involved principally in defense against the Indians. During the Colonial wars, however, it became a broader question since it was associated with the raising of Colonial militia. 

Until well into the Civil War period conscientious objection remained a local or State affair. Finally, both the Federal and Confederate Governments recognized the issue in their legislation. But it was not before World War I that conscientious objection was a national problem from the first day of a Federal draft program and that the treatment of conscientious objectors assumed some degree of uniformity throughout the land.

In the early history of this country, objectors who opposed war on religious grounds were sometimes excused from military or naval service, but in many cases they were imprisoned and often they were subjected to heavy taxes or fines for the support of military campaigns. 

As time went by it became a general custom to excuse from armed service those who hired a substitute or who paid what was called a commutation fee. Such provisions afforded a means whereby an objector could be true to his conscience and not bear arms although it 29

CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION 

should be understood that such arrangements were in general not set up especially for that purpose nor used exclusively by conscientious objectors. Furthermore, such procedures were not entirely satisfactory either to the Government or to the objector himself. They were not in operation following the Civil War and were completely dis avowed at the time of World War I. 

First Provisions for Noncombatant Service 

2 From time to time efforts were made, either by the objectors or by their governments, to find a type of service which their religious views would allow them to perform in the armed forces, one which would not be directly connected with the bearing of weapons. Among the 

13 original colonies Massachusetts (1661) ¹, Rhode Island (1673) and Pennsylvania (1757) were the first to include what might be termed noncombatant service provisions in their laws. The Pennsylvania legislation was passed by its assembly on March 29, 1757, and was of rather comprehensive nature as shown in the following quotation from the act:

All Quakers, Mennonists, Moravians, and others conscientiously scrupulous of bearing arms, who shall appear on any alarm with the militia, though without arms, and obey the commands of the officers in extinguishing fires, suppressing insurrection of Slaves or other evil-minded persons during an attack, in caring for wounded, conveying intelligence as expresses or messengers, carrying refreshments to such as are on duty, and in conveying to places of safety women and children, aged, infirm, and wounded persons, are free and exempt from the penalties of the act.'

Following that date the idea appeared occasionally in other Colonial and in State enactments. One interesting State proposal was made in North Carolina during the early days of the Civil War before the Confederate Government assumed complete central regulation of its draft. This proposal was for conscientious objectors to labor in the salt works of the State as an alternative to armed service. The significance here was that such "noncombatant" duty might have been conceived as operating outside of the armed forces whereas previously this kind of service was generally associated with military or naval personnel. At any rate the idea gradually arose of noncombatant duty outside as well as within the armed forces. This gave two alternatives to the compulsory bearing of weapons in time of emergency. The first, noncombatant service within the Army, was carried on in the

During all of this history there were at least two and perhaps three types of conscientious objectors according to the service they would perform. First were those who were willing to accept almost any duty in the armed forces except that involving the use of weapons; second, men who were willing to serve only outside of the military and naval organization; and third, those unwilling to perform any duty. The 1940 provisions attempted for the first time to meet the problem for the second group. 

William Penn and Conscientious Objection

In Colonial days religious liberty was the primary cause for the coming of Quakers, Brethren, Mennonites, and perhaps others of the pacifist church group to America. Particularly was this true of those who settled in Pennsylvania, because William Penn had made it clear that religious freedom would be granted to everyone in his colony. The following excerpt along these lines is from Penn's 

"Charter of Privileges to the Provinces and Counties of Pennsyl vania," approved in assembly, October 28, 1701:

I do hereby Grant and Declare that no person or persons, inhabiting in this Province or Territories, who shall Confess and acknowledge One Almighty God, ~ the Creator, Upholder and Ruler of the World, and Profess him or themselves obliged to Live Quietly under the Civil Government, shall be in any Case molested or prejudiced in his or their person or Estate because of his or their Conscientious perswasion or Practice, nor to be Compelled to frequent or maintain any Religious Worship, place or ministry contrary to his or their mind, or to do or suffer any other act or thing contrary to their Religious perswasion."

Thereby he voluntarily retrenched his power to "Levy, muster and train all sorts of men.' 997 It appears from Dr. Frederic A. Godcharles' history of Pennsylvania that the Quakers composed the majority of the assembly in the early 1750's and previously. On November 25, 1755, an act was passed "ordering and regulating such as are willing and desirous to be united for military purposes within the Province" and in this act the op-

Attitudes During Colonial Wars With the Indians 

Information regarding the attitude of nonresistant churches toward war between the colonists and the Indians is fragmentary. However, enough is available to disclose the general point of view. The 

Christopher Sowers, father and son, are credited with the following expression of the Quaker viewpoint:

As it is not only the aim of the Quakers, but also the faith-principle of many others, that one should not strike with the sword but put it in the sheath, that one should do good things to the enemy, that one should look for peace and for a long time many Germans have offered that-if it were possible to make a lasting peace with the Indians without bloodshed-the Germans would contribute according to their fortunes-to many poor people's lives being saved on both sides, etc. It is made known herewith that all those who have or still get the same opinion shall give * what they want to contribute voluntarily.10

In a similar connection a Pennsylvania historian, U. J. Jones, makes the following statement regarding the Brethren:

In the first place, let it be understood that we are in no particle indebted to them for one iota of the blessings of government we enjoy. They are strict nonresistants; and in the predatory incursions of the French and Indians, in 

1756-63; and, in fact, during all the savage warfare, they not only refused to take up arms to repel the savage marauders and prevent the inhuman slaughter of women and children, but they refused in the most positive manner to pay a dollar to support those who were willing to take up arms to defend their homes and their firesides, until wrung from them by the stern mandates of the law, from which there was no appeal. 

They did the same thing when the Revolution broke out. There was a scarcity of men. Sixty able-bodied ones among them might readily have formed a cordon of frontier defense, which could have prevented many of the Indian massacres which took place between 1770 and 1780, and more especially among their own people in the Cove. But not a man would shoulder his rifle; they were nonresistant! They might, at least, have furnished money, for they always had an abundance of that, the hoarding of which appeared to be the sole aim and object of life with them. But no; not a dollar! They occupied neutral ground, and wished to make no resistance. Again: they might have furnished supplies. 

And they did furnish supplies to those who were risking their lives to repel the invaders-but it was only when the almighty dollar accompanied the demand.

Dunkard was later subjected to excommunication action by his church. 

In spite of this, he rebuilt the mill. But the Dunkards, who had been his main support, refused to patronize him any more, and he was finally forced to abandon his business.12 

Recognition During the Revolution 

In the early days of the American Revolution each colony organized its own militia and all able-bodied white male citizens within broad age limits were asked to band together for the common defense. Those who had scruples against so doing were called "nonassociators." The 

Assembly of Pennsylvania again gave full recognition to its conscientious objectors by addressing a plea for mutual understanding and cooperation to all citizens on June 30, 1775:

The House taking into consideration that many of the good people of this Province are conscientiously scrupulous of bearing of arms, do hereby earnestly recommend to the Associators for the Defense of their Country, and others, that they bear a tender and brotherly regard toward this class of their fellowsubjects and Countrymen; and to these conscientious people it is also recommended, that they cheerfully assist, in proportion to their abilities, such associators as cannot spend their time and substance in the public service without great injury to themselves and families.13

During the summer of 1775 the Continental Congress likewise adopted a strong resolution on July 18 stating that the religious beliefs of nonresistant groups would be respected, but admonishing them regarding their behavior. This resolution read:

As there are some people who from Religious Principles cannot bear Arms in any case, this Congress intend no Violence to their Consciencies, but earnestly

12 Ibid., pp. 215–216. 

13 Votes and Proceedings of the House of Representatives of the Province of Pennsylvania.

recommend it to them to Contribute Liberally, in this time of universal calamity, to the relief of their distressed Brethren in the several Colonies, and to do all other services to their oppressed country, which they can consistently with their Religious Principles."4

Thus the tradition of a democratic approach to believers in nonviolence which had grown up with a number of the colonies was again reiterated by them and in addition it was espoused by the Continental Congress for all of the citizens in all of the colonies. The latter was done even in a time of national peril just as the early Colonial commitments had been made in the face of emergencies due to Indian dangers.

A Revolutionary Controversy over Objection 

However, there apparently was a growing feeling in Pennsylvania and perhaps elsewhere that those of nonresistant faiths were "getting off too easily," as far as helping in the war of the Revolution was concerned. Patriotic interest and the difficulty of financing military campaigns caused protests to mount against the leniency shown conscientious objectors. A memorial regarding the problem was therefore presented to the House of Representatives of the Province by the officers of the Military Association for the City and Liberties of 

Philadelphia on September 27, 1775. The essence of this was:

The Memorialists, with great Concern, perceive that fatal Mischiefs will arise to the Association from the Lenity shown towards Persons professing to be conscientiously scrupulous against bearing Arms;-that People sincerely and religiously scrupulous are but few in Comparison to those who upon this Occasion, as well as others, make Conscience a Convenience;-that a very considerable 

Share of the Property of this Province is in the Hands of People professing to be a tender Conscience in military Matters;—that the Associators think it extremely hard that they should risk their Lives and injure their Fortunes in the Defense of those who will not be of the least Assistance in this great Struggle ;that the Memorialists therefore humbly conceive that some decisive Plan should be fallen upon to oblige every Inhabitant of the Province either with his Person or Property to contribute towards the general Cause, and that it should not be left, as at present, to the Inclinations of those professing tender Conscience, but that the Proportion they shall contribute, may be certainly fixed and determined.15

On October 20, 1775, a Committee of the City and Liberties of Philadelphia likewise addressed a similar petition to the House. The following day still further petitioning was done. This was by the 

Committee of the Privates of the Association of the City of Philadelphia. The Quaker Statement on the Controversy 

"The People called Quakers," having been "favoured" with information regarding the foregoing, expressed their own concern over the matter in an address received by the House on October 27, 1775. The following are pertinent parts of this:

It is well known, that for above One Hundred Years past we, as a religious Society, have declared to the World that we could not for Conscience Sake bear Arms, nor be concerned in warlike Preparations, either by personal Service or by paying any Fines, Penalties or Assessments, imposed in Consideration of our 

Exemption from such Services.

That for many Years after becoming a distinct religious Society, our Ancestors suffered many grevious Persecutions and Oppressions for adhering to these our religious Principles, which we are convinced are founded on the Example and express Injunction of Christ our Lord and Lawgiver.

That in Expectation of being entirely relieved from the divers Oppressions, to which they were subjected on this and other Accounts, and of enjoying perfect Liberty of serving God, and of walking before him in the Way and Manner they believed to be most agreeable to him, our Ancestors were induced to leave their native Land, and encounter the Dangers and Difficulties of settling this, then a Wilderness; and although they were assured that our Honourable Proprietor 

William Penn was united with them in religious Profession and Principles, yet in order to secure this inestimable Privilege of Liberty of Conscience to themselves and their posterity in the fullest Manner they could, before they came from their native Land, they entered into a solemn Contract with him for this Purpose, as appears the 35th Section of Laws, agreed upon in England, the 5th 

Day of the Third Month, 1682, in the following Words, viz. "That all Persons living in the Province, who confess and acknowledge the one almighty and eternal God to be the Creator, Upholder and Ruler of the World, and that hold themselves obliged in Conscience to live peaceably and justly in civil Society, shall in no wise be molested or prejudiced for their religious Persuasion, or Practice in Matters of Faith and Worship, nor shall be compelled at any Time to frequent or maintain any religious Worship, Place or 

Ministry whatsoever."

We therefore earnestly entreat you carefully to guard against any Proposal or Attempt to deprive us and others of the full Enjoyment of Liberty of Conscience, and that the solemn Assurance given us in the Charter, that we shall not be obliged "to do or suffer any Act or Thing contrary to our religious Persuasion, "may not be infringed.-The Power of judging respecting our Sincerity belongeth only to the Lord of our Consciences, and we hope in a Province heretofore remarkable for the Preservation of Religious and Civil Liberty, the Representatives of the People will still be conscientiously careful that it may remain inviolate." 

Ibid., pp. 7312-7313.

After this expression had been delivered to the House each of the three groups making the representations previously referred to petitioned and remonstrated additionally and took specific exception to certain of the things the Quakers had said. Consequently the argument was drawn tighter but appears not to have been measurably advanced. The Committee of the City of Philadelphia did "positively say, that the Scriptures of the Old and New Testament must be wrested and tortured, with more than Jesuitical Art, to furnish Argument to support them (the Quakers). They also deny, that the Clause in the 

Proprietary Charter, which they cite, is by them truly construed." 

The Mennonite and Baptist Position 

Next November 7, 1775, an address or declaration, "Signed by divers persons," was presented in behalf of the Society of Mennonists and German Baptists. The purport of this was more conciliatory and is characterized by these two paragraphs: 

The Advice to those who do not find Freedom of Conscience to take up Arms, that they ought to be helpful to those who are in Need and distressed Circumstances, we receive with Cheerfulness towards all Men of what Station they may be it being our Principle to feed the Hungry and give the Thirsty Drink;we have dedicated ourselves to serve all Men in every Thing that can be helpful to the Preservation of Men's Lives, but we find no Freedom in giving, or doing, or assisting in any Thing by which Men's Lives are destroyed or hurt. We beg the Patience of all those who believe we err in this Point. 

We are always ready, according to Christ's Command to Peter, to pay the Tribute, that we may offend no Man, and so we are willing to pay Taxes, and to render unto Caesar those Things that are Caesar's, and to God those Things that are God's, although we think ourselves very weak to give God his due Honour, he being a Spirit and Life, and we only Dust and Ashes." 18 

After deliberating over all of these various documents in a committee of the whole house, that legislative body adopted among others the following "Resolves" on November 8, 1775: Resolved, 2. That it is the Opinion of this Committee, that the military Association entered into for the Defence of this Province, ought to be continued, encouraged and supported.

Resolved, 3. That it is the Opinion of this Committee, that it be recommended to all Male white Persons within this Province, between the Ages of Sixteen and Fifty Years, who have not already associated, and are not conscientiously scrupulous of bearing Arms, to join the said Association immediately. 

Resolved, 5. That it is the Opinion of this Committee, that all Male white

Persons between the Ages aforesaid, capable of bearing Arms, who shall not associate of the Defence of this Province, ought to contribute an Equivalent to the Time spent by the Associators in acquiring the military Discipline, Ministers of the Gospel of all Denominations, and Servants purchased bona fide, and for valuable Consideration, only excepted."

The amount of the "contribution" in question was first fixed at two pounds and 10 shillings annually, but was changed a number of times during the course of the Revolution.20 It was in effect a practical conscription for the nonresistant people as everyone was required to render military or naval service or to pay an equivalent in money. 

This precedent was followed by the draft laws of the Civil War, which also excused individuals from armed service upon the payment of a fine or commutation fee. 

Virginia and Maryland Laws During the Revolution The colonies of Virginia and Maryland also took significant legal action toward their conscientious objectors during this general period. 

In Virginia the laws regarding military service were at first liberal toward those who were averse to armed conflict. A law passed in 

November 1766 "(7th George III)” and entitled "An act to continue and amend the act for the better regulating and disciplining of the militia" in its provisions declared to be free and exempt 66* * all the people called Quakers.” 21

During the Revolutionary War, however, a petition was presented to the Virginia Convention on June 19, 1776,22 setting forth that the petitioners had a tender regard for the conscientious scruples of every religious society, but suggesting that the Quakers and Mennonists be subjected to the payment of a certain sum in lieu of bearing arms. 

An ordinance subsequently passed on July 5, 1776, specifically included "all Quakers and Mennonists" for enlistment in the militia but also provided that "the said Quakers and Mennonists shall not be obliged to attend general or private musters." 28

While the law of Revolutionary days in Maryland like that in Virginia, was more liberal toward nonresistant citizens than the Pennsylvania legislation, it did on the other hand discern between religious objectors and those who objected because of "other motives." 

The records show the following action by the Maryland Convention on July 6, 1776:

Resolved that the several Committees of Observation may, in their discretion, prolong the time or take security for the payment of any fine by them imposed for not enrolling in the Militia, and may remit the whole or any part of the fines by them assessed; and it is recommended to the Committees to pay particular attention, and to make a difference between such persons as may refuse from religious principles, or other motives."
