This early distinction between opposition to military and naval service on the grounds of religion or for other reasons is of importance to later developments as will be seen. 

A Proposed Constitutional Amendment After the War 

It is interesting to note that following the Revolution and the organization of the Federal Government an apparent attempt to write a conscientious objection clause into the Constitution of the United States failed in the first session of the First Congress. When the bill of rights amendments were under consideration in the House of Representatives a clause was adopted on August 17, 1789, which would have amended article I, section 10 of the Constitution to include between the first and second paragraphs "the equal rights of conscience, the freedoms of speech or of the press, and the right of trial by jury in criminal cases, shall not be infringed by any State." 25 However, since the provisions of article I of the amendments as finally adopted, mention the "freedom of speech or of the press" phrase but omit reference to "equal rights of conscience," it may be assumed that the wording was changed during the deliberations of the Senate and was not reinstated at later conference meetings with the House. 

From the Revolution to the Civil War 

Although there does not seem to have been a great deal of conflict between nonresistant church members and the Government during the period between the Revolutionary and the Civil Wars, historic peace churches apparently maintained their position anyway with reference to participation in warfare during the intervening years. For instance, records show that shortly after the Revolution many members of these churches, Quakers and others, who had favored the war, and particularly those who actually took part in the fighting, were disciplined by their organizations.26 

It appears that some difficulties were encountered during the War of 1812, because the Church of the Brethren took the following action in 1815: 

It has been discussed by us concerning the war matter, and it is agreed by all the brethren that a brother's sons who consider themselves according to the teaching of the brethren, "defenseless," and prove themselves to be such and wish to obey the teachings of the brethren, when these shall be hard pressed with the payment of fines they shall be assisted by the brethren according to the teachings of the apostle: Let us bear the burden of another thus you will fulfill the law of 

Jesus Christ.27

In 1817 the Annual Conference of the Church of the Brethren was asked, "Whether Brethren or their children may go on the muster ground or not." Similar viewpoints are said to have been expressed by this church in 1822, 1835, 1845, and 1859.29 Other evidences indicate the same general approach on the part of the other historic peace churches during this time.

Provisions Made by the States 

On the other hand a number of individual States provided exemptions for the conscientious objector. The Pennsylvania constitution of 1838 stated in article VI, section II: 

The freemen of this Commonwealth shall be armed, organized and disciplined for its defense, when and in such manner as may be directed by law. Those who conscientiously scruple to bear arms, shall not be compelled to do so, but shall pay an equivalent for personal service. 30 Other States provided through their constitutions for the exemption of nonresistance citizens from militia service in various, but often indefinite ways. For example, the constitution of Alabama, 1819, read: 

Article IV, Militia, Section 2. Any person, who conscientiously scruples to bear arms, shall not be compelled to do so, but shall pay an equivalent for personal service.⁹1 32 The constitution of Texas, 1859, contained an identical provision 2 and that of Illinois, 1818, included language as follows: 

SEC. 2. No person or persons conscientiously scrupulous of bearing arms shall be compelled to do militia duty in time of peace, provided such person shall pay an equivalent for such exemption." 83 This provision appeared likewise in the Illinois Constitution of 1870. 

In the meantime, the constitution of Iowa, 1846, made a similar statement, but also said that conscientious objectors should "pay an equivalent for such exemption in the same manner as other citizens." 35

The First Part of the Civil War 

Thus by the time of the Civil War something of a State as well as a Colonial pattern for dealing with conscientious objectors existed in legislative documents. It remained for the Federal and Confederate conscription acts of that war to give the problem recognition in national law. These two draft enactments were in themselves somewhat constructive toward settling the issue of conscientious objection and further, they gave it status as a Federal rather than a local or State question as had been the case previously. 

The passing of the Federal Militia Act of July 17, 1862, gave the President power to muster into service the militia of the ages 18 through 45. The enrollment was to be under State control unless the 

State laws were insufficient, and in such cases the President was empowered to make the necessary rules and regulations.40 A call for 

300,000 men was issued by President Lincoln on August 4, 1862, and five days later the Adjutant General issued General Order No. 99, regulating the enrollment and the drafting of these men. Neither the act nor the order was specific in the matter of exemption. However, the order did instruct the commissioner of enrollment to strike from the list the names of "all persons exempted by the laws of the respective States from military duty, on sufficient evidence, or on his personal knowledge that said persons belong to any of the aforesaid classes, whether the exemption is claimed by them or not." 41 

Substitutes and Commutation Fees

For the time being, then, the problem of handling conscientious objection, as such, was left to the individual State, as before. However, Order No. 99 did go on to provide broadly that "Any person so drafted may offer a substitute at the time of the rendezvous of the drafted militia force." 42 Within a few weeks thereafter arrangements were completed also for the conscientious objector to pay a commutation fee in lieu of service. The Federal Conscription Law of 1863 

In March 1863 Congress passed an "Act for enrolling and calling out the national forces" which had the effect of taking the administration of conscription out of the hands of the States. This law made no mention of conscientious objectors, but it did provide two methods by which anyone might be exempted from the draft. These were for the individual (1) to provide an acceptable substitute himself or (2) to pay $300 to the War Department for use in procuring a substitute. They were merely inclusions in the act of the provisions for substitutes from General Order No. 99 and the arrangements with the 

States for the payment of commutation fees. 

The Army Suggestion of Hospital Service 

Later in 1863, Gen. H. W. Halleck, General in Chief of the Army, was confronted with the question of what to do with conscientious objectors who came under his jurisdiction. Maj. Gen. John A. Dix wrote him the following letter from the Headquarters Department of the East, New York City, on October 24 of that year:

The cases of Quakers who have conscientious scruples in regard to bearing arms or paying money as a commutation from military service may be provided for without injury to the public or objection on their part by assigning them to duty as nurses and attendants in hospitals.

They do not object to being employed in nursing the sick and disabled, as it is a duty of humanity and of men capable of bearing arms, without any sacrifice of principle on the part of the Government. Several cases have occurred in this department, and I take the liberty of suggesting the adoption of the above rule to meet them and all others of the same character." 

First Federal Provisions, the 1864 Draft Law 

This suggestion of the Army was of very much more than ordinary nature in that here for the first time apparently was noncombatant service designated within the confines of the Federal forces for those who were against bearing arms. Its significance becomes more evident in connection with a new draft act which was passed by the Congress on February 24, 1864. Therein the provision for hospital service appeared and thus the new statute became the first Federal law to provide for the special handling of conscientious objectors as such. Section 

17 of the Act of 1864 read: 

43 Ibid., pp. 587-590. "Ainsworth and Kirkley, op. cit., Series III, vol. III, p. 922.

CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION 

And be it further enacted, That members of religious denominations, who shall by oath or affirmation declare that they are conscientiously opposed to the bearing of arms, and who are prohibited from doing so by the rules and articles of faith and practice of said religious denominations, shall, when drafted into the military service, be considered noncombatants, and shall be assigned by the Secretary of War to duty in the hospitals, or to the care of freedmen, or shall pay the sum of three hundred dollars, to such person as the Secretary of War shall designate to receive it, to be applied to the benefit of the sick and wounded soldiers: Provided, That no person shall be entitled to the benefit of the provisions of this section unless his declaration of conscientious scruples against bearing arms shall be supported by satisfactory evidence that his deportment has been uniformly consistent with such declaration." 

As indicated, the legislation went somewhat farther than duty in hospitals. It also initiated service in the care of freedmen. It likewise included specifically for conscientious objectors the payment of a commutation fee in lieu even of either of these noncombatant duties. 

It should be added, however, that of the three alternatives open to objectors, the latter was used to the practical exclusion of the other two. The following letter of instruction from the Provost Marshal 

General to David Neport, outlined the procedure for paying the commutation tax and for securing exemption: 

WASHINGTON, D. C., Nov. 8th, 1864.

Drafted persons who claim the benefit of section 17 of the Act approved Feb. 

24th, 1864, and desire to avail themselves thereof must first satisfy the Board of Enrollment in their respective districts that they are noncombatants, within the meaning of the law.

The Provost Marshall will then give a Certificate to this effect to the drafted man and upon presentation of this certificate to the Receiver of Commutation money, he will receive the $300 (and the amount fixed by the Secretary of War), and issue his receipt therefor in triplicate the duplicate thereof to be presented by the drafted person to the Board of Enrollment for their action. 

JAMES B. FRY, Provost Marshall General.“

Lincoln's Opinion Regarding Objectors 

President Lincoln held an understanding attitude toward conscientious objectors. In answer to people who urged him to force Friends, Mennonites, and Brethren into the Army, he replied substantially as follows: 

No, I will not do that. These people do not believe in war. People who do not believe in war make poor soldiers. Besides, the attitude of these people has always been against slavery. If all our people held the same views about slavery as these people hold there would be no war. These people are largely a rural people, sturdy and honest. They are excellent farmers. The country needs good farmers fully as much as it needs good soldiers. We will leave them

Your people the Friends-have had, and are having, a very great trial. On principle and faith, opposed both to war and oppression, they can only practically oppose oppression by war. At the end of hostilities Secretary of War Stanton said that President Lincoln and he had "felt that unless we recognize conscientious religious scruples, we could not expect the blessing of Heaven.” 49 

Conscientious Objection in The Confederacy The treatment of conscientious objectors in the Confederacy was generally parallel to that in the North. However, the convictions and expressions of the nonresistant church group against slavery as well as war brought them under more adverse criticism in the South. 

There appears to be little if any evidence, however, that the sympathies which objectors in the Confederacy may have had for the Northern cause inclined them to the commission of any overt act in favor of the Union.

Nevertheless, in the Southern States conscientious objectors were often accused of not participating in the war because of pro-Union sentiment. This was somewhat analogous to the situation during the Revolution when men believing in nonresistance were frequently branded as Tories because they refused to fight against the British, or the circumstances of World War I when some of those opposed to violence were often referred to as pro-German on the grounds that they were more or less of German ancestry. 

Liberal Treatment in North Carolina 

It has already been remarked that during the early period of the war the regulation of the draft in the South was carried on by the States, as in the North. Among the State laws of the Confederacy the militia bill of North Carolina, ratified September 20, 1861, was quite liberal toward the objector. Section 5 read in part:

Virginia's Church Membership Requirement 

In addition to the North Carolina provision requiring statements of church membership in conscientious objection, the Virginia act of March 29, 1862, specified church membership at the time of the passage of the act. It also provided for a heavy commutation fee of $500 plus 2 percent of the assessed value of the applicant's taxable property. A portion of this "Act providing for the exemption of certain parties upon religious grounds" is quoted: 

That whenever, upon application for exemption to the board of exemption, it shall appear to said board that the party applying for said exemption is bona fide prevented from bearing arms, by the tenets of the church to which said applicant belongs, and did actually belong at the passage of this act, and further, that said applicant has paid to the Sheriff of the county or collector of taxes for the city or town in which said applicant resides, the sum of five hundred dollars and in addition thereto, the further sum of two per cent of the assessed value of said applicant's taxable property, then the said board, on the presentation of the receipt of said officers for said moneys, and after the said applicant shall have taken an oath or affirmation that he will sustain the confederate government, and will not in any way give aid and comfort to the enemy of the said confederate government, then the said board shall exempt the said applicant; 

Provided, That whenever said party may be unable, or shall fail to pay the sum of five hundred dollars, and the tax of two per centum of their property, he shall be employed (when liable to military duty) in the capacity of teamster, or in such other character as the service may need, which does not require the actual bearing of arms; And provided further, That the person so exempted do surrender to the board of exemption all arms which they may own, to be held subject to the order of the governor, for the public use."

Early Confederate Legislation and Action 

In April 1862 the Confederate Congress passed a law taking over from its States the authority for the draft and providing that any conscriptee could secure exemption by the hiring of a substitute. This act contained no specific mention of conscientious objectors as such. 

About six months later, on October 11, 1862, however, a new law was passed containing a large number of exemptions, among which was one relating specifically to religious objectors as follows: 

All persons who have been and are now members of the society of Friends, and the association of Dunkards, Nazarenes, Mennonists in regular membership in their respective denominations: Provided, Members of the society of Friends, Nazarenes, Mennonists and Dunkards shall furnish substitutes or pay a tax of five hundred dollars each into the public treasury."

After the passage of the new legislation, the Confederate Adjutant 

General's Office issued the following regulation: 

Orders from the Adjutant and Inspector General's Office, 1862, Sec. VIII.— 

Friends, Dunkards, Nazarenes, Mennonites.-All persons of the above denominations, in regular membership therein on the 11th day of October, 1862, shall be exempt from enrollment on furnishing a substitute, or on presenting an enrolling officer a receipt from a bonded quartermaster for the tax of five hundred dollars imposed by Act of Congress, and an affidavit by the bishop, presiding elder, or other officer whose duty it is to preserve the records of membership in the denomination to which the party belongs, setting forth distinctly the fact that the party, on the 11h day of October, 1862, was in regular membership with such denomination."

Statement on Cause for Distrust 

There was a further indication or explanation of distrust for those who were exempted on the grounds of religious opposition to armed conflict. Judge J. A. Campbell, Assistant Secretary of War for the 

Confederacy, in his Circular No. 24 of June 27, 1864, after referring to the act of that year and to subsequent orders, made the following statement:

It is understood that a large addition has been made to these denominations since the enactment of October, 1862, from families not previously connected with them. This has been a cause for distrust and probably led to the adoption of the precise language of the act. 

The department has exercised a liberal indulgence in favor of those who held or were supposed to hold conscientious scruples upon the subject of bearing arms, but there is no reason for affording any countenance to efforts to avoid the performance of public duty by hypocritical pretenses of a religious belief, which has no root in the conscience or influence on the conduct.

There seems to be an interesting parallel, on the one hand, between the Civil War situation described by Judge Campbell concerning a religious belief which had no "influence upon the conduct," and the circumstances of the 1940's, on the other, when some men claimed to be conscientious objectors by reason of religious training and belief, but failed to follow any recognizable pattern of accepted moral or ethical conduct in everyday life. Southern Pressure on Objectors at War's Close Pressure to obtain for the Army of the Southern States the services of every man available in the latter days of the war made the position of conscientious objectors precarious. Jefferson Davis, President of the Confederacy, was particularly insistent on reducing exemptions to the draft. The last bill reported on March 18, 1865, to the Confederate Congress as signed by President Davis, was an act to diminish the total number of exemptions.60 This is said to have cancelled all of the existing exemptions which were based on religious grounds. 

Conscientious Objection from Civil to World War It appears that in the period between the Civil War and World War I there was little conflict between the conscientious objector and the Federal Government with respect to military or naval service. No need arose for conscription during the Spanish-American War of 1898 or other years of the period and at no time was pressure exerted upon objectors to enter the armed forces. Officially the historic peace churches did not turn aside from their stand regarding nonresistance, but they did from time to time offer some evidence of a more liberal attitude toward financial matters and opposition to war and with respect to recognition of those members who found that their individual consciences did permit them to serve in the Army or Navy. 

For instance, the following queries came to the Church of the Brethren conference of 1870: "Is it considered right for a brother to take or receive a pension, back pay, or bounty, for services rendered to the government before he became a member of the church?" The answer was: "We think he may be allowed to do so." 61 Again in 1878 the annual conference was asked: "A son of a sister, whose husband is living, perished in the army: Is it right, under any circumstances for the sister to draw pension from the Government?" The conference answered: "It is." 62 On the other hand, a book entitled "The Brethren's

The New Approach of World War I 

The coming of World War I to the United States in 1917 marked the beginning of a totally new period in the treatment of the conscientious objector during a period of national emergency. In this war, conscription became personal, universal, and absolute; there was no provision whatsoever for the hiring of a substitute or the paying of a commutation fee. The Selective Service law which was provided in the Act of May 18, 1917, had this to say about those opposed to war and the armed forces:

SEC. 4. * * * nothing in this Act contained shall be construed to require or compel any person to serve in any of the forces herein provided for who is found to be a member of any well-recognized religious sect or organization at present organized and existing and whose existing creed or principles forbid its members to participate in war in any form and whose religious convictions are against war or participation therein in accordance with the creed or principles of said religious organizations, but no person so exempted shall be exempted from service in any capacity that the President shall declare to be noncombatant; * * * 64 

Basic Liability of C. O.'s for Military Service 

Apparently the Nation had decided that in spite of a two-century history of leniency, conscientious objectors, like all other able-bodied citizens within specified age limits, should be liable for military service under article I of the Constitution. It was noted that section 

VIII of the Constitution read: 

The Congress shall have power: 

15. To provide for calling forth the militia to execute the laws of the Union, suppress insurrections, and repel invasions. 

What fundamental implication was this seen to have for those believing in nonresistance? It probably meant to the country that all able-bodied men were available on call as members of the unorganized militia, subject only to such laws as were enacted by Congress. 

The public had apparently arrived at this conclusion before the passage of Selective Service legislation in 1917. At any rate, the 

National Defense Act, approved June 3, 1916, as amended, had already been set up as a control in such regard. First of all, section 57 of this act provided as follows by way of a general basis:

SEC. 57. COMPOSITION OF THE MILITIA 

The militia of the United States shall consist of all able-bodied male citizens of the United States and all other able-bodied males who have or shall have declared their intention to become citizens of the United States, who shall be more than eighteen years of age and, except as hereinafter provided, not more than forty-five years of age, and said militia shall be divided into three classes, the National Guard, the Naval Militia, and the Unorganized Militia." 

Next section 59 dealt specifically with men of nonresistance faith: 

SEC. 59. EXEMPTIONS FROM MILITIA DUTY. 

* * * and all persons who because of religious belief shall claim exemption from military service, if the conscientious holding of such belief by such person shall be established under such regulations as the President shall prescribe, shall be exempted from militia service in a combatant capacity; but no person so exempted shall be exempt from militia service in any capacity that the President shall declare to be noncombatant."

Thus a positive legal approach of a Federal nature was taken to the problem of military service for those believing in nonviolence and this carried over into the Selective Service enactment of the next year. 

Selective Service Regulations 

As regards the Selective Service Regulations which were prescribed to administer the 1917 draft law, they did not deviate in any essential from the act. The second edition stated: 

Classification Rules and Principles, section 79, rule XIV.-Any registrant who is found by a local board to be a member of any well-recognized religious sect or organization organized and existing May 18, 1917, and whose then existing creed or principles forbid its members to participate in war in any form, and whose religious convictions are against war or participation therein in accordance with the creed or principles of said religious organizations, shall be furnished by such local board with a certificate (Form 1008, sec. 280, p. 225) to that effect and to the further effect that, by the terms of section 4 of the Selective Service law, he can only be required to serve in a capacity declared by the President to be noncombatant. He shall be classified, however, as is any other registrant; but he shall be designated upon all classifications, forms, records, certificates, and other writings of local and district boards in which his name appears by the insertion of a cipher (0) after his name."

Pacifist Churches Not Listed in Regulations 

Under the Selective Service program of World War I the administration of the regulations on "religious-creed members" was left wholly to the local boards of the System. No list was prepared of religious denominations recognized as existing on May 18, 1917, and professing a creed opposed to war in any form. Provost Marshal 

Gen. E. H. Crowder, in his second report (1919) to the Secretary of

War on the operation of the draft" stated that the compilation of such a list was thought impracticable. He also said that no information had ever been required of the boards showing the churches which they had recognized. However, he went on to give the following data compiled from materials in the Bureau of the Census regarding the principal churches said to profess such a tenet: 

Brethren in Christ: The Yorker, or Old Order Brethren, and the United Zion's 

Children belong to this group; they believe that inasmuch as Christ is Prince of 

Peace His Kingdom is of peace and as his subjects they should abstain from the employment of carnal forces which involve the taking of human life; for this reason the doctrine of nonresistance is a prominent feature of their belief; 

Christadelphians: Conscientious scruple as to serving in the Army in the Civil 

War was the occasion for the organization of the body under this name; 

Amana Society: The members believe war to be contrary to the will of God and the teachings of Christ;

Churches of Christ: This body has no published creed, but a leading elder stated that the churches believe in "nonresistance";

Old Order German Baptist Brethren: Denominational practice calls for non conformity to the world in war, politics, secret societies, dress, and amusements;

Placing All Inducted C. O.'s Under Military Authority 

Regardless of their claims, inducted conscientious objectors fell entirely within the authority of the armed forces under the direction of the President and of the Secretary of War. This was because all conscientious objectors, as well as other draftees, were considered to be members of the armed forces as soon as the induction order issued by their local boards became effective. The governing rule in this regard was:

Separate Treatment of Objectors after Induction 

Among the early significant orders of World War I which were issued by the War Department to the Army, regarding conscientious objectors, was that of September 25, 1917, in which it was stated that the "Secretary of War directs that selected Mennonites who report to your camp for duty be not forced to wear a uniform, as question of raiment is one of the tenets of their faith." 75 On October 10, 1917, the Secretary of War directed further that conscientious objectors be segregated and handled with tact and consideration." They were not to be treated as violators of military law and it was instructed that reports of the actions taken and of the results obtained by the Army be submitted. This and other orders were issued confidentially and it was strictly enjoined that they be not given to the newspapers; it was felt that had they "been made public at the time they would undoubtedly have been means of creating a large number of insincere objectors." 77

A Broader Scope of Exemption 

In enacting the Selective Service law of 1917, Congress had provided for the exemption from combatant service of the religious objector only. That legislative body evidently had not regarded as worthy of consideration, any objection to military service on moral or conscientious grounds unless it had a religious foundation. However, an order from The Adjutant General of the Army, under date of December 19, 1917, extended the benefit of exemption from combatant service to those claiming to have scruples against participation in warfare, even when such scruples were not based on religion. The principal part of this order read as follows:

The Secretary of War directs that until further instructions on the subject are issued "personal scruples against war" should be considered as constituting "conscientious objection" and such persons should be treated in the same manner as other "conscientious objectors" under the instructions contained in confidential letter from this office dated October 10, 1917."

It is interesting to note here some of the legislative history lying back of the enactment of the 1917 law. Regarding the requirement as written into the act that noncombatant service be provided only for those who were members of a "historic peace church," the Hon. 

Newton D. Baker, Secretary of War, stated at the Hearings of the 

House Military Affairs Committee: 

The religious-belief section is changed from that which you have in the National Defense Act, and which, in my judgment, is inoperable. In the National Defense Act you have an exclusion of any person who has conscientious beliefs against the bearing of arms. It is not exactly that language, but that is about what it is. That, of course, makes the question of exclusion purely a question of individual statement, and, as lawyers might say, of a self-serving declaration made after the event. We recommend that the provision be modified so as to exclude or exempt those who are actually members of a recognized society which has, as one of its tenets, the disapproval of war.' 79 At another time during the hearings, the following significant discussion also occurred:

Mr. QUIN. What justification can the department put up for exempting persons of religious belief against fighting? I believe everybody ought to fight, and would not propose to exempt any man. 

Secretary BAKER. Of course, the justification is that the men at the front cannot fight unless the men at home provide them with the things to fight with. 

Mr. QUIN. But I am talking about the religious exemption. 

Secretary BAKER. That is a historic question. It is a part of the policy of the Government to allow liberty of conscience, and where men are actually members of religious bodies which have entertained that view, they have never been required in this country to fight.⁰⁰ 

It appears further that at one time the wording of the bill under consideration provided for absolute exemption. The following is quoted in such regard:

Mr. ANTHONY. Would not that really be a better provision for the Government? 

Secretary BAKER. Gen. Crowder says that is provided here-partial service. 

General CROWDER. Not as applying to the religious classes.

Another interesting technical consideration was brought up in a recent book on the subject wherein it was said: 

The original draft of this provision had read as follows: "No person shall be exempted from military service in any capacity that the President shall declare to be noncombatant." After the hearings on the bill had been closed, however, and before the bill was finally brought to the floor of the House, the word "military" was stricken out, making it possible for the President to define noncombatant service as nonmilitary or civilian service, if he saw fit to do so. This change in wording was made, at the last moment, as the result of a personal appeal by P. H. Richert through the Chairman of the House Committee on 

Military Affairs.82

As will appear later, this did not make a very significant difference in the World War I program for conscientious objection. When the furlough of soldiers including objectors, to agriculture and industry was finally authorized, the action was taken under a separate law. 

However, the broadened concept of exempting any conscientious objector instead of just the religious one bore fruit later in that the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940 contained provisions which had somewhat wider coverage. 

Wilson's Definition of Noncombatant Service 

President Woodrow Wilson on March 20, 1918, issued an Executive order defining noncombatant service and expressing in comprehensive form his policy as regards men whose beliefs made them opposed to resistance and violence. This was subsequently published by the War 

Department as General Orders No. 28 on March 23 of that year.83

The first paragraph quoted section 4 of the 1917 Act and declared certain service within the Army as noncombatant. This included duty with the medical department wherever performed. It covered also any service in the Quartermaster Corps and Corps of Engineers, if performed in the United States, and certain service in these organizations abroad. 

81 Ibid., p. 88. 

83 Guy F. Hershberger, War, Peace, and Nonresistance (Scottsdale, Pa.: The Herald 

Press, 1944), p. 116. 

83 Statement Concerning Treatment of Conscientious Objectors in the Army, op. cit., pp. 

18, 39-41.

CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION IN AMERICAN HISTORY » 57 

The second paragraph provided for two classes of conscientious objectors: first, those who had received the Certificate of Exemption from Combatant Service (PMGO 1008) from their local boards, and, second, those who objected to participation in war "because of conscientious scruples but have failed to receive certificates as members of a religious sect or organization from their local board." It directed the assignment of all these men to noncombatant service to the extent they were able to accept such service "without violation of the religious or other conscientious scruples by them in good faith entertained." Commanding officers were directed to explain the character of noncombatant service, as defined, and to secure acceptance of the order insofar as possible. Upon acceptance of noncombatant service each soldier was to be given a certificate which would "thereafter be respected as preventing the transfer of such persons from such noncombatant to combatant service by any division, camp, post or other commander under whom said person may thereafter be called to serve, but such certificate shall not prevent the assignment of such person to some other form of noncombatant service without his own consent." As far as feasible, noncombatant assignments were restricted to the medical department in the absence of a specific request for assignment to some other branch. 

The third paragraph contained a requirement for monthly reports on men who were unwilling to accept noncombatant military service. 

Such men were to be segregated and handled with tact and judgment. 

Commanding officers were instructed to impose no "punitive hardships" upon these men but not to allow any consideration beyond exemption from "active military service."

The fourth paragraph recommended uniformity of penalties in sentences of courts martial and prescribed confinement in the United States disciplinary barracks in cases of desertion. The final paragraph provided for the revision of court martial sentences imposed prior to this order with a view to possible remedial action by the President.

Noncombatant Service Outside the Army As indicated by the last three paragraphs of the President's policy statement and by General Orders No. 28, the Army was experiencing difficulty in getting some inducted objectors to cooperate in its program of noncombatant duty. This particular issue was further recognized by the Secretary of War in an order dated April 27, 1918. It directed, for instance, that any conscientious objector should be promptly brought to trial by court martial (a) if his attitude in camp was sullen and defiant, (b) if his sincerity was questioned, or (c) if he was active in propaganda.

In the meantime, however, officials of the historic peace churches had become interested in the situation. They had requested of President Wilson and Secretary Baker and of Provost Marshal General Crowder, who was in direct charge of the draft, that conscientious objectors to noncombatant military service, be assigned to noncombatant activities in agriculture and peaceful industries.84 Thus the idea of duty outside of the armed forces which appeared at least in the State of North Carolina during the Civil War again came to mind in connection with Federal conscription during World War I. The precedent for the-work-of-national-importance concept of 1940 was in process of development. 

As early as September 1, 1917, a committee of Brethren had an interview with Secretary Baker to discuss the problem in general. It is said that on the occasion of a previous meeting of a Mennonite committee with the Secretary certain statements had been made verbally which had been summarized as follows: 

1. That none of our brethren need serve in any capacity which violates their creed and conscience. 

2. When they are called, they should respond at the place designated on their notice. 

3. From the place designated on their notice, they should go with others, who are drafted and called, to the training camp. 

4. Report to the army officers the church to which they belong, and their belief in its creed and principles. 

5. This nonresistant position will place them in detention camps where they will be properly fed and cared for. 

6. In these camps, they will not be uniformed or drilled. 

7. A list of services considered noncombatant will be offered, but they need not accept any in violation of their consciences. 

8. Those who cannot accept any service, either combatant or noncombatant, will be assigned to some other service, not under the military arm of the government. 

9. Our ministers will be allowed to visit the brethren at these camps and to keep in touch with them. 

10. Our ministers will be privileged to give this information and advice in private or in public meetings. 85 At the conference with the Brethren's committee this statement was brought to the attention of the Secretary. After reading it over carefully, he said that it was substantially what he had told the Mennonite committee, except that item No. 8 contained commitments which he was not yet ready to make. To the Brethren, he is reported to have said:

It would not be within my province, at this time, to say finally: "Those who cannot accept noncombatant service will be assigned to some other service not under the military arm of the government." It may possibly be so, but that would

An Opinion on Outside Noncombatant Service 

A detailed opinion, issued shortly thereafter for the Secretary of War, evidently was developed because of the issue on whether conscientious objectors could substitute service outside of the armed forces. It was released by the Judge Advocate General of the Army and stated that under existing laws duty in the Red Cross or on farms in the production of food could not be considered as a means of relief from noncombatant military service. Congress had apparently been considering the question also and following the opinion of the Judge Advocate General took action to rectify its legislation in such regard. 

Congressional Authorization of Furloughs 

On March 16, 1918, an act of Congress provided for the Secretary of War to grant furloughs without pay and allowances to enlisted men, and on May 31, 1918, the acting Judge Advocate General advised the Secretary of War that he was now authorized to furlough conscientious objectors under the new law.87 88 Provisions for farm and industrial furloughs were thereupon established by orders from the Adjutant General of the Army under dates of June 1, June 10, and July 30, 1918. In general these orders provided that a monthly report as to the industry of each person so furloughed should be received from disinterested sources and that the furlough might be terminated upon receipt of a report that the man was not working to the best of his ability. They also said that bona fide employment should be obtained at the prevailing wage rate for the class of work in which the man was engaged, and that no person should be recommended for furlough who did not voluntarily agree that he would receive for his labor an amount no greater than a private's pay, plus an estimated sum for subsistence, if such was not provided by the employer, with any additional amount which was paid for his services being contributed to the American Red Cross. 

Creation of a Board of Inquiry 

On June 1, 1918, the Secretary of War constituted a board of inquiry which visited various Army camps during the remainder of the war period to hold hearings for men who claimed to be conscientious objectors. This board was composed of a representative of the Judge 89

These men were to interrogate personally each individual whose case was referred to them and to recommend what action was to be taken. 

It was the function of the board to determine the sincerity of men professing objection, both as to refusal to perform noncombatant service and with regard to the performance of combatant service. 

It was provided that in exceptional cases the board might recommend furlough for service in France in the Friends' reconstruction unit. Two other types of special duty were established. One of these was work in reconstruction hospitals of the medical department of the Army where the patients were not to be returned to military service. The other was labor in the reclamation branch of the Quartermaster Corps where the activities comprised laundry, salvage, clothing renovation, shoe repair, transportation repair, and motor truck company service.

Discharge of Conscientious Objectors 

Conscientious objectors who were assigned to noncombatant service were discharged on the same basis as were other soldiers with similar assignments. War Department orders dated November 29 and De cember 11, 1918, provided for the release of sincere conscientious objectors who had not been assigned to duty, and also for the recall and discharge of furloughed men "after consultation with the employer to detemine whether it is in the best interest of all concerned, and at the request of the soldier." 96

Conscientious objectors who had been furloughed to the American Friends Service Committee for work in France were apparently discharged early in 1919. Copies of War Department correspondence available in the National Archives war records office show that such action was contemplated as of January 2, 1919. The men were to be separated with the understanding that they would continue to serve the Friends committee in its reconstruction work in France and that the committee would assume all responsibility for and expense of bringing them back to the United States when their term of service with the committee expired.

As regards conscientious objectors in the Army who were totally uncooperative, a letter addressed to the Hon. James W. Wadsworth of the United States Senate under date of February 14, 1920, by General Peyton C. March, Chief of Staff, in speaking of the "so-called conscientious objector class" stated "only six remain in confinement at the Pacific branch, United States disciplinary barracks." 97 The sentences of all objector prisoners were eventually commuted, however, and the last one was released from prison in November, 1920.98

The form of separation for this type of objector was neither honorable nor dishonorable but was a simple "blue ticket" discharge. The reason for separation was stated as "this is a conscientious objector who has done no military duty whatsoever and who refused to wear the uniform."

CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION IN AMERICAN HISTORY » 63 A Statement on World War I Experience 

The Third Assistant Secretary of War issued a statement through the Committee on Public Information under date of September 28, 1918, summarizing the manner of handling conscientious objectors near the end of the war, part of which follows: 

The War Department's policy regarding conscientious objectors has from the beginning been based on the provisions of the Federal draft law and subsequent Executive orders. It has been the liberal American policy of according a measure of self-determination to the few who will in all sincerity have not been able to adjust their minds to the needs of the present sudden and desperate emergency; to whom direct participation in the war would violate religious convictions, as well as a sense of self-respect and integrity of character. 

In dealing with objectors the difficulties have not been primarily those of policy, but of practical procedure. First of all the insincere have had to be differentiated from the sincere, and forced into full service or subjected to fitting penalties. The second difficulty has concerned the disposition of sincere objectors in ways that would conserve the manpower of the Nation. This has been complicated by misunderstandings and by peculiar local situations; but with growing experience many complications have been eliminated as requisite governmental machinery to this end has been perfected. 

The usual procedure as thus far developed is as follows: A draftee is certified as a conscientious objector by his local board on proper presentation of facts. 

On call he goes to a cantonment as does any other drafted man. He there has a hearing before a board of inquiry on conscientious objectors, * The board of inquiry passes on the sincerity of objectors. Those adjudged insincere are required to perform regular military service, in default of which they are subjected to court martial and remanded to the disciplinary barracks at Fort Leavenworth. Those adjudged sincere are encouraged to enter noncombatant military service; and many have done so. But those whose convictions prevent this are furloughed to various forms of service under the jurisdiction of a civilian commissioner of the department who has supervisory and recommendatory powers. The vast majority of objectors have been lifelong members of religious sects the tenets of which forbid participation in war. Most prominent among these are the Society of Friends, the Mennonites, the Dunkards, the Christadelphians and various minor sects such as True Lights, Holy Jumpers, and others little known outside of restricted and isolated areas. A large proportion of the Friends have been furloughed by the board to the Friends' reconstruction unit, an organization operating under the American Red Cross in the work of rebuilding devastated areas in France. Others are furloughed mainly into agricultural service * * In other instances, objectors are furloughed in groups to harvest apple, corn, or other crops in danger of loss because of local labor shortage; to undertake work of land reclamation; to carry on large scale farming operations in the 

West, or to reduce the labor shortage in State institutions for defectives, which are often in dire straits because their regular force has been cut down by the Army draft or drawn off by their high wages current in outside employ

In short, every effort is being made to respect the sincere scruples of a small minority of our people, at the same time that their power to contribute to the Nation's efficiency is turned to good account. There is unquestionably strong sentiment in many quarters against the granting of immunity from military service to any group in our population, however small. But many objectors 737977°-50-—vol. 1- -6

are not without the courage of their convictions. They would resist compulsion to the end. We might imprison or shoot them. But Prussian practices such as these would hardly appeal in a Democracy. On the other hand, a method which conserves the manpower of the Nation, and accords to furloughed objectors a lot that is endurable and serviceable, but in no sense pampered, will, it is believed, commend itself to the common sense and practicability of the American people." 

Comments of Harlan Stone 

Some of the philosophy held during World War I by the late Chief Justice of the United States, Harlan F. Stone, in regard to conscientious objection is very interesting. As a member of the Army's Board of Inquiry he was in close touch with those opposed to warfare and armed forces. In concluding this chapter, therefore, three paragraphs are quoted from an article which he wrote for the Columbia University 

Quarterly several months after the end of the War:

There remains the larger question whether there is any basis in morals or sound policy for exempting the conscientious objector from liability to military service. It has long been the settled policy of the English common law that conscientious or good motives afford no legal excuse for acts which transgress a rule of law. Libel or blasphemy that good may come, or the practice of acts defined by law to be unlawful, because the doer believes them to be moral or religious, has never been considered by the English law to be a defense to a criminal charge. Viewed in its practical aspects, however, there may be and probably is a very radical distinction between compelling a citizen to refrain from acts which he regards as moral but which the majority of his fellow citizens and the law regard as immoral or unwholesome to the life of the state on the one hand, and compelling him on the other to do affirmative acts which he regards as unconscientious and immoral. The action of the state in compelling the citizen to refrain from doing an act which he regards as moral and conscientious does not in most instances which are likely to occur do violence to his conscience; but conscience is violated if he is coerced into doing an act which is opposed to his deepest convictions of right and wrong. The traditional view of the common law that right motives are no defense for crime and should not stay the hand of the law gives very little clue, therefore, to the sound method of dealing with the conscientious objector to war, in the realm of either morals or policy. However rigorous the state may be in repressing the commission of acts which are regarded as injurious to the state, it may well stay its hand before it compels the commission of acts which violate the conscience. 

It is the easy but undiscriminating and shallow way to dispose of the case of the conscientious objector by denouncing him as a coward and slacker. 

That many, if not most of his numbers, are muddle-headed and inconsistent in their theories of life increases the difficulty of the problem; but their evident sincerity and willingness to suffer to the end rather than to yield up their cherished illusion make impossible the wholesale condemnation of the conscientious objector as a coward and a slacker. That any considerable number of our citizens at a time when we were making our supreme national effort should defy our laws and refuse to participate in it is a serious matter; but the violation of the conscience of the individual by majority action is likewise "Statement Concerning Treatment of Conscientious Objectors in the Army, op. cit., pp. 

49, 50.

CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION IN AMERICAN HISTORY 65 

a serious matter, and the statesmanship which would shut its eyes to facts and say that cowardice only is involved is singularly lacking in penetration and in any constructive policy.

The ultimate test of the course of action which the state should adopt will of course be the test of its own self-preservation; but with the limitation, at least in those countries where the political theory obtains that the ultimate end of the state is the highest good of its citizens, both morals and sound policy require that the state should not violate the conscience of the individual. All our history gives confirmation to the view that liberty of conscience has a moral and social value which makes it worthy of preservation at the hands of the state. So deep in its significance and vital, indeed, is it to the integrity of man's moral and spiritual nature that nothing short of the self-preservation of the state should warrant its violation; and it may well be questioned whether the state which preserves its life by a settled policy of violation of the conscience of the individual will not in fact ultimately lose it by the process. Every ethical and practical consideration which should lead the state to endeavor to avoid the violation of the conscience of its citizens should therefore lead a wise and humane government to seek some practical solution of this difficult problem.100 

Résumé 

Regarding America's history of conscientious objection, the import for 1940 of the statement made by Chief Justice Stone is that so advanced a view was held at the end of World War I. His idea that a democracy like the United States may restrain action even though it is sanctioned by belief but should not coerce in opposition to conscience, was drawn from the Nation's past. 

The settlement of this country was due in part to its offering a haven for peace-loving men and women. Consequently there have always been citizens opposed to war, resistance and violence. Although a proposed "freedom of conscience" clause was not included in the United States Constitution, a number of the State constitutions which were adopted between the Revolution and the Civil War contained provisions on conscientious objection. In addition, national laws were eventually passed dealing with the subject. 

In early Colonial times the problem of the objector was a local one. 

Its main basis then as later was membership in pacifist churches having extensive backgrounds opposed to armed conflict. In consequence, the Continental Congress strongly resolved that religious beliefs of nonresistant groups should be respected. 

During the Civil War both Northerners and Southerners who objected to war found themselves in a dilemma, being also against slavery. Nevertheless the Confederacy as well as the Federal Government gave legal recognition to "members of religious denominations" who were opposed to bearing arms and allowed them to secure substitutes or pay commutation taxes or fees. The North in its 1864 

100 Harlan F. Stone, "The Conscientious Objector," Columbia University Quarterly, vol. 

21, October 1919, pp. 253–272.

Enrollment Act even went as far as also providing for noncombatant service within the Army by assignment to work in hospitals and in the care of freedmen. Thus the Civil War ushered in the first national legislation with special provisions for conscientious objectors. 

From the Civil War to World War I there was some liberalization of church principles in opposition to resistance measures during a national emergency. In addition, the Selective Service law of 1917 took an entirely new approach. Service became personal, universal and absolute for those liable. Substitutes and commutation fees were not allowed. However, noncombatant service within the Army was provided at the outset for "a member of any well-recognized religious sect" forbidding participation in war and eventually there was a furlough arrangement for civilian duty. Thus the stage was set for the more democratic provisions in the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940 covering both noncombatant service within the armed forces and work of national importance under civilian direction for the registrant conscientiously opposed to war "by reason of religious training and belief."

î 

IV LEGISLATIVE PROVISIONS ON CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION, 1940-47 

The prospect of religious freedom in America was one of the reasons for its early and later settlement. This meant the continuous presence of conscientious objectors in the United States and especially in its pacifist churches. The general public and local, State and national governments thus became acquainted with the religious background of conscientious objection and with methods for meeting the problem in times of emergency. In consequence, the Selective Service law of 

1940 contained not only the philosophy of service for every liable person but also that of duty which would not violate the consciences of men opposed to war and armed forces. 

Conscientious Objection in the Burke-Wadsworth Bill 

The Selective Training and Service Act of 1940 was approved and became effective on September 16, 1940. When this legislation was introduced in Congress it was known as the Burke-Wadsworth bill and was titled, “A bill to protect the integrity and institutions of the United States through a system of selective compulsory military training and service." It was presented in the Senate as S. 4164 on June 

20, 1940, and the next day in the House of Representatives as H. R. 

10132. Section 7 (d) of the original version had to do with the matter of conscientious objection and read as follows: (d) Nothing contained in this Act shall be construed to require or compel any person to be subject to training or service in a combatant capacity in the land and naval forces of the United States who is found to be a member of any wellrecognized religious sect whose creed or principles forbid its members to participate in war in any form, if the conscientious holding of such belief by such person shall be established under such regulations as the President may prescribe; but no such person shall be relieved from training or service in such capacity as the President may declare to be noncombatant.¹

Suggested Changes in the C. O. Provisions 

As has been seen, such provisions were similar to those covered by the Selective Service law of 1917. In the consideration of the 1940 

1 Hearings on S. 4164 before the Senate Committee on Military Affairs, 73d Cong., 3d 

Sess. (Washington: 1940), p. 3. 67

< 

bill, however, a number of suggestions were made for changes. These may be generalized under four headings: broadening the basis of the conscientious objection or belief, providing for special methods of classifying conscientious objectors, extending the type of service to be required of or permitted by objectors, and providing for civilian rather than military control.

These four points, about which there was considerable conflict, will be explained briefly and the issues regarding them set forth, mentioning in detail some of the amendments and testimony offered in connection with section 7 (d). Then the changes actually made by Congress will be traced through the various committee prints of the bill. 

Objection a Personal Matter 

The first of these issues was whether to cover by the provisions of the Burke-Wadsworth bill conscientious objectors other than those who were members of historic peace churches. Such question came up in considering whether to include members of nonpacifist churches since they ordinarily would hold an individual or a minority viewpoint rather than a group or majority approach within their own organizations. This developed into the issue of whether the matter of conscientious objection should be made one at all of personel religious belief. Eventually the discussion turned to conscientious ob jectors who had arrived at their conclusions by reason of philosophical, political or economic reasoning. The final decision was to eliminate the church membership requirement entirely, but to qualify the provision by making it apply only to a person "who, by reason of religious training and belief, is conscientiously opposed to participation in war in any form."

Special Consideration on Appeal 

The next question was whether to provide in the 1940 law a special classification procedure for the registrant who claimed to be a conscientious objector. It was proposed that all persons making such claims should be listed on a register by their local boards, and then referred to the Department of Justice for inquiry and hearing, after which they would again be considered by their local boards. 

At this point the usual appeal rights accorded to all registrants would apply and either the registrant or a representative of the local board could appeal the classification given by the Department of Justice. Under the provisions finally adopted, however, classification was first made by the local board, the same as for any other registrant, but conscientious objector cases were to be referred to the Department of Justice for investigation, hearing and recommendation in all instances where an appeal was taken.

LEGISLATIVE PROVISIONS OF CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION, 1940-47 » 69 Work of National Importance 

Regarding the third point, the original Burke-Wadsworth bill provided only that conscientious objectors might be assigned to "training or service in such capacity as the President may declare to be noncombatant." It was pointed out in such connection, however, that during the latter part of World War I certain conscientious objectors had been assigned to civilian work through administrative procedure, and it was suggested, therefore, that provision for assignment to such work be made a part of the new draft law. It was further recommended that such conscientious objectors as thought they could engage in no work under the direction of the government be granted absolute exemption. The first suggestion was accepted by the Congress and incorporated into the Selective Service Act of 1940 as work of national importance. Absolute exemption was not provided for any type of objector, however.

Civilian Direction and Civilian Trial 

The final point which became an issue, was on the administrative control of the conscientious objector after he had entered the service of his country. During World War I and under the original provisions of the Burke-Wadsworth bill, conscientious objectors who were inducted for any type of service, like all other draftees, were still under the general control of the armed forces. It will be recalled that men who were assigned to farm work and other industrial tasks during World War I were given their final discharges through the Army. 

In the 1940 law, however, provisions were finally made that the service required of the conscientious objector who was opposed to any military duty, be under civilian direction. Furthermore it was also provided in section 11 of the act that any person charged with a violation of the Selective Service law be tried in Federal Court instead of under military court martial as was most often the case during World War I. 

In such connection, representatives of the Church of the Brethren, the Mennonite Church, and the Society of Friends had prior to the consideration of the 1940 bill presented statements expressing the historic conviction of these groups. The occasions were February 

12, 1937 and January 10, 1940. When the representatives of the three pacifist groups visited the President in 1940 a part of the letter which they left with him read as follows:

As you know, in the last war the United States Government finally authorized such nonmilitary humanitarian service to be substituted for military service, and furloughed conscientious objectors to this relief work or to farm labor. But this arrangement was provided only after months of confusion and distress, and only after repeated conferences between our representatives and officials of the War Department, because of the lack of any previously established policy. Since we understand that plans are now being formulated for mobilization of the Nation's

manpower if war should come, and since the need for dealing with conscientious objectors would again emerge to confront Government agencies, we venture to suggest the advantage of advance discussion of the problem with the appropriate officials. We should much appreciate the opportunity for such discussion and are prepared to make concrete proposals to such officials regarding procedures for handling conscientious objectors and types of service which might be provided. 

In this connection we also venture to suggest the desirability of again setting up a civilian agency for dealing with this problem. There is a precedent for this in the action of President Wilson in 1918.2

Quaker Requests at the Senate Hearings 

As the hearings on the Burke-Wadsworth bill progressed during 1940 a number of men testified on conscientious objection before the Senate Military Affairs Committee. These included Mr. Harold 

Evans representing the Religious Society of Friends; Mr. Paul Comly 

French of the Friends' General Conference; Dr. Charles S. Longacre representing the Seventh-Day Adventist Church; the Rev. John M.

Swomley, Jr., of the National Council of Methodist Youth; and Dr. 

Howard K. Beale from the American Civil Liberties Union. 

During this testimony the representatives of the Society of Friends early indicated the main issues. In his appearance before the Senate 

Committee on July 10, Mr. Evans made these specific requests: 

Section 7 (d) of the bill, exempting from combatant service members of certain religious sects which hold pacifist beliefs, merely follows the provisions of the selective service law of 1917, which was enacted as an emergency measure, and which in this phase of it did not work out very satisfactorily, I think, either to the Army or to those most concerned. We would respectfully urge that this section of the bill be amended, if the bill is to be passed, so as to follow in general the British National Service Act of 1939. We would specifically ask that it provide: 

1. For handling conscientious objectors at all times by civilian rather than by military authority. 

2. For placing conscientious objectors on a special register, as they do in England. 

3. For complete exemption for those found to have sincere convictions against all forms of compulsory service, and for the exemption of others from such service as they cannot conscientiously accept. 

And finally, we ask for the same treatment for all conscientious objectors, regardless of membership in any historic peace church, because we feel that this is a matter not of membership in the Society of Friends, of Mennonites or Dunkards, but is a matter of the individual's conscience. As you have heard this afternoon, there are numbers of Catholics and there are numbers of Methodists and others who hold the same view.

Adventist Views Before the House Committee 

The first to testify on the conscientious objection question before the 

House Military Affairs Committee was Dr. Longacre of the Seventh day Adventist Church. This was on July 25, whereas he had spoken to the Senate committee on July 10. However, because his testimony was more complete on the latter occasion, it is mentioned here. Regarding the members of his church he said: 

We (the Adventists) are not pacifists nor militarists nor conscientious objectors, but noncombatants. But as to the noncombatant (the Adventist) he merely believes that he should not take human life. But he is willing to cooperate with his Government in any capacity that he can, without having to violate his conscience in regard to taking a life. We are noncombatants. 

He then proposed the following amendment as an addition to section 7 (d) as it appeared in the first version of the Selective Service bill: 

Nothing in this act contained shall be construed to require or compel any person who is drafted and is a member of any religious sect or organization whose creed or principles forbid its members to participate in war in any form or to bear arms in combative service; or any person, though a member of an organization whose creed or principles do not forbid the bearing of arms but who individually has religious scruples against the bearing of arms, to take any other than noncombatant military training courses offered by the Government." 

Following this Dr. Longacre went on to testify: 

President Wilson, you remember, was given the authority to define what constituted noncombatant service in the World War, and the definitions he laid down as to noncombatant service and the lines of work he prescribed were in full agreement with our religious convictions on that subject. I do not think anybody could have laid them down any more clearly than he did. Our denomination has appointed a war service council, and in that council we have laid down certain lines of work. The Mennonite Position 

When Mr. Amos F. Horst appeared before the House committee in behalf of the Mennonite Church on the same day, July 25, he set forth the position of his church. He used a part of the 1937 general conference statement which has already been quoted in chapter II. Thereafter he proposed, in behalf of the Mennonite Church the following amendment: 

Delete section 7 (d) and substitute the following: 

"(d) Nothing contained in this act shall be construed to require any person to be subject to training or service in the land or naval forces of the United States who is conscientiously opposed to participation in war in any form, nor to require any person to be subject to training or service in such forces in any capacity to which he is conscientiously opposed. All persons claiming such conscientious objections shall be listed provisionally at the time of their registration on the register of conscientious objectors. There shall be established in the Department of Justice a bureau of conscientious objectors under the direction of a commissioner, who shall be a civilian and shall be directly responsible to the Attorney General and who shall administer this subsection 7 (d) of the act under such regulations as the President may prescribe." 

Respectfully submitted for consideration and adoption by the peace problems committee of the Mennonite Churches of the United States.

Differences in Individual Conscience 

Shortly after he had presented the suggested amendment to the committee, Dr. Beale pointed out some differences of individual conscience:

There are degrees of conscientious objectors. There are the absolute objectors, and they would say that they could not take up arms against anybody; and there are others, there are people who would say that they can defend their own shores and nothing else; and the people I am talking about, I believe, in general, believe in nonviolence to the extent that they could not take up arms against anyone, but they certainly do not approve of that sort of people and would use great moral force. And I still believe that has validity in the world against people who are unpatriotic and un-American." 

Dr. Beale also said:

Some of these objectors, whether nonreligious or religious, can do noncombative service. Some feel that they cannot do even that, and this is a matter of personal conscience, not a matter that you can reason on; and some feel that they can do noncombative military service; some feel that they can do civil service under civil control, not service in the Army. And this very small group of them feel that they cannot do anything."

75 1 We, the undersigned students of Union Theological Seminary, wishing to register our protest against the use of the method of war to settle international disputes because we believe it inconsistent with Jesus' teaching of love for friend and enemy, which he himself practiced and enjoined his followers to do likewise, do petition the Congress of the United States to include in the Burke-Wadsworth bill, now being drawn up, provisions for the registration of conscientious objectors to war similar to those in the British draft act. Testimony of Mr. Paul Comly French

Mr. French of the Friend's General Conference also appeared before the House committee on July 25. His testimony is most significant in the light of future developments. Taken at its face value, and considered with Committee Prints Nos. 3 and 4 of the Senate, it indicates at the same time the turning point in the hearings and for most practical purposes the final shaping up of the Burke-Wadsworth provisions regarding conscientious objectors. At this time he said:

During the past week we have talked with members of the Senate Military Affairs Committee and with members of the War Department who are testifying before your committee and before the Senate committee in the hope that we might jointly work out some common ground for the treatment of conscientious objectors that would protect their viewpoint and protect the position of the Government.

Yesterday, at the War College, we worked out a proposal, a proposed substitute for 7 (d), with Colonel O'Kelliher, of the Army (the Joint Army-Navy Committee on Selective Service), which was presented to the Senate committee today, which in the main, I think, covers the position and would protect the Army and protect the conscientious objector.

During the last war, or after the war, Major Clegg (Kellogg) of the Adjutant General's Department, who served on the board of inquiry for the conscientious objector, wrote a book and said he found from the War Department experience that the act at that time was not completely satisfactory in its operation, either to the Army or to the conscientious objector. It was a problem that the Army had to face and that he felt that after the war was over it would be wise if someone gave the matter some thought, that before another emergency arose some definite plan could be prepared. 

16 Ibid., pp. 191-2 (signatures omitted).

We have agreed with him and have prepared this outline, or rather, the War Department has, after we have discussed it with them and tried to reach a common ground. It provides, in general, for a registry of persons who claim conscientious objection to war at the time they are registered under the draft on a provisional register. The Senate committee bill, I understand this morning, has been reported out, I am not sure yet.

It provides that the Department of Justice would see the record of every person who registered as a conscientious objector and would then hold a hearing and inquiry and then report their findings back to the local draft board, whether the person was a conscientious objector and should justly be treated as such. 

It would provide for two forms, or three forms, under this proposal, one that the man was conceded to be a conscientious objector to war as a result of hearing and inquiry, and was willing to perform noncombatant service in the Army, he would be so assigned.

If he felt conscientiously unwilling to perform noncombative service, the wording was that he might then be assigned to service of national importance under civilian control; and the third provision in this draft was that if they found his objections were not deep conscientious convictions, then his name would be removed from the provisional register of conscientious objectors, and he would be assigned to military service.

We would like to see another provision in it which the War Department did not agree to. We would like to see complete exemption for a very small group of absolutists who conscientiously feel unable to perform any service in the war. 

In the World War this amounted, in the entire draft, to 509 men. But they are persons of deep convictions; they feel that they cannot do anything which contributes in any way to the Military Establishment. 

You may not agree with them entirely, but they are deeply convinced that their position is completely right, and in keeping with their religious faith." 

Court Martial Opposition 

Mr. Raymond Wilson of the Society of Friends likewise testified and among other things explained to the House committee the Friends' objection to possible military supervision of conscientious objectors: 

We feel that the administration of this ought to be in the hands of the Department of Justice or some civilian agency, so that the procedure is a civilian one, instead of court martial.18

Mr. Arthur J. Edwards, representing the Council for Social Action of Congregational and Christian Churches, also spoke to the House committee on the same subject. He said that the specific amendment to the proposed Selective Service enactment which he had in mind and which he did present had already been incorporated in Senate Committee Print No. 4. However, he went on to make the point, later incorporated into the law, that violators of the act should be prosecuted under civil law rather than under court martial, as was true in connection with the draft legislation of 1917.
