The Proposed Quaker Amendment 

Returning to the conscientious objector provisions, a substitution for section 7 (d) of the Burke-Wadsworth bill which was left with the House committee by Mr. Wilson and Mr. French of the Friends' organizations during their appearance last referred to above, read as follows: 

Nothing contained in this act shall be construed to require any person to be subject to combat training or service in the land or naval forces of the United States who, by reason of religious training and belief, is conscientiously opposed to participation in war in any form, and is so found to be a bona fide objector as hereinafter provided. All persons claiming such conscientious objections shall be listed on a register of conscientious objectors at the time of their classification by a local board, and persons so regstered shall be at once referred to the Department of Justice for inquiry and hearing. After appropriate inquiry by the proper agency of the Department of Justice, a hearing shall be held by the Department of Justice regarding the character and good faith of the objection. 

The Department shall, after hearing, if the objection be sustained, recommend that the objector shall (1) be assigned to noncombatant service in such capacity as the President may designate as noncombatant, or (2) if found to be a conscientious objector opposed to participation in war in any form, that he shall be assigned to work of national importance under civilian direction, or (3) if said objection is not sustained, the local board shall be immediately notified thereof, and the name of such objector shall then be removed from the register of conscientious objectors, and such objector thereafter be subject to classification. 

Should such conscientious objector of the local board disagree with the findings of the Department of Justice, said local board shall immediately refer said case to the appeal board having jurisdiction for final determination.25 

Religious Training and/or Belief 

The effect of the Quaker substitution was a direct one in that it was inserted as a replacement in both the Senate and House versions of the proposed Selective Service law. Section 7 (d) in the original Burke- 

Wadsworth bill of June 20, 1940, was patterned very closely after the conscription act of World War I (May 18, 1917) as indicated early in this chapter. The language of the first version of section 7 (d) was continued verbatim in section 6 (d) of the Senate Prints No. 1, July 

23, 1940, and No. 2, July 25, 1940, but after Mr. French and Mr. Wilson had presented their suggestion, it was substituted and the bill included this entirely new statement: 

24 Congressional Record, Proceedings and Debates of the 76th Cong., 3d Sess., vol. 86, pt. 10 (Washington: 1940), p. 10895. 

25 Hearings on H. R. 10132, op. cit., p. 211. 

737977°-50-vol. 17

Nothing contained in this act shall be construed to require any person to be subject to combat training or service in the land or naval forces of the United States who by reason of religious training and belief is conscientiously opposed to participation in war in any form," 

At the instigation of Senator Guffey of Pennsylvania the word "or" replaced the word "and" in section 6 (d) of Senate Print No. 3 making the phrase in question read: "by reason of religious training or belief." 26 Finally, on the representations of Col. Victor J. 

O'Kelliher of the Joint Army-Navy Selective Service Committee, however, the word "and" was restored in section 6 (d) of Senate Print 

No. 4, and the phrase so remained thereafter.27

There was considerable difference in the "both" idea conveyed by the “and” and the "either" concept which arose from the use of the disjunctive "or". The former tended to eliminate conscientious objectors who developed their beliefs in the absence of definite religious training, as well as those who were trained in religious groups but had no personal convictions opposed to military service. Settling upon the word "and" militated against those who had attained a religious belief against participation in war without affiliation with or indoctrination by a formal training establishment of a religous nature. 

The Selective Service System having the above information on a possible more liberal intent of Congress, however, did not apply too strict an interpretation in this regard during its 62 years of operation.

Liberties Union. However, this identical wording was also used in an amendment suggested by the Friends during the same committee session on the Burke-Wadsworth bill. The Bill as Reported to and Passed by the Senate The Burke-Wadsworth bill was reported out of the Senate Military Affairs Committee on August 5 and reprinted as reported. There were no changes in the conscientious objection provision from Print No. 7. At this time the majority report included this statement regarding the conscientious objector question:

The measure is fair both to a person holding conscientious scruples against war and to the Nation of which he is a part. It provides for inquiry and hearing by the Department of Justice to make recommendations as to whether a person claiming deferment because of conscientious objection to war is or is not a bona fide conscientious objector. If his contention is made in good faith he may not be selected for combat service, but may be selected either for noncombatant service, or for national work under civilian direction. The rights of the conscientious objector and of the Government are fully protected against possible local prejudice, influence, or passion, by provision for appeal to a board of appeal." 

The only statement in the minority report related to this question was the brief statement that: "This minority does approve the provisions for registration and its exemptions." 30

The conscientious objector provisions remained unchanged as to wording when the bill was eventually passed by the Senate on August 30. At that time, however, the section was numbered “5 (e)."

Conference Reports on the Bill 

The Burke-Wadsworth bill as passed by Congress then went to conference to harmonize the differences between the Senate and the House. 

The following is taken from the "Statement of the managers on the part of the House" in making their conference report of Sep tember 12, 1940 on the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940. 

The Senate bill provided that nothing therein contained was to be construed as requiring any person to be subject to combatant training or service who by reason of religious training or belief is conscientiously opposed to participation in war in any form. All persons claiming such exemption because of such conscientious objections were to be listed on a register of conscientious objectors at the time of their classification by a local board, and their names at once referred by the local board to the Department of Justice for inquiry and hearing. After appropriate inquiry by the appropriate agency of the Department of Justice, a hearing was to be held by the Department of Justice in the case of each such person with respect to the character and good faith of his objections. If the objections were found by the department to be sustained, it was to recommend that (1) the objector be assigned to noncombatant service as defined by the President, or (2) if the objector was found to be conscientiously opposed to participation in such noncombatant service that he be assigned to work of national importance under civilian direction. If after the hearing the objections were found not to be sustained, the objector and the local board were to be immediately notified, the name of the objector was then to be removed from the register of conscientious objectors, and the objector was thereafter to be liable for the training and service provided for in the bill. If within five days after the date of the findings by the Department of Justice, the objector or the local board gave notice to the other of disagreement with the findings, the local board was to refer the matter for final determination to an appropriate appeal board. 

Under the House amendment the character and good faith of the objection of a conscientious objector were to be determined by the local board, subject to the right of appeal by the objector to an appropriate appeal board. 

Under the conference agreement, if the objections are not sustained by the local board in the first instance, the objector is given the right to appeal to the appropriate appeal board. Upon the filing of such appeal, the appeal board is directed forthwith to refer the matter to the Department of Justice for an inquiry and hearing. After appropriate inquiry by the proper agency of the 

Department of Justice, a hearing is to be held by the department with respect to the character and good faith of the objections. If the Department finds the objections to be sustained it is to recommend to the appeal board (1) that the objector, if he is inducted under the act, be assigned to noncombatant service "Ibid., p. 11753–54.

as defined by the President, or (2) if it is found that he is conscientiously opposed to participation in such noncombatant service, in lieu of such induction that he be assigned to work of national importance under civilian direction. 

In making its decision, the appeal board is to consider the record on appeal from the local board, together with the recommendations, which it is not bound to follow, by the Department of Justice. All persons whose claims for exemption under this provision because of conscientious objection are sustained are to be listed by the local board on a register of conscientious objectors." 

The conference report presented in the Senate on the following day was in almost the same words." Thus the Department of Justice again assumed a role in the processing of conscientious objectors but its work came into application following that of the Selective Service local board and did not relate to any but objector cases which came up for appeal consideration. Such procedure was simple and did not involve much duplication of effort. 

The C. O. Provisions Finally Adopted 

There seem to have been no objections in either the Senate or the House to the conference report and the wording thus agreed upon in conference became section 5 (g) of the Selective Training and Service 

Act of 1940: 

[Nothing contained in this act shall be construed to require any person to be subject to combatant training and service in the land or naval forces of the United States who, by reason of religious training and belief, is conscientiously opposed to participation in war in any form. Any such person claiming such exemption from combatant training and service because of such conscientious objections whose claim is sustained by the local board shall, if he is inducted into the land or naval forces under this act, be assigned to noncombatant service as defined by the President, or shall, if he is found to be conscientiously opposed to participation in such noncombatant service, in lieu of such induction, be assigned to work of national importance under civilian direction. Any such person claiming such exemption from combatant training and service because of such conscientious objections shall, if such claim is not sustained by the local board, be entitled to an appeal to the appropriate appeal board provided for in section 10 (a) (2). Upon the filing of such appeal with the appeal board, the appeal board shall forthwith refer the matter to the Department of Justice for inquiry and hearing by the Department or the proper agency thereof. 

After appropriate inquiry by such agency, a hearing shall be held by the Department of Justice with respect to the character and good faith of the objections of the person concerned, and such person shall be notified of the time and place of such hearing. The Department shall, after such hearing, if the objections are found to be sustained, recommend to the appeal board (1) that if the objector is inducted into the land or naval forces under this act, he shall be assigned to noncombatant service as defined by the President, or (2) that if the objector is found to be conscientiously opposed to participation in such noncombatant service, he shall in lieu of such induction be assigned to work of national importance under civilian direction. If after such hearing the Department finds that his objections are not sustained, it shall recommend to the 

38 Ibid., p. 12038.

LEGISLATIVE PROVISIONS OF CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION, 1940-47 » 87 

appeal board that such objections be not sustained. The appeal board shall give consideration to but shall not be bound to follow the recommendation of the Department of Justice together with the record of appeal from the local board in making its decision. Each person whose claim for exemption from combatant training and service because of conscientious objections is sustained shall be listed by the local board on a register of conscientious objectors.40 

Later Legislative Proposals

During the 62-year life of the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940, as amended, several attempts were made to change the conscientious objection provisions. Mr. Thorkelson, of Montana, introduced a bill in the House of Representatives (H. R. 

10545) on September 23, 1940, which was entitled, "A bill to define the status of conscientious objectors under the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940." Only section 3 of this bill affected the Selective 

Service law. It read: 

SEC. 3. All registers of conscientious objectors required to be kept under the 

Selective Training and Service Act of 1940 shall be open to public inspection in the offices of the respective local boards on Monday of each week between the hours of 9 o'clock antemeridian and 4 o'clock postmeridian during the operation of said act. On the first day of each month, it shall be the duty of the respective local boards to deliver to the Government Printing Office, by registered mail, a complete list of the conscientious objectors appearing upon their respective registers up to that time; and on or before the first day of the succeeding month it shall be the duty of the Government Printing Office to publish for free distribution, as a public document, the names (alphabetically arranged) and addresses of all conscientious objectors appearing upon the lists furnished by such local boards. Failure to perform any of these duties shall subject the guilty person or persons to the penalties prescribed in section 11 of said Selective 

Training and Service Act of 1940. 

This bill was referred to the Committee on Military Affairs but no report was ever made regarding it.

A Bill Designed to Eliminate Section 5 (g) 

Mr. Thomas of Oklahoma introduced the following bill (S. 315) in the Senate on January 11, 1943:

To amend section 5 of the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940, as amended, by striking out subsection (g) thereof relating to exemption from combatant service of conscientious objectors. 

Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled, That section 5 of the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940, as amended, is amended by striking out subsection (g) thereof.

A hearing was held on this and another bill, not concerned with conscientious objection, on February 17, 1943. At this time a rep resentative from the National Headquarters of Selective Service pointed out that the bill was presented as a result of a resolution of the 

40 Public Law No. 783, op. cit., section 5 (g).

American Legion in Oklahoma, but that it did not have the endorsement of the National Department. He then read the following paragraph of a communication from Mr. Bruce Stubblefield, Executive 

Secretary of the National Legion, which indicated opposition from that level:

At the time of our national convention in Kansas City, there were some resolutions presented with reference to conscientious objectors, but the resolutions were rejected by the committee that considered them, feeling that the Army was handling the proposition satisfactorily under the circumstances, and also feeling that it would not be proper to take these men into the Army because of their attitude and the further fact that no commanding officer would want to go into battle with a conscientious objector.“ 41 Speaking for the War Department, a representative stated: 

We are opposed to the repeal of section 5 (g) of the act, mainly because of the fact that the type of people who are conscientious objectors would cause a lot of trouble in the Army. While the War Department does not endorse the conscientious objector's view regarding his obligation to his country, we believe that the present solution is proving satisfactory as to the disposition of these people, and the ones we have that are willing to perform noncombatant service, as a group, are performing satisfactorily, and for those reasons we are opposed to the bill S. 315." 

The Director of Selective Service, Major General Lewis B. Hershey, also testified against the bill, part of which testimony was as follows: 

There has not been a report made by the Selective Service System on S. 315, and therefore my testimony on that must be considered with the limitation that I do not presume to represent the Presidential program viewpoint, or the viewpoint of the Chairman of the Manpower Commission. 

The Selective Service System believes that the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940, as amended, has, as a practical matter, reasonably solved a rather distressing situation, as in all wars, that of what to do with those whose conscience prevents them from participating in full measure in the Army. 

S. 315 provides not only for the elimination of all such civil work, in lieu of service in the Army, but also noncombatant service in the Army, itself, and while I do not presume to testify from the Army's viewpoint but from sources within the Army, I would like to say that I am opposed to S. 315." 

This so-called Thomas amendment was eventually tabled by the 

Senate Military Affairs Committee.

August 10, 1942; dependency benefits for conscientious objectors, January, 1945; overseas service, June 30, 1943; Federal Government employment, March 10, 1943; the appropriation of funds from conscientious objector services (1) for the Office of Foreign Relief and 

Rehabilitation Operations, September 14, 1943, (2) for expenditure by the United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration, January 3, 1945, (3) for needy dependents, January 10, 1945, and (4) for the International Children's Fund of the United Nations, February 13, 1947; the induction into the armed services of objectors who failed to comply with the rules governing operation of work of national importance, April 2, 1945; and the discharge of conscientious objectors both in the armed forces and in Civilian Public Service 

Camps, June 26, 1945. Review

The fact that there were no changes in the conscientious objector provisions of the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940 during their 62 years of existence was perhaps an indication of their careful development. These provisions made four distinct advances over previous national legislation on conscientious objection. The first was a broader definition for objection which based it upon conscientious opposition to participating in war by reason of religious training and belief. In World War I the basis was the narrower one of membership in any well-recognized religious sect or organization forbidding participation in war; that of the Civil War under the final enactment of the Federal Government (1864) was membership in a religious denomination conscientiously opposed to bearing arms. 

The second step forward was to allow the Selective Service registrant to file an appeal with the appeal board in the event the local board did not sustain his claim for exemption from combatant or noncombatant training and service. The System's board of appeal then referred the case to the Department of Justice for inquiry and hearing, which agency after taking such action made recommendation to the appeal board on the type of service. Neither the World War I nor 

Civil War enactments contained such special instruction. 

The third was a new provision for assignment in lieu of induction, to work of national importance under civilian direction. Likewise provided for was assignment upon induction by the armed forces to noncombatant duty as defined by the President. The 1917 law made provision only for service within the armed forces in any capacity declared by the President to be noncombatant. Later, however, furlough from the Army to farm and industrial work was provided by another law. The Federal Enrollment Act of 1864 said that inducted objectors should be assigned as noncombatants by the Secretary

of War to duty in the hospitals or the care of freedmen or should pay the sum of $300 to be applied in benefiting sick and wounded soldiers.

The fourth improvement was removing the control on work of national importance entirely from the armed forces and placing the direction of such work under civilians. This was not the case either in 1917 or 1864. The Selective Service Act of 1940 also provided that its violators would be tried in the Federal courts of the land and not by military courts martial as was the procedure during both previous occasions of national conscription. 

As a result of this progress, there were prospects among registrants opposed to war of (1) somewhat greater cooperation in both combatant and noncombatant service with the Army and Navy and (2) of much greater cooperation in duty outside of these organizations under civilian control. Those averse to any kind of service were not exempted, however; they were violators of the law and subject to its penalties.

V 

CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTOR REGULATIONS 

Regarding the conscientious objector provisions of the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940, the President of the United States was authorized, as in the case of other military manpower procurement provisions, "to prescribe the necessary rules and regulations" for their administration. The law established noncombatant service within the armed forces or work of national importance under civilian direction as the way in which a registrant opposed to war should perform his obligation when selected for induction. The general regulations of Selective Service covered the operations of the System with reference to conscientious objectors and in addition special regulations were issued on the Civilian Public Service Camps which were set up in connection with work of national importance. 

The details of the regulations-both general and special-appear in the text and the appendices of the book. The purpose of this brief chapter is but to introduce them in one place now as a preparation for their later discussion and presentation. 

Original Regulations of 1940

The Selective Service Regulations were issued in two editions, the first of which was composed of six separate volumes, dated from 

September 23, 1940 to October 22, 1940.¹ Each volume set forth the procedures for one phase of the administration and operation of the System. The volumes were divided into sections and paragraphs which were numbered consecutively throughout the entire set. Thus the first section and paragraph of volume I were numbered I and 101, respectively, and the first section and paragraph of volume III, XV and 301. These original regulations, revised by 127 amendments, were in effect from the time of their issuance until February 1, 1942, when the first printing of the second edition appeared. 

1 Vol. 1, Organization and Administration, and vol. 2, Registration, were prescribed by

Executive Order No. 8545, of Sept. 23, 1940. Vol. 3, Classification and Selection, by Executive Order 8560, October 4, 1940. Vol. 4, Delivery and Induction, by Executive Order 8574, October 22, 1940. Vol. 5, Finance, by Executive Order 8561, October 4, 1940. 

Vol. 6, Fiscal Standards, by Executive Order 8570, October 18, 1940. 

91

< Conscientious Objector Regulations in First Edition 

The first edition of the regulations contained provisions relating to the classification of conscientious objectors, to their assignment to work of national importance under civilian direction and to special appeal procedures for them. Likewise included in a separate unnumbered volume was a series of paragraphs entitled, Camp Regulations. Inasmuch as the major conscientious objector operation of Selective Service was one of classification, most of the general regulations pertaining to this phase appeared in volume III, Classification and Selection. 

Classes Available for the Objector

As first prescribed, the regulations provided a special class only for the objector who was unwilling to perform any military or naval service but who would accept assignment to work of national importance. Paragraph 361 stipulated:

In Class IV-E shall be placed conscientious objectors who are classified for civilian work in accordance with paragraph 365. 

This provision was not changed during the 6½ years of the System's existence.

With reference to the objector who was available for noncombatant service, paragraph 364 (b) provided the following on means of identification: 

Whenever a registrant is thus determined to be available for noncombatant service only, the local board shall indicate this by placing an "O" after the letter indicating his subclass on all records, reports, orders and other papers on which the registrant is mentioned by name. For example: Class I-A-0, Class I-B-O, Class I-D-O, or Class I-E-O. 

Thus Class I-A-O identified the conscientious objector willing to perform noncombatant duty, who was available for general military service, and Class I-B-O the objector available for limited service. 

Later by Amendment No. 72 to paragraph 365, effective June 13, 1941, registrants available for work of national importance in Class IV-E who possessed but limited physical fitness were identified as "Class IV-E (limited service)." On August 31, 1941, this designa tion was changed to Class IV-E-LS by Amendment No. 86. By the same amendment Class IV-E-H was established for the registrant formerly in IV-E or IV-E-LS who had reached his twenty-eighth birthday without having been assigned to work of national importance. Finally, after the entry of the United States into World War 

II, the urgent manpower needs of the Army caused the elimination of all limited service classes. Amendment No. 73 to the second edition, August 18, 1942, provided, therefore, that Classes I-B-O and IV- E-LS should no longer be used for conscientious objectors with limitedservice qualifications. It also provided for the discontinuance of 

Class IV-E-H.

CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTOR REGULATIONS » 93 Classification and Appeal Procedures Section XXV of volume III, Classification and Selection, set forth the classification process as it related to conscientious objection, outlining the procedure for the filing of claims of conscientious objection, for the classification of objectors opposed to combatant service only and for the classification of those opposed to all military service, and providing for a register at local boards of all objectors whose claims were sustained.

The conscientious objector had the same rights of appeal as every other registrant. In addition, special appeal procedures were prescribed by the regulations. Paragraph 375, as originally written, stipulated that when the appeal of an objector was taken to the board of appeal, unless the registrant was placed in Class II, III, or IV (other than IV-E), his file should be forwarded to a United States 

Attorney for an advisory recommendation of the Department of Justice before the board of appeal was permitted to make its decision. 

Later, October 27, 1943, after paragraph 375 had become section 627.25 in the second edition of the regulations, the Department of 

Justice was relieved of some of the additional burden placed upon it by the conscientious objector hearings through Amendment No. 183.

This amendment authorized the board of appeal to classify into Classes IV-E and I-A-O claimants of such classification without first referring the case to United States Attorney.

Civilian Public Service Camp Regulations 

The special regulations to the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940, known as Camp Regulations, which were to be established for Class IV-E objectors who had been assigned to work of national importance under civilian direction, provided the rules and procedures for the administration and operation of the Civilian Public Service 

Camps. Authorized by Executive Order 8675, February 6, 1941, these special regulations vested in the Director of Selective Service authority to "designate or determine work of national importance under civilian direction." Contained in 23 paragraphs, they specified the responsibilities of a Camp Operations Division in the National Headquarters of the System and of the administrative personnel for the camps; defined the functions of a National Service Board for Religious Objectors to develop with Selective Service plans for utilizing objector registrants in work of national importance; provided for health standards in the camps, a safety program, an educational program, and work and camp operations; and designated authority for certain operational procedures.

Revision of Volume III, First Edition 

Volume III, Classification and Selection, in the first edition of the regulations, was revised September 3, 1941, to make its provisions

current with amended procedures. No change in the organizational structure of the volume was made, however. The important changes which occurred in the provisions relating to conscientious objectors have already been indicated.

CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTOR REGULATIONS » 95 The Second Edition 

Three printings to the second edition of the regulations were issued. 

The first printing became effective February 1, 1942. 

In the second edition the physical arrangement used in the first or original edition was changed. In place of separate "volumes", "sections" and "paragraphs" the regulations were divided into "parts" numbered from 601 to 692 and sections, such as 601.1 and 692.1. A conversion table showing the relations between the "parts" and "sections" of the second edition and the "paragraphs" of the first edition was included. A total of 125 amendments was made to this first printing of the second edition.

The second printing of the second edition covered the regulations from February 1, 1943 through July 31, 1945. This printing incorporated the changes in the regulations made by amendments issued during the preceding year ending February 1, 1943, and included subsequent amendments Nos. 126 to 334, inclusive.

The third printing of the second edition contained the regulations as effective July 31, 1945, and amendments Nos. 335 to 423, inclusive. 

The inclusion of these amendments made the regulations current through March 31, 1947.

Under the revised form in which the second edition of the regulations was issued, five parts related exclusively to objectors willing to accept work of national importance only. Part 651 was headed, De termination of Acceptability of Persons for Work of National Im portance Under Civilian Direction;

Part 652, Assignment and 

Delivery of Persons to Work of National Importance Under Civilian Direction; and Part 653, Work of National Importance Under Civil ian Direction. The Camp Regulations were contained in Parts 691 and 692.

Determination of Acceptability 

Part 651 set forth the procedures as related to the final-type physical examination for determining the acceptability of Class IV-E registrants for work of national importance under civilian direction. 

Every registrant in Class IV-E had to report for a final-type physical examination before being accepted for such work. An Order to Re port for Final-Type Physical Examination (DSS Form 48A) was mailed to the registrant by the local board when his order number was reached for this purpose. Following such examination the local board either retained the registrant in Class IV-E if he had been found qualified, or reclassified him in Class IV-E-LS if qualified for limited service only, or in Class IV-F if disqualified. This procedure was eliminated with the amendment of the Selective Training and Serv- 737977°-50—vol. 1- -8

CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION 

ice Act, by Public Law 197, effective December 5, 1943, which provided that a registrant could request and receive a preinduction physical examination when his induction appeared imminent. Previously, examination was only given after the registrant had been called up for induction. 

Assignment and Delivery

Part 652 specified the manner in which Class IV-E registrants were to be assigned and delivered to work of national importance under civilian direction. Assignment was made by the Director of Selective 

Service upon being notified by the local board on a Conscientious Objector Report (DSS Form 48) of the objector's acceptability. The registrant was then ordered to report for this work by the local board following its receipt of an Assignment to Work of National Impor tance (DSS Form 49) from the Director. Transportation to the 

Civilian Public Service Camp was provided by the System. Like inductees into the armed forces Class IV-E, registrants were assigned to such work for the duration of the emergency and 6 months thereafter. 

Work of National Importance 

Part 653 related to work of national importance. Under the authority vested in the Director of the Selective Service System to "establish, designate, or determine work of national importance under civilian direction" regulations were provided for the administration and operation both of Government-operated and church-operated Civilian Public Service Camps. Administratively, both were under the civilian direction of Selective Service and technically under the supervision of the Government agency concerned. The regulations directed that funds for the Government-operated camps should be provided by the System, and that such expenses of camps sponsored by the National Service Board for Religious Objectors as wages, clothing, feeding, housing, hospitalization, and all other costs of operating should be borne by that organization. 

The regulations further stipulated that assignees should be paid $5 a month and be furnished with "subsistence, proper clothing for the performance of their duties and such other personal supplies or equipment" as seemed necessary. By Amendment No. 236 to section 653.3 (e), effective June 7, 1944, the Director of Selective Service was authorized to provide in lieu of these necessities a cash allowance. The same amendment also provided for a physical examination of the assignee as soon as he arrived at camp to determine whether there had been any change in his physical or mental condition since his preinduction physical examination, and extended the responsibility of the Director to supervision and control over all projects.

CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTOR REGULATIONS » 97 

After an assignee had completed his period of service, section 653.14 provided that he receive a certificate of release from active participation in work of national importance and that he be transferred to a reserve for 10 years until he had attained the age of 45 or until he was discharged, whichever occurred first. The assignee remained in Class IV-E at his local board. 

Sections 653.15 and 653.16 authorized the Director of Selective 

Service to release an assignee from work of national importance prior to his completion of service, either to volunteer for induction into the armed forces and take up combatant or noncombatant duty, or under conditions which would likewise permit release of a member of the armed forces. An amendment to section 653.15 effective March 

16, 1943 (Amendment No. 40), relieved assignees who were discharged to volunteer for military or naval service from having to submit first to a physical examination. 

Camp Regulations, Second Edition 

The Camp Regulations, issued as a separate series of paragraphs in the first editions, were incorporated in the second edition as Part 691, Rules for Camps Operated by the National Service Board for Religious Objectors, and as Part 692, Rules for Government-Operated Camps. Among the more important amendments to these parts was 

Amendment No. 128 to section 691.13, effective February 23, 1943, which provided upon order of the Director of Selective Service for a physical examination by the medical advisory board of an assignee who in the opinion of the camp physician was "physically unfit to perform work of national importance." Amendment 222, effective May 5, 1944, revise Part 691 in its entirey. This amendment also provided minor administrative changes in the new provisions. 

Part 692 was likewise revised in its entirety May 5, 1944, by Amendment No. 223. Most of the changes effected thereby related to camp discipline with more flexibility given the camp director in determining disciplinary measures. An additional amendment (No. 298) effective April 3, 1945, provided for more prompt action by the camp director in regard to a. w. o. 1. absences of assignees. Under the new procedure, the camp director was instructed to make a report immediately to the Director of Selective Service on assignee departures or absences without permission in contrast to the 10-day interim previously stipulated. The amendment also provided that any disciplinary action already taken by the Director or camp director or lack of such action should in no way be considered a necessary precedent for prosecution of the assignee for violation of the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940, as amended.

Conclusion The above compilation and the preceding materials of this chapter indicate that both the general Selective Service Regulations on ob-

jectors and the special ones for their camps tried to carry out the spirit and the letter of the World War II legislation on conscientious objection. What is more, these rules which the System used to execute the C. O. provisions were prepared in the light of pertinent Congressional hearings of 1940 and the church backgrounds and wartime experiences in the United States of men opposed to resistance or violence. In other words, observance was given to the basic philosophy of the enactment that liable men must serve during an emergency but within the confines of their beliefs.

VI 

THE OBJECTOR WHO PERFORMED NONCOMBATANT SERVICE 

The law and the regulations upon which the 1940–47 operations of Selective Service were based provided that conscientious objectors inducted into the armed forces could perform such duty in a noncombatant way. The legislation and the rules of administering it went even further by also providing, in lieu of induction, for assignment to work of national importance under civilian direction if noncombatant service was a violation of conscience. 

No provisions were made, however, for the registrant who was opposed to war, resistance or violence and would accept neither induction for noncombatant duty nor assignment to work of national importance. This individual, who would perform no service whatsoever, was a violator of the law and subject to the penalties thereof. 

In such regard the American public held firmly to its 1940 philosophy that every liable person must give some kind of service in time of emergency, a concept which had been developing since early colonial times through acquaintanceship and experience with conscientious objectors and their church backgrounds.

During World War II there were few objectors who would not perform any kind of service. Those who did work of national importance were much more numerous. More numerous still were those who performed noncombatant duty. The present chapter deals with this latter group which objected only to combatant service. 

Conscientious Objectors as Noncombatants 

During World War II Selective Service furnished for induction into the armed forces approximately 25,000 conscientious objectors who were opposed to military or naval training and service of combatant nature. They were willing to perform noncombatant duty, however, and in order to distinguish these registrants from men objecting to any and all types of service with the armed forces, the term "conscientious cooperators" was sometimes used. The conscientious cooperator although wishing to support his government, was forced to decline participation in overt acts of war and bloodshed because of the dictates of conscience. As has been seen specific pro- 105

vision was made in section 5 (g) of the Selective Service Act for such men to "be assigned to noncombatant service as defined by the President" and thus not violate their beliefs. This was in the original law and was not amended at any time during the 62 years of the System's operation.

Recording of Objection on Registrant's Questionnaire 

When a man registered with Selective Service no specific opportunity was given him to indicate conscientious objection. However, the Questionnaire (DSS Form 40) which the System usually had him prepare shortly after registration provided a means whereby he could make such position known. This form always constituted the first official request for information upon which to base a registrant's classification. The part of the questionnaire referring to conscientious objection was found on page 6 and in the last version of the form used by Selective Service, prescribed January 31, 1942, it read as follows: 

SERIES X. CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION TO WAR 

Instructions.—Any registrant who, by reason of religious training and belief, is conscientiously opposed to participation in war in any form shall sign the statement below requesting a special form of conscientious objector (Form 47) from the local board which must be completed and returned to the local board for consideration.

By reason of religious training and belief I am conscientiously opposed to war in any form and for this reason request that the local board furnish me a special form for conscientious objector (Form 47) which I am to complete and return to the local board. 

Three earlier editions of Form 40 contained a slightly different wording. In the first edition, prescribed September 24, 1940, the registrant was asked to indicate whether he was opposed to combatant military service or to noncombatant military service. The second edition was prescribed January 3, 1941 and the third May 26, 1941. They did not include other than minor changes in series X.¹ 

The Special Form for Conscientious Objector (DSS Form 47),² re ferred to in the questionnaire, consisted of four pages and gave the registrant an opportunity to specify a claim of exemption from combatant training and service or one of complete exemption from all military or naval training and service and in the event of the latter to request assignment to work of national importance under civilian direction. The Form 47 provided information on religious training and beliefs, general background and participation in different organizations. Additional provision was made for references and the regis- 

1 Appendix F, Item No. 83. 

2 Appendix F, Item Nos. 86 and 87.

THE OBJECTOR WHO PERFORMED NONCOMBATANT SERVICE . » 

107 trant was expected to support his claim by an affidavit. Form 47 is later discussed in more detail. 

The Routine Deferment of Many Objectors In the regular process of selection the conscientious objector was first considered for classification by his local board without any regard to his claim on DSS Form 47. If he qualified for exemption or deferment from service on the same grounds as any other registrant, that is, for legal, dependency or occupational reasons, he was so classified and no classification attention was given to his Form 47. In other words the local boards of the System were instructed by the general regulations of Selective Service to give consideration first to placing any registrant-conscientious objector or other in the classes provided for exempt and deferred persons. The man's board was to investigate and pass upon his claim of conscientious objection only if, but for such claim, he would become available for combatant training and service become eligible for physical examination by the armed forces and for induction if found qualified upon such examination. 

Class I-A-O 

In the event the local board did not find the conscientious objector eligible for exemption or deferment upon its first consideration of his case along with those of other registrants, it then moved to determine the validity of his conscientious objector claim. If the claim could not be substantiated, he was placed in Class I-A as available for combatant military or naval service. A substantiation of his claim, however, made him eligible for Class I-A-O, noncombatant service in the armed forces, provided his DSS Form 47 indicated his willingness to be assigned to that type of duty. Class I-A-O, then, was the classification used by the local board to designate the so-called conscientious cooperator, the objector who was found to be available for noncombatant service.

The general Selective Service Regulation dealing with this class was section 622.12 and read as follows in the final edition: 

Class I-A-O: Available for noncombatant military service; conscientious objector. In Class I-A-O shall be placed every registrant who would have been classified in Class I-A but for the fact that he has been found, by reason of religious training and belief, to be conscientiously opposed to combatant military service in which he might be ordered to take human life, but not conscientiously opposed to noncombatant military service in which he could contribute to the health, comfort, and preservation of others.

If the Class I-A-O registrant later passed his physical examination and was inducted for noncombatant service, the local board classified him I-C, member of the armed forces, which was the same classification as that applied to any other inducted registrant.

It will be noted that Class I-A-O was the regular one for service availability except that the letter "O" was added to signify that the registrant was an objector. During the time Selective Service operated under the first edition of its regulations, September 23, 1940, to February 1, 1942, conscientious objectors available for service were not given a separate classification, but the local board was instructed to place an "O" after "I-A” on all records, reports, orders, and other papers which mentioned the registrant by name. At the time of the publication of the second edition of the regulations, however, a distinct classification instead of just an identification, was provided, namely, Class I-A-0.³ Class IV-E 

In addition to the conscientious objector with the unsubstantiated claim who was placed in Class I-A and the one with the valid claim willing to perform noncombatant service who was put in I-A-O, there were two other types not exempted or deferred in the routine process of selection. One of these was the registrant determined to be available for service and having a valid claim whose Special Form for Conscientious Objector (DSS Form 47) indicated that his beliefs would permit him to accept only work of national importance under civilian direction. His local board designated him Class IV-E, available for such work. After qualification through physical examination he was assigned to duties of this nature and the board continued him in this classification. More will be said about this type in subse quent chapters. 

A Special Appeal Procedure 

The other type of objector not exempted or deferred in the regular process was the Class I-A, I-A-O or IV-E registrant who was not satisfied with such classification by his local board and decided to appeal it. For him Selective Service had a special procedure. If he appealed to the board of appeal and this unit upheld the local board classification, his case was referred to the Department of Justice. This was provided for by the act and implemented by the regulations (sec. 

627.25 of the second edition). When cases were so referred, a special 4

Then, but only then, was the objector subject to penalty for law violation if he did not accept the local board's classification. Succeeding chapters will likewise deal with this type of case. 

The Liberal Approach to Classification 

In the main the general procedure for the classification of conscientious objectors applied equally to all types of them. However, there was some tendency, among Selective Service local boards, when it came to distiguishing between Class I-A and Class I-A-O, to give the registrant claiming objection the benefit of any reasonable doubt by placing him in Class I-A-O. This tendency arose because for practical purposes the distinction between the two classes amounted mainly to a question of assignment within the armed forces after induction. 

The general feeling was that other things being equal it was advisable to give the man the type of assignment he requested. This would tend to make him a better soldier to the extent of the personal acceptability of his duty. There was never a time during the war when inducted men were not being needed for assignment to noncombatant work in considerable numbers. Hence, this liberality seemed a practical approach.

Selective Service Jurisdiction Over Classification 

It was the policy of the War Department to recognize that Selective Service had exclusive jurisdiction over the classification of all registrants and especially over those claiming conscientious objection. 

Where men were certified to an induction station by the System as being in Class I-A-O this classification was considered final. 

The procedure in this regard was for the local board to enter on a Delivery List (DSS Form 151) the name of each registrant who was being forwarded for induction. If he was in Class I-A-O that fact was stated after his name in the column of DSS Form 151 headed "Remarks." For each man listed as being forwarded there was likewise sent to the induction station his Report of Physical Examination and Induction (DSS Form 221) which also carried a notation regarding his classification. This was under section II, item 17, of DSS Form 

221 which read as follows: 

17. Determination of local board: (a) Registrant classified in class 

(b) Date of classification

In this connection, Instruction No. 1 for Form 221, as amended, 7/18/46; subject: Completion and distribution of Form 221, paragraph 

2, (b), (3) read:

(3) ITEM 17. No entry will be made in this item for registrants forwarded for preinduction physical examination.—A registrant's classification and the date of his classification will be entered under this item (a) for registrants classified in Class I-A or Class I-A-O immediately prior to the time the registrant is forwarded for induction * * * If the registrant has been denied a claim for classification in Class I-A-O or Class IV-E at any time, the local board shall enter opposite item 17 a statement to that effect. 

Thus the System and the War Department attempted to make sure that the objector's classification accompanied him for assignment purposes after his induction. However, it was provided further by the 

War Department that when inductees still claimed to be conscientious objectors to combatant duty, after having their claims denied by their local boards, they were to be questioned fully in this regard by a chaplain. Upon the recommendation of the chaplain, the Army reception center commander might assign such men to medical units, that is, to noncombatant service. This decision was one of assignment and not classification, though, and neither the records of the armed forces nor of the local board were ever amended to show reclassification from I-A to I-A-O. 

War Department Consideration of Inducted Objectors 

Inductees who had been placed in Class I-A-O by their local boards were assigned exclusively to medical training centers or to medical units or detachments. An assignment of this kind was based on the same principles used for the assignment of other inducted personnel. 

Once assigned, the conscientious objector was not transferred to combatant service except upon his own written request. 

On the other hand, inducted men not classified by Selective Service as I-A-O who still claimed religious scruples to combatant duty, might be reassigned from combatant units to medical units or installations, if in the opinion of a commanding officer who was authorized to transfer enlisted personnel, their claims were honest and warranted. However, the record in such event were not changed to show that the individual was an objector.

Within the Army, conscientious objectors were subject to all Army Regulations, including those on training and discipline with the exception of bearing arms or being trained in their use. The last directive of the War Department in this regard was paragraph 2 of Circular No. 160 issued June 4, 1946.5 

Once in a while the records sent by the local board to the induction station showed a conscientious objector with a valid claim in Class I-A rather than I-A-O. This error occasionally resulted in his misassignment to combatant training and service. Upon the man's later making representations to the National Headquarters of Selective 

Appendix C, Item No. 23.

THE OBJECTOR WHO PERFORMED NONCOMBATANT SERVICE >> 111 

Service, the information which he provided regarding such assignment was verified through the State Director with the local board of his jurisdiction. The erroneous assignment was thereupon called to the attention of The Adjutant General of the War Department which 

Department cooperated promptly in rectifying that mistake.

Presidential Definition of Noncombatant Service 

The 1940 law provided that the types of military or naval service to which noncombatants could be assigned would be defined by the 

President. Accordingly, on December 6, 1940, Executive Order 8606 (5 F. R. 488) was issued by President Franklin D. Roosevelt. It was entitled "Definitions of Noncombatant Training and Service." After citing the pertinent provisions of the act, the President declared that the following was noncombatant service: (1) service in any unit which was unarmed at all times, (2) service in the medical department wherever performed, and (3) service in any unit or installation the primary function of which did not require the use of arms in combat, provided the individual's assignment in such unit or installation did not require him to bear them or to be trained in their use. He further declared that noncombatant training consisted of training in all the military subjects except marksmanship, combat firing, target practice, and those subjects relating to the appointment of weapons. 

The War Department circularized this Executive Order in Bulletin 

No. 43, December 27, 1940, and then issued Circular No. 2 on January 

4, 1941, to implement it further." In turn, information regarding the issuance of this War Department circular was furnished with explanations to all local boards and other agencies of Selective Service through the medium of Local Board Memorandum No. 51, dated 

October 28, 1941.8

Restriction of Assignment to Medical Corps After the entry of the United States into World War II, it appeared advisable for the War Department to restrict the assignment of conscientious-objector personnel entirely to the Medical Corps. This part of the Army was most free at all times from having to bear arms. Its members operated during warfare under the protection of the international provisions adopted by the Geneva Conference.

The change in assignment policy was made by issuing War Department Circular No. 29 on January 25, 1943.

Entering the war meant a very great increase in the number of inductions and consequently in the number of objectors for noncombatant assignment. There would be battle casualties as well as more soldiers, and the Medical Corps must therefore grow. It needed personnel of the conscientious-objector type. In addition, these men were generally interested in the specific task of saving human life as opposed to its destruction through violence. Further, some of the forms of noncombatant service which had been defined by the President contributed directly to the resistance efforts of the Army. 

International Legal Status of Noncombatants

Mention has been made of the protection afforded the unarmed Medical Corps of the United States Army and the armies of other countries by the international provisions adopted at the Geneva Conference. In consequence, a brief statement on the legal status of noncombatants in international warfare may be of interest. The term "noncombatant" is used in two different senses by international military law. It is applied both to the unarmed inhabitants of an invaded country and to those members of the armed forces of a belligerent country who are nonfighters. Article III of the Hague Conferences of 1899 and 1907 specifies that "The armed forces of the belligerent parties may consist of combatant and noncombatants." " 

J. M. Spaight, authority on international military law, says that noncombatants form that part of the armed forces "whose function is ancillary to that of the fighting men and who do not themselves oppose the enemy arms in hand. The troops of the commissariat and intendance, of the veterinary service, of the pay and accounting department, and orderlies, clerks, and bandsmen, are noncombatants in the sense of article III. So, too, are the medical personnel and army chaplains, who, however, are further protected by the Geneva Convention." "10 The Geneva Convention of 1864 made provisions that "have developed into an organized system of protection and immunity for all the personnel of recognized religious, medical, and nursing service." 11

Personal Safety Not the Concern of Objectors 

It is in no wise intended to imply here that American conscientious cooperators who engaged in noncombatant service during World War II did so to seek personal safety. The present purpose is merely to 

J. M. Spaight, War Rights on Land (London: Macmillan & Co., 1911), p. 34. 

10 Ibid., p. 58.

T. J. Lawrence, The Principles of International Law (6th ed., N. Y.: D. C. Heath, 1915), p. 421-2.

THE OBJECTOR WHO PERFORMED NONCOMBATANT SERVICE » 113 

point out that wherein the Geneva Conventions were honored and observed, medical units became the only ones in the Army where the conscientious objector could reasonably be guaranteed freedom from the necessity of being armed and trained in the use of arms. 

This general immunity from attack granted only to medical and religious personnel had its beginning in 1190. Before this time to be plundered and killed was the usual lot of the wounded on the field of battle. At the siege of Acre, during the Third Crusade, the order of 

Teutonic Knights was founded to tend the wounded. For some centuries after this the task of caring for the wounded was left to private and ecclesiastical benevolence. Then, in the seventeenth century, countries began to send a small number of surgeons and chaplains and a few field hospital units along with their armies. 

The distinctive international sign of humanitarian and noncombatant service in time of war is now a red cross on a white background, although Turkey uses a red crescent and Iran a lion and red sun. This emblem was adopted in 1864 as a compliment to Switzerland for taking the lead in calling the first conference of 12 countries in that year on medical services in the armed forces. The conference article reminded the Moslem countries that the adoption of this sign had no religious significance:

As a compliment to Switzerland, the heraldic emblem of the red cross on a white ground, formed by reversing the federal colours, is retained as the emblem and distinctive sign of the medical services of armies." 

The Medical Corps of the American armed forces as well as those of other countries display the red cross emblem conspicuously at all times.

The Willing Service of I-A-O Men 

Class I-A-O objectors apparently fitted well into the units to which they were assigned during World War II. In fact upon inquiry the 

Surgeon General of the Army said that any question of their service as such had never been brought to his attention. The commandant of a large Army medical center stated that although hundreds of these men were received in his training center "only those who refused to do anything were brought to my attention." He said that he would judge that there were not over 10 in that category during a period of almost three years.

Conscientious Objectors in the Navy Much reference has been made to the War Department and the Army as regards the assignment of conscientious objectors to noncombatant service, but thus far nothing has been said about the Navy 

12 Spaight, op cit., p. 454.

Department in this connection. The Navy, however, did not figure in such assignments until February 1943. Prior to that month this branch of the armed forces placed no calls for inductees upon the Selective Service System. Neither the Navy nor the Army accepted an avowed conscientious objector of any kind for voluntary enlistment. 

They only received this type of personnel through induction. 

Furthermore, the Navy generally viewed as problematical the acceptance of Class I-A-O inductees for the reason that in time of battle all of the men serving on a ship had special assignments for combatant duty. Even members of the medical corps were assigned to ammunition stations when not actually engaged at dressing stations. Nevertheless some I-A-O men were accepted for assignment to shore bases, construction work, and medical duties. The total number of conscientious objectors in the Navy was very small, however, although the quality of their service according to Navy informants did not differ from that of other personnel assigned to similar duties. 

The Discharge of Noncombatant Personnel 

When it came to the matter of discharge from the armed forces, the Class I-O-A men received exactly the same consideration as others who had served. No provisions were made either by the War or the Navy Department for their being handled in any different manner. In addition, there were no provisions made, in connection with their separation papers, for special notation of the fact that they were conscientious objectors. 

High Honors for Some Noncombatants

It is known that at least one conscientious objector received a Congressional Medal of Honor and the American Legion in his native city made him a life member. It is said that the members of his infantry division on Okinawa regarded him as their most courageous comrade, who stayed alone on a high and bitterly contested escarpment from which his companions had been driven. At various times during his service he was able to remove from the battlefield a total of 75 wounded men who without proper medical attention faced almost certain death. 

Another case just as outstanding was an objector who claimed objection to any armed service and was assigned to civilian work. Later he requested induction for noncombatant duty with the Army and a month following that he applied for combatant service. Before the end of the war he had been awarded the Purple Heart, Croix de Guerre, and Good Conduct decorations.

Digest Thus the objector whose conscience was opposed only to combatant duty in the armed forces made his contribution to the American effort

THE OBJECTOR WHO PERFORMED NONCOMBATANT SERVICE » 115 

during World War II. His belief would not permit him to cooperate in the degree of accepting combatant training and service like the vast majority of inducted Selective Service registrants, but his record otherwise was such that he became known as the "conscientious cooperator." 

Conscientious objectors who performed noncombatant duty totaled some 25,000 over the 612 years of the System's operation. Eventually some of them through rationalization of conscience and interest in the security of the United States applied for combatant service in the Army. On the other hand a few sought release to do work of national importance. In all three instances they were, of course, abiding by section 5 (g) of the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940, as amended, wherein were contained the provisions for conscientious objection.

Most objectors of this type performed noncombatant duty with the Army. They were assigned either to a medical training center or a medical unit or detachment which branch of the service was the freest from bearing arms and was protected in warfare as such by the international agreements of the Geneva Conference. This type of noncombatant duty was among those defined by the President in accordance with the 1940 law. Since the armed forces needed Medical Corps staff and the conscientious objector was interested in saving not destroying human life, his noncombatant duties were mutually agreeable and his service thereby of great value during the battle activities of 

World War II.

VII THE OBJECTOR WHO DID WORK OF NATIONAL IMPORTANCE 

As already indicated, conscientious objectors whose beliefs would not permit them to serve in the armed forces (Class IV-E registrants) were less numerous during World War II than those who felt that they could perform noncombatant duty with the Army or Navy (Class I-A-O men). Nevertheless registrants opposed to any kind of service with military or naval organizations constituted a major problem for Selective Service even though their numbers were small. The basic law and the regulations of the System, in accordance with the general attitude of the United States resulting from long familiarity with the backgrounds and problems of objection, provided that such individuals during the national emergency of 1940-47 must serve in work of national importance under civilian direction. The purpose of this chapter is to detail the manner in which the man liable for duty but averse to induction into the armed forces even for noncombatant service, was registered and classified IV-E and then assigned to civilian work.

Conscientious Objectors in Work of National Importance The best available figures indicate that from the beginning of the 

Selective Service program in 1940 a total of 11,887 Class IV-E regis trants served as assignees to work of national importance in the Civilian Public Service Camps of the country. They did not "conscientiously cooperate" as did the Class I-A-O men by accepting combatant service but they did give limited cooperation of another type. Additionally it was reported by the Department of Justice that 1,624 men were convicted from October 16, 1940 to June 30, 1946, as failing to report for such work. This made a total of 13,511 individuals classified by the local boards of the System as objectors to military or naval service and given valid and final assignment orders for civilian work. In comparison with the men serving in the armed forces during the war, this was a ratio of slightly less than one to 1,000. 117

The Problem of the Complete Objector 

The 1,624 convicted persons mentioned above were opposed to both noncombatant duty and civilian work-to any and all kinds of service. 

Thus their objection was absolute or complete and they were entirely uncooperative, which constituted a violation under the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940, as amended. In addition to the enforcement problem created by this noncooperation, it was also problematical for the reason that matters of personal conscience and religion were difficult to determine. It also presented difficulties in that some registrants asserting a "tender conscience" toward war, were touchy to the point of contentiousness and a peculiar kind of belligerency. 

Fortunately, such registrants constituted but a minority of this very small group of complete objectors. Further treatment of them will appear later.

Registration and the Preparation of Questionnaires In the operations of the System the specific provisions for conscientious objection which were contained in section 5 (g) of the Selective Service Act of 1940 were integrated with the other procurement provisions of the law. That is, the conscientious objector was handled like any other registrant, except to the extent provided in section 5 (g). In the matter of registration, for instance, no exceptions or special arrangements were made for objectors. The registrant's answers to certain questions were written by a registrar on the front of a Registration Card (DSS Form 1). On the reverse side of the form some characteristics of the man's appearance were also noted by the registrar whereupon the registrant read and signed the card or made his mark. The registrar then made out a Registration Certificate (DSS Form 2) attesting to the fact of registration and gave it to the individual. Neither of these cards provided for the recording of conscientious objection. Some registrants wrote on one or both of the forms that they were objectors. This served no practical purpose for Selective Service but the System made no particular objection to its being done.¹

It has been mentioned that every registrant was required to fill out a Selective Service Questionnaire (DSS Form 40) as the basis for classification by his local board. "Series X" of this form provided special coverage for conscientious objection as has been seen.

THE OBJECTOR WHO DID WORK OF NATIONAL IMPORTANCE » 119 Special Form for Conscientious Objector (DSS Form 47) 

The signing of series X by the registrant constituted a request that the local board furnished him with a Special Form for Conscientious Objector (DSS Form 47) to use in substantiating his claim of exemption either from combatant service or from all military or naval duty. 

The Form 47 was to be returned to the local board within 5 days of its receipt by the registrant. It was provided for by section 621.3 of the general regulations which read as follows: 

621.3. Special form for conscientious objector.-A registrant who claims to be a conscientious objector shall offer information in substantiation of his claim on a Special Form for Conscientious Objectors (Form 47) which, when filed, shall become a part of his Selective Service Questionnaire (Form 40). The local board, upon request, shall furnish to any person claiming to be a conscientious objector a copy of such Special Form for Conscientious Objector (Form 47).* 

Form 47 was an extremely important document in cases of conscientious objection. It became the basis for Selective Service classification by the local board if the man was not routinely exempted or deferred from training and service in Class IV, III, or II during the regular classification and selection process for all registrants. The objector was not limited to this form, however, in presenting claimant information. Not only was it specifically stated that extra sheets of paper might be attached to Form 47 if more space was needed, but registrants in general were encouraged to file any additional information which they deemed pertinent. 

The general heading of Form 47 showed the registrant's order number, his name and address, the stamp of his local board, and the date upon which it must be returned to the board. The following stipulations were then made:

INSTRUCTIONS 

A registrant who claims to be a conscientious objector shall offer information in substantiation of his claim on this special form, which when filed shall become a part of his Questionnaire. 

The questions in series II through V in this form are intended to obtain evidence of the genuineness of the claim made in series I, and the answers given by the registrant shall be for the information only of the officials duly authorized under the regulations to examine them. 

In the case of any registrant who claims to be a conscientious objector, the local board shall proceed in the ordinary course to consider all grounds of deferment before passing upon his claim to be a conscientious objector. The procedure for appeal from a decision of the local board on a claim for conscientious objection is provided for in the Selective Service Regulations.

There followed five parts, entitled "Series I-V," each with lined spaces for the entry of information. 

Form 47 Requirement for Claim to be Specific

In series I, claim for exemption, of Form 47, the registrant was offered two statements, A and B. He was instructed to sign either but not both. By signing statement A, he indicated that he was a conscientious cooperator, willing to serve in a noncombatant capacity in the armed forces. But by signing statement B, he showed that he was willing only to be assigned to work of national importance under civilian direction in lieu of induction into the land or naval forces. 

Statement A read as follows: 

A. I am, by reason of my religious training and belief, conscientiously opposed to participation in war in any form. 

I, therefore, claim exemption from combatant training and service. I understand that if my claim is sustained I will be inducted into the land or naval forces, but will be assigned to noncombatant service as defined by the President. 

Statement B was: 

B. I am, by reason of my religious training and belief, conscientiously opposed to participation in war in any form and I am further conscientiously opposed to participation in noncombatant service in the land or naval forces. I, therefore, claim exemption from combatant training and service and if my claim is sustained, I believe that in lieu of induction into the land or naval forces, I should, because of any conscientious objection to noncombatant service in the land or naval forces, be assigned to work of national importance under civilian direction.

Explanation of Beliefs on Form 47 

Series II, religious training and beliefs, was at once the most personal and important part of the Form 47. In it the registrant was asked to explain the nature and source of his belief. He was asked to name the person on whom he relied most for religious guidance. Then a blank was provided for a brief discussion of his belief regarding the use of force. Finally, he was offered an opportunity to set down instances of personal action and behavior or public expression which he thought demonstrated the sincerity of his claim. 

Reporting of Background, Organizations and References 

Series III, general background, of Form 47 provided space for detailed information regarding the man's education, occupations, residences, and parentage.

THE OBJECTOR WHO DID WORK OF NATIONAL IMPORTANCE » 

121 Series IV, participation in organizations, afforded opportunity for listing the names of organizations in whose activities the individual had participated. First, he was asked to tell of any membership in military organizations or establishments. Then detailed information was requested regarding his religious affiliation. Finally, there was a request for information regarding any organizational membership, not religious or military.

Series V, references, provided space for identifying persons who could supply information regarding the sincerity of the man's professed convictions regarding war.

Following this information, the form provided space for signature and an oath or affirmation witness.
