It was not even necessary to give a reason for the appeal or to advance arguments regarding the matter, although this was permissible. Nor was there need to specify what classification was thought to be more equitable. 

Any person claiming to be a dependent of a registrant or any person having filed written evidence of the occupational status of a registrant, might appeal. But any such appeal, including that taken by the registrant himself, was required to be made within 10 days after the date the local board mailed the Notice of Classification (DSS Form 57). An extension of this appeal time might be granted, however, for sufficient reasons under most circumstances.

The appeal agent of a local board had the right of taking an appeal in the case of any registrant. The Director of Selective Service and the State Directors of Selective Service also had very broad appeal rights with respect to individual cases.

Special Consideration for C. O.'s on Appeal 

The conscientious objector provisions of section 5 (g) in the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940, which established a special appeal procedure for Class IV-E, I-A-O or I-A objectors, were implemented by section 627.25 of the general regulations which, in 1944 and later, read as follows: 

627.25. Special provisions where appeal involves claim that registrant is a conscientious objector.—(a) If an appeal involves the question of whether or not a registrant is entitled to be sustained in his claim that he is a conscientious objector, the board of appeal shall take the following action: (1) First determine whether the registrant should be classified in one of the classes set forth in section 623.21 in the order set forth except Class IV-F for physical or mental disability and, if it so determines, it shall place the registrant in such class; or (2) If it determines that the registrant should not be classified in one of the classes set forth in section 623.21 and the registrant has claimed classification in Class IV-E, determine whether to place the registrant in such class, and if it so determines, it shall place the registrant in Class 

IV-E; or 

(3) If it determines that the registrant should not be classified in one of the classes set forth in section 623.21 and the registrant has not claimed classification in Class IV-E but has claimed classification in Class I-A-O, determine whether to place the registrant in such class and, if it so determines, it shall place the registrant in Class I-A-O; or (4) If it determines not to place such registrant in one of the classes set forth in section 623.21 or in Class IV-E or in Class I-A-O under the circum stances set forth in subparagraphs (1), (2), or (3) above, it shall transmit the entire file to the United States Attorney for the judicial district in which the office of the board of appeal is located for the purpose of securing an advisory recommendation from the Department of Justice.

THE OBJECTOR WHO DID WORK OF NATIONAL IMPORTANCE » 125 

No registrant's file shall be forwarded to the United States Attorney by any board of appeal, and any file so forwarded shall be returned, unless in the "Minutes of other actions" on the Selective Service Questionnaire (Form 40) the record shows and the letter of transmittal states that the board of appeal reviewed the file and determined that the registrant should not be classified in one of the classes set forth in section 623.21 (except Class IV-F for physical or mental disability) or in Class IV-E or Class I-A-O under the circumstances set forth in subparagraphs (1), (2), or (3) above. (b) The Department of Justice shall thereupon make an inquiry and hold a hearing of the character and good faith of the conscientious objections of the registrant. The registrant shall be notified of the time and place of such hearing and shall have an opportunity to be heard. If the objections of the registrant are found to be sustained, the Department of Justice shall recommend to the board of appeal (1) that if the registrant is inducted into the land or naval forces, he shall be assigned to noncombatant service, or (2) that if the registrant is found to be conscientiously opposed to participation in such noncombatant service, he shall be assigned to work of national importance under civilian direction. If the Department of Justice finds that the objections of the registrant are not sustained, it shall recommend to the board of appeal that such objections be not sustained. (0) Upon receipt of the report of the Department of Justice, the board of appeal shall determine the classification of the registrant, and in its determination it shall give consideration to, but it shall not be bound to follow, the recommendation of the Department of Justice. The board of appeal shall place in the Cover Sheet (Form 53) of the registrant both the letter containing the recommendation of the Department of Justice and the report of the hearing officer of the Department of Justice.10

When the regulations were first promulgated it was provided that if a board of appeal classified a man claiming to be a conscientious objector in a deferred or exempt classification, Class IV, III or II, the file could be returned to the local board of origin without forwarding the case to the United States attorney for a recommendation on the objection claim. Otherwise, the board of appeal would refer the claim to the Department of Justice for advisory recommendation. 

On December 15, 1942, it was additionally provided that in a case where the local board had classified the registrant in IV-E or in a case where the registrant had claimed objection to combatant service only and the local board had classified him I-A-O, the board of appeal might affirm the classification of the local board without referring the case to the Department of Justice. Still later, on October 27, 1943, it was provided that if the registrant claimed classification in Class IV-E or I-A-O, the board of appeal might classify the registrant in accordance with his claim without forwarding the case

It relieved the Department of considerable unnecessary work and also expedited the operation of the System. As it was, more than 12,000 of what may be termed the more questionable cases of conscientious objection, were investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation of the 

Department of Justice. 

Cases Handled by the Department of Justice 

However, if the board of appeal did not place the objector making the appeal in an exempt or deferred class (IV, III, or II), or classify him according to his claim, the procedure was as explained by Mr. 

Joseph C. Duggan, who handled much of this work for the Department of Justice from the beginning of Selective Service to June 1945: 

If it determines not to classify the registrant in any of the deferred classes, and is of the opinion that the registrant is not entitled to a conscientious objector classification (or desires an advisory opinion before considering the conscientious objector claim), the board of appeal may not affirm the local board classification in Class I-A without referring the case to the Department of Justice for investigation and hearing on the conscientious objector claim. 

Reference to the Department of Justice pursuant to section 5 (g) of the act and section 627.25 (a) (4) of the regulations is effected by transmitting the file to the United States Attorney for the Federal judicial district in which the board of appeal is located. The United States Attorney thereupon examines the file to determine whether the Department of Justice has jurisdiction and, if he so determines, the file is transmitted to the nearest field office of the Federal Bureau of Investigation. The investigation in this type of case is an inquiry into the character of the registrant, and is undertaken to determine whether he has the religious training and belief required by the statute, whether he is sincere, and whether his daily conduct is consistent with his professed claim for exemption as a conscientious objector.

Upon completion of such inquiry, the registrant's file and the investigative report are then transmitted to a Special Assistant to the Attorney General designated as hearing officer under section 5 (g) of the Selective Service Act. 

The hearing officer thereupon issues a "notice of hearing" to the registrant and furnishes him with a copy of the instructions governing the conduct of the hearing. The notice of hearing allows the registrant 10 days in which to appear, and informs him that he may bring any witnesses or documentary evidence to the hearing in order to substantiate his claim. The hearing officer has no power of subpena and the appearance of the registrant is entirely voluntary. While no exact counterpart of the hearing officer is known to the 

System, he is a quasi-judicial officer who acts in a capacity analagous to that of a trial examiner.

After concluding the hearing, the hearing officer prepares a report in triplicate in which he makes a recommendation to the Department of Justice. This report containing findings and conclusions of law, together with his recommendations relative to the registrant's classification is transmitted to the office of the Assistant to the Attorney General in the Department at Washington for examination and review.

THE OBJECTOR WHO DID WORK OF NATIONAL IMPORTANCE » 127 

It is possible that the report may be returned to the hearing officer with a memorandum of disagreement from the Department. If, however, the Department concurs in the findings of the hearing officer, it proceeds to make a recommendation to the Board of Appeal from which the case originated. This recommendation is generally made by adopting, approving, and concurring in the advisory recommendation of the hearing officer to the Department. Upon return of the file, together with a recommendation to the board of appeal, the administrative function of the Department in conscientious objector cases is complete." 

Appeal to the President 

Still another opportunity, an appeal to the President, was offered to the Class IV-E, I-A-O or I-A registrant who had claimed the right accorded a conscientious objector, but whose claim had not been sustained either by the Selective Service local board or by the System's board of appeal. This was the usual appeal to the President and was the same right accorded any other registrant. However, such right was available only if one or more members of the board of appeal dissented from the classification given. An appeal to the President could be made by the registrant, any person who claimed to be a dependent of his or any person who had filed written information as to his occupational status, at any time within 10 days after the mailing by the local board of the Notice of Classification (DSS Form 57) informing the registrant that the local board classification had been affirmed or changed by the board of appeal. The local board under certain circumstances might permit a person such an appeal even though the 10-day period had elapsed. 

An appeal to the President might also be made by a State Director of Selective Service or by the Director of Selective Service. Such an appeal by a State Director or by the Director was usually taken after special or unofficial requests for action were received from a registrant or from an organization representing the registrant, for instance, the National Service Board for Religious Objectors. Ordinarily an appeal to the President which originated with a director of the System was taken for the purpose of making certain that there was uniform action throughout the State or the Nation. 

In addition, it was taken only when such action appeared necessary in the national interest or to avoid an injustice. Regarding Presidential appeals, mention should be made here that the President delegated this responsibility to the Director of Selective Service who set up a Presidential Appeal Board at National Headquarters to act as the classifying agency in this regard.

Classification Always Subject to Change 

No Selective Service classification was permanent. This held for all registrants including conscientious objectors. The regulations stated that each classified man and each person who had filed a request for the registrant's deferment, should report in writing any fact that might result in the registrant being placed in a different class. The local board was to keep itself currently informed of the status of classified men, and they might be questioned or given physical or mental examinations by the board or upon the order of the board. 

Employers, Government agencies, and individuals might be required to furnish such information.

It was provided that the local board might reopen and consider anew the classification of a registrant upon his written request or that of certain other parties, if there were written information presenting facts not considered when he was classified previously but which might now justify a classification change. Such action could be taken by the board after a man had been ordered to report for service only if it first specifically found there had been a change in the registrant's status resulting from circumstances over which he had no control. 

This prohibition did not apply to a State Director of Selective Service nor to the Director of Selective Service, however. The board was required to reopen and consider anew the classification of a registrant upon the written request of a State Director or the Director. Upon the receipt of such a request it was to cancel immediately any outstanding order to report, except that after a registrant had left the local board for delivery pursuant to an Order to 

Report for Work of National Importance (DSS Form 50) the board was to reopen and consider anew the classification of the registrant only upon written request by the Director to that specific effect.12

The Physical Examination of Objectors 

Conscientious objectors to all military or naval service (Class IV-E men) were given the same type of physical examination as any other registrant. This was done chiefly in the interest of uniform physical standards. The pertinent provisions of the general regulations in such regard are found in section 629.2 (c) and (d) and in 1944 read as follows: 

(c) The local board shall also mail an Order to Report-Preinduction Physical 

Examination (Form 215) to each registrant classified in Class IV-E when his order number is reached (without regard to whether he has requested or will request a personal appearance before the local board and without regard to whether an appeal has been or will be taken) in the process of ordering Class

129 1 I-A and Class I-A-O registrants to report for preinduction physical examination under the provisions of paragraph (b) of this section." 

During the early operation of Selective Service the local board secured through local physicians an examination for each assignee to work of national importance. In spite of this, some assignees arrived at Civilian Public Service Camps with defects which disqualified them for work. It therefore became necessary, after the assignee arrived in camp, to order him before a medical advisory board for reexamination. If this examination showed him disqualified for service, he was released from the camp. Such procedure was expensive for the Government and also dislocated the assignee in his civilian pursuits. In addition, there still remained in some camps numbers of men who apparently did not qualify physically. As a result, National Headquarters eventually sent a medical officer into each Civilian Public Service Camp for the purpose of giving an on-theground examination to those men who appeared to have physical disabilities. Further discharges were then made upon the recommendation of this officer.

In previously discussing section 622.51 (a) of the general regulations on the classification of conscientious objectors in IV-E it was pointed out that the original Selective Service provisions for such action permitted the man to be placed in Class IV-E after physical examination by the local board. This local examination later came to be commonly known as a "screening examination" and it was given to all registrants alike. Upon classification, after this physical examination, the Class I-A and I-A-O registrants were to be forwarded to an induction station for examination and admission to the armed forces and Class IV-E registrants were to be assigned to work of national importance. No specific provision was made at that time for a second physical examination for Class IV-E registrants comparable to that given to Class I-A and I-A-O registrants at the induction station. However, when the second edition of the regulations was promulgated on February 1, 1942, it contained part 651, determination of acceptability of persons for work of national importance under civilian direction, and provided for a supplementary or second examination. Then on December 5, 1943, any registrant, including the objector, was allowed by Public Law 197 (78th Cong., 1st Sess.) to request and receive a preinduction physical examination when his induction or assignment seemed imminent.

A Certificate of Fitness for the Objector 

After passing a preinduction examination, the objector received a Certificate of Fitness (DSS Form 218) indicating his acceptability for service. The terminology used on this certificate referred to military or naval service. The use of such terminology was a practical guarantee to the man seeking civilian duty that he had received the same type of physical examination as that given to registrants considered for induction into the armed forces. The local board was required to mail the original of this certificate to the objector immediately after his physical examination whether he was in Class IV-E I-A-O or I-A. 

Army Discharge for Assignment to Civilian Work The provisions of section 622.51 (b), quoted above, were promulgated as a result of a special agreement made May 17, 1944, between 

Undersecretary of War Robert Patterson and the Director of Selective 

Service. This agreement provided that War Department general prisoners who claimed to be conscientious objectors and who had been convicted only of offenses involving a refusal to participate in military service, including unauthorized absence and desertion, might make an application in writing for discharge other than honorable from the Army (blue certificate) and for assignment to work of national importance under civilian direction. 

Upon transmittal of the soldier's request to the National Headquarters of Selective Service, his local board file and any other pertinent available material were procured and examined. After studying the file, the Director recommended approval or disapproval of the request to the Adjutant General of the War Department. If, upon receiving a recommendation of approval, the War Department decided to discharge the soldier, the Director when notified to this effect by the Adjutant General, took steps to have the man placed in Class IV-E by his local board. The registrant was then processed for assignment to a Civilian Public Service Camp in much the same manner as any other Class IV-E registrant, except that he was ordered to report for work of national importance through the local board nearest to the disciplinary barracks where he was in confinement. In addition, the War Department kept him in custody until the System completed arrangements for his reporting to camp and until he could be sent to camp immediately upon his release from the barracks. 

Not many cases of this kind were referred to Selective Service by the War Department during the latter months of operation and, as far as is known, no soldier was released from the Army for the purpose of being assigned to work of national importance in a Civilian Public Service Camp except where he had been court martialed pre-

Abstract 

In such fashion, then, Selective Service registrants whose consciences would not allow them to perform either combatant or noncombatant service in the armed forces of the United States during World War II, were processed through the local boards of the System for assignment to work of national importance under civilian direction. 

Their beliefs did not permit them to cooperate in the national emergency of 1940-47 to the extent of men who were inducted for combatant duty or objectors who accepted induction for noncombatant service. Nevertheless, their participation in civilian work met the requirements of the conscientious objector provisions (sec. 5 (g)) in the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940, as amended, and their contribution to the American effort in this capacity was generally useful and often exceptionally so. 

The objectors who did work of national importance from 1940 to 1947 numbered almost 12,000. This amounted to a ratio of but one in 

1,000 when compared to the total number of men serving in the armed forces during that period. Although the registrants in civilian work were but half as numerous as those accepting noncombatant duty and their approach to the problem of violating conscience was some different, they were nevertheless classified by Selective Service in the same manner as the noncombatant person or for that matter any other individual registered with the System. The only classification departure for this type of objector was that provided for appeal by the 1940 law.

The man whose faith caused him to accept only assignment to civilian work, registered and prepared his Selective Service Question-

Like the noncombatant person he then prepared a Special Form for Conscientious Objector (DSS Form 47) to substantiate his claim in detail. He was first considered for classification on the basis of the Form 40 without reference to his objection claim, just as was the noncombatant claimant, and if placed in Class IV, III, or II, as not available for training and service, no classification attention was given to his Form 47. If considered available, however, and his objection claim was found valid by the local board, the board placed him in Class IV-E, available for assignment to work of national importance, which was different from the Class I-A-O, available for assignment to noncombatant service in the armed forces, given to the other type of objector. In the event his claim was not substantiated by the board he was put in Class I-A-O or even I-A, available for combatant duty. 

When the registrant did not agree with his classification he could very easily and readily appeal it to his board of appeal. If that unit would not exempt or defer him, or honor his claim, it referred his case to the Department of Justice for investigation, hearing, and recommendation. After such action if the classification was still IV-E and the registrant did not accept assignment to civilian work he was a violator of the Selective Service Act. 

In preparation for a civilian work assignment, the Class IV-E man was given exactly the same physical examination as the Class I-A-O or I-A registrant and the results noted on his Report of Physical Examination and Induction (DSS Form 221). If he qualified for such assignment, he was issued a Certificate of Fitness (DSS Form 

218). A Conscientious Objector Report (DSS Form 48) and his Form 

221 were mailed from the local board through State Headquarters to National Headquarters in order that his actual assignment to a Civilian Public Service Camp could be made. National Headquarters did this in conjunction with the department of the Federal Government mainly concerned with the work of the particular camp. It then forwarded an Assignment to Work of National Importance (DSS Form 49) to the local board which in turn sent the IV-E registrant an 

Order to Report for Work of National Importance (DSS Form 50). 

It is interesting to note that some objectors in Civilian Public Service Camps eventually applied for induction for combatant or noncombatant service in the armed forces. From time to time also some who went to prison rather than serve in the camps, later requested parole and assignment to civilian work. In both instances the voluntary action of the registrant significantly increased his contribution to the general effort of his country during a period of great emergency.

VIII GENERAL PRINCIPLES AND POLICIES OF OBJECTOR CLASSIFICATION 

The classification of conscientious objectors by Selective Service during its operation of 1940-47 has been discussed specifically for registrants in Class I-A-O, available for noncombatant service in the armed forces, and in Class IV-E, available for work of national importance under civilian direction. It is also of significance to discuss the main precepts of the System which formed the basis for such classification and selection. Likewise important are the relationships of these fundamentals to the Selective Service Regulations; the Selective 

Training and Service Act of 1940, as amended; the American history and the church backgrounds of conscientious objection; and the underlying philosophy of the System-service by all liable men so selected, but such duty within the dictates of conscience. 

Two Proposals for Classifying Objectors 

As already pointed out two ideas, or principles, regarding the Selective Service classification of conscientious objector registrants were in conflict when the conference committee of the United States Congress in 1940 came to harmonize the differences between the Senate and the House versions of the Burke-Wadsworth conscription bill. Both legislative bodies had provided in their versions of the bill that special hearings be held in connection with the classification of each person claiming to be an objector. The Senate following largely the request of certain church groups, had provided that such hearings be conducted by the Department of Justice; for this the House had substituted hearings by the local boards of the System. 

Experience has shown the value of the compromise finally agreed upon whereby the local board first classified the objector the same as any other registrant without the requirement for a hearing. Then, if an appeal was taken, there was provision for an inquiry, hearing and recommendation by the Department of Justice. Thus the Department of Justice was relieved of handling cases where the local board and the registrant were in agreement on classification, a situation which prevailed for a decided majority of objectors. 135

General Acceptance of Local Board Classification 

The fact that this agreement was achieved between Selective Service and the conscientious objector in a large proportion of cases was to the great credit of both local board members and objectors. Figures to be presented in detail later show that over 50,000 registrants were classified I-A-0 or IV-E. Other partially incomplete records indicate 5,438 men as having been placed in these classes by boards of appeal or through an appeal to the President. On the basis of this information it would appear that nearly ninety per cent of the registrants classified as conscientious objectors received such classification at the hands of their own local boards.

Thus the originally proposed plan of having the Department of Justice hold hearings and make recommendations for all men claiming conscientious objection would have constituted an unnecessary procedure. In addition had the Department been required to conduct hearings on all of these cases, it would have been charged with a burdensome responsibility. As it was the Department found necessary the handling of between twelve and thirteen thousand cases. 

Difficult Cases 

Even though classification by the local board was accepted in a great majority of the objector cases, there was considerable disagreement over the remaining small number. Religious and other groups representing those who claimed conscientious objection, usually wanted the System to be liberal in recognizing such claims. It is true under ordinary circumstances that they were willing for the claims of the insincere to be denied, but their interpretations of insincerity often varied widely from those of Selective Service. 

The issues were drawn when objector registrants who were not satisfied with their classifications, noted appeals to the boards of appeal. 

Seldom was an appeal taken when the local board classified a man in accordance with his claim. Although the Director of Selective 

Service, a State Director or another official of the System might disagree with the board's decision, it was usually his feeling that the interest of the Government in getting the classification changed would not justify the effort involved and the delay incident to such action. 

Local and Appeal Board Strictness 

On the whole, Selective Service local boards tended toward strictness in judging the validity of conscientious objector claims and making classifications of such registrants. There were perhaps two principal factors involved in this. The first was the quite natural and common tendency on the part of local board members to classify ac-

GENERAL PRINCIPLES AND POLICIES OF OBJECTOR CLASSIFICATION 

137 cording to their own feelings of fairness, justice, impartialness as enjoined by the 1940 law. If their action was the source of disagreement or regarded as unjust they would freely remind the registrant of his right to appeal. A second factor was that local board members were in close touch with the situations of their communities and the feeling of the great majority of people toward objector registrants was not too sympathetic, especially after America's entry into the war late in 1941. Added to both of these was the fact that many conscientious objectors assumed somewhat unreasonable, belligerent, or obnoxious attitudes toward their local board members. 

The System's boards of appeal on the other hand were removed in a measure from the local communities and were inclined to be more lenient with the registrant who was opposed to warfare and armed forces. In addition, the boards of appeal received the detailed analyses of cases which were made by the hearing officers of the Department of Justice and were provided, in most instances, with the Department's recommendations. Appeal board members very seldom knew or saw the registrants in question and their approach was therefore more impersonal.

The Liberality of Presidential Decisions 

Although the Presidential Appeal Board, which handled appeals to the President and was located at the National Headquarters of Selective Service, was frequently the target for attack by various religious groups because it was composed of military men, it actually proved to be the most liberal unit of Selective Service in granting conscientious objectors the classifications to which they felt entitled. 

These officials of the System had a very keen sense of their duty and obligations under the act. They operated under a rather liberal interpretation of the law and realizing that the Presidential Appeal Board was where final decisions were made, they conscientiously attempted to carry out this responsibility in moderation. Moreover, they were men of wide experience at handling major difficulties in classification policy.

The liberal approach of its members sometimes brought the Presidential Appeal Board under severe criticism from within Selective Service itself. Undoubtedly there were some objectors assigned to 

Civilian Public Service Camps who did not belong there, but it was doubtful whether they belonged in the noncombatant service of the armed forces either. On the other hand, some of the cases of worst behavior in Civilian Public Service Camps, assuming for the moment that this constituted a reason for their not belonging there, were those where the registrant was placed in Class IV-E by his local board and an appeal was never taken on such action.

« 

CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION 

To continue in this paradoxical direction, a considerable number of men who were placed in Class I-A after claiming classification in I-A-O or IV-E, and some who were classified I-A-O, would not accept the finality of their appeal decisions. They were therefore arrested, tried, and convicted for law violation in the civil courts and sentenced to prison terms. By being willing to serve prison terms in lieu of noncombatant duty or civilian work, it may be assumed that they proved the sincerity of their conscientious objection claims.

The Policy Effect of Wide Experience 

Over and above the experience which National Headquarters had in conscientious objector cases through the activities of the System's 

Presidential Appeal Board, its Camp Operations Division handled hundreds of cases and had intimate contact with many which involved special problems. This had a tremendous effect upon the over-all classification policies which were established for the classification of individuals averse to resistance and violence. While most local boards had but a few instances of objection there were a very large number of cases considered by National Headquarters over the 6½ years of the System's operation and their impact served to establish valuable patterns as guides to the Nation as a whole. 

Aside from the opportunity afforded to gain a more complete understanding of the conscientious objector through the handling of many cases, there was the fact that National Headquarters was the only unit of Selective Service permitted access to the Federal Bureau of Investigation reports on men claiming to be objectors. Such reports covered the lives and activities of objector registrants as they were investigated while their cases were before a board of appeal. Close contact with the prosecution of objectors who were law violators, the handling of objector parolee cases, and conferences with the War Department on disciplinary problems where the soldier claimed conscientious objection, also combined to influence the national policy on the objector and to incline it toward liberality. 

Another somewhat motivating factor in the development of liberal classification policies was that the Nation was engaged in an all-out war effort and that prior experience had shown the armed forces often impeded where overzealousness had forced men claiming objection into combatant service. Because of their sincerity many such men later developed into disciplinary cases while on duty. 

From another standpoint if the objector did not accept induction for combatant service, he became a delinquent, and the Nation lost not only the contribution he would have made as a noncombatant or civilian worker, but it also had to assume the added burden of his

GENERAL PRINCIPLES AND POLICIES OF OBJECTOR CLASSIFICATION >>> 139 

apprehension by the Department of Justice, his prosecution in the Federal courts and in the event of conviction his incarceration by the 

Bureau of Prisons. 

Dual Role of the Director on Presidential Appeals 

As regards the Presidential appeal of objector classifications, the Director of Selective Service had a dual function. In the first place, all appeals to the President were actually decided by the Director on a delegation of authority from the President and through applying the recommendations of the Presidential Appeal Board. In the second place, the Director exercised authority in any case to take an appeal either to a board of appeal or to the President. 

The authority for the Director of Selective Service to appeal classifications was a general authority not restricted to the cases of conscientious objectors, nor was it even restricted to classification actions. 

The Director might appeal from any determination of a local board or of a board of appeal. This authority was held also by State Directors of Selective Service and was specifically granted by Sections 

627.1 and 628.1 (a) of the general regulations: 

627.1. Appeal by Director and State Director.—(a) Either the Director of 

Selective Service or the State Director of Selective Service as to local boards in his State, may appeal from any determination of a local board. 

(b) Either the State Director of Selective Service or the Director of Selective 

Service may take such an appeal at any time.¹ 

628.1. Who may appeal to the President from any determination of a board of appeal.—(a) When either the State Director of Selective Service or the Director of Selective Service deems it to be in the national interest or necessary to avoid an injustice, he may appeal to the President from any determination of a board of appeal. He may take such an appeal at any time.' 

The National Service Board for Religious Objectors began early to bring to National Headquarters reports of alleged error in the classification of individual claimants of conscientious objection by local boards in various parts of the country. At that time, however, the 

Board was requested to send such communications direct to the appropriate State Headquarters. Later it was realized that, in connection with the consideration of cases brought to the Presidential Appeal Board through procedural appeal, it would also be well to have a section within National Headquarters to accept and process these nonprocedural appeals.

State Origination of Most Presidential Appeals 

The taking of objector classification appeals to the President by the Director and the State Directors became a procedure whereby a general uniformity of action could be achieved. National Headquarters always encouraged the taking of informal requests for appeal action to State Directors first of all, but it did not hesitate to proceed upon its own in the absence of action by State Directors when such was thought necessary. The prompt and frequent action of State Directors in this regard, however, resulted in the Director himself having to take very few appeals on conscientious objection to the President. 

Separate figures for conscientious objectors are not available, but up to September 1, 1945, State Directors initiated general appeal action in 44,774 of the total Presidential appeal cases as compared to only 

1,437 by the Director.

Special Procedure for Objector Delinquencies 

Because a considerable number of objector cases involving delinquency were found to have resulted from faulty classification procedure or to be contrary to national policy, it was finally deemed advisable to have all such cases reviewed in National Headquarters prior to their being reported to a United States attorney as law violations. Accordingly, late in the experience of the System, the regulations were changed and the new procedure made effective. 

However, it was not placed in operation due to the expiration of the 

Selective Service Act on March 31, 1947.8 

It was believed the adoption of this procedure would accomplish two things. First, it would insure more uniform treatment and obviate classification which was not in accordance with national policy. Second, it would enable Selective Service to assure the Department of Justice that the classification of a man referred for prosecution was accurate. 

General Considerations in Objector Classification

The question of the classification of difficult conscientious objector cases was usually resolved in the last analysis either on the question of whether the registrant came within the general purview of congressional exemption as a religious objector "to all war" or whether, in spite of being technically within the scope of the law, he was personally insincere. These two issues were closely related and interwoven. But a relatively clear distinction was usually possible from an exhaustive review of the facts in a given case, from giving great * As provided by Amendment No. 423 (12 F. R. 2126) to sec. 642.41 (a), effective March 

31, 1947 of the Selective Service Regulations, second edition (Washington: 1942, 1943, 1945). Sec. 642.41 was originally provided by Amendment No. 181 (8 F. R. 14115), effective November 1, 1943.

GENERAL PRINCIPLES AND POLICIES OF OBJECTOR CLASSIFICATION » 141 

weight to pertinent material on both current and previous actions and statements.

The Selective Training and Service Act of 1940 stated that a conscientious objector was one who was "opposed to participation in war in any form." From this was deducted the basic idea or concept of opposition "to all war" and the fundamental assumption that such objection would have been held in peacetime as well as in time of war. 

Consequently information on previous service in military or naval organizations, or on refusal to enroll when opportunity was specifically offered, as in school training units, constituted factual material of great value in considering and interpreting the objector's beliefs. 

The law stated further that such conscientious objection should be "by reason of religious training and belief." Positive data on training of this nature were often available and always valuable as contributory evidence. In considering the claims of conscientious objection, the 

System naturally started with the historically known basis for such claims and with the current expressions of individuals representing conscientious objectors at the time of the enactment of the 1940 law. 

These were applied in accordance with the approach of the Congress to the views expressed in the committee hearings of 1940 on the Burke- Wadsworth bill for selective service. 

Paul French's Interpretation of the Act 

Additionally and especially in view of the many discussions during the war years on the congressional intent of the 1940 law, a memorandum given to the System by Paul Comly French, field secretary of the Friends War Problems Committee, under date of October 23, 1940, is very significant. This was written as a suggested guide for local boards in classifying conscientious objectors. It is particularly important because it reflects the thinking of an individual who not only held a prominent position among the representatives of a large group of objectors but who also was closely connected with the writing of some of the most essential parts of the conscientious objection provisions. It read as follows: 

A person shall be deemed to be conscientiously opposed to war in any form if in good faith and in conformity to his sense of right and wrong or in conformity to the dictates of his conscience he objects to war or to the preparation for war. 

The opposition of such persons shall be deemed to be based upon religious training and belief if such opposition is accepted by such individual as a part of the belief, faith or doctrine of any religious denominations, sect or organization of which he is a member, or if arrived at as a result of other religious training as herein defined or as a fixed belief through ethical or moral considerations. Religious training shall include any training whether conducted individually or in classes or groups, through courses of study or individual or other forms of instruction, which has for its purpose the recognitions, service and adoration of God or a

CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION 

god and the development of a way of life based upon a conception of man's relation to God or a god and to his fellow men.'

The Importance of the Registrant's Conduct 

In the classification activities of the Selective Service local boards, appeal boards and Presidential Appeal Board with reference to conscientious objectors, considerable importance was attached to the generally expressed standards of conduct which were held suitable for members of each of the different peace churches. It was felt that observance of such standards by objector registrants was rather conclusive proof of their sincerity. The System was mindful, however, that these standards were usually set up by the organizations in question as ideals of conduct. But if an objector claimed affiliation with a certain church denomination, deviation in conduct from the accepted standards of the group was reason to doubt his sincerity. 

The whole matter of religious conscientious objection was considered a personal matter. Each case was approached separately and primarily from the registrant's personal viewpoint. For instance, there was one case where a member consulted three elders of his church as to whether certain contemplated employment was consistent with the view of the group. Two of the three elders advised against the employment, but the man accepted the position in accordance with the advice of the third. In this instance, the registrant's action was held to be not inconsistent with his personal convictions and, since his record was otherwise good, his claim of conscientious objection was allowed. 

It was reasoned that men should be judged by the whole of their training, belief and conduct. Isolated items needed to be fitted into the whole picture. As an example, it was not the practice to base the denial of a registrant's claim of conscientious objection on his failure at age 18 to have joined the church with which he later affiliated, if that church made a practice of urging membership only after a person reached adulthood. Nor was it fair to reason that an individual was irreligious just because he had broken the church or civil law in some instance in the past.

Influence of Many Factors on Classification 

As this chapter has indicated, the classification of conscientious objector registrants during the national emergency of 1940-47 was influenced by many and varied factors. These factors operated singly or jointly with respect to classification or to classification principles or policies. In other words when the classification of a man opposed to war and armed forces assumed difficult proportions with his Selec- Unpublished document on file at National Headquarters, Selective Service System, Washington.

GENERAL PRINCIPLES AND POLICIES OF OBJECTOR CLASSIFICATION 

143 tive Service local board, it then became the subject of very exhaustive consideration by the System.

In addition to personal sincerity, as shown by training, belief and conduct, the following factors have also been among those mentioned: the intent of Congress in passing the conscientious objector provisions of the Selective Service Act; the administrative interpretations of the law; the underlying principles of the objection held; the approach of the local board, appeal board, Presidential Appeal Board, State Director, Director and the President; public opinion as expressed by both local groups and those of broader areas; status as parolees from civil or military prisons; and court interpretations of the legislation. 

A very considerable factor which has been mentioned but needs further attention was the study given to difficult cases by the Department of Justice and the recommendations made by it. This included factual information presented by the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the recommendations of the various Hearing Officers who had been appointed to hear the objectors individually. 

Department of Justice Report on Objector Cases 

The Department of Justice made a statistical report on its activities with reference to conscientious objector cases as of June 30, 1946. A total of 12,342 cases were reported as having been handled and closed by the Department. Detailed statistics were included in this report on geographical distribution, age, race, education and occupation, but such analysis was for a distinct segment of objectors and is not presented here. The cases covered were largely registrants whose claims had been denied in most instances by both a local board and a board of appeal.

Nevertheless a few generalizations may be made using these data. 

One is that the largest number of the cases handled by the Department of Justice were from New York, the most populous State. Yet of the registrants actually classified as conscientious objectors the largest number were in Pennsylvania. This suggests that there were more objectors in New York than in Pennsylvania whose sincerity was doubted by Selective Service. 

It is also of interest to note that Negro registrants figured in only 4.4 percent of the Department of Justice cases. This is only about half as large a percentage relationship as that race bore to the total registration of the System.

Comment on Claims by the Justice Department Of considerable significance from a classification standpoint was the comment of the Department of Justice in its report regarding the 737977°-50-vol. 1-11

basis of claims made by conscientious objector registrants. This comment read in part as follows:

The exempting statute as passed by Congress, which persisted without amendment throughout the entire operation of the program, specifically provided that any claim for exemption granted under the Act must be "by reason of religious training and belief." While the statute thus provided an objective standard as a basis for exemption, extreme difficulty was experienced in applying the standard because the determination of its existence in each particular case required exploration of the subjective conscience of the registrant. Except for the probative value deducible from the registrant's daily life and conduct, most of the evidence concerning the existence of his conscientious objections arose from his own selfserving statements or an appraisal of his mental state by means of the examination conducted by the Hearing Officer at the hearing. 

Of course, the Selective Service special form for conscientious objectors contained a series of questions in answer to which the registrant was supposed to outline his religious background and training. Because of the diversity of religious persuasion which is characteristic of the American people, it was decided at the outset that formal adherence to a creed, sect or denomination was not necessary in order to prove the existence of the "religiousness" necessary to sustain the claim for exemption. Accordingly in the initial circular to the United 

States attorneys and hearing officers it was provided that exemption may be granted to- (a) Those whose conscientious objections were based upon the tenets of a particular church or religious organization, and (b) Those whose conscientious objections were based upon their own scruples but who do not rely upon adherence to a particular religious doctrine or membership in any church, sect, or religious organization as a basis thereof. 

The circular then stated that: "The question in the first class of cases whether the registrant is a bona fide member of such group or denomination or sect and whether his conduct and mode of life are generally such as to indicate that he is a bona fide believer in its tenets. This group will include members of the so-called Peace Group churches as well as members of other denominations, or established churches, the creeds of which are bases for an individual belief that war is unchristian or ungodly. In the second class of cases the question is whether the registrant individually is conscientiously opposed to participation in war in general and not whether he is conscientiously opposed to participation in a particular war. In seeking to determine the state of mind of the conscientious objector, which may be difficult in the latter class of cases, the hearing officer should satisfy himself that the objections of the registrant are based upon a personal religious or ethical conviction, and not upon a political doctrine." " 

Thus the Department of Justice as well as the Selective Service System found very difficult the matter of substantiating conscientious objector claims.

The Basing of Most Claims on Religious Tenets 

Of the 12,342 cases closed by the Department of Justice on or before June 30, 1946, 6,210 or 51.3 percent based their claims either on general or specific religious tenets. Bible study, obviously having a religious connotation, served as the basis for 2,182 registrants (17.7

The Following of Justice Department Recommendations 

The question of the appeal board's approach to the recommendations of the Department of Justice is also of importance. Reference to the statute and to the general regulations of Selective Service, previously quoted, reveals that the board of appeal in finally classifying the registrant was required to give consideration to, but was not bound to follow, the recommendation of the Justice Department. Data presented in Table 4 show, however, that over three-fourths of the recommendations of the Department of Justice were carried out by the boards of appeal, and that the Class I-A recommendations were more completely agreed to by the appeal boards than any other classification recommended.

Appeal Board Agreement a Tribute to the Department 

The fact that the boards of appeal followed the recommendations of the Department of Justice in such a large percentage of cases is a tribute to the respect held for the Department and for the procedure which it developed in this connection. It was well known that these cases were carefully investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation, although the report of the investigation of that Bureau was not contained in the information forwarded to the board of appeal. In a large number of cases, however, the Hearing Officer's report, which was forwarded to the board of appeal and was placed in the registrant's Cover Sheet (thereby being made available to the registrant himself) contained references to the investigation by the Federal Bureau of Investigation. Perhaps the action by the boards of appeal reflects the persuasiveness of the reports written by the hearing officers. By way of illustration a specimen of these reports is reproduced in the appendices of this monograph." 

Justice Department Cases and Presidential Action 

Out of the 12,342 cases disposed of by the Department of Justice, 712 were eventually considered and classified by the Presidential Appeal Board of Selective Service. These cases reached the Board in one of three ways. First, the registrant, a dependent of the registrant, or a person who had filed written information regarding the

registrant's occupational activities, could take an appeal to the President in the event the registrant was classified as available for service and one or more members of the board of appeal dissented from such classification. Second, a State Director of Selective Service could take an appeal from any classification at any time. Third, the Director of Selective Service could appeal from any classification at any time. 

The National Headquarters of the System had a working arrangement with the Department of Justice in such matters. The Department informed the Camp Operations Division, which was in charge of the conscientious objection program for National Headquarters, of any case that a board of appeal classified I-A when the Department of Justice had recommended I-A-O, or had placed either in Class I-A 

or I-A-O when the Department had recommended Class IV-E. 

Upon such advice the Camp Operations Division as a matter of policy requested a postponement of induction or a postponement of the issuance of induction orders, meanwhile asking that the registrant's local board file be forwarded for examination. Thereupon an appeal to the President was almost invariably recommended and almost without exception the Presidential Appeal Board classified the registrant in accordance with the recommendation of the Department of Justice. 

This procedure was adopted because of the regard which National Headquarters held for the work of the Department of Justice on conscientious objector cases.

A study of the 712 classifications given to Justice Department cases on appeal to the President, as compared with the classifications made by the local and appeal boards, reveals that the Presidential Appeal Board was considerably more liberal than either the local boards or boards of appeal. It placed a much smaller proportion of the men in Class I-A and a much larger percentage in Class IV-E or gave them ministerial exemption (Class IV-D). Table 5 indicates these results.

The Ministerial Factor and Objector Classification 

Out of a total of 11,918 conscientious objector classifications reported for this group whose cases were handled by the Department of Justice as to advisory recommendations, only 0.2 percent had been classified as ministers (IV-D) by their local boards. The actions by the boards of appeal raised this number to 1.1 percent while on 

Presidential appeal 25.7 percent were so classified.

There arose early in the Selective Service program a problem of involvement between the classification for ministerial exemption (Class IV-D) and that for the exemption of conscientious objectors (Classes I-A-O and IV-E). This came up mainly in connection with registrants who were members of the pacifist religious sect known as Jehovah's Witnesses. In some respects these men were opposed to war and armed forces by reason of conscience, but generally speaking the claims of objections which they made were incidental to claims of being "regular or duly ordained ministers of religion." The objector who belonged to this sect was really not asking for assignment to do work of national importance under civilian direction, that is, for Class IV-E exemption, but for legal exemption as a minister from all service including civilian work. 

Jehovah's Witnesses as a Different Category 

The problem of objector classifications for Jehovah's Witnesses was further involved in that such registrants who claimed opposition to any military or naval service and in effect asked for Class IV-E, if they were not otherwise exempt or deferred in the regular selection process, apparently had no intention of reporting for work of national importance, if so assigned. Therefore, any consideration given to the validity of their objection claims served scant classification usefulness to the System.

150* 

In an effort to conserve time and effort as regards cases involving Jehovah's Witnesses, the Department of Justice worked out a general procedure to cover these and similar ones. This was set forth in the Department's Circular No. 3461, Supplement No. 9, September 

28, 1943.

Information in such regard was disseminated throughout 

Selective Service in State Director Advice No. 250, November 11, 

1943, to which was attached a copy of the Department's circular. The essential part of the procedure was contained in the following para graph from section III of the circular: 

(3) If the registrant clearly and unequivocally states that he does not desire or will not accept a conscientious objector classification, regardless of the granting or denial of classification in Class IV-D, and that he wishes to withdraw his claim for classification as a conscientious objector, the registrant should be given an opportunity to sign a statement to that effect.' 

Reference of C. O. Appeals to Justice Department 

The Department of Justice and Selective Service took the position that each time the case of a registrant who claimed to be a conscientious objector came before a board of appeal, the case must be referred to the Department of Justice for its recommendation. This was felt to be the direct application of the law. In addition such reference was necessary because new factors in the case might be brought to light by the Department's investigation and hearing. The attention of the State Directors of the System was invited to this approach through the issuance of State Director Advice No. 250-D on April 19, 1945.

As of June 30, 1946, only 58 cases of objectors had been considered a second time by the Department of Justice and only two cases a third time. In such instances the registrant's file was forwarded directly to the Department of Justice by the United States attorney receiving it. 

After this the Department made a preliminary study to determine whether it would be advisable to have an additional investigation made by the Federal Bureau of Investigation and whether it would be advisable to have a supplementary hearing by a Hearing Officer. In many cases either or both of these additional measures were dispensed with and the Justice Department reiterated its previous recommendation. 

In some cases, however, the recommendation was amended after additional information was received from the Federal Bureau of Investigation or the Hearing Officer, or both.

The report of the Department of Justice which has already been referred to, shows that in only 183 instances did the recommendation by the Department of Justice differ from that of the Hearing Officer. In 

28 of these the officer made no recommendation and in 87 cases the

A Minimum of Criticism for the Department 

The report of the Department of Justice also pointed out: 

The Department received but a small amount of criticism for the manner in which it performed its duties and functions under section 5 (g) of the Selective Service Act. True, criticism and even great pressure were received in connection with individual cases; but this office prides itself on the fact that it has been able to work out a flexible program in connection with one of the most intangible and difficult problems which arose under the Selective Service Act. 

Proceeding on the theory that the benefit of the doubt should be accorded to the registrant in most cases, the overriding intent and purpose of the Selective Service Act was kept constantly in view. 

It is believed that this office has succeeded in discharging its duty not only to the conscientious objector whom Congress intended to exempt, but also to the Government and all other inductees under the Selective Service Act who would necessarily have to serve when exemption was granted to conscientious objectors. 

The Selective Service System agreed with this general appraisal.

Objectors Who Were Really Ministers 

As already shown the local boards and boards of appeal of the System had considerable difficulty in classifying some registrants who

GENERAL PRINCIPLES AND POLICIES OF OBJECTOR CLASSIFICATION >> 

153 claimed to be "regular or duly ordained ministers of religion." The fact that there were a considerable number claiming to be both ministers and conscientious objectors was a coincidence. The claims were both related to religion but they could not be viewed as interdependent except in the cases of ministers of denominations having inclusive nonresistant doctrines. However, there apparently was a decided increase in the number of cases where conscientious objectors were placed in Class IV-D as they progressed through the Selective Service appeal procedure. In this group of cases the percentages were 0.8 by 'the local boards, 2.4 by the boards of appeal and 23.6 by the Presidential

Appeal Board. 

Two things may well be pointed out in this connection. First, the number of conscientious objector claimants placed in Class IV-D by the President, namely, 366, represents less than one-fourth of one percent of all registrants classified as ministers by the System. The other is that a large proportion of these men were members of Jehovah's Witnesses.

The Small Proportion of C. O.'s to All Registrants 

The number of men classified at some time during the operations of Selective Service as conscientious objectors and placed on the local board rosters as such represented fifteen-hundredths of 1 percent of the total registration. Since out of a total of 64,051 cases considered on Presidential appeal there were 1,558 in which a claim of conscientious objection had been made, the percentages which the objector claimants bore to the total of such cases was but 2.4 percent. Thus it may be remarked again that the magnitude and effect of the conscientious objector problem far overshadowed its numerical significance. 

General Policies of Presidential Appeal Board 

In concluding this chapter, it may be well to give a general summary of the National Headquarters policy regarding the granting of a claim of conscientious objection as outlined in the Presidential Appeal Board approach. The following is part of a statement made at the close of the first year of war in behalf of the officers who constituted the Presidential Appeal Board. It may be said fairly that this remained the view until the closing of operations:

The appeals of conscientious objectors have presented some of the most troublesome as well as the most interesting questions. Here divergent ideas broke sharply over that rock of contention presented by the congressional language "religious training and belief." Local boards and boards of appeal generally brought little sympathy to the consideration of these cases. The tendency was to insist that conscientious objections be based upon certain kinds of religious experience. Many board members held the view that such objection must arise from religious training and belief in those particular religious organizations

CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION 

which make objection to war a definite part of their creed. It was argued, for example, that a member of the Catholic Church could not possibly have a basis for conscientious objections.

Hearing officers of the Department of Justice took a somewhat broader but still limited view in their early reports. They held generally that the conviction, while limited to no particular creed, must nevertheless rest upon an easily recognizable religious background with the definiton of religion the usual somewhat formal concept. 

After much consideration, we adopted a more liberal view, based upon a conclusion that the definitions of religions and the variety of religious experience are so nearly infinite in number as to make futile any attempt to say whether this or that one met the law. The practical effect of this decision was to say that conscientious convictions held by a man reared in the environment of a religious civilization and exposed, if only subjectively, to its ethical concepts, have their roots in the same soil from which spring religious convictions, and furnish evidence from which may be drawn the inference that he recognizes a Deity or a power above and beyond the human. This view has prevailed. 

Summarization 

This statement by the Presidential Appeal Board indicated again the liberal principles and policies of classification and selection which that agency of Selective Service applied to conscientious-objector registrants during World War II. It was also evidence of the whole approach to the problem taken by the System's National Headquarters wherein the Board was located. Many factors entered into the adoption and continuation of such an attitude. The more important of these were: (1) Selective Service's own interpretation as well as that of the courts regarding the intent of the objection provisions in the 1940 law, (2) tendency for local boards as final classifying agencies to apply narrowly the System's Regulations on objectors, (3) custom for greater leniency in appeal-board classifications and Justice Department recommendations to appeal boards, (4) delegation by the President of his appeal responsibilities to the Director of Selective Service, (5) the administrative handling nationally of many objector cases from all over the United States, (6) National Headquarters access to the investigation files and hearing reports in the Justice Department on registrants opposed to war and armed forces, (7) desire to help the armed forces avoid the disciplinary problems of objectors in combatant service and to assist the Government in avoiding the court and imprisonment enforcement of delinquency penalties, (8) interest in "fair and just" selection for men conscientiously opposed to war "by reason of religious training and belief" as well as for all registrants and (9) cooperation of National Headquarters with the National Service Board for Religious Objectors. 

These factors also reveal some of the general principles and policies for classifying objectors. In addition the classification significance 

& Selective Service in Wartime, Second Report of the Director of Selective Service 

(Washington: 1943), p. 258.

GENERAL PRINCIPLES AND POLICIES OF OBJECTOR CLASSIFICATION >>> 155 

of information on the conduct, training and belief of this type registrant should be mentioned. The local board in its strict approach to substantiating the validity or sincerity of a conscientious objection claim, depended heavily upon such data as it placed the available registrant in Class I-A, I-A-O, or IV-E. The boards did well enough in this regard that 90 percent of the objectors whom they classified, accepted such action without exercising their appeal rights. 

The appeal board, which took a more lenient approach, likewise depended upon information of this type in cases forwarded to it for classifying. The same was true of the Department of Justice in making classification recommendations on cases referred from the appeal board. The Department even went further by having the 

Federal Bureau of Investigation make a special investigation of the registrant and a Hearing Officer conduct hearings for him to provide exhaustive material on conduct, training, and belief. These data were basic also when the State Director or the Director of Selective Service was considering an appeal to the President and when the Presidential Appeal Board was engaged in classifying. They were fundamental, too, in the case where the objector coincidentally claimed to be a "regular and duly ordained minister of religion" and made claim for exemption on the grounds of objection because ministerial exemption in Class IV-D had not been granted him. 

Thus the classification of a conscientious objector was based on thorough and painstaking consideration, and the sincerity of his claim for exemption from combatant service (for Class I-A-O) or any military or naval duty (for Class IV-E) was given increasingly more exhaustive and careful study if appealed. It was the whole effort of the System to pay the utmost respect to the objector registrant's claim so that his duty in the emergency of 1940-47 under the Selective Service Act could meet the dictates of his conscience as well as the needs of his country.

IX 

THE CIVILIAN WORK PROGRAM FOR CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTORS 

Both specific and general treatment has been given to the Selective Service classification of conscientious objectors who were opposed to any military or naval service during World War II and whom the local boards of the System found available for duty. It has been seen how their opposition to noncombatant as well as combatant service with the armed forces caused them, when they were selected for duty and their objection claims were substantiated, to be placed in Class IV-E, available for assignment to work of national importance under civilian direction. On the other hand, if their claims were not found valid they were put in I-A-O as noncombatant "availables" or I-A as combatant "availables."

The relationship of this type registrant to the specific objector pro visions of the Selective Service Act and regulations for World War II 

has been observed. Attention has also been given to the genesis of the civilian-work idea in the American philosophy and history of service during national emergencies and in the church backgrounds of conscientious objection. It is, therefore, time to see what was involved in the 1940-47 program on work of national importance. 

The Work Program For Objectors a New Idea 

In the planning which lay back of the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940 it was not contemplated that the statutory provisions for conscientious objectors would differ materially from those in the conscription legislation of World War I. As noted previously, the reference made to objectors in section 7 (d) of the original Burke- Wadsworth Bill was that "no such person shall be relieved from training or service in such capacity as the President may declare to be noncombatant." 1

The provisions finally adopted read in part that a man found under the act to be a conscientious objector to both combatant and noncombatant service should, in lieu of induction into the land or naval forces, 

¹ Hearings on S. 4164 before the Senate Committee on Military Affairs, 73d Cong., 3d Sess., (Washington: 1940), p. 3. 157

"be assigned to work of national importance under civilian direction." 2 

This meant that such registrants were to be in no way a part of the armed forces and in no way under military law and subject to court martial. The legislation was silent, though, on how this provision was to be administered. The matter was left entirely to determination by the President along with various other matters connected with putting the act into effect.

Existence of But Slight Precedent 

As has been noted, there was but slight precedent from World War I for the handling of such registrants. During that emergency a considerable number of conscientious objectors were furloughed from the Army into agricultural and industrial service and some to the Friends Reconstruction Unit for duty in France. There is evidence also that others were furloughed for duty in Virginia hospitals. A record likewise exists of special service in forestry work for Mennonite objectors during a short term following the year 1880, in Russia. Then in the 

American Civil War the Federal Government provided for objector duty in hospitals and in institutions caring for freedmen. However, all of this was under general military supervision. 

Early Consideration of the Civilian Work Problem 

The National Headquarters of Selective Service began work on the conscientious objector problem very shortly after the act was approved on September 16, 1940. A memorandum, dated September 

24, 1940, made the following recommendation:

Pending the completion of my study of the conscientious objector feature of the law, as it applies to the assignment of a conscientious objector to work of national importance under civilian direction, I recommend that an informal conference be immediately aranged of representatives from several national agencies, such as WPA, NYA, CCC, Public Health Service, and the Veterans'

Administration, for the purpose of- (1) Coordinating a national policy, and (2) The designation of the various types of work to be performed by such registrants, and (3) Possible methods of administration of these particular registrants in such national work.*

The President of the United States had, on August 27, 1940, appointed a special group to work with the Joint Army and Navy Selective Service Committee in planning the procurement of military and naval manpower. This was called the National Advisory Committee on Selective Service and it also participated for some time
