during the fall months of 1940 in the discussions on the problem of a civilian work program for conscientious objectors. The committee was originally composed of Frederick Osborn, W. H. Draper, Jr., Floyd W. Reeves and Joseph P. Harris. Added to it later were 

Channing H. Tobias and Wayne Coy.

The First Planning 

During the fall of 1940 the planning for a civilian work program to utilize conscientious objectors was handled by the Manpower Division at the National Headquarters of Selective Service. It was thought that perhaps the best program, at least a program capable of the most rapid development, would be one which could use certain available equipment, buildings, camp supplies and the like. Consequently, the possibilities of continuing some of the projects abandoned by the Civilian Conservation Corps were explored. With this in mind an officer, experienced in the CCC program, was secured by National Headquarters to assist in planning the "work of national importance” and a series of conferences was arranged with representatives of the CCC, the Federal Security Administration, the War Department, the Department of Agriculture, the Department of the Interior, and other agencies interested in the CCC projects. 

Surveys were then made to determine the costs and the availability of buildings, equipment, camp supplies, and other necessities. On November 20, 1940, the first actual inspection of a camp location was made. This location was outside of Grottoes, Rockingham County, Va., where Civilian Conservation Corps camp NP-4 had been operated by the National Park Service near an area having a continuing need for erosion control. The inspection of the camp was made by representatives of Selective Service, the Army, the Department of Agriculture, the National Council for Religious Conscientious Objectors, the Mennonite Church, and others. It was here that much of the pattern for later camp cooperative relations was worked out between the agencies and organizations concerned. Tentative determination was made regarding the extent of technical responsibility by the agencies, the limit of the church group participation, and other steps necessary to the setting up of a program by the System. 

The National Service Board for Religious Objectors 

Although the main burden of administering work of national importance under civilian direction was to fall upon the Director of Selective Service and his representatives working cooperatively with the representatives of the larger groups of religious objectors, the three largest peace churches had been quite active in presenting their viewpoints to the Congress when the Selective Training and Service 

---

CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION 

«K Act of 1940 was being formulated. These groups were now desirous also of the privilege of operating work units of conscientious objectors. 

It was evident that they had rather different ideas than the System for the administration of such units and it was anticipated that misunderstandings and confusion would be the outcome of separate agreements with the several groups. It was therefore suggested that one central representative body be formed through which all matters could be cleared by Selective Service.

Such an organization was therefore formed in October 1940 and was named the National Council for Religious Conscientious Objectors. 

During December 1940 the name was changed to the National Service Board for Religious Objectors. In autobiographical language its origin is explained as follows: 

As a result of our early conversations with Dr. Dykstra and Colonel Hershey our groups realized that we needed some organizational form which would permit us to discuss problems with the Government on a collective basis. It was obviously impossible for Selective Service, merely from the time element, to talk over the same problem with representatives of many religious denominations and other groups. But if a unified approach could be made to them, it seemed likely that they would be willing to listen to suggestions and proposals from us. 

The development of this thinking led to a meeting in Washington to consider the situation. That meeting recommended that a larger group be brought together in Chicago on October 4 to establish a National Council for Religious 

Conscientious Objectors. Friends, Brethren, and Mennonites agreed and the council was organized with offices in the National Press Building, Washington, D. C. Later the name was changed to National Service Board for Religious 

Objectors and all other interested groups were invited to participate." 

At first this organization represented only the American Friends 

Service Committee, the Brethren Service Committee, and the Mennonite Central Peace Committee. It continued to function throughout the war, however, and came in time to represent practically all of the larger conscientious objector groups.

Various Ideas Regarding Work for Objectors 

The suggestions and proposals variously advanced for the use and control of conscientious objectors ranged from assignment on an individual basis with no supervision all the way to Governmentoperated and strictly disciplined concentration camps. The problem was further complicated by the degree to which the various individuals and their groups were willing to go in participating in the defense effort. Some were willing to take part in outright defense work so long as it did not involve actual military or naval service, but others 

National Service Board for Religious Objectors, Camp Directors Manual, (Washington: 

rev. 1943), pp. 1-12.

THE CIVILIAN WORK PROGRAM FOR CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTORS » » 

161 were opposed even to growing crops that might conceivably be used for war purposes.

Realizing that many objectors would be strongly opposed to any type of defense work, the policy adopted was to choose work projects as unrelated to the war effort as possible. It was planned also to operate these projects through agencies which were distinctly civilian in character. It is true that in the later months of the civilian work program several projects somewhat connected with the war effort were established. One of these was even directly under the supervision of an agency of the War Department. However, only assignees who volunteered for transfer were sent to these projects. 

In the meantime, men who had been placed in Class IV-E by their local boards and whose order numbers had been reached were allowed to remain at home, causing numerous complaints from local board members and other citizens. These people complained that conscientious objectors, never very popular, were being favored, since they remained in the community while men in Class I-A or I-A-O were being inducted for training and service in the armed forces. 

Early Program an Extension of Civilian Conservation 

In time the various plans crystallized, finally emerging as the usual democratic compromise between divergent points of view. Progress was necessarily slow, such matters took considerable time, particularly in view of the fact that the religious groups wished to maintain full control of the assignees on any program and objected to any Government supervision. Some became critical because of the delay, others understood. Paul Comly French, executive secretary of the National 

Service Board for Religious Objectors, in a booklet published November 1, 1942, expressed it this way:

It takes time to work out new plans and new projects with Governmental agencies under normal conditions. And it takes even more time and energy and patience to develop a new program in fields which have no blueprints in the midst of a global war.*

It was agreed that "work of national importance" should, in the initial stages at least, be mainly a continuation of projects originated by Civilian Conservation Corps and carried on in the old camps of this agency. Such projects had been in operation for several years and had been accepted generally by the public as nationally important activities. In addition, various governmental agencies such as the Forest Service and Soil Conservation Service had projects and experienced personnel available to help in getting the civilian work program for objectors under way.

CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION More Specific Planning 

Then too, some of the churches most concerned, had already been operating work camps for their young people and it was not a long step for them to reshape such programs for the new activity involving objectors. On November 12, 1940, the following suggestions were made by letter to the National Headquarters of Selective Service by the Na tional Council for Religious Objectors: 

In line with our conversation this morning, I am submitting a specific program of work of national importance under civilian direction for boys who are judged sincere in their conscientious convictions against military training and service. 

I would suggest three types of projects. The first would be for technically equipped boys to work with Government agencies and with the Government paying all expenses. The boy, however, should not receive personally any greater pay than he would have received if he had been in the military service. I think that this type will represent a very small number of the boys involved. 

The second type of projects would be camp units operating in conjunction with Government agencies but under the administration of such organization as the American Friends Service Committee, the Brethren Service Committee, and the Mennonite Central Committee. In this type of project, the Government would assume technical direction of the work, and would pay for maintenance such as food and shelter and supply the necessary tools. The agency administrating the project will employ and pay the administrative staff including camp director, educational director, dietician, and nurse. In this type of project provision should be made so that boys might have the choice of either accepting or refusing to accept wages at the Army scale. 

The third type of project would be operated and financed by the agencies listed above and any other agencies which the Director of Selective Service might decide was competent to direct such projects. In this type of project there would be no expense to the Government, but the directing agency should have the opportunity of selecting the best boys qualified to fit into the program. 

Under type three the American Friends Service Committee now has a camp functioning on New York State Forest Lands at Cooperstown, N. Y. This camp has been in operation for some time and is equipped to immediately take up to 20 boys. The work being performed there is in conjunction with the New 

York State Forest Department and is directed toward the profitable use of submarginal land through instructing farmers on the best methods of raising trees on this land. The camp is also assisting a cooperative lumber mill which is being developed in conjunction with this program. 

The American Friends Service Committee is establishing in Patapsco State Forest about 10 miles south of Baltimore, Md., a work camp in conjunction with a Maryland State Forest Commission. This project will be available for boys between the 25th of November and the 1st of December and will be able to handle approximately a hundred persons. The plan was to use this camp as a reception center and later distribute those boys with special qualifications to smaller units approved by the Director of Selective Service. 

The Brethren Service Committee have a camp at Onekame, Mich., which is adjacent to the Manistee State Forest. They are prepared to receive 100 boys on the 1st of December and to gradually expand their facilities as necessity arises.

Under the type 2 project, the Mennonite committee is prepared to operate in conjunction with the Soil Conservation Service, a camp for 100 boys in

Selective Service Plans for Camps 

Among the questions being discussed within the System at this time were the following: (1) financing the civilian work program for conscientious objectors; (2) types of work to be undertaken and possible locations for them; (3) legal questions involved in the program; (4) quotas or the numbers of conscientious objector registrants who would be assigned; (5) methods by which local boards would report objectors to National Headquarters through State Headquarters; (6) allowing objectors to volunteer for civilian work; (7) the status of the civilian worker after one year's service; and (8) parole of Selective 

Service violators from prison to civilian work. 

By the early part of December 1940 it was generally agreed that it would be necessary for the President, by Executive order, to (1) define what constituted work of national importance under civilian direction and to give authority to the Director of Selective Service to issue detailed definitions and regulations regarding it; (2) give the Director supervisory control over the program; and (3) authorize the Director to call on other Government departments and agencies and private organizations to cooperate in carrying on the work with funds furnished from appropriations of the System or from private sources. 

It was understood that pursuant to the above, the Director would need to: (1) secure the appropriation of adequate funds; (2) issue special Selective Service Regulations defining the work and prescribing rules for assignment thereto and for the general direction of the program; and (3) set up the necessary administrative controls of Selective Service for (a) planning and continuing of the program, (b) controlling of the assignment and delivery of men from local boards through State Headquarters, and (c) giving inspection and policy supervision to the program.

Attention was also being given to the details of establishing camps, along with those for administrative organization. It was suggested that the following data on each proposed camp should be obtained: (1) a statement of the work project available and a letter of approval from the technical agency which would direct it; (2) one regarding constructional work equipment needed and, if available, where and by whom to be furnished; (3) a statement of technical personnel needed and when and where available; (4) information on ownership, leases,

´or control of camp sites and records of the same properly executed; (5) a statement of ownership or control of all camp improvements and records of the same; (6) one on camp supervisory personnel, that is, the names and other pertinent data and by whom furnished and when available; (7) letters of approval for occupancy by (a) the corps area medical officer of water supply and sanitation and (b) the corps area quartermaster officer of building equipment; (8) advice on the availability of all utilities-water, electricity, telephones, etc.; (9) information regarding the adequacy of camp equipment; (10) letter if possible from the United States Public Health Service that this agency could and would make inspections within reason when requested; (11) local information as to whether the camp was acceptable to the community in which it was situated; (12) evidence on the acceptance of bond to the System by the National Service Board for Religious Objectors; (13) a statement regarding the camp medical and hospital facilities available; and (14) one on the need for the camp which would meet approval.

Presidential Approval of the General Plan On December 19, 1940, the Director of Selective Service presented a memorandum regarding conscientious objectors to the President of the United States after having previously secured the approval of the various governmental agencies concerned. This memorandum was personally approved by the President. It presented the plans reviewed above. Following the concurrence of the White House, letters were exchanged between the National Service Board for Religious Objectors and the National Headquarters of the System, clearing the last obstacle to beginning the operation of camps for work of national importance under civilian direction. 

By January 7, 1941, the Director of Selective Service, in cooperation with the National Service Board for Religious Objectors, had tentatively selected nine camp sites and was making preliminary arrangements with the interested agencies. By January 10, reports were furnished on camps which had been inspected and on general equipment needs.

Civilian Public Service Camps 

With the publication of this order definite progress was possible. 

In March of 1941, five camps were selected for "immediate use." In 

April the first set of special or camp regulations was drawn up by Selective Service prescribing the government of the camps and setting forth the duties and responsibilities of the agencies involved. On 

May 8, the Camp Operations Division was established at National Headquarters with the duty of obtaining, equipping, and operating the camps and assigning to camp the men classified in Class IV-E. 

The camps for conscientious objectors were originally referred to as National Service Camps. However, the National Service Board for 

Religious Objectors came to refer to them as Civilian Public Service Camps. Finally, the System itself officially recognized this as the designation for the camps.

The First Men Ordered to Camp 

The first group of men was ordered to report to Camp No. 3 at 

Patapsco, Md., on May 15, 1941.9 This camp was under the supervision of the Friends, but, as was usually the case in their camps, the members of that church were in the minority. The registrants sent to this camp were varied and heterogeneous with regard to religion, education, and occupation. Some went willingly, believing they had a duty to perform; other were resentful and suspicious. More than one was surprised not to find the barbed wire and guards of the concentration camp which his imagination had led him to expect. ?Filed in the Federal Register, February 8, 1941 (6 F. Factors in Selecting Work Projects and Camp Sites 

Once the broad outlines of the civilian work program were established, Selective Service was able to orient itself with regard to many of the major problems involved. During at least the first half of the period when the Camp Operations Division was in existence a great deal of attention had to be paid to the matter of selecting projects. It was a much broader question than merely the picking of a type of work which was "of national importance." The following factors were judged to be the most important in selecting projects: 

1. Was the project important to the Government in the emergency, considering the manpower available, and was the project the most important thing that could be done at the time? Would it continue to be important with the changes which would probably occur in the situation? 

2. Would conscientious objectors perform the work? It would have been useless to select projects which objectors would not do wholeheartedly; filling the jails with them because they would not work would not solve the problem of having them perform service for the Nation. 

3. Would the public tolerate the objector in the community where the project was to be located? It would have been useless again to attempt a project in a community where the local population so threatened or harassed the objector that he could not do a creditable job. In many cases the cooperation of the citizens of the community was necessary. 

4. Would other employable labor be displaced? No projects could be attempted which would displace labor already employed, nor were projects located where funds and labor were already available. 

5. Would the project raise political controversy? It would not do to have objectors in a community where their presence might become a political issue.

Supervision by the Interior and Agriculture Departments Because of the uncertainty regarding the number of conscientious objectors who would be sent to the camps and the difficulty of getting Government agencies to accept the responsibility for the camp work projects, it was decided to restrict the setting up of the early camps to the supervision of the Forest Service and the Soil Conservation Service in the Department of Agriculture and of the National Park 

Service in the Department of the Interior. Of the first 25 camps established, 12 were under the Forest Service, 11 under the Soil Conservation Service, and 2 under the National Park Service. 

The Civilian Work Program in 1942 

With the complete abandonment of the Civilian Conservation Corps program in 1942 more and more projects of the highest priority with full equipment and comparatively new barracks became available to Selective Service. Consequently, quite a number of the original camp sites were disregarded in favor of more desirable ones. Some of the initial projects were never considered to be of the highest priority either by the technical agencies directing them or by the System. 

However, due to the necessity of providing work for conscientious objectors which would place them in service and take them from their home communities, such projects were used. 

While, generally speaking, the camp program of Selective Service was made up of abandoned Civilian Conservation Corps projects, there were exceptions. Camps were established in New England in order to repair the extensive damage caused by a severe hurricane in the States of New Hampshire and Massachusetts. Additional locations were at Merom, Ind., Hagerstown, Md., and Lincoln, Nebr., where no buildings used by the Civilian Conservation Corps were available, but where extremely valuable erosion control projects were located.

The Hospital Phase of the Program 

In 1942 it became increasingly evident that the camp work program would not be satisfactory for all conscientious objectors. Many registrants were assigned to work of national importance who would, for varied reasons, never adapt themselves to its heavy manual labor requirements. Considerable thought had to be given therefore to other available and acceptable projects. While many Americans felt that the objector was entitled to the rights provided him in the 1940 law, there were just as many who believed he was being treated as a member of a "privileged" class. Consequently, additional projects were difficult to develop. Public opinion and the necessity of maintaining the war effort prevented the use of conscientious objectors

THE CIVILIAN WORK PROGRAM FOR CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTORS » 

169 in the fields of education and social welfare work where there was a possibility that they might spread their philosophies and thus interfere with the winning of the war. 

A large number of requests had been received for the use of assignees in general hospitals, tubercular hospitals, and mental hospitals during the early part of 1942. Since many objectors indicated they would welcome such duty, an experimental unit was installed at the Alexian Brothers Hospital in Chicago during the month of March that year. 

In June of 1942 a unit was also established at the Eastern State Mental Hospital, Williamsburg, Va. These projects, particularly the one at Williamsburg, were approved only after a most extensive survey into the possibilities of this type of service. Experience at the two units showed that a successful operation could be developed in this field. As objectors available for assignment increased in number a great many were ultimately assigned to this phase of the whole program. In fact so many requests were received from hospitals for assignments to this kind of work, once the program had proven satisfactory, that it became necessary to limit them to State mental institutions only. Later, this limitation was waived in order to provide men for Veterans' Administration facilities. 

Food Production Assignments 

Among other program activities investigated and finally adopted was one calling for the utilization of assignees in food production. 

Two factors entered into the use of objectors for this purpose. First, in World War I some conscientious objectors were paroled for farm use, and, second, in World War II farming was the only vocation. many of the men from rural areas had acquired. When the labor situation on farms became acute as a result of the industrial and armed forces displacement of farm workers, the Department of Agriculture began looking into all available sources of new manpower, and the objector came under consideration in this connection. 

A series of meetings were therefore arranged between Department of Agriculture representatives, staff members of the United States Employment Service, the National Service Board for Religious Objectors and staff members of the Selective Service System. These conferences discussed many difficulties which had to be overcome. Some of the problems had to do with (1) the priorities of certain labor shortage areas, (2) methods of selecting assignees for farm work, (3) methods of supervising them and (4) whether or not wages were to be paid, and, if so, on what basis. Considerable time was required to work out all of the details, but four different plans for this phase of the civilian work program eventually became effective. 

The first of these plans provided for the use of assignees from regular Civilian Public Service Camps on farms within a radius of 15 miles

after certification had been made by the county agent and the county employment office that there was no available labor from other sources. The second plan provided for the use of conscientious objectors on dairy farms in certain counties to be selected by the Department of Agriculture and approved by the United States Employment Service as to the nonavailability of labor. The third program looked to the use of such individuals as dairy herd testers in States where the loss of testers was resulting in the abandonment of the testing program. The fourth plan called for the establishment of units at experimental stations or at agricultural colleges where labor shortages had reduced their programs to the point of retarding the food production program of the Nation. 4 It was determined by the groups concerned that the farmer, the dairy testing association or anyone else using the farm labor of objectors, would pay the prevailing rural wages of the community. The wage was to be established by the local county wage board and was subject to revision semiannually. The payment of the wages was to be made by the labor user to the National Service Board of Religious Objectors which, in turn, through a preaudit system, would pay allowances to the assignees to be used by them for clothing, other miscellaneous needs and medical, dental and hospital expenses, insurance premiums, and transportation to and from the camps in which they had been on duty. The balance of the fund was to be forwarded to the 

National Headquarters of Selective Service for deposit in the United 

States Treasury. 

The conscientious objectors, before wholeheartedly accepting this program activity, had to be convinced that none of the money so collected would be used for purchasing war machines or materials of war. This was arranged through the establishment of a special deposit account in the Treasury, which impounded the money and provided that it could not be spent until after the termination of hostilities. 

Volunteering for Medical Experiments 

No chapter relating to the establishment of the civilian work program would be complete without a reference to the use of assignees as "guinea pigs" on research subjects. This work was the responsibility of the Office of Scientific Research and Development and of the Office of the Surgeon General of the Army. It appealed to many conscientious objectors because, they felt that through volunteering for such projects they could show the public generally that they were not afraid to submit themselves bodily to any worthwhile experiment which would result in the saving of life or improvement of health and living conditions. Requests for these programs started slowly, but increased as it became evident that the assignees would be satisfactory subjects and were willing to volunteer in adequate numbers. The latter

THE CIVILIAN WORK PROGRAM FOR CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTORS » 171 

was very important inasmuch as such assignments were made only on a voluntary basis.

Other Program Activities 

As time passed and as men became available, Selective Service gave consideration to almost any type of project sponsored by Federal or State agencies which would be accepted by the public and would further the general war effort. Ultimately several projects were approved having to do with the control of hookworm and malaria in certain areas of Florida and Mississippi. A public-health program was sanctioned in Puerto Rico. A weather-mapping program came into being under the direction of the United States Weather Bureau. 

The United States Coast and Geodetic Survey obtained approval for the use of assignees to run surveys. The Forest Service, Department of Agriculture, submitted and had approved the use of objectors as parachute fire fighters in the less accessible western forest areas. 

Before the conclusion of the program, consideration was given to the use of specially trained men on detached duty with the Forest Service. This was done only after the claim had been made and substantiated that valuable work of the bureau could not be done otherwise because of the impossibility of obtaining the services of properly educated and trained individuals. Men with the proper qualifications were found in the ranks of objectors and were assigned to this detached duty.

The Success of the Camp Phase 

The discussion of the last few pages is not intended to give the impression that the basic camp phase of the civilian work program was not satisfactory and that it was necessary to develop other activities because of that fact. To remove any doubt it may be stated that, in the opinion of Selective Service, no program would be successful for conscientious objectors which did not provide for some camps. It was in the camps that a screening procedure became possible and permitted the proper reassignment of men to projects for which they proved qualified. At the same time too it could be determined whether or not a man was going to cooperate with the program as a whole. 

Neither should it be supposed that all projects which were suggested proved to be acceptable. Many, submitted chiefly through interested church groups, were not approved because in the opinion of the System such activities might create difficulties in the relationships between 

Selective Service and the public. 

The Manner of Establishing Camps and Projects 

While at the inception of the program it was, in some instances, very difficult to establish camps or projects due to resentment against

172. 

the conscientious objector, the task later became relatively simple. 

As already indicated the demands for men among the special projects eventually became much greater than the supply of volunteers. The selection of projects, the comparing of the needs for each program phase with those of another, became the problem of the Camp Operations Division in National Headquarters. However, it was here that proper public relations, availability of housing without rehabilitation costs, labor needs in relation to the war effort, and other factors had to be given increasingly serious consideration. This was much more the case as time went on than when the program first started and when the prime objective was to remove registrants exempted on the basis of objection from their home communities. 

The general interest in the whole civilian work program became such that upon occasions National Headquarters was given very material but unexpected help by outside sources in the establishment of camps and projects. To give an idea of such assistance the pertinent facts in a few instances will be outlined. The examples chosen are by way of illustration only and do not necessarily constitute a typical sampling of the establishment of camps or projects or of the various avenues through which information or requests were received. 

Examples of Outside Help 

. In one instance, information was received through a Federal agency of the possible availability for camp purposes of abandoned Civilian Conservation Corps buildings, in good condition, with all of the necessary equipment for their operation and maintenance. This advice continued by saying that a valuable forest-fire-fighting program was located in the immediate vicinity for which labor could not be provided due to its isolation, and that, in addition, a valuable research project not then provided with personnel was also situated near there. At about the same time the National Service Board for Religious Objectors made known its willingness to accept this particular site for the operation of a camp by either the Mennonite Central Committee or the Brethren Service Committee. After investigation, confirming the facts presented, the project was set up by Selective Service as work of national importance.

In another instance, a letter was received by the Director of Selective Service from the Director, Division of Territories and Island Possessions and the Administrator, Puerto Rico Reconstruction Administration, indicating that informal discussions had been had between representatives of that office and the National Service Board relative to the establishment of a public-health project. This appeared to be an excellent program and was, after examination, given approval. 

As the hospital phase of the program was being established, a letter was received from the superintendent of a State mental institution,

THE CIVILIAN WORK PROGRAM FOR CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTORS >>> 173 

enclosing communications from the Governor of the State, the mayor of the city in which the institution was located, the Committee for Industrial Organization and American Federation of Labor representatives, the American Legion, and the Veterans of Foreign Wars. 

These enclosures pointed out the need for labor at the hospital and that the organizations writing would appreciate the establishment of a unit of conscientious objectors there; also that no public relations problems would be created by such action. After checking on the project, it was given approval. 

In one case, a petition requesting the establishment of a camp was received through a Member of Congress. It set forth that a 

Civilian Conservation Corps Camp was being closed, that the project was nowhere near completion, that the State had appropriated $30,000 for the work, that the involved counties had appropriated an additional $20,000, that it was the most "important and beneficial work done in this part of the country for the past several years,” and that in the event the project was continued many thousands of acres of agricultural land would be made available for cultivation and additional thousands improved. Statements were attached to the effect that veterans' organizations had been approached and had given a favorable response to an objector camp. Further, the Governor of the State wrote, expressing his approval. This request, upon investigation, proved to deserve a high priority and was likewise approved. 

Statistics on Work Camps and Projects 

A total of 151 camps were set up by the Director of Selective Service on individual orders.10 Information regarding these projects is presented in Appendix G, Item No. 119. In this item all of the projects or camps are shown by number with the camp names, locations, operating groups, technical agencies, the camp capacities or authorized maximum strength, and the dates when the camps were individually approved and closed.

A true picture of the operation of the Civilian Public Service Camps is not easily derived, however, from figures on the number of such camps and other details. For example, all dairy-farm units were, for purpose of administration, placed under the camp No. 97 designation; whereas the work was actually carried on in 34 county units in 15 different States. And the dairy-herd testing program was officially known as camp No. 100 but it had units in 14 different States. 

Camp No. 115 was assigned to the Office of Scientific Research and

The Subdivision of Some Camps 

A slightly different situation in most of the regular work camps caused some division of another type among them. This was particularly true in those under the supervision of the Forest Service, the National Park Service, and the Soil Conservation Service when it was necessary during given periods to set up smaller camps outside of the main camp areas. These were established at many outposts, especially during the fire seasons, to make it possible for men to get to critical districts as soon as possible. The use of these small camps also made it possible to accomplish more work in various situations, because of the elimination of excessive travel time. 

Small camps, when composed of six or more objectors, were usually referred to as side camps. If they contained five men or fewer, they were generally called spike camps. Some of the main camps had as many as 12 of these side or spike camps, and at times registrants were even sent to other areas at the request of the regional headquarters of the technical agency assisting Selective Service in its camp operations. The transfer of objectors to the side and spike camps was, at the convenience of the technical agency, arranged between the operating church group and the technical agency and did not require the prior approval of the System. 

Four of the Civilian Public Service Camps established on paper, that is, by the issuance of the usual orders, never in fact became active units. These were all hospital camps. The first three of them were not activated because of local opposition to the work. The other was authorized just prior to VE-Day and was never placed in operation due to lack of assignees. 

The Discontinuation of Foreign Projects 

In the course of events two foreign-relief projects were developed for conscientious objectors as a phase of the general civilian work program. They were discontinued in their infancy, however, by 

Congressional action. These units had been provided for by official orders and some men had been assigned to each at the time the work, part of which had been started here in this country, was interrupted. 

One of these projects, to be located in Chunking, China, was to consist of rehabilitation, sanitation, nutrition, public health, and other services as designated by the Ministry of Public Health for the Gov-

Provided further, That no appropriation contained in this act shall be used for any expense pertaining to (1) the instruction, education, or training of class IV-E conscientious objectors in colleges, (2) the service of such conscientious objectors outside the United States, its Territories, and possessions, (3) the transportation of such conscientious objectors to or from any college or any such service, or (4) the compensation of military or civilian personnel preforming any services with respect to the matters set forth in (1), (2), or (3) above after the enactment of this act, except any services which may be necessary promptly to terminate any such class IV-E conscientious objector college or foreign-service projects existing on the date of the enactment of this act; 11 This matter was fully discussed in Congressional Committees, with hearings held before both the House and Senate subcommittees of the Committee on Appropriations prior to the enactment of the bill (H. Similar riders were likewise attached to subsequent appropriation bills throughout the remainder of the war period. 

Control of All Camps by Camp Operations Division 

All of the Civilian Public Service Camps were under the general con trol of the Camp Operations Division at the National Headquarters of the System as previously indicated. They were operated under the authority of the Director of Selective Service according to regulations and orders promulgated by him pursuant to Executive Order No. 

8675 of the President of the United States, issued February 6, 1941, and quoted above. Their direct supervision, however, was by that agency or department of the Federal Government primarily concerned with the project or projects being carried on by the camp. 

As regards the church-sponsored camps, their operation was under a dual system of supervision in which the project work was carried on by the camp superintendent, who was an employee of a governmental agency or department, while the camp life was conducted by a camp director selected by the sponsoring church group.

Most of the church camps were operated by the Friends Service

This fact is of no particular significance, though, because the project was simply an administrative expedient for permitting the assignment on "detached service" of a number of registrants to assist the Board in its camp activities work. Certain of the camps were cooperative, in that a number of religious agencies participated. 

In the spring of 1943, it was decided to open up a few Governmentoperated camps for those assignees who objected to serving in camps under religious sponsorship. Some assignees had expressed a desire to be transferred to Government camps to relieve the churches of financial burden. There were also those who wanted such transfers in order to have a better opportunity for expressing their aversion to conscription. In the revised Special Form for Conscientious Objector (DSS Form 47), put into use at the time, registrants could indicate their choice of a religious or a Government camp. 

The Government-operated camps were similar to the other regular work camps, except that the responsibility for both the work project and camp life was entirely assumed by the Federal Government. In other words, the Government in operating these camps had the entire responsibility for the general maintenance and sanitation of the camp and for the clothing, feeding, housing, medical care, supervision, and control as well as the work of the assignees. 

A total of eight camps was operated by the Federal Government at one time or another. Four of these were at first conducted as church camps but later taken over by the Government. One was first sponsored by a church agency, but under a different number designation. 

At no single time were more than five such camps in operation, however.

A complete manual for camp directors was issued under date of May 10, 1944, by Selective Service.12 This set forth the manner in which the general administrative directives applied to camps and detailed certain additional things or matters in which changes were to be made. A subsequent chapter will discuss at greater length the differences between church-operated and Government-operated camps.

Special Rules for Each Type of Camp 

Although the Civilian Public Service Camps had more points in common than otherwise, there were special directives for certain types of projects. For instance, Administrative Directives Nos. 6, 16, 16R, 20, 21, 22, and 23, from National Headquarters 13 covered special agricultural work for the most part. Parts of the first four also governed the use of assignees in emergency farm labor. Administrative Directive No. 18, outlined the conditions under which men were assigned to research or "guinea pig," projects. Administrative Instructions, Nos. 1 to 4, covered the general administration of the hospital units.

The Uniqueness of the Civilian Work Program 

As stated earlier, the entire civilian or camp work program for conscientious objectors was without much precedent in the United States. 

The administration and operation was somewhat experimental, and both the sponsoring church groups and the technical Government agencies concerned were in a sense pioneering in the field. Selective 

13 Appendix D, Item Nos. 24-74, Organization Instructions, complete texts of all significant administrative directives and memoranda.

Service hampered neither the church groups nor the cooperating agencies with many regulations and rules. There was set up, however, a force of field representatives whose duty it was to coordinate the program for the System and to insure that the best possible use was made of the services of the assignees. These representatives had wide latitude in the settlement of misunderstandings or disputes at the camp or project level.

At the beginning of the civilian work program there were but few camp regulations and other written instructions. The latter were in letter and sometimes mimeographed form. After 62 years of continuous operation only 31 administrative directives and 4 administrative instructions 14 had been issued directly affecting all types of work projects, that is, all phases of the program. Three of these dealt with discharge, 10 were replaced by revised issues in the series and some of the others had to do with demobilization or such matters as hours of work and holidays to be observed. Changes in the special 

Selective Service Regulations, directives, or instructions for camps were only made as a result of actual operations, usually as a result of the recommendations of the field representatives or as a result of conferences with interested groups called upon to improve project conditions.

In the hospital and agricultural phases of the program, particularly, meetings were necessary and unusually valuable for the reason that these projects had been set up on a much more "trial and error" basis than was true of the regular camps. In the latter, there were the precedents of the Civilian Conservation Corps to adapt, modify, and follow. 

Two major conferences were held concerning the hospital and training school activities. These were attended by directors of State mental programs, superintendents of institutions, representatives of the National Service Board, staff members of the various cooperating church agencies, representatives of the United States Public Health Service, and members of the staff of the Camp Operations Division, National Headquarters, Selective Service. To one of these conferences also came conscientious objectors from the various institutions. At these meetings all of the approaches to the activity were discussed and in some instances revisions were made in the regulations or directives. 

Much of the success attained in the hospital phase was attributable to the constructive work of the conferences which were also held on the agricultural activity. Representatives of the Department of Agriculture, the United States Employment Service, the church groups, and other organizations also met from time to time in conferences to improve operating conditions in the farm labor projects.

Résumé Statement 

This kind of cooperation was largely responsible for the success of the civilian work program carried on by the conscientious objectors of World War II whose beliefs would not permit them to accept either combatant or noncombatant service with the armed forces. Although the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940 provided for it, the average American citizen was somewhat skeptical of an objector program on work of national importance under civilian direction. The concept was fairly new and the country had almost no experience in applying it. The whole proposition at first looked much like a special privilege or unwise arrangement for Selective Service registrants who were averse even to performing noncombatant duty with the Army or Navy of the United States in a time of emergency.

By the end of the 6½ years experience which the System had with the program, however, there was a marked difference in attitude throughout the country. A careful selection of work projects or activities and their location together with their skillful operation caused the demands for the program to exceed its facilities. This was the result of painstaking efforts by the National Service Board for Religious Objectors and other church organizations, of technical agencies in the Federal Government, such as the Department of 

Agriculture, and of the Camp Operations Division, National Headquarters, Selective Service. 

Basically, the civilian work or work-of-national-importance program was a camp operation. Civilian Public Service Camps were set up for the program. At these camps the Class IV-E assignees were accepted from the local boards of the System, given fundamental training in camp life and work, observed for special aptitudes and tried out as to general cooperation with the program. Most of the camps, which numbered 151 in all, were sponsored by churches or groups of churches who had directors stationed at them to conduct what was termed the "camp life" of the units. The actual work was under superintendents, however, who were employees of the Federal agencies mainly concerned with the projects of the camps. A total of eight camps, however, were at one time or other operated entirely by the Government without any church sponsorship. 

The regular work of the average camp was a single manual project like soil conservation, forestry service, or land reclamation, and the personnel of the unit was stationed in the camp all of the time. However, as the program developed many camps assumed more than one project, and the objectors on duty in them were dispersed throughout the area covered by the projects and even into adjoining or separate districts. Some camps even had no work project of the regular kind,

their personnel all being engaged on special projects and numbers of them being on detached assignments. The special projects, several of which were highly specialized in nature, covered such widely different activities as hospital service, scientific research, and dairy-herd testing. Therefore the work-of-national-importance idea for conscientious objectors became a program with many phases or activities and resulted in a distinct and valuable contribution to the emergency effort of 1940-47.

X 

CIVILIAN PUBLIC SERVICE CAMPS FOR OBJECTORS 

Beyond the civilian work program for Class IV-E objectors, the operation of its Civilian Public Service Camps during the national emergency of 1940-47 is also worthy of consideration. The Class

IV-E registrant of Selective Service, as will be recalled, was one to whom any service in the armed forces, either noncombatant (Class I-A-O) or combatant (Class I-A) was a violation of conscience. 

When a local board of the System found him to be available for such duty and to possess a valid conscientious objection claim, he was, therefore, classified in accordance with the 1940 law and the general regulations for assignment to work of national importance under civilian direction. The establishment of the work program and the operation of the Civilian Public Service Camps was a practical effort to observe the dual approach of the law, first, that every liable and selected person should serve, an attitude held by the general public, and, second, that such duty must be within the confines of conscience, as advocated by pacifist and other churches. 

Arrival of the Objector in Camp

When the conscientious objector arrived at the Civilian Public Service Camp after having been forwarded and furnished travel there by a local board, he reported to the camp director or his representative. 

In most instances, that is, except where the unit was Governmentoperated, the director was an employee of the church or church group sponsoring the camp as has been mentioned. Upon the assignee's reporting to the director his arrival was recorded and he was made acquainted with the camp personnel and the first things which he would be required to do. The camp director had already received by mail five copies of the assignee's Order to Report for Work of National Importance, DSS Form 50.¹ He therefore certified the arrival of the registrant in the space provided on the form and mailed four of the copies to the National Headquarters of Selective Service. 

The other copy was retained in the camp files. 

¹ Appendix F, Item Nos. 95 and 96. 181

In the event the assignee did not reach the camp within 48 hours after the date scheduled for his arrival by the local board, the director there was required to report such fact by air mail to the Director of Selective Service. Under no circumstances did the camp director communicate directly with a local board of the System. 

An Additional Physical Examination 

2 The first assignment of the objector at the Civilian Public Service Camp was to the camp doctor. The preinduction examination which the registrant had already passed was final insofar as his acceptance in camp was concerned. This supplementary examination was necessary to determine the acquiring of a communicable disease or a general physical or mental change between the time of the preinduction examination and the date of reporting to camp. A complete record of the assignee's physical condition was made at the camp and sent to National Headquarters in cases where it was felt that there had been a deterioration in the man's condition since the preinduction examination. However, such men were necessarily retained in camp or hospitalized pending instructions from the Director of Selective Service.

Immunization Against Disease 

With few exceptions all objectors were inoculated against typhoid and vaccinated against smallpox within 48 hours of reporting to a Civilian Public Service Camp. These inoculations and vaccinations were given by the physician in attendance at the camp. Upon completion, proper notations were made on the assignee's record at the camp headquarters. The few exceptions to this general practice were men who claimed their religious beliefs prevented immunization, and they were required to sign statements relieving the camp director and the System of all responsibility for failure to comply with the stipulation of the special Selective Service Regulations for camps in this regard.

Orientation and Issuance of Equipment 

Before an objector was detailed to any specific duty he was informed about the camp regulations and about the minimum requirements of Selective Service and of the technical agency in charge of the work project. An orientation course was given in which information covering the relationship of various jobs to the work project and the overall program of the technical agency was given. Attendance at these meetings was mandatory on the part of assignees released by the camp director to a work project, unless specifically excused by the project 2 The discussion here relates to practices during the latter years of the operation. 

VII has a more complete coverage of the problem of physical examination. Ch.

) superintendent. Rules of safety were given each registrant because the prevention of accidents and the encouragement of work safety were the main objects of this first training. In these orientation classes the men were acquainted also with rules governing leaves of absence, furloughs, health activities, and camp discipline. 

In the Government-operated Civilian Public Service Camps, that is, in camps having no church sponsorship, all assignees were given their full allotment of camp and work clothes during this early period. In the church-sponsored camps the objectors were supposed to have their own work clothes, but in the event an assignee did not have such clothes, he was fitted out by the church administration. 

Special Assignments for Volunteers

When this orientation period was completed, a conscientious objector was assigned to the civilian work program according to his qualifications and the needs of the project or projects. Every effort was made to place a man in a job that suited his physical condition and education. Many skilled positions had to be filled and operators of special equipment were always in demand. However, most of the work consisted of ordinary out-door labor which required physically fit young men. There were experiment stations and special units in various parts of the United States, and these required men with special technical skills. After an assignee had worked 3 months in the original work camp he was considered eligible for the special units. Assignment to all special work was on a voluntary basis. It was necessary in each case for a registrant to indicate a desire for the special type of work and also to submit evidence of satisfactory mental and physical condition.

Undesirability of Premature Project Discussions 

Although it was desirable to prevent such occurrence, upon occasions a feeling of unrest arose in the camps and special projects. This was due primarily to the interested church groups giving out information on the planning of additional projects before such projects had been accepted by the Director of Selective Service. In the event the planned projects did not materialize some dissatisfaction developed among registrants who had become prematurely interested in them.

A Handbook Description of Camp Life 

Information in the camper's handbook of one Civilian Public Service Camp contained a good over-all view of the assignee's relation to the camp with particular emphasis on orientation of the new arrival. 

This was a church-operated camp and the booklet was the product of the operating agency, the Mennonite Central Committee. The hand-

book is quoted in its entirety, except for the table of contents and a two-page map of the camp grounds. Some condensation of the material has been made to conserve space, but the wording has not been altered:

FOREWORD 

For some time it has been felt that a camper's handbook would be a valuable aid to men who transfer to our camp or such men as come as new assignees. 

Our camp has now been operated by the Mennonite Central Committee since the first group of men came to open it October 21, 1942. Many things have happened in the period of time from then to now. It would be impossible to mention all of these and their importance to the life of this camp in the brief space available in this book. Many of the events have no importance other than that they were stepping stones to what we have now. Some of the things which we have now will serve a similar purpose. 

While it is clear that with the changing of the personnel of the camp various minor adjustments have to be made, it shall be kept in mind that certain basic considerations are always present as Mennonite Central Committee concerns, Briefly, the following concerns should be mentioned: 

1. That at all times, at work or at play, we live the life consistent to the convictions which brought us to camp in the first place. That calls for a positive 

Christian witness. 

2. That so far as is consistent with the dictates of your conscience you cooperate with all existing agencies operating this camp. Your coming to camp indicates you are willing to do so. 

3. That as far as possible, so long as it does not interfere with the operation of this camp, you be given the right to religious freedom and worship as your conscience gives you guidance. 

4. That your individual physical needs be met wherever possible and consistent to group living.

To carry out these concerns is at best a man-sized task. We can never hope to accomplish them without your help. We are confident that we can count on you. With your help we may look to success.

HISTORY AND LOCATION OF CAMP 

Our camp is one of many former CCC camps of this area. Most of these camps are now closed and dismantled. Our camp was one of the last ones to be built. As a matter of fact when it was taken over by the MCC, part of it had not been completed. It also served as a dumping place for many other of the 

CCC camps which had been ordered closed.

MCC took over this camp on October 19, 1942. The opening staff included: 

John Synder and Phil Frey, MCC; Paul G. Tschetter, Dale Nebel, Oscar Wiebe, Miss Marie Groening, and Miss Edna Peters. On October 21, 1942, a carload of assignees arrived from CPS No. 28, Medaryville, Ind. Two days later 97 new assignees coming from various midwestern States arrived. And so the picture has been changing ever since camp was opened. 

Camp is located in Pennington County, S. Dak. We are about 40 miles due west of Rapid City and are truly "in the heart of the hills." We are about 2,500 feet higher than Rapid City and a little under a thousand feet higher than Hill City. 

Our elevation is 5,737 feet. Camp is located on Castle Creek. To the west of us is Flag Mountain which is said to be the third highest peak in the Black Hills and is right around 7,000 feet above sea level. We are about 15 miles northwest of Hill City.

CIVILIAN PUBLIC SERVICE CAMPS FOR OBJECTORS > 

185 The history of our camp would also include some reference to the Deerfield Dam which we are helping to build. The dam is to meet a twofold purpose, namely, to be a reservoir (8,000 foot-acres of water) for a much needed water supply for Rapid City, and be a reservoir (7,000 foot-acres of water) for the Rapid Valley irrigation project near Rapid City. The need for this water supply dates back to pre-World War I days, and has increased as Rapid City grew to industrial maturity. Irrigation farming, the State cement plant, the school of mines, mining operations, lumbering, and cattle grazing have all been factors in the growth of Rapid City. The original survey was undertaken about 5 years ago by the Bureau of Reclamation. Much of the preliminary work was done by 

WPA, CCC, and, just before our coming, private labor. Most of the work you see can be attributed to CPS labor.

SUGGESTIONS FOR CORPORATE LIVING 

You no doubt see the necessity of understanding each other, when it becomes necessary for a large group of men to live together in rather close contact. In an ideal system where everything "clicks" it should not be necessary to have any rules or regulations. Unfortunately, no one is perfect nor is there a system which is perfect. Thus the necessity of an understanding. 

There is another angle to our living together. Some of the things we are asked to do, do not lie in the realm of our own choice. In other words, because of the fact that Selective Service or the Mennonite Central Committee has a much larger over-all view of the general problem of administrating civilian public service, they may be called on or think it desirable for the program to ask of us certain things which we may not understand or wholly appreciate. So far as 

MCC is concerned, I am certain they will always wish to deal with you in the spirit of Christian love.

Locally, in those things which affect us and do not directly relate to general administrative policies determined by others, we wish at all times to be friendly, cooperative, considerate of all groups, helpful, and above all things Christian in spirit. To that end the camp staff has been placed here and to that end the camp council has been established. 

It is quite clear that this type of living is of a much higher order than the "thou must do thus and thus" variety. It certainly appears to be more in harmony with the Christian spirit. However, no one will deny the fact that it is a much more difficult way. It assumes that you are honest in motive and purpose. It requires a constant self-discipline. It places group values ahead 

Due to the uncertainty of the afternoon session, the entire afternoon session may be changed to another afternoon.

of personal gain. It emphasizes the positive characteristics of Christian living.

Statistics on Objectors in Camps 

Complete statistical information showing the flow of registrants into and out of the Civilian Public Service Camps is presented in Table No. 

8. This table and Table No. 17 in chapter XV which gives detailed information regarding the reasons for discharge by month of discharge, differ slightly from other statistics kept by the Camp Operations Division, National Headquarters, Selective Service. In developing this table the data were compiled as of the actual date of arrival in and departure from camp, except for objectors separated by reason of delinquency and men known as Civilian Public Service

Ordinarily, the statistics of the Camp Operations Division were kept according to the date when registrants were assigned by National Headquarters and when their discharge was reported to National Headquarters. It was necessary for the System, the churches or operating agencies and the Federal Government or technical agencies to have figures so based for planning purposes. Such data gave somewhat larger figures than those reflected in Tables No. 8 and 9, however, because on this basis assignees were counted as being in camp before the actual date of arrival and dischargees were counted as having left some time after actual departure.

Regular and Special Camp Projects 

Various technical or Federal agencies used conscientious objectors on work of national importance during World War II as has been seen. 

By securing this labor assistance they were able to carry on important projects and functions to an extent that would otherwise have been impossible. Without such help some activities would have had to be abandoned. This was especially true in the experimental and scientific research fields.

It has been noted that all of the regular projects of the civilian or camp work program to which registrants were first assigned upon reporting to camp, were operated by different bureaus of the Department of Agriculture and Interior. In the Department of Agriculture there were three bureaus so engaged, namely, the Forest Service, the 

Soil Conservation Service and the Farm Security Administration. 

Bureaus similarly engaged in the Department of the Interior were the National Park Service, the Bureau of Reclamation, the General 

Land Office, and the Fish and Wildlife Service. 

In addition to the regular projects there were also the special ones which were established beginning with March 1942. After camp assignees had served a reasonable time, that is three months on the regular ones, they were allowed to volunteer for service on the special projects. These special projects included units under the direction of the Agriculture Labor Administration and the Extension Service of the Department of Agriculture, the Coast and Geodetic Survey and the Weather Bureau of the Department of Commerce, the Office of Scientific Research and Development, the Office of the Surgeon General of the Army, the Public Health Service, the Puerto Rico Reconstruction 

Administration, and various State training schools and Veterans' 

Administration and State mental hospitals. 

Distribution of Camp Assignees by Project 

As previously stated, the Civilian Public Service Camp program began with all conscientious objectors doing the same general type of work as that formerly undertaken by the Civilian Conservation Corps. 

In fact, the majority of men were so engaged throughout the entire operation. At the time when the camps had their greatest personnel strength in the fall of 1946, it is true that more men were assigned to the special projects of mental hospitals and training schools than to any single regular project. However, registrants assigned to the Forest 

Service, the Soil Conservation Service, and the National Parks Service alone outnumbered the training school and hospital attendant group.

Table No. 9 has been prepared to show the number of men working under the different technical or Government agencies at the end of October in each calendar year. October was chosen because in that month of 1945 the camps were the largest in size of any time during the 62 years of operation. Reference to this table gives a good general picture of the number of assignees by type of project for each year. 

A great deal of effort was expended in the Civilian Public Service Camps to select the best qualified men for the special work assignments. 

This would not only benefit the project but it would also utilize the experience and knowledge of the objector to the maximum. In this screening process men were found who had the necessary schooling and experience to perform special tasks far beyond the work they were doing on regular projects. Some of them did not choose to volunteer for special assignments, however, and still others were not physically or mentally suited or did not have the cooperative attitude necessary to justify their transfer.

Variations in Working Hours up When the first special Selective Service Camp Regulations were set for the C. P. S. Camps it was provided that:

1 The hours of work on the project at any camp will be determined by the technical agency. No limitation is set on the number of hours that an assignee may be asked to work in any given day or week." 

This stipulation was arrived at after several conferences between the Camp Operations Division at National Headquarters and the National Service Board for Religious Objectors. It was the opinion of the System and other Federal agencies that an 8-hour work day would be proper. However, some of the religious farm representatives were in favor of longer hours because of their "sun-up to sun-down" work background. The agreement finally reached was that each camp should set up its own requirements as long as they met with the approval of the technical or Government agency concerned with the work project or projects. Disputes in this regard were to be referred to the Camp Operations Division for final decision. 

The camp regulations likewise specified that in addition to the regular hours of work the assignees would be subject to emergency calls by the project superintendent of the technical agency, at any time, for the purpose of fighting forest fires or for work in connection with other emergencies affecting life or property. The freedom which was thus given for local determination caused a wide variance not only in the number of work hours, but also in the time allowed for travel to and from projects and for lunch periods. Then as the assignees of the various camps became acquainted with one another and began to exchange correspondence, complaints arose among those who found themselves in camps requiring longer hours. This led to the issuance of the following instructions:

Beginning March 1, 1942, and continuing until further notice, assignees will be lined up available for turn-over to technical agencies at 7:30 a. m. daily. 

They will be under the supervision of the technical agency until they are returned to camp at 5 p. m. The hours 7:30 a. m. to 5 p. m. daily include all necessary travel time, and three-quarters of an hour should be allowed for lunch. 

On Saturdays the hours of work shall be from 7:30 a. m. to 12 noon, but the superintendent may turn back to the camp director not to exceed 25 percent of the men turned over at work call for camp duties, and the superintendent may use such additional men as he sees fit for project work at the camp site. Men turned over to the camp director for camp duties will work the same hours as the men in the field, and their labor will be properly supervised by the camp director or his authorized representative.

The foregoing hours of labor will in no way affect the liability of assignees for emergency calls by the project superintendent at any hour of the day or night for work of an emergency nature.*

These new working hours were observed until the end of the year 1942, when, in accordance with the President's request that all Federal

Subject: Hours of Work: 

In accordance with joint resolution of Congress No. 171, Executive Order No. 

9289, and the President's request that all Federal agencies work a minimum of 8 hours per day 6 days per week, previous instructions concerning hours of work are hereby rescinded and the following will apply. 

Beginning January 2, 1943, or as soon thereafter as these instructions are received and continuing until further notice, the hours of work in Civilian Public Service Camps will be from 7:30 a. m. to 5 p. m. Monday through Saturday of each week except for such holidays as may be authorized for Federal employees. 

The hours 7:30 a. m. to 5 p. m. daily will include all necessary travel time and 1 hour to be allowed for lunch.

On Saturdays, the superintendent may turn back to the camp director not to exceed 25 percent of the men turned over at work call to be used for the day on camp duties. Men turned over to the camp director for camp duty will work the same hours as the men in the field, their labor being properly supervised by the camp director or his authorized representative. At the discretion of the project superintendent the above hours for beginning and ending work may be reasonably modified to meet local variations in hours of daylight and in those camps where the project requires that work be done in shifts, changes may be made to meet such conditions providing the total hours or days per week remain the same. Neither will the foregoing hours of labor in any way affect the liability of assignees for emergency calls by the project superintendent at any hour of the day or night for work of an emergency nature. 

Administrative Directive No. 5 was issued January 15, 1943 to cover this matter. It used almost the same words as the circular quoted above, but noted the fact that the provisions of the directive would not apply to hospital and other special units. In this latter connection it was provided that registrants assigned to such hospitals and units would work the same hours as the regular civilian employees stationed therein."

After VE- and VJ-Days, working hours in the Federal Government were reduced to 44 hours per week and the hours of work in the C. P. S. Camps were similarly adjusted by Administrative Directive 

No. 27 issued August 17, 1945. This was soon followed by Administrative Directive No. 28 on August 29, 1945, which made a further reduction to 40 hours per week. Each of these directives also made certain minor adjustments in the matter of lunch periods, travel time, and the like.
