Administrative Directive No. 1 was replaced by Administrative Directive No. 3 and, on February 1, 1945, by Administrative Directive No. 4. Each made similar provisions regarding the hours of work of assignees in hospital and special units.

Administrative Directive No. 29, issued August 29, 1945, made provision for the observance of holidays. Previous provision had been for the observance of such holidays as were generally authorized for observance in the Federal Government. During the war period 

Christmas, however, was the only day so observed.

Monetary Allowances to Objectors in Camps At the beginning of the civilian work program no consideration was given to providing allowances of money to the assignees in the Civilian Public Service Camps. However, it was soon recognized that as a result many were faced with some privation. For one thing, their personal appearances indicated a need for such articles as toilet and shaving soap, razor blades, tooth powder, brushes, combs, shoe polish and similar items. In March 1942, the churches sponsoring the camps decided to give each assignee $2.50 per month for such personal necessities. This became the general rule for a period of about 18 months, when two of the sponsoring churches raised the amount to $5 per month. In Government-operated camps, it should be added, the allowance was always $5 per month for each assignee. 

The Housing of Camp Assignees in Barracks 

The assignees in the work camps were usually housed in barracks that accommodated 40 or 50 men each. As a general rule each camp unit had four or five barrack buildings which took care of from 150 to 200 men. The units ordinarily had, in addition to these buildings, an administrative building, a mess hall, a kitchen and a pantry. One of the barracks or another suitable building was usually set aside for religious purposes. There were also education, recreation and storage buildings, bath houses, latrines, and laundry facilities. Adjoining these were the technical service buildings comprising administration and storage buildings, garages, tool sheds and repair shops. 

Medical Care and Sanitation Each C. P. S. Camp had a physician who was responsible for the health of the objectors stationed there. Arrangements were made with the nearest local hospital of suitable nature for assignees to be admitted upon the order of the camp doctor. The camp director along with the doctor was responsible for holding a daily sick call and the doctor was available at all times for an emergency call.

The sanitation of the camp unit was the responsibility of the camp director, with the advice of the camp doctor, and the unit was subject to inspection from time to time by representatives of the United States or State Public Health Service. The minimum standards of sanita tion were the same as those applicable to the units operated under the 

Civilian Conservation Corps.

Food Service in the Camps 

Considerable difficulty was experienced with the camp mess in the early days of the operation. This was due to a number of factors. 

One was the inexperience of the men who were given kitchen duty. 

There were few trained cooks among assignees. Then, too, the dietitians in the camp units at first were not experienced in feeding men on work projects. Government rationing of certain foods added to the problem. The camps, being classified as institutions, had small rationed food allowances per assignee. This created considerable difficulty because the objectors in the camps were doing hard manual labor for which the food requirements were greater than those of ordinary civilian work. In addition the camps were often not popular with local merchants and frequently even authorized articles on ration could not be procured. The distance from large markets was another handicap for many units.

However, the food situation improved in most camps as a result of experience. Schools were established to which cooks, bakers, and dietitians were sent, and manuals and cook books were provided. 

Pressure was exerted upon the sponsoring agencies to increase the daily food allowance for each man. The raising of this allowance from 30 to 40 cents per day in several units made a material difference. In such connection it should be pointed out that the money allowance for food was supplemented in most cases by produce from a camp garden or farm and by donations from associated churches and individuals.

In the administration of the camps there was an understanding between the church representatives and the technical agencies that when it was necessary to send registrants out in small groups of six or more to the side camps in isolated areas the cost of feeding these groups would be the joint responsibility of the church and technical agency. At the side camps, cost figures were kept, and the technical agency met the expenses which were over and above the food allowance at the main unit.

At spike camps which were the small sub-units consisting of five men or less, the assignees were considered on detached service from the main camp and the technical agency provided the entire cost of subsistence. When objectors from the main unit were detailed to other areas or special duty the technical agency provided all travel expenses, food and shelter. In the Government-operated camps the men were given food allowances on the same basis as those serving in the Army, except that the per diem allotment was certified to the camp director for each succeeding month on the basis of the actual per diem expenditures of the Army for the preceding month. 

8 For additional information reference should be made to Administrative Directives Nos. 

1, 3, 4, 16, 18, 20, 21, 22, Appendix D, Item Nos. 24, 26, 27, 39, 42, 44, 45, 46, respectively.

Laundry Service 

One of the greatest problems of the camps at the start was the washing and ironing of clothing and bedding. Many camp units had small commercial laundry equipment left over from Civilian Conservation Corps days. Such equipment was operated by the registrant assignees of the Civilian Public Service Camp and usually a crew of three did the washing for the average size camp. Under ordinary circumstances ironing services were also limited, though there was no restriction on the number of rough dried work articles laundered in spite of the problem of washing facilities. 

Commercial laundry equipment was not available for purchase during much of World War II and many camps therefore used two or three family-sized washing machines. However, this light equipment was not satisfactory for the hard and continuous use demanded of it. 

Motors and bearings were a constant source of trouble and there were often long delays in repairing them. Some of the camps designed and constructed their own laundry equipment which proved more satisfactory.

Provisions for Education 

The general educational program for objectors who were assignees to the civilian or camp work program, was the responsibility of the camp director; special on-the-job training, however, was carried on by the project superintendent. Administrative Directive No. 17, issued October 1, 1943,⁹ amplified section 691.15 of the special Selective Service Regulations for camps 10. and outlined the job-training and orientation which were within the province of the project superintendent, and the additional technical training which was the responsibility of the camp director. In addition, many of the camps had more or less definite programs of elective educational study and work project training. It was therefore suggested in Administrative 

Directive No. 17 that project training activities be placed in the hands of an assignee selected for that purpose by the superintendent after consultation with the director.

The Providing of Recreation by Church Groups 

The sponsoring or operating agency, through the camp director, was responsible for all of the recreational activities at the camp unit during the off-hours from work. As a rule, each unit had a recreational supervisor who arranged programs of sports. Most camps had papers, magazines, and books. Practically every camp had a motionpicture projector, and moving-pictures were shown each week. When transportation was available sight-seeing trips were made to points 

• Appendix D, Item No. 41. 

10 Appendix B, Item No. 3.

of interest within the area where the units were located. In the 

Government-operated camps a special welfare allowance was provided by the Government partly for recreational purposes. It amounted to $1 per man per month for the first 100 of a camp and 50 cents per month for all over that number. However, the use of Government vehicles for recreational purposes was prohibited." 

The Providing of Religious Services 

In the church-sponsored camps all of the religious activities of objectors were under the supervision of the camp director. The camp units had regular services on the Sabbath and Holy Days and these generally were in charge of the church administration represented at the particular camp. However, the assignees at a given unit might belong to several different religious denominations and so groups of registrants who desired a service conforming to their church beliefs, when such were not available, usually made arrangements of their own at the camp. Each man was likewise given the privilege of attending any local church in the community where the unit was located, and the use of Government vehicles for this purpose was authorized. 

In the Government-operated camps an attempt was made to provide religious services through a chaplain from the Federal Council of Churches of Christ. This plan did not succeed very well due to lack of interest on the part of the assignees in such camp units. 

Furlough Privileges of Camp Assignees 

The assignees in objector camps were given similar privileges to those of the enlisted men in military or naval service as far as absences from camp were concerned. Liberty or leave during nonworking hours or on nonworking days and furlough from camp for periods including working time was provided. Provision was also made for absence from the camp unit in a sick or illness status. These matters were subject to control by special rules and by the camp director. The rules were set up in Administrative Directive No. 7. They were later revised by the issuance of Administrative Directive No. 31 on October 

10, 1945.12 It should be added here perhaps that the suspension of the privilege of absence from camp or the reduction of furlough time were the only measures which could be taken by a camp director for disciplinary purposes.

Assignees Eligible for Transfer to Special Projects 

Assignees to Civilian Public Service Camps were eligible for transfer to special projects and units after they had served at least three months in a regular work camp and demonstrated that they were

qualified for special assignment. In most cases of this kind, a representative of the special unit would visit the work camp to select from applicants those whom he felt had satisfactory qualifications. When selections had been made by him, applications for transfer were forwarded to the Camp Operations Division at National Headquarters, and, if they were approved, the transfers were then effected. 

When transfer was made at Government expense, it was under the general provisions of sections 608.44 and 608.45 of the special Selective Service Regulations for camps. Prior to July 20, 1945, the transportation accommodations furnished assignees were similar to those furnished to military personnel. Due to the large military movements at that time, however, it became necessary to make some modification of previous policy. Special instructions issued that date were as follows: 

1. In view of the extreme shortage of pullman cars, it is deemed necessary to curtail pullman travel for assignees being transferred or discharged. 

2. Effective this date, transportation for assignees being transferred or discharged will be provided on the following basis: (a) On journeys of 48 hours or less, coach travel will be provided. (b) On journeys of more than 48 hours, the usual pullman accommodations will be provided, if available. Tourist class accommodations will be used whenever possible. 

3. When assignees have been ordered to transfer and where pullman travel is allowed but where such accommodations cannot be secured, assignee will proceed by coach on the date ordered for start of travel from camp, farm, hospital, or special unit. 

4. In order to relieve the pressure upon railroad transportation, bus transportation, if available, will be utilized on all travel of short duration. 

5. The foregoing rules will control all travel of assignees in hospital, “guinea pig", and farm units as well as camps.

Objectors on Detached Service 

As already indicated, the National Service Board actually operated but one camp itself. This project was an administrative expedient for assignees which the Board was permitted to use on detached service in Washington to assist in its camp activities work office. After VE-Day these three committees became extensively engaged in relief work in Europe and permission was granted for some of their detached service registrants to work in other places preparing food and clothing for shipment abroad. 

Out of the 151 Civilian Public Service Camps, the Friends and the Brethren church groups operated about 30 each, the Mennonites, nearly 60, and the remainder were operated by scattered church groups or by the Government. The National Service Board and the sponsoring or operating groups, or the operating groups working through the Board, cared for the personal needs of the assignees while in the camp units.

In a church-operated unit the camp staff usually consisted of a director, assistant director, certain supervisors, a nurse and a dietician.

The National Service Board also served as a clearing house for the assignment of conscientious objectors to Civilian Public Service Camps. 

When the Camp Operations Division at the National Headquarters of Selective Service received a Conscientious Objectors Report (DSS 

Form 48) indicating that a registrant in Class IV-E had been called for civilian work, the man's name, together with a statement indicating his preference for a church- or a Government-operated camp, was submitted to the National Service Board. The Board thereupon sent the man a copy of its pamphlet, "The Conscientious Objector under the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940” which presented the background of the civilian work program and gave considerable information on the types of projects available and the methods of assignment to them. It contained specific instructions about what the man should take to camp with him and some details regarding what would occur upon his arrival. The Board also sent the objector a Questionnaire (NS 101) on which he was to submit information about himself and his wishes concerning camp assignment. After reviewing the information contained in this Questionnaire and consulting with the individual's church organization, the Board made a recommendation to the Camp Operations Division regarding the camp to which the registrant should be assigned.

Federal Ownership of Property and Equipment 

Most of the property and equipment at the objector camps belonged to the United States Government. It had been acquired by Selective 

Service through the liquidation of the Civilian Conservation Corps. 

When the National Service Board for Religious Objectors took over the administration of a camp, arrangements were made whereby the National Service Board could accept as a loan from the System whatever property was available for housing and other purposes. 

The Camp Operations Division set up a system of accountability and the National Service Board provided a bond in the amount of

CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION 

$500,000 to cover the transfer of and responsibility for this Government property. The Division, however, assumed the loss of all equipment worn out through normal work activities. When the field representatives of the Division visited the camp units they acted as property inspectors and examined all worn out items. If the condition was the result of normal project work, the inspector would recommend to the property officer of the Camp Operations Division that the worn out items of equipment be dropped from the records of the Board without cost to the sponsoring religious group. 

When property was lost or damaged and there was a question of negligence, it was necessary to make a survey. Information and facts surrounding the misuse or disappearance were gathered and studied for the purpose of fixing the responsibility. If it developed that reasonable care had been exercised, the religious agency was released from responsibility.

When the evidence indicated carelessness or theft, the shortage was charged to the National Service Board. After the camps had all been closed, the entire outlay of property and equipment had been accounted for with the exception of items valued at approximately $11,500. This amount was billed to and paid for by the Board. On the basis of the gross number of men housed in Civilian Public Service Camps, the loss amounted to less than a dollar per man for the entire period of occupancy.

Safety Regulations 

At the beginning of the civilian work program it was decided that the safety regulations established during the Civilian Conservation Corps operation would likewise be satisfactory for the Civilian Public 

Service Camps. Copies of Civilian Conservation Corps Safety Regu lations were made available to all project offices in sufficient quantities so that a copy could be placed in the hands of each foreman and other key employee.

Suggestions and instructions were issued to camp superintendents and directors from time to time amplifying and defining more specifically the safety regulations for matters peculiar to the Civilian Public Service Camps. Instructions were released also upon occasion to clarify reporting and other procedures incidental to the safety program.16 

All accidents resulting in injuries to assignees, loss of life, or damage to or destruction of property were considered the responsibility of the 

16 Administrative Directive No. 9, issued April 15, 1943, and Administrative Directive 

No. 13 issued April 12, 1943, Appendix D, Item Nos. 31 and 35; also the Daily Report of

supervisory personnel of the technical or Federal agency, if the accident occurred during working hours. An employee responsible for the enforcement of safety regulations was subject to disciplinary action if it was shown that the accident could have been prevented by the exercise of proper vigilance on his part. The camp director was held responsible for all safety measures during the time the assignees were not actually working on the project or projects of the technical agency.

In the opening months of the civilian work program, the technical agencies experienced a great deal of difficulty regarding matters of safety due to indifference on the part of assignees. Because of this and to give himself assistance in this regard the camp or project superintendent appointed a safety assistant. This assistant was usually selected from among the assignees. He was expected to be a man of mature judgment and capable of obtaining the cooperation of the other objectors. He was to devote his entire time and effort to safety measures and it was hoped that he would be more effective with the assignees themselves than would the representative of a technical agency. The result was that in camps where there were assignee safety assistants the frequency of accidents was much lower than in units where the objectors could not be interested in permitting one of their own number to take this responsibility. 

Duties of the Assignee Safety Assistant 

The duties of the assignee safety assistant at a C. P. S.

Camp were in general as follows: 

1. To keep a close check on equipment and working conditions from a safety standpoint through a weekly general inspection made in person. The superintendent also designated various project employees to report regularly to the assistant regarding equipment, working conditions, and other safety matters. 

2. To advise the superintendent each week of the results of his personal inspection and these employee reports. 

3. To discuss with the heads of various crews the hazards which might be encountered when a new project was about to be initiated. 

4. To make periodic inspections of the various work projects at the request of the superintendent. The time set for such an inspection was at the discretion of the superintendent since it required the assistant to be away from his regular job for a short period. 

5. To prepare monthly reports on Report of Illness or Injury (DSS

Form 51-B) and submit copies to the project superintendent for transmittal to the proper authorities.

6. To make narrative reports of all accidents charged to the technical agency which reports were to be kept available for inspection in the camp files. 

7. To submit a monthly report of his activities to the superintendent in order to obviate the possibility of overlooking important phases. 

8. To act as chairman of a safety advisory committee, and to assist the superintendent and the foremen in conducting a mass safety meeting of assignees each month. 

Allocation of Accident Costs 

All expenses incidental to accidents and sickness were the responsibility of the churches in camps which they operated even though the accident or sickness may have occurred on a work project. In the 

Government-operated camps, the Government assumed this responsibility. Where the Government became involved in paying for medical and dental care, the schedule of fees of the Veterans' Administration was used for purposes of reimbursement. The Camp Operations 

Division adopted the Veterans' Administration schedule for the reason that it was believed to be based upon a broader and more representative experience than that of any other agency. 

Special Safety Emergency Units 

Special safety emergency units or crews of objectors were organized, trained and made available for disaster relief in the Civilian Public Service Camps. These were also available to communities within a 

100-mile radius of camp locations. The services of such assignees were offered to the Director of the Office of Civilian Defense where their use was desired by a local authority of this agency. Emergency units were not assigned to definite communities, in instances of this kind, but any civilian defense council could request the assistance of a unit for use in emergencies which arose in connection with any disaster.

The special safety emergency units organized in a camp for this purpose consisted of a leader, two truck drivers, one mechanic, six first-aid men, four cooks and assistants, six stretcher bearers and four utility workers. Each unit had the necessary transportation facilities, stretchers and first-aid kits and such other equipment and supplies as could be assembled and maintained. The names of registrants selected for these units were made a matter of record by the camp director.

The crews of the emergency units were prepared to give assistance in rescue work, in demolition and clearance, road repair, and emergency feeding and housing. They were available for the use of evacuation authorities and in rendering first aid, if needed. The statistical

J 

 

reports received from the camps located in the Midwest indicated that 15,490 man-days were actually contributed by the units in relief work following such disasters as tornadoes and floods in various communities.17

Objectors Assigned to Special Hospital Projects 

Turning from the operation of Civilian Public Service Camps as regards regular projects of the civilian work program, to their functioning with reference to special projects it can be said that men assigned to care for the mentally ill in hospitals and training schools were given the same food, provided the same quarters, had the same laundry service and worked the same hours as the regularly appointed personnel of these institutions. It would have created many administrative and other difficulties to have handled regular employees in one way and conscientious objectors in another. For one thing, work schedules would have been impossible to maintain under such an arrangement. Assignees doing this type of work were provided a monthly allowance of $15 by the institution which they were expected to use in providing themselves with clothing, other than uniforms required by the institution, toilet articles, and other miscellaneous items. Originally the allowance was $2.50 per month with the institution being required to provide clothing and toilet articles. However, experience proved this to be impractical of administration due to varying State laws, regulations or restrictions. Dental, medical, or hospital care necessary to keep the assignee fit for work was also provided by the institution.

In most institutions of this kind registrants were given immediately upon their reporting, an intensive training under the direction of physicians, nurses, and attendants. Naturally, some of the institutions went much further than others in this direction. The resultant efficiency of the objector, however, was a clear reflection of the intensity of the training provided.

A conscientious objector was usually appointed by the hospital superintendent as an assistant director of the group of assignees stationed in the institution. The superintendent himself served as the director. It might be added that among the duties of the assistant director was to keep a record of leaves, furloughs, and a "check-out" book which accounted for the time each assignee left and returned to the institution. It was possible for the institution head to stop a registrant from leaving the institution grounds if conditions warranted. 

This was seldom done, however, and hardly ever without first obtaining the permission of the Camp Operations Division. The assistant director was also charged with the responsibility of the educational 

17 Appendix E, Item Nos. 75-82.

CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION 

and recreational activities for the men assigned to the hospital. The cooperating church groups assisted in this regard and often definite training in foreign relief, missionary work, language, psychiatric care or other subjects was an additional inducement for men to volunteer for special project work in a particular institution. 

Special Food Production Work 

Conscientious objectors who volunteered for and were assigned to special food production work on dairy farms, in dairy herd testing or at experiment stations were provided with an allowance of $15 per month, paid by the employer. This amount was to provide them with clothing, toilet articles and other necessities. In addition, they were covered by insurance against death and accident and were given essential dental, medical, and hospital care. The last mentioned expenses were met from wages paid by the employer. It has previously been explained that the farmer, the herd-testing association or the institution using the special services of assignees in these ways paid the prevailing wages established by a county wage board. The expenses referred to above were deducted from these wages and the balance deposited with the United States Treasury in a special fund. 

Men assigned to special farm labor projects worked the hours observed by similar labor in the particular community of their location. Provisions were made for them to attend church services of their choice in near-by cities or towns. A system of furloughs, of shorter duration than in the regular camps, was provided. 

Scientific Experiment Activities 

Perhaps the special projects for which the fewest instructions were issued by the Camp Operations Division were those where objectors volunteered and were assigned as subjects of scientific experimentation. 

These projects were often referred to as "guinea pig" activities and their very nature precluded the issuance of directives. Registrants so assigned were expected to be on continuous duty under constant surveillance for the entire period of the actual experiment. This was in order that the effects of the experimental use of various foods or drugs could be continuously observed. The supervision required for experiments of this nature made it necessary for assignees to be placed entirely at the disposal of the project director. The director controlled the hours of experimentation and of recreation or leisure and decided when it was desirable to give the men "recuperative" furloughs. However, before a special project of this kind was set up the technical agency agreed that the assignees would be paid a $15 monthly allowance for clothing and other needs; that they would be provided with food, special clothing and laundry; and that they would be covered by

insurance to cover any hospital or medical care. It likewise assumed the responsibility for dental care, while the man was under its direction.

Another plan for administration was developed for men assigned to special projects under the direction of the United States Coast and Geodetic Survey. These involved mobile camp units operating in several States. The technical supervisors, as well as the assignees, had to furnish themselves with meals, laundry and certain facilities. Housing, in the form of tents or trailers, as well as cots and bedding were supplied by the Survey. It was necessary, however, to provide the conscientious objector with funds which he could use to secure other necessary facilities. To take care of this a per diem arrangement was worked out which enabled the assignee to provide himself with food, clothing, laundry, insurance against sickness and accident, and incidental expenses.

This per diem allowance was subject to change in order to meet local conditions.

Other Special Projects 

It would appear that with each new type of special project developed, it became necessary to set up a new system of administration to take care of the needs of assignees and yet at the same time comply with the rules, laws and regulations under which the technical agency functioned. In the case of registrants assigned to the United States 

Weather Bureau project, they were generally considered much the same as men in regularly operated camps when it came to food, quarters, laundry, hours of work, furloughs, recreation and education. 

However, they were provided by the Weather Bureau with $15 per month, and from this supplied themselves with clothing, toilet articles, sickness and accident insurance, and other necessities. 

With respect to the public health group of special projects in Florida, Mississippi, and Puerto Rico the interested church groups defrayed most of the expense. In Puerto Rico the territorial authorities provided quarters but all traveling expense to and from the island and food, clothing, and allowances were supplied by the church groups. 

There were no Federal contributions of any kind. In Florida and 

Mississippi the State health authorities provided housing, material, and equipment with which to do the work; Selective Service loaned beds, bedding, kitchen equipment and certain housekeeping supplies; and the church groups provided the assignees with all other requirements.

Special Projects in General 

While the foregoing indicates the many and varied conditions under which special projects operated, one general requirement prevailed.

When a conscientious objector had volunteered and had been accepted for service on a special project, the transportation expense from the original camp to the point of new duty was the responsibility of the technical agency operating the project. When a registrant had served his minimum term and had been authorized for return to "the nearest available camp," or where the services of an assignee were no longer desired, for any reason, the expense of the return was also borne by the technical agency. In the farm labor project the transportation charges were deducted from the wages paid by the employer. Where the expense was borne by the Federal Government, all agencies using conscientious objectors on special projects were directed to use the same methods of travel, the same meal allowances and the same room allowances as were provided men in camps who were transferred to other duties.

General Review 

It will have been observed, then, that the Civilian Public Service Camp which started out in 1941 to be much like the Civilian Conservation Corps unit of previous days, acquired more and more uniqueness as World War II progressed. At first, C. P. S. Camps were established jointly by the National Service Board for Religious Objectors, the Agriculture and Interior Departments of the Federal Government and Selective Service to conduct a civilian work program of national importance for conscientious objector registrants of the System whose beliefs did not allow them to serve in the armed forces. When in the routine process of selection these men were determined to be available for such duty, they were assigned to this type of camp in lieu of induction by the Army or Navy.

In the beginning, Civilian Public Service Camps were engaged upon projects involving little else than heavy manual labor. All of their objector assignees were stationed within the camp proper and it was a fairly self-sufficient unit as to living and working activities-quarters, food service, clothing, laundry service, and medical care; orientation, conditioning, and specialization; equipment and allowances; sanitation and safety; education, recreation, and religious services; furloughs and transfers; control, direction, administration and supervision. 

Gradually the scope of the projects widened for many camps and much of their personnel became deployed. This made for greater dependency upon the Federal, technical, or project agency and less participation by the church, sponsoring or operating group and by the administra tive agency, the Camp Operations Division of Selective Service. 

As has been seen, the regular projects of the civilian work program for C. O.'s which were in operation at the average C. P. S. Camp covered

such things as forestry, soil conservation, farm security, national park, reclamation, general land, and fish and wildlife activity. At the other extreme, operating out of special camp units in some instances, were the highly specialized projects of rescue, demolition, clearance, road repair, feeding and housing work of an emergency nature and, in the more standard categories, of caring for the mentally ill in hospitals and training schools; assisting in food production through dairy herd testing, experiment station and farm work; becoming the subjects of scientific experiments; and helping on coast and geodetic surveys and public health programs. Such phases of camp work could not be effectively operated except by very substantial reliance upon the technical agency.

XI 

THE WORK ACCOMPLISHED BY OBJECTORS IN C. P. S. CAMPS 

Some indication of the accomplishments of conscientious objectors in Civilian Public Service Camps during World War II has already been given in discussing the operation of the camps and the development of their work programs. A more comprehensive account of the efforts of these Class IV-E registrants is therefore in order. Their consciences, it will be recalled, did not permit them to accept service in the armed forces, so when they were selected as being available for such duty, Selective Service assigned them in lieu of induction to work of national importance under civilian direction. In this way the 

System provided a means for them to fulfill their obligation under the 

Selective Training and Service Act of 1940. 

Man-Days and Main Types of Work Performed 

A total of 5,931,632 man-days of project work was accomplished by objector assignees in Civilian Public Service Camps from May 1941 through March 1947. This figure represents the net hours devoted to work of national importance and does not include time spent in camp maintenance and other nonproject work or on sick leave or furlough. A complete account of the total man-days of work performed at the various projects is included in the statistical tables of 

Appendix E. 

The work accomplished can be divided into two kinds. The larger amount of 4,042,147 man-days was devoted to what may be termed the conservation of natural resources. This work was done mainly under the regular or manual type of project and the supervision of the United States Departments of Agriculture, Interior, and Commerce. The smaller amount of 1,889,485 was performed in the socalled conservation of human resources and was of the special type project and under State mental hospitals, the Veterans' Administration, the Public Health Service, the United States Office of Scientific Research and Development, the Surgeon General of the Army and a few State-aided general hospitals. 209

Some Outstanding Accomplishments 

It would be difficult to designate as most important any one project of the civilian work program for Class IV-E registrants of Selective Service. It may be of interest, however, to point out a few accomplishments which were very noteworthy. For instance, the assignees to 

C. P. S. Camps constructed and maintained 2,000 miles of fence, 475 miles of new telephone and electric power lines, 814 miles of new truck trails and 7,640 miles of stock and foot trails. Some 173,000 man-days were spent in tree nursery work and approximately 40 million trees were planted in areas needing reforestation. Eighteen hundred miles of new fire hazard reduction work was done on firebreaks, trails and roads, and 48,000 man-days were devoted to fighting forest fires. Several dams were completed which provided water for irrigating large tracts of arid land. Adding together the days spent on wartime food production in all of this type of project, there were more than a million so contributed. Much other forestry, soil conservation, and national parks work that had been handicapped by the loss of manpower was, through the camp program of the System, provided with labor to carry on these activities of conserving and preserving natural resources.

In the field of conserving human resources 1,512,896 man-days were spent in State mental hospitals, 120,403 man-days in veterans hospitals, and 105,473 in public health work. Additionally the office of the Surgeon General of the United States Army and the Office of Scientific Research and Development benefited through the use of 150,713 man-days in special projects and research work. 

Different Types and Quality Rating of Work Performed 

The succeeding pages of this chapter will present brief summaries on the type of work done in the different kinds of camps. It should be recognized in reading these summary statements that certain projects are more readily described than others and that the results achieved by some are more easily pictured. No inference should be made that a type of camp not fully described was considered less important than those described in detail. 

An estimate of the accomplishments or achievements of each camp in the total of 151¹ was made by the staff of the Camp Operations Division on the basis of personal knowledge of the work done, on the work records of the units and on the statements made by the Federal or technical agencies. This composite quality rating showed 52 percent of the camps as good, 42 percent as satisfactory, 4 percent as unsatisfactory and 2 percent as very poor. 

1 Appendix G, Item No. 119, List of 151 C. P. S. Camps.

THE WORK ACCOMPLISHED BY OBJECTORS IN C. P. S. CAMPS >> 211 Work Accomplished by Forest Service Camps The Forest Service of the United States Department of Agriculture was the technical agency of Civilian Public Service Camps located in National and State forests, primarily for the control of forest fires. 

It carried on a year-round program of disease control; fire presuppression; construction and maintenance of roads, trails, fire towers and communication lines; nursery operation; reforestation; and other work. All of this tied into the protection and preservation of forests. 

In the western part of the country, especially, the importance of such work went far beyond the protection of valuable timber, because the social and economic life of many communities depended upon the preservation of cover in the mountains to prevent floods and maintain a water supply. The bulk of the work in these camps was manual labor, strenuous and exhausting in the case of fire fighting, and it required young, physically fit objector registrants. However, the 

Forest Service needed and secured, or trained, Class IV-E assignees having any one of a variety of skills or specialized knowledges. This ranged from the operation and maintenance of motor vehicles, tractors, and other power machinery through construction, surveying, and engineering, to the scientific knowledge and experience that could be used in the forest experimental station. Objectors were used additionally as office workers and in the construction, operation and upkeep of communication equipment, including radios and telephones. 

One camp was organized which trained and used a selected group of assignees as parachute fire fighters for the control of fires in remote and inaccessible forests. Forest Service Camps were widely scattered, in order to provide as much fire protection as possible with the few men available.

The Chief of the United States Forest Service in the Department of Agriculture made a survey of all regional foresters who had operated conscientious objector projects and summarized their opinions as follows: 

EVALUATION OF PROGRAM 

The Forest Service was, of course most willing to respond to requests of the War Department, Selective Service System, and any official agencies to help in any way with problems resulting from the war. In addition we appreciated the CPS assignees as a source of manpower when many types of labor were virtually unobtainable during the war. While the labor of the assignees was not, as you know, very efficient as a whole, there were certain types of work in which the assignees performed unusually effective services. This covered such projects as fire-fighting, including smoke-jumping, "white-collar" research undertakings, some special fire-prevention activities and, from certain camps, farm labor.' 

2 Official correspondence on file at National Headquarters, Selective Service System, Washington.

The National Park Service Camps 

Camps under the supervision of the National Park Service in the Department of the Interior were located in many National and State parks. All the parks had fire-fighting and forest-protection projects similar to those of the Forest Service and, in addition, had to preserve and maintain the park improvements, which represented a large Government investment. Two examples of comments on the work of these camps show the kinds of opinions expressed. Superintendent, Mr. 

Blair Ross, of the Great Smoky Mountain National Park, made this statement:

In the early part of 1944 several incendiary forest fires occurred in the northeastern section of the park. The labor used in fighting these fires was secured mostly from the CPS camp at a time when it was almost impossible to hire such labor in the surrounding country. It is difficult to evaluate the worth of the CPS camp to the park in such a case. The assistant chief ranger of this park states that the services of the assignees on fire suppression work were satisfactory.

Mr. Edward D. Freeland, superintendent of the Shenandoah National Park, wrote:

During the war years, approximately 25 percent of the camp strength went out to surrounding counties to help farmers with their crops when other labor was not available. With our own appropriations drastically cut and labor of any sort at a premium, we were able, through the assistance of CPS crews, to maintain our roads and trails, buildings, and protection structures; to man fire look-outs; to secure trained and equipped fire-suppression forces immediately during emergencies; and to do numerous small maintenance jobs that otherwise would have had to go undone. As a result, we were able to keep the park in a reasonably good state of repair and to provide much more efficient forest protection than would have been possible without the use of this labor.* 

Camps Engaged in Soil Conservation Work 

C. P. S. Camps of the Soil Conservation Service in the Department of 

Agriculture were located in farming areas where they carried on a program of erosion control, water conservation, drainage, nursery operation, development of pure strains of seed and preservation of land. The type of conservation work done varied with each camp unit. In some localities fence relocation and the laying out of fields for contour farming and strip cropping was the most important work, while in others terracing and the construction of waterways and check dams was of first importance. One camp was engaged in the rechanneling and reclamation of a large drainage canal, and the labor of another was largely confined to a nursery which provided trees for field planting and new varieties of grass seed. A unit was assigned to an experimental station to provide technical assistance in & Ibid.

the study of water run-off and erosion control. Basically the soil conservation work required intelligent manual labor, but there was a need for assignees with skills, such as mechanics, clerks, and equipment operators, as well as those with technical training in engineering, farm planning, and the laboratory work of the experimental stations. 

In addition, the C. P. S. Camps supplied the bulk of the emergency farm labor available to the surrounding area for the production and harvesting of essential crops when other help was not available. 

The Farm Security Administration Camps The Farm Security Administration of the Department of Agricul ture was engaged in arid land reclamation at the farm level. After a water supply had been developed and brought to the land, it was necessary to get onto the fields for irrigation and to place the farms in condition for occupancy and production. This work consisted of clearing, land leveling, construction of lateral ditches, roads, buildings and other improvements on land which is fertile when watered. 

Several of these units were completed and brought under farm cultivation through the activities of the C. P. S. Camps. Besides the usual mechanical and clerical skills needed in any camp, these projects required objectors who could operate many types of land-leveling and earth-moving machines, do engineering and engage in a variety of construction work ranging from carpentry to building with concrete and steel. A total of 8,100 acres were brought under irrigation cultivation during the war as a result of such projects of the civilian work program of Selective Service. 

Results Obtained by Bureau of Reclamation Camps

The Interior Department's Bureau of Reclamation with the assistance of C. P. S. Camps completed the construction of a number of large earthen dams for water storage purposes. This construction work had been started by the Civilian Conservation Corps to provide water for civilian consumption and irrigation. The project had been approved, and was granted material and equipment priorities, by the War Production Board. One of the dams built had a storage capacity of 180,000 acre-feet; it was 100 feet in height with a crest length of 17,700 feet. It was designed to provide water for 50,000 acres of new land and a supply for an additional 8,000 acres when they could be brought under irrigation. The other dams were smaller in storage capacity and length but of about the same height. Subsidiary activities necessary to the main jobs included the operation of sawmills, gravel pits, rock crushers, and extensive repair shops, the construction of roads and buildings, and the cutting and clearing of timber from the reservoir sites. The work required skill in the

various phases of construction, such as engineering and drafting and the operation and maintenance of trucks, tractors, and earth-moving machinery. A Reclamation Bureau report on the work of one

Camps Doing General Land Office Work 

Camps of the General Land Office in the Department of Interior (later known as the Bureau of Land Management) were located in the West on forest lands which had been recently acquired by the Department. In addition to fire protection, roads and trails were needed and a large amount of surveying, mapping and timber cruising was necessary. This required assignees with engineering training to make maps and lay out roads and trails, others with the ability to make timber surveys or tabulate the results and those with the usual skills needed in forest camps of the System's civilian work program to operate road building machinery, fall timber and do maintenance work.

Fish and Wildlife Camps 

Under the sponsorship of the Fish and Wildlife Service, Department of Interior, a group of Class IV-E registrants were assigned to the experimental station at Bowie, Md., for work on a variety of research projects. Some of this was manual labor, but other jobs required selected men with scientific training. This agency also operated the Government camp at Germfask, Mich. The work at the Germ- Ibid.

The CPS camp was installed on the Patuxent Research Refuge, Bowie, Md., in 1942. Our agency was faced with a very critical situation at this time as a result of loss of personnel to the war agencies. The majority of our development, maintenance, and research programs were being held in abeyance or had been discontinued as hopeless.

The assignment of the camp has enabled us to advance our development and research program far beyond what we probably would have realized or accomplished by normal operations during normal times. We are proud of the records and accomplishments of the camp. 

Mental Hospitals and Training Schools 

This project group as well as the remaining projects which are discussed, constituted the ones usually referred to as "special projects”. 

Registrants who were assigned to the mental hospital work as well as to the farms and other projects yet to be covered, were individuals who had first been assigned to regular camp activities for a minimum of 90 days. During that time the objector had to demonstrate his ability to accept discipline and to work under normal conditions before being considered for a special-type project. 

In the beginning of the mental hospital and training school phase of the civilian work program, medical officers from the institutions themselves often visited the Civilian Public Service Camp and selected men for the projects. These medical men thus determined the adaptability of the individual for the hospital and school activity. 

Approximately one-fifth of all the Class IV-E assignees of Selective 

Service worked in mental hospitals or training schools. Many of • Unpublished report on file at National Headquarters, Selective Service System, Washington.

these institutions were finding it impossible to maintain staffs of qualified employees; their employees were constantly leaving to take positions in industry where the wages were much higher and the work less confining. However, their inmates were wards of society and must be given care. The work involving as it did, service along humanitarian lines, had a strong appeal to the conscientious objector. 

Assignees from the C. P. S. Camps performed work at the hospitals and schools as attendants, technicians, clerks, farm laborers and the like. Doctors who were assigned as objectors were practically without exception placed with these hospitals. Units at these institutions varied in size according to: 

1. The population of the institution. 

2. Its labor needs. 

3. Available quarters for housing assignees.

When the civilian work program for the conscientious objectors of the System was being terminated a communication was addressed by the Camp Operations Division to all institutions who used these men on this type of special project. The superintendents were asked to give their comment—whether good or bad-concerning the value of the assignees. Most of the replies were favorable; others did not speak so highly of the Class IV-E registrant. In order to illustrate the range of the superintendent's comments, the following excerpts from their letters are given:

The entire group of assignees reached the CPS camp unit in January 1944. 

We immediately assembled the group and informed them regarding the work and tried to inspire them with interest in the care of the mentally ill. Subsequently a series of 15 lectures were given to the entire group. These lectures covered such subjects as institution hygiene and sanitation; personal hygiene and sanitation for the patients; first aid; observation of patients; tact with patients and general care of the mentally ill. Several months later the group was gotten together again and given lectures regarding psychology, mental hygiene, and mental health.

The group assigned to this unit were all of the Mennonite faith. They came from the middle Southwest, largely from farming areas. We found these men to be sincere, loyal, and cooperative. They were extremely helpful and as a matter of fact I do not see how we could have operated this institution during the war without their assistance. I would like to make the following comments with regard to this CPS unit: 

1. During the entire time that this group has been at this institution, I have never heard a complaint from the relative of a patient, or any other employee, regarding the behavior of any one of these assignees. 

2. There was only one instance where disciplinary measures were used. This was in the case of an assignee whom we believed to be paying too much attention to a boy of 16 who attended the same church as the assignee. In this instance the assignee was confined to the premises of the hospital for a period of 1 month. 

The friendship with this 16-year-old boy continued and the assignee was then transferred away to another camp. 

3. During the entire existence of this camp we have had no instance of AWOL or malingering.

Another assignee

When I hear so much about the difficulties which have arisen in certain other units, I am surprised that we have gotten along here with practically no difficult situations of any kind. I believe the success of this camp has been largely due to the religious training of the men and the fact that they were all of one faith.

The CPS unit at this hosptial was closed out on May 30, the last man in the unit being released on that day. Looking over in retrospect the 3 years of service given by the camp, I cannot but say that it was of definite value to us, and helped carry us through a critical stage in manpower during the years of the war. However, in spite of the war now being over, we have not been able to fully replace the CPS men.

The men in our unit conformed very well to rules and regulations, and were intelligent in their approach to their tasks. Some of them were, of course, intellectually much above the type of work they were required to do; and it is unfortunate they could not have been used in a type of work more in keeping with their education and training. Some, I think, were fakirs as far as having any religious objections to army service, and in one instance at least, a man stated that he had no religion. 

I think the 4-E classification is poorly conceived. 

In my judgment the pay of $15 a month for the work these men did was very unjust and a pitiful hardship on some men who had families. 

Replying to your inquiry of May 25, I regret to have delayed answering;

I have no criticism of your administration, or the CPS system. The conscientious objectors assigned to this hospital did excellent work, and materially helped us in conducting the hospital when other help was scarce. Some of the boys were neurotic and psychopathic in make-up and never should have been inducted into the service. Our group was under the supervision of the Brethren; consequently, they were properly advised and encouraged to do the right thing.

Personally, I feel that the C. O.'s are selfish and uncooperative. They resented working under rules and regulations. They were also critical of the work of others. I feel that the problem of conscientious objectors, in general, when not founded on a recognized religious basis, in time of war should result in disenfranchisement. Not even the United States, as powerful as it is, can stand when its citizens remain divided and uncooperative, when threatened with danger of extinction from the outside world.

I feel that the office of camp operations of the CPS system has done an excellent job.

The unit was opened on April 8, 1943. During its existence 69 men were assigned to the unit, and its maximum strength was 40. We have had five assistant directors. We transferred 26 men from this unit to other units and discharged 43 outright. The total number of man-days was 8,826. 

In general the services of these men were good, and they were a real help to the hospitals in a very critical period. I do not know how we should have continued to operate without them. There was a time when I had less than 

30 regular ward employees to take care of approximately 1,100 men. We noted a considerable letdown in the quality of the work following VJ-day. This was due in part to the resentment of the men at enforced servitude after that time, and to the fact that the older and more stable employees of the unit were dis-

charged, and were in part replaced by younger men less mature in their judgments and viewpoints. The operational difficulties of the unit I think came about through a dual control, the director taking his orders from Selective Service, and the assistant director taking his order from a church board. 

I believe it will be well, in any future set-up, not to have this dual control, and I think that the church board supervision tended to create in the individuals a feeling that they were a group aside in the hospital, and it lead to considerable spying activity which did not lend itself to good cooperation. Fortunately, I think the Mennonite group was quite free of this, but I found myself embarrassed on a number of occasions by requests from the church board to do things which I had no instructions from the National Board to do. 

We were desperately short of attendants for at least 3 years and the objectors seemed to feel that if they gave us good service we would keep them indefinitely because of the fact that they were giving us cheap labor. In fact, they had tacked on their bulletin board literature sent out from Washington, D. C., to that effect. Probably these men were not entirely to blame for some of their positions, since the visiting ministers at times seemed to agree with them in their attitude. These ministers seemed to feel that they could give me orders which would conflict with your written instructions left with me by Mr. Shott in June 

1944. This was particularly true concerning them leaving the institution when sickness or death occurred in their family. They felt that they should be paid for the time they were not here working; whereas, our other employees would lose the time, despite the fact that one paragraph in your instructions states very distinctly that the CPS men should eat the same food, live in the same quarters, and receive the same time off duty as the regular civilian employees. 

On the whole, I have found even the assistant director, to be unfair and unreasonable, so that one could scarcely blame the other employees for taking the position which they did take. We admit that our institution is far from perfect, but nevertheless, we gave our inmates about as good care and attention as that given to mental cases in our large, wealthy Eastern States. We admit that we are using entirely too much restraint, but when one has but 11 night attendants and 17 day attendants for 900 insane patients, they surely are justified in resorting to restraints and seculsions. 

During World War I, I worked in an Iowa institution where we had Amish Dutch objectors. Those boys made no trouble for us whatsoever, despite the fact that their relatives did not live more than 60 miles away. I assume that we will not have many conscientious objectors left by July 1, and I assure you that we will not have any great regret at terminating this type of service. We expect we will again be short of attendants when our young people return to complete their high-school work about September 1, but I hope that we shall not be compelled to resort to conscientious objector help, at least until World 

War III puts in its appearance. 

I have taken considerable time to summarize my opinions and experiences regarding the use of conscientious objectors in mental hospitals. 

One's opinions vary when considering the value of CPS as it relates to mental hospitals. There is no denying that when these groups of men were organized to work in the hospitals the situation was serious and theoretically their assistance should have been of inestimable value. From there on, however, the theory began to break down and there were increasing difficulties. 

In my opinion, Selective Service would have accomplished more by declaring these so-called conscientious objectors unfit for military service because of

THE WORK ACCOMPLISHED BY OBJECTORS IN C. P. S. CAMPS » 219 

mental disorders and let it go at that. It is my further opinion that they are a group of men who are anarchistic in their thinking and general plan of living, and by and large are the most selfish group of men I have ever had dealings with.

Therefore, when I attempt to make an evaluation of this portion of the Selective Service program, it is my opinion that it has been a decided disappointment and a practical failure.

It is my further opinion that the program would have been more satisfactory if it had been organized and administered under strict military discipline.'
