Agricultural Labor Administration Work 

The use of conscientious objector assignees by the Agricultural 

Labor Administration of the Department of Agriculture as year round laborers and technicians in food production resulted in 

786,326 man-days of labor and the earning of $1,549,152.28 in wages up to the end of the civilian work program. An additional 138,674 man-days of emergency work was performed by men in regular Civilian Public Service Camps who supplied day labor for the production and harvesting of vitally needed farm crops within a 15-mile radius of the camp units. Wages earned by these emergency day laborers on farms amounted to $711,596.55. In addition, these and other assignees worked thousands of man-days of labor in the production of food for consumption at the mental hospitals and training schools and at the work camp units themselves. This was not recorded as farm labor, however.

The farm labor camps were divided into three general groups: those for individual dairy-farm laborers, those for Dairy Herd Improvement Association herd testers and those for State college agricultural experiment station workers. As has been pointed out, wage payments were required for all types of farm labor. The general standard used was the going wage of the community for year-round single farm hands where room, board, and laundry were furnished. 

The only exception to this rule was that the hourly wage rate for day labor was the standard used in setting wages for emergency farm labor. A ruling of the Comptroller General required that all moneys paid as wages for assignee farm labor, less necessary expenses, be deposited with the United States Treasury where it was placed in a special fund to be held until the termination of the national emergency. 

'Official correspondence on file at National Headquarters, Selective Service System, Washington.

Dairy Farm Labor 

The acute shortage of labor in some dairying areas led to the development of a plan, in conjunction with the War Food Administration and the Extension Service of the Department of Agriculture, under which qualified Selective Service assignees, who volunteered, were transferred from the regular camps to jobs on dairy farms. 

These objectors worked as farm laborers on selected dairy farms in counties recommended and approved by the War Food Administration as being important in dairy production and having a shortage of dairy-farm labor. The employer paid the prevailing wage of the community for this help, as stated above, and the money, less an allowance to the assignee for the purchase of clothing and other necessities and a deduction for administrative operating expenses, was paid into the United States Treasury. At the close of the civilian work program the extension services in the States operating dairy-farm labor projects were asked to evaluate this type of camp activity. Here are examples of such evaluation:

The good work these assignees did is further evidenced by the fact that they were taken into the homes of farmers whose own sons were in the armed forces and were treated as members of the family. They quickly established themselves in the community, and in local churches, and neighbors who had scoffed and criticized, were soon requesting the opportunity of employing a conscientious objector. They did their work with dignity. They were always given the best jobs in this county only because they deserved them. We know of no instance where an assignee refused to do any work given him, or grumbled at the long hours he was forced to work because the farm was short of manpower. On the other hand we heard of many cases where the boys offered to go into the field on Sunday or after the usual day's work was done to plant or harvest a crop. In every instance where an employer sold out or moved to a smaller farm, numerous requests were received from neighbors for the transfer of the conscientious objector to their farms, demonstrating that they were, by far, the very best help we were able to obtain during the war years. 

This program supplied labor at a time when it was badly needed by the dairy industry in this county and, as a whole, the program was successful; however, one of the most outstanding defects in the organization and administration as I saw it was the fact that conscientious objectors were in charge of the camps from which we secured our labor. This involved too-sympathetic an attitude on the part of the supervisor who visited the area. It would seem to me it would be much more advisable to have a disinterested party who could evaluate the affairs of the worker and the affairs of the dairyman so that when problems arising as to administration came up this person would not be swayed in his decision by his own personal belief or sympathy. To me this is the most outstanding defect.

We attempted to place these workers in dairies where they would perform the greatest service toward the supplying of a needed food product during the war. As a whole, with one or two exceptions, we had very little difficulty with our employers because they were selected on the basis of their ability to handle labor as well as their ability to produce dairy products.

THE WORK ACCOMPLISHED BY OBJECTORS IN C. P. S. CAMPS 

221 Another defect that seemed apparent during the program was the lack of corrective measures when workers were a. w. o. l., or walked off the jobs, or refused to work. Under the present program the only corrective measure that seemed to be apparent was the deduction of furlough time. It seemed to me that a better system of correction, or punishment if you wish to call it that, should be in force because in my opinion after serving in the armed forces myself it seemed to me that these workers should be handled with the same type of corrective measures as a man who is in the armed forces. Present organization of the program does not allow for such corrective measures and as a whole it seemed to me to be very weak in that respect. 

In closing, I would like to reiterate my statement that the program as a whole supplied a source of needed labor and also the workers, with the exception of a certain percentage, seemed willing in most cases to do their duty with a minimum of petty complaints or personal grievances. 

Dairy Herd Testing 

A number of camp assignees from the System were selected and trained by State agricultural colleges for work as herd testers with various dairy herd improvement associations. A few of these objectors were also used as technicians in artificial dairy herd breeding associations. An assignee herd tester sampled and tested the milk from individual cows once a month for about 25 dairymen and then estimated feed costs per cow. This information was used by dairymen in deciding how to improve production and when to eliminate unprofitable cows. In such connection it might be added that the testing loads of assignees varied from 350 to 900 cows. New Jersey testers averaged 690 cows, Michigan 456, Pennsylvania 515, Iowa 390, Illinois 486, and New York 613. The 108,105 cows tested yearly in these States averaged 512 per tester. The associations paid for the services of these registrants under the same arrangement as that followed by the individual dairy farmer on the dairy farm labor project. 

The Pennsylvania State Dairyman estimated that an assignee doing such work might increase milk production considerably more as a herd tester than as a milker or herdsman. The New Jersey Extension

Dairyman reported that, “just as soon as the dairy herd improvement association program discontinued, milk production dropped" materially. The pay of a regularly employed tester varied from $1,500 to $2,000 per year. Assuming that the average pay would amount to $1,800, therefore, the assignees performing these duties, who jointly put in 565 man-years of work, made a contribution having an estimated value of $1,000,000. Extension Services made comments along the following lines regarding this project as it was ending: 

The use of conscientious objectors as testers enabled approximately 800 more Illinois dairy farmers to maintain continuous dairy herd improvement association records throughout the war period. As a whole the assignees were comparable in ability to the association peacetime testers. A few of the men assigned 

8 Ibid.

to Illinois were very outstanding. On the other hand, a few lacked ability or because of attitude caused considerable trouble. More care in selection of assignees was needed. 

As I see it, the administrative set-up could be improved by having representatives of Selective Service as area supervisors. Many of the assignees who tried to get by with as much as possible would, in my opinion, have conducted themselves differently had they been responsible to an area supervisor not so sympathetic to them.

Our experience with conscientious objectors as dairy herd improvement association supervisors in Maryland was very satisfying. As a whole, the testers did a remarkably fine job and lifted the plane of dairy herd improvement association work done in Maryland to a new level. 

On the other hand, I do feel that some corrections could be made in financial arrangements which might be beneficial. In many instances there was a misunderstanding between the Extension dairyman and the dairy herd improvement association officials as to just how much could be spent for each item. Then also, many of the dairymen, in their appreciation for the fine work the testers were doing, forgot that these boys were actually in the Army and more or less broke up the morale of the testers in other counties by being too liberal with them.

I also feel that from the church standpoint we didn't get enough supervision of the boys and what supervision we did get didn't help but hindered. Many times the church supervisor merely cried with the boys and that didn't help the situation in the least. On the other hand, I think the club could have been wielded a little stronger and the whole program would have worked a little smoother as a result.

The program has made it possible for over 800 dairymen to continue record keeping in their herds during a period when it was impossible to obtain the services of an adequate number of civilian testers. The quality of work done by conscientious objector testers has been entirely satisfactory in every case except one. This exception was due to a lack of ability and not to any lack of conscientious effort. A large percentage of the conscientious objector testers have set a standard of work that will be hard to maintain with available civilian testers and Association members are appreciative of the service they have had. 

While all the conscientious objector testers with the one exception did acceptable work, a few failed in some other respect. Without exception all of the conscientious objectors that were Brethren, Friends, or Christadelphians were extremely conscientious in their work and fitted themselves into the situation and their work remarkably well.

As a group the men in the CPS program that had experience with dairy herd improvement association work were superior to men who are usually obtained during peacetime conditions from civilian ranks. The men from the 

Mennonite unit and the Brethren service had a considerable amount of initiative coupled with a definite desire to work. The farmers were very well pleased with the service and received the men in a very cordial manner. The CPS program was the salvation of our improvement work in dairy cattle breeding throughout the State. The cows enrolled in the associations would have not been kept at their high level of production without the dairy herd improvement association program. In New Jersey one can safely say that the continuation of the dairy herd improvement association program accounted for an estimated

THE WORK ACCOMPLISHED BY OBJECTORS IN C. P. S. CAMPS >>> 223 

additional production of 19 million pounds of milk a year. Experience taught us that just as soon as the dairy herd improvement association program discontinued, milk production dropped about 1,000 pounds per year per cow.' 

Dairy herd improvement association records were also used to determine the ability of sires from high-producing dams to beget highproducing heifers. Bulls so proven were used in artificial breeding which greatly multiplied their usefulness. The value of this work was almost beyond estimate due to its cumulative effect. 

Agricultural College Experiment Stations 

Assignees were placed with a number of State agricultural college experiment stations to relieve the labor shortage and enable these institutions to carry on with work that otherwise would have been discontinued. Some of the experiments had been under way for 50 years or more, and a great deal of their value was in the continuity of the work and records. Higher yielding strains of seeds were being developed and propagated and considerable time and effort were being devoted to the study of animal and plant diseases. A few qualified men were engaged in research work, others had technical jobs and the remainder supplied the farm labor needed at an experiment station. In general, such men were employed under the same financial arrangements and other conditions as the men on dairy farms. 

A questionnaire sent to experiment station directors in late 1944 revealed that only 29 percent of the assignee tasks were of a common labor type, 39 percent were rated as skilled labor, 24 percent were technical and 7 percent were scientific jobs. When the project was terminating experiment stations evaluated it as follows:

The labor made available to the station from CPS Unit 104 was extremely valuable and made it possible to continue many phases of work having a direct relation to food production. Had it not been for the labor from the camp, many phases of our wartime program would have been seriously handicapped and some phases discontinued because of inadequate help. 

The selection of personnel for the camp was well handled. At the beginning, prospective assignees were screened prior to their acceptance at this camp. As you are aware, the assignment of men to an experiment station requires a more careful selection than to less technical work. Among the group at this camp many were graduates or students from institutions above high-school level, and several had previous professional backgrounds which could be kept active during their period of service. In fact, we have added several men, after discharge, to the staff of the station to perform jobs for which they were especially well adapted. If future needs should exist, we would hope for the opportunity to again select men from the service who would fit into a college community and have such capabilities that could be utilized both to the benefit of the station and the men themselves. • Ibid. 737977°-50—vol. 1- -16

- 

Generally, the men were capable workmen and did exceptionally well considering conditions. They enabled us to continue with important work, whereas without them it would have been almost impossible to get the work done. 

Naturally, the men varied in ability and in the attitudes with which they approached their respective jobs. 

The most important criticism I should like to make is that the church, in this case, the Mennonite Central Committee, was given too much responsibility for and authority over the assignees. Under the arrangement, the church (which was quite natural) used its responsibility and authority to try to more thoroughly indoctrinate the assignees with pacifism. It seems somewhat paradoxical that a country, fighting for its very existence, will not only exempt men from military service but make it possible for them to be more thoroughly indoctrinated in pacifism than would have been possible otherwise, and to provide the funds, even if indirectly, which made this possible.10 

Malaria and Hookworm Units 

Two State health projects of the Civilian Public Service Camps involved disease control, one in Florida, consisting of three units, and the other in Mississippi, with one unit. The work was largely malaria and hookworm control and the teaching of general sanitation through mosquito elimination, the screening of houses and the construction of sanitary privies. Besides making sanitary surveys of the counties in which the camps were located and doing the required construction work, it was necessary in some instances because of shortage of materials, to cut and mill timber in order to obtain the needed lumber for building. These special projects of the civilian work program were sponsored by the United States Public Health Service and supervised by the State boards of health at no cost to Selective Service. Funds were provided by the religious organizations operating the camps and by the states and communities in which the work was done. 

Puerto Rican Medical Units 

A medical unit project was set up for Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands. This special camp project was divided into a number of small units dispersed throughout the islands. Centers were established to provide medical, surgical, hospital, ambulance, dietetic and welfare service for people in areas which previously were without any of this kind of care. Out-patient service was provided along these lines and the population was given instructions in health and sanitation, and trained in home nursing. Objectors assigned to this duty by the 

System had special qualifications and included doctors, nurses and technicians of various kinds. The project was jointly operated and financed by the Brethren, Mennonites, and Friends under the sponsorship of the Puerto Rican Reconstruction Administration with the approval and some assistance from the insular health department.

225 

Special Experimental Projects 

A group of selected volunteers from among camp assignees were used as experimental subjects in various medical research projects under the supervision of the Office of Scientific Research and Development and the Surgeon General of the Army. Besides acting as subjects for tests, the assignees assisted with investigations and experiments of various kinds having to do with problems of diet, nutrition, climate, altitude and certain diseases. These projects were quite important, and had a high priority among the various special phases of the civilian work program. Usually, no special training was required for such service, selection being based on physical condition and temperament.

Numerous magazine articles appeared in scientific publications giving details regarding the participation of conscientious objectors in these experimental projects. In addition, a number of pamphlets were published on the work. The bibliography at the end of the text for this monograph contains references to such reports. 

Coast and Geodetic Survey

The Coast and Geodetic Survey of the Department of Commerce had experienced considerable difficulty in obtaining qualified men for its field staffs while, at the same time, the mapping of certain areas of the country was urgently required. A unit of Class IV-E assignees was therefore organized by Selective Service to assist with this work. 

Objector registrants on this project had to be able to stand hardship and exposure and also to have enough technical background for training in the required surveying and mapping procedure. 

Weather Bureau 

In addition to its other duties, the Weather Bureau of the Department of Commerce had undertaken during World War II to compile data from past weather reports and plot it on a series of weather maps. The information was badly needed, but the work was delayed due to a shortage of civilian personnel. In consequence a C. P. S. 

Camp of objectors was established by the System under the supervision of the Weather Bureau to carry on this special project. It required men with skill in drafting and map making or with clerical or statistical experience.

Accomplishments as Measured in Financial Terms 

In the preceding paragraphs the work accomplished by conscientious objectors assigned to work of national importance has been discussed, but no specific reference has been made to the costs of this civilian work program. It should be borne in mind that Class IV-E registrants assigned to the regular or special projects of this program did

CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION 

not receive any pay nor were they given any of the routine allowances available to men inducted into the armed forces. For this reason alone the cost of operating the program was naturally low. Attention is also invited again to the fact that in the majority of Civilian Public Service Camps the costs of food, clothing, utilities, recreation, and allowances to the men were not an expense of the Federal Government. 

At all camps technically directed by the Departments of Agriculture and Interior, whether existing as church-operated or Governmentoperated camps, Selective Service funds were provided to the technical bureau to defray the salaries of its own personnel which was necessary to the supervision of the work. The System also provided money for the operation and maintenance of equipment essential to the job and for the purchase of new heavy equipment, tools, and materials with which to complete the project. In Government-operated camps food, clothing, cash allowances for the men, and all other expenses were provided by funds from Selective Service. 

Eliminating any reference to the amount contributed by the various church groups cooperating in the program and considering the fact that 3,194,436 man-days of labor were provided to camps operated directly by the Agriculture and Interior Departments, the total cost to the Selective Service System from May 1941 to March 1947 was $4,731,558. This constituted a man-day cost of but a fraction over $1.48 per day. Such cost did not include the number of days lost through sickness, leave, arrest, or overhead camp work. 

Money From Work on Special Projects 

It was found that the average monthly salary paid to State hospital attendants in States where conscientious objectors were assigned was $68. Deducting from the result $15 for the monthly allowance of the registrant and an amount for transportation and medical and dental care over and above that provided regular employees, there was an estimated maximum saving to the States of approximately $4,286,519 through this project. 

Another group of conscientious objectors was assigned to certain institutions of the Veterans' Administration. These registrants performed a total of 120,403 man-days of work. The entrance pay scales for regularly employed attendants in these institutions ranged from $1,320 in 1943 to $1,697 in 1947. On the basis of such wages and taking account of monthly allowances, transportation and extra dental and medical care, it is estimated that this project effected a maximum saving of around $535,141 for the Veterans' Administration. Analysis A financial summary for most of the projects not mentioned above, is difficult because the final costs were not made available to Selective

THE WORK ACCOMPLISHED BY OBJECTORS IN C. P. S. CAMPS » 227 

Service. As will be recalled, money was only provided by the church and Federal agencies as it was required. Moreover, no objective evaluation was placed on the work done in connection with the various research projects. Obviously the monetary total was considerable, however, and the contribution of the Civilian Public Service Camps to the national welfare was of a wider dimension than money terms alone could indicate.

Of great significance is the fact that the conscientious objectors of the System who according to their beliefs could accept only work of national importance, did accomplish many major tasks. Likewise noteworthy is that on the whole these Class IV-E registrants performed such duty well. The situation wherein they were often under some supervision from three directions-church group, technical agency, and Selective Service-must have served to complicate camp life and work for them as well as for their supervisors; nevertheless they rated satisfactory in accomplishment. As this chapter and those which follow show, all too frequently, there were individual conscientious objector assignees to the C. F. S. Camps and small groups of the same who were a source of deterring irritation to satisfactory operation. In the main, however, the assignees fulfilled their obligation under the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940 in a creditable manner and without complaining personally.

XII 

THE PROBLEM OF CAMP ORDER AND DISCIPLINE 

Much time has been devoted to the Selective Service registrant of 1940-47 whose conscience made him object to both combatant and noncombatant service in the armed forces. It has been noted that when the basic law of the System was passed, there were provisions for this type of objector to be assigned, in lieu of induction, to work of national importance under civilian direction. These provisions stemmed from the general concept-service for everyone selected-and the specific church and historical philosophy-duty within the observance of religious faith. They were reflected in the general regulations of Selective Service which said that if such a registrant was chosen for duty and possesssed a valid claim of conscientious objection he was to be placed in Class IV-E and given an assignment to civilian work. 

In consequence, the System along with the peace churches and certain agencies of the Federal and State Governments, developed a civilian work program for the Class IV-E objector which operated by means of Civilian Public Service Camps. The sound planning of this program and the general satisfactoriness of its operation in the camps has been discussed. Furthermore, the types of regular and special camp projects have been presented along with the value, quantity, and quality of the work accomplished. 

As this usually good story has unfolded, there have been significant references to the problem of camp order and discipline. This problem has been noted as being due in the main to a very small number of 

Class IV-E registrants. Relating these experiences in delinquency is not a pleasant task. In addition there may be a tendency for the reader to accord them undue emphasis as compared to the whole civilian work program. Nevertheless, a monograph on conscientious objection would be incomplete without their presentation. 

The Root of the Problem 

The discharge of objector assignees from Civilian Public Service Camps by reason of delinquency totaled but 500 to 600 during the entire 62 years of Selective Service operations. This was only about 229

5 percent of the approximately 12,000 Class IV-E registrants assigned to the camps for the period. Compared with the some 36,- 

000,000 militarily liable registrants in the System, or the 10,000,000 inducted for combatant and noncombatant service with the armed forces, or even the 50,000 classified as conscientious objectors of all kinds, the number of such discharges was insignificant. Yet the story of order and discipline in the C. P. S. Camps was much broader than just a discussion of the few recalcitrants who were separated from duty because they were delinquent.

It should first be pointed out that there were four distinct types of objector assignees in the camps. By far the largest group were those who were cooperative in every respect. They did a satisfactory amount of good work on the projects and led well-regulated lives from all angles during "off-duty" hours. They constituted no problem of discipline whatsoever. The second group, a minor one, was also composed of good assignees, but they were of a type somewhat prone to be influenced, and created some difficulty to that extent. Their conduct depended to a degree upon whom they were working or living with and also whether they were being observed by camp officials. 

Another group, much smaller still in numbers, was made up of assignees who were opposed to the civilian work program in principle, but who advocated nonviolent passive resistance to it, patterning their actions after Mahatma Gandhi. The fourth and smallest group were those who desired open and united rebellion, sabotage, and violence in their demonstrations of noncooperativeness. 

These last two groups hardly belonged in C. P. S. Camps, but they accepted such assignments, not having the honesty or courage of their convictions to refuse and stand court trial as law violators. Therein was based the problem of camp order. The presence of this type of 

Class IV-E registrant, sometimes referred to as a pseudo-religious objector, created difficulties of extremely critical nature in some camps and in so doing tended to cast disrepute upon the whole first effort of the United States in work of national importance under civilian direction.

Lack of Prompt Court Action a Factor 

Although not universally practiced, it had been generally recognized for a long time that a claim of conscientious objection carried with it a connotation of "influence upon the conduct" or of deportment "uniformly consistent with" such a declaration.¹ Therefore, the assignment under the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940 of sincere objectors to a civilian work program in lieu of performing duty with the armed forces or serving a sentence in prison was fundamentally 

1 Ch. III.

THE PROBLEM OF CAMP ORDER AND DISCIPLINE >>> 

231 sound. However, the disciplinary measures provided by the law were insufficient for the control of camp delinquents, such as, the pseudoreligious objectors described above. The difficulty was that, in removing the Class IV-E objector from the direction of military organizations, the act left recourse only to the Federal courts for any discipline other than the restriction of camp privileges, such as furlough. The latter proved, in most instances, to be but a minor deterrent. 

Coupled with this situation, the United States attorneys during the early part of the program seemed hesitant to refer these delinquent cases to the Federal courts. Inexperience in the field apparently caused them at first to regard such cases as minor infractions of the law. The result was a long delay before delinquent individuals were brought to trial. In one instance, a United States attorney even went into a C. P. S. Camp and endeavored to talk the recalcitrant objectors into reforming their ways. Failing in this, he did not continue actively with their prosecution.

Then in one court where trials were held for many early cases, the Federal judge interpreted the law in a peculiarly liberal way and was extremely lenient as to penalties. Men who pleaded guilty were found not guilty upon the instruction of the court; others were placed on probation after conviction. The initial laxity of the United States attorneys and the leniency of this one Federal court alone made the maintenance of proper order and discipline in the C. P. S. Camps of this area and others very difficult. There undoubtedly would have been less assignee misconduct if the Department of Justice had uniformly prosecuted with vigor and promptness. In this connection it is recalled that section 11 of the 1940 law read: "Precedence shall be given by courts to the trial of cases arising under the act." 

Failure To Prosecute Deserters

As a rule Selective Service did not have this much difficulty in obtaining the prosecution of outright desertion except in the latter months of the operation. In one group of six cases, however, the Justice Department failed to prosecute after the offenses had been reported and action requested. These objectors deserted a C. P. S. Camp in May of 1946, and four months later the Department suggested that the registrants were then eligible for discharge, although they had continued meanwhile in a desertion status. The System felt that since the men had not completed the required length of service at the time of violation they should not be issued discharges in the usual manner. The 

Department of Justice then replied that the United States attorney "had expressed the view that public policy does not demand the prosecution of these cases. Consequently, no further action in these cases

is contemplated by this Department." It would appear that in this instance the United States attorney tended to place himself somewhat in the position of the judge or the jury. The basic law of 1940 provided for the trial of violators in section 11; it seems, therefore, that the sworn duty of the attorney was to place the deserters on trial. 

Most United States attorneys were cooperative, however, and prosecution and convictions were secured for both delinquencies and desertions in a large percentage of cases. 

Prospects of Remedial Segregation 

Sincere religious objectors, who had been assigned to the civilian work program, were amenable to reason and, in general, performed a good day's work on the camp project or projects. However, it was not always possible to separate these registrants from what may be termed the agitators. In some church-operated units the directors, being church representatives, were not inclined to segregate men because of the church attitude of religious tolerance. This left the sincere but easily influenced objectors exposed to their few noncooperative companions. The result upon occasions was a demoralizing effect for the whole group. Such demoralization even extended beyond the work projects. Thus it is probable that some objectors suffered psychological effects difficult to overcome.

In the church-sponsored camps discipline was the responsibility of the camp director and, in general, this was a fairly satisfactory arrangement. The director, himself a conscientious conscientious objector, usually tended to be sympathetic and favorably inclined toward the objector and therefore secured his cooperation without great trouble. The church representatives were inclined to predicate their policy of administration on the theory that all assignees were conscientious and sincere, and sometimes the troublesome person took decided advantage of this approach.

Against the advice of Selective Service, most church-operated camps were set up on a self-government basis. This gave each assignee an equal voice in camp government and resulted in an extreme degree of individual freedom outside of working hours. In fact about the only effective check on freedom during off-duty hours was the penalty against desertion. Many of the problem-type assignees had considerable education. They were well fitted by training and experience to argue their ways of life. Often they were more persuasive even than the administrators of the camp. 

Their early segregation in special camps would therefore have had some advantage to the operation of the entire camp program. Even- 

Letter of September 10, 1946, to the Director of Selective Service from the Assistant

Varieties of Misconduct 

Many of these problem assignees to the civilian work program possessed qualifications for the highly specialized projects of the C. P. S. Camps but their noncooperative attitudes prevented their selection in these regards and so they continued as common laborers. 

In unskilled capacities they were often quite adept when trying to "botch their jobs," to use a phrase from one of them. They did not always refuse to work but sometimes moved articles of light weight one at a time instead of carrying a reasonable load. Or they carried dirt with shovels by spoonful-size loads. Or they required a separate order for each movement on a job. In one reforestation camp some of them, when sent to weed plant beds, managed instead to trample the young seedlings they were expected to tend and to break down the shade covers placed over the beds. As a whole, they also spent much time criticizing and ridiculing their project or technical foremen.

Upon occasion these malcontent "men 'gainst the state" placed bottles in front of rubber-tired vehicles, took a Government truck without permission and brought liquor into camp, broke windows out of a camp foreman's quarters, battered down doors with rams, caused the destruction of foodstuffs by breaking into a pantry and trampling valuable supplies on the floor, damaged electric generators and truck engines by placing sugar in the gas supply, caused buildings to be burned, refused to keep either their persons or quarters clean, decorated one dining hall with swastikas and at times raised Japanese and German flags on flagpoles reserved for the 

United States flag.

A staff member of a Civilian Public Service Camp, who observed the problem of misconduct at first hand, made this division of conscientious objectors: "Second mile men" and "men against the State." Regarding the first, he wrote, "One group felt that the times called for 'sacrificial service' and 'second mile' cooperation. Men of this group went quietly to Civilian Public Service Camps after their local boards had certified to the religious validity of their objections to military service. They served there quietly and well, *". He characterized the other group as "The men who resisted, who left camp, who refused to cooperate, * * *" Regarding those who "remained in

C. P. S. Camps and resisted both Church and State at that level, *" he used this language, "* ** employ sabotage against the State when men accustomed to reasonably * * * * 

3 George B. Reeves, Men Against the State (Washington: Human Events, Inc., 1946), p. 13.

efficient work habits deliberately slow down, botch their jobs and act the parts of able-bodied imbeciles." 

It should be constantly borne in mind, however, that the perpetrators of these gross outrages in order and discipline were a very small minority of the Class IV-E registrants assigned to work of national importance under civilian direction.

Resistance in Church-Operated Camps 

Most of the outstanding misconduct occurred in the Governmentoperated C. P. S. Camps as would be expected. Some of these units, it will be recalled, were organized specifically to segregate agitator elements for remedial purposes. In addition, the objector who was a recalcitrant to the civilian work program often requested a transfer to the Government camp so that he could register more effective opposition to the whole civilian work program. However, some destructive malcontent did occur in the church-operated camps. 

In checking over the reports made from time to time by the field representatives of the Camp Operations Division in the National Headquarters of Selective Service, it is noted that the many minor and the few serious disturbances which took place in the churchsponsored units were handled in various ways by the camp directors. 

The situation of the problem assignee was not due to the church but to the Government, and the director was a patient man, so ordinarily he managed to get along somehow with this type of assignee. Such arrangements were in the main not satisfactory but they nevertheless existed.

This often made it difficult for Selective Service to obtain enough direct evidence to prosecute the offender. Sometimes it was only through the continual inspection of a camp that National Headquarters gained knowledge of trouble there. At other times the difficulty only came to attention through the report of a technical agency whereupon a field representative of the System was immediately dispatched to the unit. Upon rare occasions the camp director would even transfer the trouble-maker to his own administrative organization and keep the violator from coming to the attention of the technical agency or Selective Service. These are not representative illustrations, of course, but they do indicate that the System and the technical or project agency interested in the work of a camp, did not always receive the outright cooperation of the church group in matters of order and discipline. Undoubtedly the desire of the churches to give the program a greater appearance of success to the general public was a factor in such instances. However, experience • Ibid.

THE PROBLEM OF CAMP ORDER AND DISCIPLINE » 235 

indicated the shortsightedness of not dealing outwardly and directly in problems of camp delinquency.

Resistance at the First Government Camp Mancos 

While it is difficult to establish a date on which the first efforts of the noncooperators against the Government proper had their inception, it can be definitely said that such noncooperation stemmed principally from those "absolutists" in the C. P. S. Camps who lacked the courage of their convictions to face prison sentences rather than to comply with the Selective Service law of 1940. They preferred seemingly to accept assignment to the civilian work program with the idea of proving it inadequate through a planned process of sabotage. 

When the first Government-operated camp was established at Mancos, Colo., in July 1943, many of the early arrivals indicated that they would be difficult to discipline. It was said by some of the more belligerent that the mass of assignees to the camp would eventually develop some sort of organized resistance against the Government. 

There were enough cooperative registrants among the first group, however, to prevent open united demonstrations. 

At the Mancos camp, the general attitude of most assignees was one of cooperativeness. Many efforts were made by dissident elements to organize the unit along the line of partial resistance, but this failed to materialize. Large numbers would not participate at all and the differences of opinion among the noncooperators on methods of demonstration could not be reconciled. It is true that many Mancos assignees were prosecuted by the United States Department of Justice but these delinquents were individualists rather than organizers of resistance groups.

A Special Camp for the Maladjusted-Germfask 

During April 1944, the Fish and Wildlife Service opened a Government camp at Germfask, Mich. This unit was established to assist the Government in wildlife research work and to provide a special camp for those assignees who did not make an adjustment at other camps, including the one at Mancos, Colo. In addition, this unit was set up in cooperation with the Michigan State Board of Mental Hygiene to make observations and studies of noncooperative objectors who were believed to be mentally and physically deficient. 

Most of the noncooperators at Mancos were transferred to Germfask, in order to relieve the Mancos work project of the problems of order and discipline which were accumulating. Primarily because of the activities of these problem cases and the uncertainty of the medical advisory boards of the System as to the status of many cases, it was determined to use this new camp in the special analysis of the

- 

physical and mental fitness of problem assignees. As a result many recalcitrant objectors were eventually discharged and reclassified 

IV-F. 

The Germfask camp was closed May 31, 1945, and transferred to Minersville, Calif. Local public relations at Germfask were never good. There was general opposition and dissatisfaction of the community as regards the camp which had been brought about by the conduct of assignees both on the job and during off-work hours. At this camp demonstrations of noncooperativeness against the Government and the local community were made by various individuals. There were no organized mass demonstrations; here, as at Mancos, the malcontents were not able to agree on methods of demonstrating against the Government. Shortly before the Germfask camp was closed, Selective Service discharged and reclassified many of the assignees. 

This closing was at the time when assignees were being given discharges due to age and length of service. The reclassifications were to IV-F and were the result of examinations by the camp's special medical advisory board.

The Report of the Germfask Project Superintendent 

It is appropriate and valuable at this point to quote in full the final report of the Germfask project superintendent: 

Early in the late war emergency, the Fish and Wildlife Service learned that Selective Service intended to establish work camps throughout the United States, composed of conscientious objectors. These were for the most part to be administered by Federal agencies.

Having an inoperative CCC camp at the Seney refuge, completely adequate insofar as housing facilities were concerned, and still in possession of all working equipment such as heavy machinery and small tools, the Service petitioned for such a camp. For some time no action was taken, though advice was received that the Seney camp was in the high priority list, and would be allocated as soon as the availability of objectors permitted. Eventually it transpired that there was no possibility of setting up additional new camps, and an offer of a recalcitrant camp was made.

The Service accepted this type of camp, assuming that even if the assignees were hard to get along with, they could be brought to a tractable state of mind through good treatment, or failing in that by the exercise of disciplinary methods as must exist in the regulations formulated by Selective Service, under Federal laws. Service officials were in this respect overly confident. 

On May 12 the advanced cadre of 12 assignees arrived and increments of various size continued to arrive until by the end of the month 40 objectors were in camp. 

Subsequent increases brought the total up to a normal strength of 75 to 85 assignees.

THE RECALCITRANT OBJECTOR 

The types of assignees sent to the Germfask camp for purposes of screening the bad from the good in the then existing camps throughout the county beggar description. At first glance they appeared to be, physically at least, much like the run of mankind inducted into the armed services. The outstanding peculiar-

THE PROBLEM OF CAMP ORDER AND DISCIPLINE >>> 237 

ity about them was the almost universal lack of expression in the eyes. Their laughter, if any, likewise had a vacant quality. Most of the objectors avoided a meeting of glances and kept their eyes focused on the floor or ground. Quite a number wore beards, and some of these achieved a Christlike appearance, though as we were to learn the impression was to be dissipated of any inner saintliness of spirit. Insofar as education was concerned, the objectors ran the gamut of the extremes, from the rather poorly schooled to the profusely educated. In background there were sons of ministers, scions of the wealthly, and some with prison records. Professions represented were many, and there was a quota each of engineers, artists, professors, lawyers and what-not. Potentially the group had the makings of a very fine community group, and excellent prospects for self-sufficiency as a work unit. Actually, these dormant talents were to be exercised in raising Hell instead of paying back to the Nation the price of escaping military duty. For that reason, in the following lines, we avoid using the word "conscientious" when referring to the Germfask objectors. No one who has not been closely associated with them for a substantial period of time could believe that such people could exist outside an insane asylum. 

Races represented included the white, black, and yellow. 

Practically all denominations were claimed by the objectors, and there were combinations or patchworks of several. There was a small group of Theosophists, and too many nonbelievers who expressed their religion as atheism. 

And it seems to us too, after trying to find the key to the souls of many individuals, that some of the ideologies were made up from day to day as the mental writhings of the subject conceived them. 

There was a minority group of political objectors composed of men who were not in sympathy with the current war. Also some who were apparently just mad at the Government for personal reasons. And not to be forgotten were those who are suspected of being friendly to the enemy. The camp troubles were not spontaneous we know; the hidden leadership was too well oriented in the art of causing dissension and mass action to be other than well schooled agitators. 

As for character, we'll pass lest it seem that we draw conclusions before the fact.

Any discussion of the loyalty of the objectors seems idle. At least we are confused, for they wouldn't fight for their country. But strangely they cherished their "rights" above the average American, and bellyached on the slightest pretext about habeas corpus, slavery, injustice, and liberty and the constitution. 

Camp lawyers made the most of it, and were continually needling the administration by quoting the law, or the regulations where they could possibly gain anything by doing so. 

So in the vast majority, the assignees were a bad lot of men who managed to escape the moral obligations an American is born with. The dozen or so sincere and really conscientious objectors were, of course, just the opposite. These poor fellows were assigned to keep camp functions going, and they did bear the burden of the dirty work, though they suffered severely from association with the recalcitrants and from the mangling and filthing their cause received as a result. 

BEHAVIOR OF THE OBJECTORS 

The administrative personnel which were employed to supervise the work and camp activities, were carefully selected for their solid reputation in the community, as well as their supervisory qualifications. They were fair-minded, tolerant; just the type to work with conscientious objectors. With a superior steward, splendid working equipment and the know-how to accomplish things, it was felt that the camp would go to town on work projects.

238. 

<CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION 

However, trouble began the first day, when it was plain that few of the men would work. It seemed that the big objection (at first) was the lack of pay. 

When we expressed our conviction that the price of a whole skin seemed to be the wage they were getting, they readily found other excuses, until we realized that we could expect no work unless the individual felt willing to give it. 

Likewise we learned that camp discipline could not be effected, that men could malinger on the sick list, refuse to work, go a. w. o. 1. up to 10 days, destroy property, and do pretty much what they wanted in camp without paying the penalty.

From May 12 to June 9, the camp director patiently bided his time, studying the regulations and building cases against the recalcitrants; then picked up his evidence and hit the trail for the district attorney's office, after assuring the camp supervisory personnel that he would be back with a carload of United States marshals and the authority to throw the malcontents into jail. 

But it was not to be. He was dumbfounded to learn that the law could not help us, except in case of desertion. Desertion was defined as absence without leave for 10 or more consecutive days. Anything less was to be handled by camp discipline, i. e., additional work.

We explained that we couldn't get the men to work in the first place and saw no chance of using extra work as a weapon unless they could be forced to do so by full implementation of the regulations. We cited the case of the assignee who, when ordered to sweep the dust off a stake truck platform, spent all day sweeping two-thirds of it (the total should have taken 5 minutes at the most) and then went on the sick list next day. We also detailed the process necessary to force an assignee to chop down a tree; how it was necessary to order every blow, every withdrawal of the ax, and point to the exact spot the axe was to fall each time; how the men would drive staples on the fencing project, not over the wire but beside it, above or below it and maybe putting in 50 staples when one would have done the trick. The district attorney then explained that an assignee could not be tried for failure or refusal to work unless the act was sworn to by the proper number of competent witnesses. In other words, for example, if a work unit of 25 men carried on as described, not much could be done because there was no standard of work recognized in the law. But if one or more of the men refused to work, he could be tried, provided there were a preponderance of witnesses on the accusing side to support the claim. It would seem that at least 26 witnesses were needed in the case cited, or counterclaims by the assignees would neutralize the evidence. 

A discussion of camp offenses, such as indecent exposure, destruction of property, assault and battery, failure to obey orders, and disloyalty to the United States, brought to light that such cases must be serious and flagrant, and that many were civil cases within the province of State courts. 

So we appealed to State authorities, to the State police and local courts and did have some small measure of success with camp offenses, until the assignees brought their high-powered lawyers and flush treasury to bear; then the State authorities found it too expensive to fight appeals or deal out long jail terms which had to be financed by the county funds. 

The local State mental hospital, willing to help if possible, needed enabling legislation to handle Federal wards. Later, when this was obtained, all assignees sent there for observation, confinement, and treatment were returned marked sane and healthy.

So we were up to our necks in trouble with no hope in sight. Our philosophy and decision was to hang on until the situation got bad enough, when the Government would have to do something about it.

THE PROBLEM OF CAMP ORDER AND DISCIPLINE >> 

239 

THE RESISTANCE MOVEMENT 

Stating frankly that they fully understood the limitations of the regulations and the law, the objectors made things as bad as possible, opining that if they were well behaved they would get nothing at all. Whereas if they were bad enough they might be discharged as unfit for "confinement" in a conscientious objectors camp. In the light of what eventually happened they were right about that, for many a bad actor was eventually discharged on one ground or another. 

Some felt that it might help their cause if they served prison sentences, others felt that their martydom in prison might sway public opinion in their behalf. 

These were willing to go to prison and probably most of the desertions which brought prison sentences were sought in this way. Some 22 objectors from this camp were sentenced to Federal prisons as a result. Twenty-one were discharged for one reason or another, by far the minority for physical or mental unfitness. 

The counter play of the administration was based upon the realization that the objectors might in time overplay their hand and bring about enough public resentment to inspire remedial legislation. Therefore, at no time did the supervisory personnel attempt to abuse, or mistreat, deprive of allotted food, or depart from the word or spirit of the regulations in its handling of the assignees. 

What trouble they had they brought upon themselves. 

And they made plenty. They deliberately and persistently sought to break up the camp functions. They made life as miserable as possible for the supervisory personnel, thinking they would quit and the camp would eventually break up for want of supervisory personnel. And it is true that there was a large turnover in that location. There were five stewards (cooks) for instance, four camp managers (not counting the one who stayed only a half day), two project superintendents, three foremen, and five different doctors gave full and fair treatment and conscientious medical service, though patently disgusted and hopeful of getting away.

THE PUBLIC REACTION 

Public opinion of the conscientious objector was undoubtedly much the same in the district as that which would have been found anywhere. Most likely it was compounded of some little sympathy, some pity, some contempt, and in' the minds of a few, a tinge of admiration for men that could take the rap in support of religious conviction. This compound of opinion sagged sharply when word got about that the men were not conscientious objectors, but the dregs of the better camps. It hit bottom when the newspapers published an account of the fact that the assignees would not work, and feeling mounted to indignation when it became public knowledge that the objectors were destroying good food at a time when even the common sort of provender was being strictly rationed. If the assignees had been decently behaved, and done a reasonable amount of work, unquestionably the true conscientious objector would have done much toward improving public opinion in his special case. Instead, the public mind in this region has been prejudiced for a long time to come 

MEDICAL FACILITIES 

Medical service provided was of the best obtainable. In the first phase of camp life a local physician was obtained to take care of what was expected to be a minor matter. However, the assignees soon seized on the opportunity and conjured enough cases to make it necessary to have a doctor, if not on duty, at least available most of the time. 737977°-50-vol. 1—17

« 

CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION 

The records show that five different physicians served the assignees, and in addition specialist service was engaged when the case ran out of the orbit of the general practitioner. Of the total of 20,510 man-days available in the duration of the camp, 3,994 were consumed by the "sick." It is estimated most generously that one-tenth may have been really ill. 

The morning report for the month of July reveals the assignees' sense of humor. Thus six men in consecutive order in the B's and C's were sick most of the month; all of the four K's were sick all month, as were both of the 

S's and half of the H's. The total monthly average of men sick was about 12. 

This offered an escape opportunity for the assignee escape from work, and possibly from the objectors' camp. A number took this route and were eventually discharged. The case of John Menzies was one in point. Menzies went sick December 13 and remained in bed (during working hours) until May 19, a total of 150 days.

The doctors can hardly be blamed, for they were conscientious men and loath to running the risk of making a bad guess, even when fairly certain that assignees were faking illness. 

WEAKNESSES OF THE SYSTEM 

Good and bad objectors should not be mixed in a work camp. If the former is in the minority, the aggressive recalcitrant dominates, and the neutral-minded fellow is prone to go from the balancing point in the downward direction. 

Undoubtedly many of the assignees had domestic worries. The most common was lack of income while confined in a CPS camp. 

The writer doesn't believe that objectors should be relieved of any obligation to their Nation in time of war. However, if these men cannot be screened more carefully so as to exclude the coward and the political and radical objector, obviously serious penalties should be inflicted on the recalcitrant. 

Perhaps the bad actors should be educated in the first principles of life. That is, they might be segregated entirely from their fellow citizens by being placed in an isolated location or a large island, and given an opportunity to work and fight to survive, which is, after all, the heritage our freedom-loving forefathers passed on to us.

By subtracting the cost of the materials incorporated into the project we have a net cost of $75,334.14 for 2,626 man-days of labor accomplishment, such as it was. 

Apparently this would approximate $30 a day for common labor. 

However, one can merely look at the accomplished work today and assure himself that 10 men could easily do the work in 6 months at a cost of not over $6,000.

Therefore, the camp is evaluated at the cost of materials in the amount of 13,000-odd dollars and labor at the value of $6,000 or a sum total of $20,000. 

This is one-fourth of the amount of the money expended. 

Further examination of these figures seems to reveal that if it cost $75,000 to do $6,000 worth of labor, the relative efficiency of the objector labor (plus the help of the working foremen) was one-twelfth. In other words the assignee labor cost 12×$30 or $360 per day, truly a fantastic figure. 

The Fish and Wildlife Service benefited by acquisition of all the camp buildings and the working equipment formerly the property of the Civilian Conservation Corps. For this we are grateful. The camps were donated to veterans organizations, churches, and other public agencies to square ourselves for the trouble our objectors caused. We hope now to forget the episode. 

Organized Resistance at Minersville

As indicated by the superintendent's report, much of the trouble at Germfask originated with a small number of assignees and gradually spread to include others. When the transfer to Minersville, Calif., was made, the leaders of the nonviolent recalcitrants had been eliminated 5 Unpublished report on file at National Headquarters, Selective Service System, Washington.

at Germfask through the process of reclassification and discharge. 

Upon the arrival of the assignees at Minersville it was therefore more evident than ever that the minor group of the badly maladjusted would attempt to control the entire group of objectors there. In the first news letter published at Minersville, for instance, an editorial written by one of the most active of the malcontents indicated the approach which the noncooperating assignees were to take from then on: 

THE INEVITABLE GAP 

The business of establishing a new camp, in particular, Camp Germfask, at Minersville, makes clear once again the gap that exists between the thinking of the assignees and the thinking of the administrative personnel. The camp director, Bliss Haynes of the Forest Service, is no stranger to the few of us who knew him as project superintendent at Coleville. We know him to be a thoroughly fair-minded, kind, and personable gentleman. He is naturally anxious to make the kind of progress in this new location that the Forest Service values. He has his responsibilities to his organization and he means to make as much progress as is possible in a CPS set-up. It is immediately obvious that the rest of the camp administration is friendly toward us. Few CPS camps have been as fortunate in this respect as the new Germfask. 

Despite all this, a gap in outlook between Germfask men and their administrators still exists. And there is nothing short of terminating this forced labor system that will bridge this gap. In the next weeks and months we feel that it is as certain as the setting sun that antipathies of an insoluble nature will arise across this gap.

It requires no extraordinary foresight at Minersville to anticipate a repetition of the Germfask, Mich. "trouble." Nor is it reasonable to expect that a continuation of officially-inspired suppressive measures will quash the "trouble." 

There are three courses which the administration of Camp Germfask may take. 

They may muddle through and accept a poor work record. They may "crack down" and accept the unpleasant fruits of this familiar policy. Or they may withdraw from the system. We hope that they choose the last. 

The story of CPS is unchanged. The gap still exists. At Camp Germfask we begin again a chapter with which we are already fully acquainted. 

In spite of this beginning there seemed to be no more of an organized movement for protest at Minersville than there was in Germfask. 

Many individuals in Minersville belonged to the so-called troublemaker category, but there was no open rebellion by any group of assignees. 

The camp had a series of acts of sabotage that started with destroying equipment and ended with the burning down of the mess hall and storage building. However, circumstances indicated that these were the work of only two objectors at the most. 

An Attempt at Concerted Action in Government Camps 

Between the opening of the Mancos camp in July 1943 and December 1945, following VE- and VJ-Days, there was little evidence of an • Mimeographed camp publication issued by assignees; copy on file at National Head quarters, Selective Service System, Washington.

organized plan of resistance in the Government-operated units. The problem of order and discipline which had been growing slowly for some time did develop at a more rapid rate, however, after VE-Day. 

Incidents of antisocial behavior, of refusals to work and even of open violence became more numerous. There was a further increase after 

VJ-Day. 

This was to be expected with the end of the war and the type of maladjusted assignees which constituted much of the objector personnel of the Government camps. When these camp units had been established, it will be recalled that some of the problem type individuals immediately asked to be transferred to them. Others were sent to the 

Government units upon request of the church administration or the initiative of Selective Service. By the close of hostilities in Europe the seeds of discontent and noncooperation had therefore taken root. 

As an example of the more serious trouble which was contemplated in December of 1945, "The CPS-GI”, a mimeographed newsletter of the noncooperative group in the Mancos camp stated: 

This issue of the CPS-GI is dedicated to organizations that we feel CO's should be interested in, both now and after demobilization. Included are four pages of information on such organizations. We recognize that a great difference of beliefs and temperament exists, nevertheless we believe that the opportunity for finding common ground is much greater than generally accepted. This issue is published as an aid to individual investigation of groups acceptable to those who wish to join with others in progressive pacifist action. 

Quoting further:

In the last 2 weeks the Mancos “radicals” opposition to conscription has taken on a creative outlet.

Most so-called trouble makers in both church and Government camps eventually end up at Minersville, Calif. (formerly Germfask, Mich.). The recent mass exodus of 12 Mancos assignees to the "Alcatraz” of conscientious objectors camps was regarded by the majority of those directly affected as a promotion. 

One of the group adequately expressed transferee feeling by stating “Thanks, Mr. Thomas."

Director Thomas naively assumed that the transferring of slow-downers, suspected saboteurs, and nonconformists would quell the contagious disobedience. 

Thomas first began transferring men to Lapine, Oreg., then Germfask, Mich., and now Minersville, Calif. He has not faced his problems and they still go unsolved.

There are always others ready to take the places of those liquidated. 

The different attitudes of the two camps are distinctly noticeable. At Mancos the general attitude is one of submissive tolerance. That the CPS system is not one of service is recognized, but little opposition is forthcoming. The obedient response to project orders is discouraging to those anxious to thwart totalitarian dictums.

At Minersville, foremen rarely tell a man to work; rather internees are told to go to their stations. And nothing more is said. Constant tension prevails between internees and administration. Officials are frustrated because of inability to perform duties responsibly. Vigilance on the part of internees prevents a great deal of administrative action from becoming reality. CPS is recognized
