as a definite slave-labor program, and moral honesty prevents cooperation. 

As CPS throughout the Nation grinds on on its last legs (we keep telling ourselves), I feel sure that general unrest and dissatisfaction will break out into active nonviolent noncooperation, a fitting end for CPS.' 

Copies of this news letter were distributed widely in all of the other Government camps and in some of the church-sponsored units. 

Agitation at the Glendora Unit

In February of 1946, prior to the transfer of the camp at Glendora, Calif., from church to Government sponsorship, an organization of assignees, calling themselves "The Irresponsibles," published an open mimeographed letter to the United States Forest Service which introduced the first real attempt of resistance action by a group. The letter is quoted in part:

For 4½ years you have helped administer a civilian public service camp; now you plan to completely administer it. In so doing we feel that you have not been, and are not now, aware of a number of facts concerning the CPS system. We wish to call these facts to your attention while there is still time to consider them and to act upon them. First, CPS is a slave-labor punitive system dangerously similar to that evolved in Germany and is seriously threatening our American democratic way of life. Second, CPS men have for several years given their labor grudgingly and are increasing resistance to this vicious system; you can expect less and less collaboration from them in perpetuating it.

With these things in mind we are concerned, not so much for ourselves who have been enslaved, but because CPS threatens the democratic society we know. 

Using CPS as a precedent, bills that would make us a total state have already been introduced in Congress. So far they have been defeated, by a too-narrow margin, but the precedent remains, the bills only waiting for a few more votes. 

The second factor of which you seem unaware is an increasing resistance to the CPS system. For several years we in Glendora have done as little work as possible because we did not like being slaves. During the last year, however, we have come to see clearly the threat CPS offers to society; from this stems the present resistance. We do not care to aid in our own enslavement and feel a responsibility to our country and to mankind to make a totalitarian-breeding system unsuccessful. Our fight is not with you; it is with the system. It is not because of personal animosity that we refuse to collaborate with you, but because we wish to make the system unsuccessful. To be sure, slaves do not usually like their masters and you must recognize this byproduct of an evil system if you allow yourselves to be entangled. Our goal is not to fight you; our goal is to destroy CPS. Sincerely, Quoting further from the same newsletter:

THE IRRESPONSIBLES RESISTANCE NOW! 

CPS has been too successful for any of us to have clear consciences about our roles under the system; it is time that we settle with ourselves. If we believe 

Copy on file at National Headquarters, Selective Service System, Washington.

THE PROBLEM OF CAMP ORDER AND DISCIPLINE >> 245 

that CPS is an evil system, it is our moral duty to resist it and its operation. 

We have made CPS succeed so far; we can keep it from succeeding more. We have the manpower; we have the brainpower; do we have the willpower? 

The greatest difficulty that we pacifists have is that we are apt to talk and have meetings rather than act. Procrastination is a psychological evasion of action. We find it easy to put off action merely because we are afraid of action; when the prearranged date arrives we set a new one. We speak of March 1do we mean 1948?

How do accountable men, whole men, react to such a system as CPS? How can they resist nonviolently? There are a number of techniques that can be used singly or in combination to help make CPS an unsuccessful experiment in conscription: 

1. We can refuse to take responsibility for the project; that is the job of the camp administrator and his aides-they get paid for it—let's not help them evade the obligations of their positions. We can only take orders. 

2. We can slow down and do as little work as possible; we can at least keep the project part of CPS from operating smoothly. The merits of this method are that a few men can start a slow-down, that it can bog a project, and that it is not illegal. Generally those who slow down should be on project, not in administrative positions, overhead, or positions of responsibility. 

3. We can refuse to work; it is rumored that this is illegal-but it is sometimes necessary to break the law. The project suffers when men do not work; the primary advantage over the slow-down method is that the individual has more time to spend in a constructive manner. 

4. We can walk out of CPS; this method enables a man to personally escape the evils of CPS. To render CPS ineffective and to be socially worth while a walk-out must be done by 99.44/100 percent of the men. 

5. We can practice sabotage. This method of resistance is advocated by many pacifists and has been practiced in some CPS camps. A program of sabotage, for success, must have clearly defined goals and close organization.³ 

On March 1, 1946, the camp at Glendora was opened as a Government camp. It was evident upon this change of sponsorship that some very definite plans had been made by the belligerent assignees. However, it took considerable time to identify the leaders and to secure evidence to prosecute them. Several outstanding agitators and troublemakers were identified as the Government investigators proceeded with the initial screening of the camp personnel. Two of these were given orders to transfer to the Minersville, Calif., camp upon the advice of the United States attorney. They refused to transfer and were thereupon reported to the attorney for prosecution. 

An Organized Effort at Glendora 

On April 24, 1946, 25 assignees at the Glendora camp refused to perform assigned duties. They gave as the reason what they termed the "arbitrary" action of the officials of the System in ordering the transfer of the two agitator objectors from the unit. This situation was reported promptly to the United States attorney at Los Angeles, Calif., on April 25 and prosecution was requested. Upon the ad- 

8 Ibid.

- 

CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION 

vice of the Attorney General, however, such prosecution was delayed. As time elapsed the circumstances grew progressively worse until on May 15, 1946, 82 assignees from Glendora were involved. 

Shortly after the United States attorney had been advised of these law violations and was determing the proper steps to take, he was advised by the Department of Justice, Washington, D. C., to hold arrests and prosecutions in abeyance until a full and complete investigation and report could be made and submitted by the Federal Bureau of Investigation. When such report had been prepared it would be examined by the Department and a recommendation for action would be made.

The Spread of Resistance to Other Camps 

While this was transpiring the problem of order and discipline became more acute at some other Government camps. The numbers joining the resistance movement at these units were increasing daily and the situation appeared to be getting out of hand. The Civilian 

Public Service Camps involved were located at Cascade Locks, Oreg.; 

Three Rivers, Calif.; Mesa, Ariz.; Philadelphia, Pa.; Gatlingburg, Tenn.; Bowie, Md.; and Big Flats, N. Y. In consequence, several conferences were held between representatives of Selective Service and the Department of Justice during May 1946, with a view to encouraging early and speedy prosecutions. It was readily apparent that prosecution was the only available remedy for halting the trend which had begun. The System, however, was confronted with what seemed to be a reluctance upon the part of the Department of Justice to prosecute these cases even though there was substantial evidence of law violation. In the meantime, the situation became critical enough that the technical or Federal agencies operating the camps in question were making plans to discontinue the project use of objector assignees to the civilian work program. 

Trial and Conviction of Leaders 

On May 18, 1946, only 6 men were arrested out of the 82 involved for over 15 days in the disturbance at Civilian Public Service Camp No. 

76, Glendora, Calif. The six arrests did not serve to deter the others from their subversive activities; instead they continued in a refusalto-work status, and some of the more active resorted to the sabotage of Government property. A conference between representatives of the 

Department of Justice and Selective Service was therefore held on 

May 27, 1946, and subsequently 51 more men were arrested.

The trials of this group of violators were originally set for July 30, 1946; however, they were postponed four successive times and the registrants in question were not finally brought to trial until March

THE PROBLEM OF CAMP ORDER AND DISCIPLINE » 247 

8, 1947, approximately one year after the offenses had been committed. 

During the time that elapsed between the first arrests and the date of the trials in March 1947, 25 of the assignees involved in the difficulty requested to be returned to camp to resume their project duties; this was done and the court cases against them were dropped. Thirtysix more cases were discharged by the United States attorney to facilitate the handling of the trial. The 21 remaining objectors were identified as having been the leaders in the resistance movement at Glendora and the worst of the group of violators. They were prosecuted and convictions obtained for all of the 21 in the Los Angeles Federal court.

The End of the Disturbance 

On May 1, 1946, 40 men engaged in a similar disturbance at Civilian Public Service Camp No. 46, Big Flats, N. Y., in sympathy with the 

Glendora movement. A report of the matter was made to the United 

States Attorney, Buffalo, N. Y. On May 10, the Federal Bureau of

Investigation completed its examination and report covering the situation at the unit. Selective Service was thereupon informed that the attorney at Buffalo wanted to arrest and initiate prosecutive action against all participants in the trouble. However, the Department of 

Justice instructed him from Washington to arrest only those who could be identified as troublemakers and ringleaders. Following this six men were arrested on May 20 who persisted in their refusal to perform assigned duties. These were the only ones who continued in the refusal-to-work status after May 15. The others, after refusing for 15 days, reported for duty. All six arrested were tried in the 

Federal court at Buffalo and were convicted. 

At the other camps throughout the country where there had been sympathetic demonstrations, all of the assignees returned to work and it was not necessary to prosecute any of them. 

Public Reaction to the Resistance Movement 

During the prolonged investigation and apparent disregard by the Department of Justice of problem assignees in the C. P. S. Camps, many newspapers and civic and patriotic organizations, especially those that knew the situation as it existed within their own communities, published strong editorials and wrote critical letters of protest. 

Some organizations, such as the American Legion, passed resolutions condemning the lack of action on the part of the Government. The national executive committee of the Legion at its May 1946 meeting, in response to resolutions from Legion posts throughout the Nation which were interested in the prosecution of conscientious-objector delinquents, passed unanimously the following resolution directed to the President of the United States:

Whereas, it has been called to the attention of The American Legion that many conscientious objectors assigned to work of national importance have refused to work in California, New York, and in other States, and Whereas, only a small percentage of these men have been arrested and none prosecuted through inactivity or procrastination on the part of the office of the Attorney General of the United States, and Whereas, this condition constitutes a laxity in law enforcement by the office of the Attorney General of the United States, and results in an unfair discrimination against men in uniform who have honorably served our country and obeyed its laws now therefore Be it resolved that the national commander be authorized to bring the above facts to the attention of the President of the United States to the end that prosecution be carried forward as provided under Selective Service laws and regulations.

Thus it can be seen what inroads upon the general good will of the Nation toward work of national importance under civilian direction were made by the dissident actions of a handful of unbridled assignees. 

Their utterly selfish and uncontrolled activities came near to bringing the normally good operations of the entire program and its camp units into gross disrepute.

Opinions of Technical Agencies Operating Camps 

The final report of the superintendent of the Germfask camp gave a good account of disciplinary problems at camp level and the opinions of other technical or Federal agencies operating such units, are also of significance in this connection. As has been seen, most of these agencies admitted the value of the camp project work done by conscientious objectors. However, most of them, like the Germfask superintendent, also made reference to the delinquency phase encountered in the employment of the objector. For instance, a report from a regional administrator of the Bureau of Land Management in the Department of Interior stated: 

Because of lack of authority to enforce discipline in problem cases both camp management and project administration was more difficult than would have been the case had there been adequate provision for corrective disciplinary action for agitators and noncooperators. Representatives of Selective Service were most cooperative and sympathetic in this problem, but the lack of basic authority in the Selective Service Act to correct such conditions made it impossible to initiate adequate disciplinary measures. Because of the fact that it was necessary to refer disciplinary cases through civil courts a great deal of delay was involved and in many instances when such cases finally came to trial, sentences were inadequate or cases were dismissed. Such results naturally encouraged others toward noncooperation as the punishment was often less severe than remaining in camp and working.'

The Chief, Forest Service, Department of Agriculture, made some pertinent comments as a result of a survey among that agency's Regional Offices to which conscientious objectors had been assigned. • Ibid.

THE PROBLEM OF CAMP ORDER AND DISCIPLINE » 249 

If the need for a program similar to the CPS should ever arise again, full cost of the program should, we believe, be borne by the Federal Government. We doubt if any outside group, such as the “historic peace churches,” should be called upon to contribute food, clothing, or financial support to the program. 

Our field men in general feel that: (1) the establishment and operation of programs, camps, and projects should be solely a function of the Federal Government. (2) There should be no active participation in the actual functioning of the program or any control of the assignees by any religious body or group. (3) 

In the event of possible future interest by any religious body or association in a similar program, such interest should be confined to an advisory board serving at the national level in a strictly consultive capacity. 

The problem of obtaining compliance with camp or work regulations was difficult in some of the camps. It is believed the other suggestions set forth in this letter, if carried out, would do much to improve the morale of the assignees and facilitate conduct of a similar program, including compliance with the necessary work and camp regulations. However, there would still remain the problem of dealing with that small percent of men who refuse to conform to reasonable regulations and who are so disruptive to the discipline that must go with a program of this type if it is to be well ordered. It is suggested special consideration be given to ways and means of rapidly, effectively and with justice removing chronic malingerers and malcontents from the work groups and projects. In some cases this might call for speeding up action on the part of civil law enforcement and judicial agencies in prosecuting actual violators of the laws upon which any program was based. In most cases, however, the failure to comply with camp and work regulations was not, in the recent program, of a type warranting action in the courts. It is this phase of discipline within the organizations that especially deserves consideration.10

Here again is indicated the key importance of order and discipline in the whole civilian work program for the Class IV-E objector registrant of Selective Service. 

Suggestions for Dealing with Recalcitrants 

Some strong opinions have been presented in this and preceding chapters regarding the few assignees in the C. P. S. Camps who attempted to break down the respect of the entire group for law and order. Their purpose was to render unsuccessful the whole civilian work program, and, as a result, these presentations of opinion had to be made, regretful though they might be. This monograph on conscientious objection, among other things, must call striking attention to the individuals in the camps who through wilfully creating disciplinary problems sought to undermine the best efforts (1) of most 

Class IV-E registrants, (2) of the churches, (3) of the technical agencies, and (4) of Selective Service to justify the forward-looking provisions of the 1940 law.

With the end of World War II these progressive conscientious objector provisions and the System's application of them became a significant part of the American tradition for utilizing during a national 

10 Ibid. 41

<CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION 

emergency the services of citizens whose beliefs did not permit them to bear arms. This important experience must therefore be guarded historically; it may have great future significance in connection with fulfilling an obligation for duty within the limits of faith. In consequence, an effective answer needs to be found to the often-heard question of the camp delinquent, "Well, what are you going to do about it?" and to the statement of some that "We're hot potatoes, too hot even for the Attorney General to handle !"

Part of the problem of camp order and discipline may have been indigenous with the fundamental approach to the type of objector who was generally assigned to civilian work during the 1940-47 emergency. Perhaps in developing the special legal provisions, classification procedures and work program for him, sight was lost of the fact that outside of his possessing a conscience which did not permit him to serve with the armed forces, he was very much the same kind of a person as the average citizen of the United States. However, in comparison with the registrant who performed combatant duty in the Army or Navy, or even the C.O. accepting noncombatant service therein, he may have been somewhat imposed upon on the one hand and catered to on the other. 

To illustrate, he performed a duty to his country by his project activities in the camp and yet there was scant attention given to his welfare along such lines as pay, allowances, and allotments. From the other standpoint Selective Service in its selection, classification and assignment of the Class IV-E registrant, and the System, the churches, and the technical agencies in the operation of the living and working activities in the camps were very considerate in most respects. Less economic hardship for the objector assignee and his family, coupled with a more direct selective process and a more effective camp organization, might result in less delinquency. More incentive to serve in a civilian capacity, even though it might involve the hazards of duty overseas occasionally under gunfire circumstances, would perhaps result in a better appreciation by the conscientious objector of the selection process and of camp order and discipline. At least, under such conditions, this might be expected from assignees cooperative in every respect, from those cooperative but easily influenced and even from the "passive resisters." It might mean nothing to the few bent upon active law violation though it would tend to give them less grounds for such behavior.

For the active recalcitrant, malcontent, maladjusted registrant in camp a more effective procedure of selection and organization must therefore be developed. The basic law and the regulations of 

Selective Service must provide more discriminating selection for

THE PROBLEM OF CAMP ORDER AND DISCIPLINE » 251 

assignment by the System and prompt action for discipline at the camp. There should be but one authority within a camp, preferably a Government official who is an employee of the technical agency concerned with the project, and when an assignee refuses to obey orders, to work, to keep his person and quarters clean or to conduct himself in reasonable fashion, the camp director should be empowered to place him under detention pending a thorough hearing and investigation by himself and his church, Selective Service, medical, legal and other staff. Upon the continuation of the refusal, if the orders are reissued following the hearing, the director should have authority to extend the detention and to refer the case to (1) a regional and Presidential board of church, Selective Service, medical, legal, and other representatives for prompt action; (2) to the United States attorney for immediate arrest and prosecution; or (3) to the System for prompt reclassification and induction into the armed forces.

XIII 

THE OBJECTOR WHO VIOLATED THE LAW 

Regarding matters of law violation, most of the attention so far has been given to conscientious objectors (Class IV-E registrants) who failed to comply with civilian work assignments during the Selective Service program of 1940-47. Those creating problems of order and discipline by counseling or aiding in such evasion among other assignees at Civilian Public Service Camps, have also been mentioned. 

Likewise noted were those failing to report for work of national importance to the local boards of the System or to the camps. 

These three types of violations pertained only to registrants selected for service who objected to both combatant and noncombatant duty with the armed forces. Objectors were also involved in three additional types of violations: failure of the Class I-A-O registrant to report for induction into noncombatant service and failure of any C. O. to return his Selective Service Questionnaire (DSS Form 40) or to register. The last three were also pertinent for other registrants. 

Definition of a Delinquent 

A conscientious objector who violated the basic law of the System by failing or neglecting to perform one of the above duties was termed a delinquent. Delinquency was somewhat broader than this for the objector, and for other registrants, too, as will be seen from the general regulations which were in effect March 31, 1947: 

601.5. Delinquent.—A “delinquent" is a man liable for training and service under the provisions of the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940, as amended, who fails or neglects to perform any duty required of him under the provisions of the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940, as amended, and regulations made pursuant thereto. 

The main concern of the present chapter is with the law violations or delinquencies of objectors along the six lines already detailed. 

Monograph No. 14, The Enforcement of the Selective Service Law deals with the entire problem of violation.

253

The Trial of Violators by Civil Authority 

Before discussing the six types of delinquency further, however, it should perhaps be said that during World War II the enforcement of Federal conscription was, for the first time in the history of the United States, made the sole responsibility of civil authority. All law-violating conscientious objectors were therefore proceeded against in the Federal Courts under the criminal provisions of the Selective 

Training and Service Act of 1940. 

The Penalty Provisions of the Act 

Attention should likewise be given to the enforcement provisions of the 1940 Act. They were contained in section 11 which read as follows: 

Any person charged as herein provided with the duty of carrying out any of the provisions of this act, or the rules or regulations made or directions given thereunder, who shall knowingly fail or neglect to perform such duty, and any person charged with such duty, or having and exercising any authority under said act, rules, regulations, or directions who shall knowingly make, or be a party to the making, of any false, improper, or incorrect registration, classification, physical or mental examination, deferment, induction, enrollment, or muster, and any person who shall knowingly make, or be a party to the making of, any false statement or certificate as to the fitness or unfitness or liability or nonliability of himself or any other person for service under the provisions of this act, or rules, regulations, or directions made pursuant thereto, or who otherwise evades registration or service in the land or naval forces or any of the requirements of this act, or who knowingly counsels, aids, or abets another to evade registration or service in the land or naval forces or any of the requirements of this act, or of said rules, regulations, or directions, or who in any manner shall knowingly fail or neglect to perform any duty required of him under or in the execution of this act, or rules or regulations made pursuant to this act, or any person or persons who shall knowingly hinder or interfere in any way by force or by violence with the administration of this act or the rules or regulations made pursuant thereto, or conspire to do so, shall, upon conviction in the district court of the United States having jurisdiction thereof, be punished by imprisonment for not more than 5 years or a fine of not more than $10,000, or by both such fine and imprisonment, or if subject to military or naval law may be tried by court martial, and, on conviction, shall suffer such punishment as a court martial in any case arising under this act unless such person has been actually inducted for the training and service prescribed under this act or unless he is subject to trial by court martial under laws in force prior to the enactment of this act. Precedence shall be given by courts to the trial cases arising under this act. 

Thus the law of 1940 provided that no person should be tried by a military or naval court martial in any case unless such person had actually been inducted into the armed forces. The United States 

Supreme Court further construed the language of the act to mean that the Congress did not intend "to subject to military jurisdiction those who are unwilling to come to the defense of their Nation in its

THE OBJECTOR WHO VIOLATED THE LAW » D 

255 hour of peril" and held that the armed forces had "no authority to exercise force for the purpose of inducting selectees into the service." 1 

No Special Treatment for Delinquent Objectors 

It should also be said that under the 1940 Act a registrant who claimed conscientious objection was subject at all times to the same provisions as any other man with liability thereunder. Only two special things were expected of the conscientious objector and they were in nowise required. One was preparing and submitting to his 

Selective Service local board the Special Form for Conscientious Objector (DSS Form 47) which detailed his claim. Failure to fill out and return this blank was not considered a violation of the law; it had only the effect of withdrawing the claim of objection which had previously been made in the Questionnaire (DSS Form 40). 

The second special item was the opportunity offered the objector to appear before a hearing officer if his claim was referred to the Department of Justice by an appeal board of the System. However, in this, as in the other instance, failure to put in an appearance was not considered a delinquency; it merely became another item of information to the Department in the making of its recommendation for his classification.

Failure to Register, Return Questionnaire or Report for Physical 

A return may now be made to the types of violation for which conscientious objectors became delinquent, were indicted, prosecuted, and convicted if found guilty. Objectors who failed or refused to register or to return their Questionnaires were for the most part registrants absolutely or totally opposed to combatant, noncombatant, civilian or any other service whatsoever. They were completely noncooperative or uncooperative and in the main would serve prison sentences rather than perform any type of duty under the Selective Service Act. This was true to a lesser degree of those who failed to report for physical examination because a number of other factors entered into the matter of examination. Often a registrant who claimed objection to service in the armed forces was classified as available for such duty and called up for his physical during that early period of the System's operation when passing the examination meant almost automatic induction. This was before preinduction physical examinations were given at the induction stations and also when a selectee was assumed to have taken the oath if he was in the group to which it was administered.2 

¹ Billings v. Truesdell, 321 U. S. 542, 64 S. Ct. 737 (1944). 

2 Consult special monographs on Enforcement of the Selective Service Law (No. 14) and Physical Examination of Selective Service Registrants (No. 15). 

737977°-50-vol. 1——18

Although objectors failing to report for examination were clearly violators of the law, such delinquency was due to their feeling that they were entitled to be in Class I-A-O as available for noncombatant service, rather than in I-A available for combatant duty where they had been placed. The same was true of objectors claiming Class IV-E, available for civilian work, who were classified either in I-A-O or I-A. Their behavior was in accordance with the dictates of conscience. They chose prison rather than the violation of belief. This is discussed further in connection with parolees, amnesty, and the new procedure of section 642.41(d) in the general regulations. 

Refusal to Report for Work of National Importance 

Very few conscientious objectors in Class IV-E had a valid excuse for failing to report for work of national importance in a Civilian Public Service Camp. For the most part these noncooperators were absolutists, that is, total objectors who refused to accept any service whatever, even though they had complied with the registration and classification provisions of the law. One "absolutist" expressed his opposition to any kind of duty, and also his helplessness of achieving complete success in this regard, as follows in a letter to his local board which is on file at the National Headquarters of the System: 

No matter what I do as a living being on this earth, my very existence as a citizen and potential taxpayer of this country can be interpreted into being a conscious contribution to the war effort. The only way I could truly be a conscientious objector would be to absolve myself of all activities which in any way could be viewed as helping the war effort. This state of being can be achieved only by suicide, the destruction of my own life, which is itself an indirect aid to the war effort.

When an objector failed to comply with an Order to Report for Work of National Importance (DSS Form 50), information regarding him was provided the United States attorney by his local board on a Delinquent Registrant Report (DSS Form 550). If the board be lieved that by reasonable effort it might be able to locate the registrant and secure his compliance, however, it could delay the mailing of the 

Form 550 for a period not in excess of 30 days.

It might appear that some objectors were justified in their refusal to accept even a civilian work assignment. But a sounder legal course would have been for them to comply with the Order to Report for Work of National Importance and then to test their claims for absolute objection through application for a writ of habeas corpus. 

However, in the latter months of the Selective Service operation, rulings of the Supreme Court held that defendants could raise the ques- • Falbo v. United States, 320 U. S. 549; Billings v. Truesdell, 321 U. S. 542; Estep v. 

United States, 327 U. S. 114; Smith v. United States, ibid.; Gibson v. United States, Dodez v. Same, 67 S. Ct. 301.

THE OBJECTOR WHO VIOLATED THE LAW 257 

tion of the validity of their classifications as a defense in Federal court. This they had not been permitted to do previously. 4 One registrant who thought he should have been deferred from any service but who would have been satisfied with a IV-E classification by the System, reported for induction as an objector and then filed a writ of habeas corpus to obtain his release. Others with similar feelings might have tried this, but it would have been more difficult to succeed in cases where eligibility for deferment was claimed than where the claim was to a statutory-exempt status, such as that of a minister of religion. In the case cited the assignee was successful in securing a release but not by showing he was wrongly classified. 

He was released on the claim that he had been deprived of a procedural right.

Failure To Perform Duties in C. P. S. Camp 

Registrants who after reporting to camps failed to comply with orders, were sometimes characterized as "men against the State." 

They were reported to the Department of Justice for refusal to comply with an order of transfer, for absence without leave or taking unauthorized leave, and for refusal to work. The first and second were sometimes regarded as types of desertion, since they involved refusal to report to or remain in camp. Violations resulting from failure to perform camp duties, then, generally constituted "desertion" and refusal to work. 

Other Violations

Objectors who were convicted of counseling or aiding evasion at camp or otherwise were a type apart from the others. 

In this connection there appears to have been no question involved regarding their classification as C. O. violators in IV-E.

Other violations were such minor things as failure to carry a classification card. This was considered a technical violation and was sufficient grounds for holding a registrant in custody by police officers until his status could be verified or until more serious charges were preferred. There seems to have been only one record of the actual prosecution of a C. O. for failure to have his classification card in possession.

Ordering Delinquents To Report for Service 

During the latter part of Selective Service operations it became the practice to classify an objector or other registrant, even if he failed to return his Questionnaire (DSS Form 40), and to order him up for

service although he had not reported for a preinduction physical examination. This change took place on November 1, 1943, when section 

642.12 of the general regulations was amended by Amendment No. 181 (8 F. R. 14115). Delinquents who had not already been classified at the time of the change, as well as registrants who became delinquent in the future, were to be placed in a class available for duty. The effect was one of eliminating delinquents who failed to return their Questionnaires or to report for examination. If they persisted in refusing to comply, they became delinquent for failure to report for induction or assignment and were referred to the Department of Justice. 

The change was a general one adopted for all registrants in the interests of a more effective operation of the System. 

It should perhaps be mentioned also at this point that whenever any local board suspected a person, other than one of its own registrants, of being a delinquent, the general regulations provided for it to advise such person by letter of its suspicions and direct him to submit evidence concerning his Selective Service status to the board. 

He could even be directed to appear personally before the board. 

Thereafter, unless the board was convinced he was not a delinquent, it was required to report the matter in a letter to the United States attorney. This procedure did not play much of a role, however, as regards conscientious objector delinquents.

Action by National Headquarters 

As mentioned much earlier, both official and unofficial questions sometimes were raised with National Headquarters of Selective Service on the classifications of objector and other registrants who had been reported to the United States attorney. Such inquiries were occasionally made even when registrants were being tried in court. If National Headquarters became convinced that the person was clearly entitled to an exempt or deferred classification, it arranged for prosecutive action to be postponed or for court trial to be recessed for continuation later, so that the registrant's case could be reviewed by the Presidential Appeal Board and an advisory opinion expressed for the assistance of the prosecution or the court. 

At a later period in operations the Director of Selective Service sometimes went as far as advising the Justice Department of his opinion in instances where it was strongly felt by National Headquarters that the objector or other registrant had been erroneously classified. He would also recommend at such times, that consideration be given to returning the case to the local board of jurisdiction with a view to further classification action, and, if necessary, appeal to the appropriate board of appeal or to the President. Such recom-

THE OBJECTOR WHO VIOLATED THE LAW » 259 

mendation was made in but a very few cases, however. Along the same line a number of cases were returned to local boards by United States attorneys for the correction of procedural classification errors and in other instances the courts refused to convict registrants for reported delinquencies, feeling that they had not been given the exempt classifications to which they were entitled. 

A decision was also made by the Director that cases of delinquency involving any religious question in a classification action were to be reviewed in State and National Headquarters before the delinquencies were reported to the United States attorney. This policy was based upon two premises. The first was that where the registrant claimed improper classification or procedure, a State Director or the Director should make the appropriate appeal to assure further consideration. 

It was believed likewise that when a case had been reviewed by a State Director and the Director of Selective Service and they had concurred with the local board classification and had found that all procedural action had been proper, it could be more expeditiously handled by the United States attorney. The decision to provide for such review was not made until a short time before the expiration of the act. It was contained in paragraph (d) added to Section 642.41 by Amendment No. 423 to the regulations, effective March 7, 1947, which read as follows: 

(d) Whenever a delinquent registrant has injected the element of religion into his classification, claiming to be a minister of religion, a student preparing for the ministry, or one who is conscientiously opposed to participation in war, he shall not be reported to the United States attorney on Delinquent Registrant Report (DSS Form 550) until his file has been reviewed by the State Director of Selective Service and by the Director of Selective Service. In any such case the local board shall forward the Delinquent Registrant Report (DSS Form 550) together with the file of the registrant to the State Director of Selective Service, who shall review the file and transmit it to the Director of Selective Service with his comment and recommendation. The Director of 

Selective Service shall review the file, take such action as he deems necessary, and return the file to the local board. When the registrant's delinquency still exists after the taking of any action indicated by the Director of Selective 

Service the local board shall mail the Delinquent Registrant Report (DSS Form 

550) to the United States attorney. If the registrant again becomes delinquent after the completion of any further procedure in his processing and classification as was indicated to be necessary by the Director of Selective Service, the local board shall then prepare and mail a Deliquent Registrant Report (DSS Form 

550) to the United States Attorney without again referring the file of the registrant to the State Director of Selective Service or to the Direcor of Selective Service."

quency or suspected delinquency of conscientious objectors and other registrants which were made by the local board to the United States attorney. In some cases the delinquencies reported were found later to be of a technical nature only. For example, some men who had voluntarily enlisted in the armed forces were charged with failure to report for induction. Then, too, other registrants reported for delinquency had failed to receive orders and information of that nature which had been sent to them by their boards. 

The Liberal Consideration Given to Delinquents 

In the processing of objector and other registrant violators of the Selective Service law both the Department of Justice and the System were mindful of the fact that the purpose of the 1940 Act was "to increase and train the personnel of the armed forces of the United States." Accordingly, those charged with the enforcement of the law attempted through education and persuasion to secure compliance with its provisions, if possible, rather than to prosecute, convict and incarcerate. Ordinarily every effort was made and every opportunity was given registrants to comply. If they had unknowingly or unwillingly become delinquents or if, after having willfully become delinquents, they offered compliance, it was usually accepted in lieu of prosecution. Opportunities to comply were often granted to registrants even after they had been indicted and were facing trial; in some instances even after conviction but before sentencing. 

Justice Department Statistics on Delinquent Objectors 

The Department of Justice compiled statistics on convictions of all Selective Service delinquents by fiscal years through June 30, 1946. This information was broken down to give separate figures for those who claimed to be conscientious objectors. According to 

Justice Department reports slightly more than 6,000 of the approximately 16,000 convicted violators of the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940, as amended, were professed religious or conscientious objectors. About a third of these objector cases had had their claims affirmed by the classification actions of the System but then were convicted for failure to report under an assignment to work of national importance in a Civilian Public Service Camp or for refusal to comply with the orders or rules at such camp after having reported for service there. The claims of the other twothirds either had not been examined or had been denied by one or more classification agencies of Selective Service.

From Oct. 16, 1940, to June 30, 1942, there were 386 convictions, from July 1, 1942, to June 30, 1943, 1,685, and from July 1, 1943, to June 30, 1944, 2,292. 1,826 of the 2,292 defendants convicted from July 1, 1943, to

Nearly two-thirds of the Jehovah's Witnesses were convicted of failure to report for induction and more than 1,102 for refusing to report for work of national importance. Of the 155 Negro objectors who listed themselves as belonging to non-Christian religious groups, 99 or about two-thirds failed to register and 21 to report for induction. 

Most of these registrants listed themselves as Moslems and as such they did not feel obligated to serve in the armed forces of the United States.

The C. O.'s representing the larger religious congregations were confined to the larger of the so-called peace churches, such as the

Society of Friends and the Mennonites. As a rule, violations by members of these groups were in rough proportion to the size of the church membership demonstrating that opposition to the law was not concentrated in any one group. In this category, as in most of the others, a majority of convictions were for failure to report for induction. However, there was a scattering of other types of offenses, except quite significantly that none of the members of the large religious groups were convicted for counseling or aiding evasion. 

Equally important was the fact that this was the only category of religious affiliation that had no such type of delinquency. 

Registrants described as "political, philosophical, and rational objectors" included those who apparently based their objection on political and social philosophy regarding war rather than on religious training or belief. Individuals who refused to comply with the law for purely political reasons, that is, for reasons of political nature which were not associated with a professed objection to all war, were not included in these statistics. Examples of such objectors were members of the Nationalist Party in Puerto Rico who opposed the authority of the United States on that island, certain American citizens of Japanese ancestry who either professed loyalty to Japan or objected to their exclusion from military zones, and certain German and Italian sympathizers.

Jehovah's Witnesses 

Further comment should be made on the large group of Jehovah's Witnesses who were convicted for delinquency. It is important to remember that as a rule they were not denied exemption from combatant or noncombatant service as conscientious objectors. Many were not classified as objectors at all but this was partly due to their refusal to request or accept such classification. Also more than any other group, they refused after classification and even after conviction to cooperate in the work program in lieu of a prison sentence. The 

Jehovah's Witnesses usually sought complete exemption from all service the same as that accorded under the act to ministers of religion. 

They based this approach on the principle that every member of their group was considered by them to be the equivalent of an ordained minister. While many Jehovah's Witnesses were classified as ministers by Selective Service, the courts repeatedly held that active membership in the group did not automatically entitle the individual to ministerial exemption. 6

The Jehovah's Witnesses contended that they had no legal obligation for submitting to induction or to work of national importance

Since they believed they were arbitrarily classified by the System, whenever denied a ministerial exemption, they refused to comply and had to be prosecuted. By refusing to comply they deprived themselves of the opportunity to appeal their classifications, and to have them tested in court by means of habeas corpus proceedings after induction.

In 6,086 of these cases the defendants professed some type of religious conscientious objection to complying with the provisions of the act (Table No. 11). This amounted to almost 40 percent of the total delinquency convictions, which seems rather large in view of the fact that ministers and ministerial students were granted exemptions or deferments. On the other hand, 4,411 of these cases were Jehovah's Witnesses.

Religious Affiliation of Convicted Objectors 

As already stated, Jehovah's Witnesses constituted well over twothirds of the total number of registrant objectors convicted of violation or delinquency under the provisions of the 1940 Act. More than one-third of these were in the fiscal year ending 1943 and nearly 30 percent in fiscal 1944.

Examination of the figures for individual years discloses a striking trend. Convictions secured during the first year and one-half of operations, from October 16, 1940, to June 30, 1942, resulted in sentences about one-half of which were from more than 6 months up to and including 2 years, while 35 percent resulted in more severe sentences. 

In the fiscal year ending June 30, 1943, only 20 percent of the convicted persons received sentences ranging from 6 months plus to 2 years, while 75 percent were given more severe sentences, that is, more than 2

years to, and including, 5 years. About the same distribution can be noted in the year ending June 30, 1944, except that while the percentage of more severe sentences were about the same as to total, a larger proportion of them were in the 5-year group.

The Last Report of the Justice Department 

On June 30, 1946, 271 conscientious objector cases were still pending before the Federal courts. A total of 118 of these involved Jehovah's 

Witnesses, 83 of whom were charged with failure to report for induction, 19 with refusing to report for the civilian program and 16 with failure to comply with orders and regulations after having reported to Civilian Public Service Camps. The remaining 153 of the pending cases included 12 who failed to report for induction and 141 cases who did not comply with instructions after reporting for work of national importance.

In the last year for which a statistical report was available from the Department of Justice, fiscal year 1946, the only increase in the number of cases was for noncompliance at Civilian Public Service Camps. The large number of cases in this category was due to efforts on the part of a small number of conscientious objectors who challenged the validity of the civilian work program and willfully created problems of order and discipline. 

As of June 30, 1946, only 1,199 convicted objectors were still serving sentences in prison. Of these, 1,046 or almost 90 per cent were Jehovah's Witnesses and only 153 were conscientious objectors who did not involve a claim of being ministers.

269 From this statistical information and from details furnished by an examination of the individual files of these cases it appears likely that a number of parolees, convicted for failure to register or failure to perform certain other duties connected with classification, later became convinced that compliance would have been proper in their It also seems likely that further information, education, and persuasion might have decreased the number of delinquents who, because of claiming conscientious objection, failed to comply with requirements as to registration and keeping their local boards informed about themselves. Indeed, related data showing a reduction in the number of convictions for this type of violation after June 30, 1943, support this interpretation, although the age and number of the new registrants may also have been important factors. Brief Generally speaking, violations of the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940 by conscientious objector registrants were of six kinds: failure to (1) register, (2) return Selective Service questionnaires and (3) report for physical examination; refusal (4) to report for induction into the armed forces or for assignment to civilian work of national importance and (5) to obey orders at C. P. S. Camps; and (6) counseling or aiding evasion in these and other respects. 

The penalty provisions of the World War II law established 5 years of imprisonment or a fine of not more than $10,000 or both for violators and designated civil trial in the Federal courts for such delinquency. However, Selective Service and the Department of Justice desiring the maximum operation of the act for its primary purpose of procuring manpower for the armed forces, were in one sense very liberal as to enforcement. In cases of violation the first and continuous effort was to secure compliance by the registrants and in such event to drop the charges of delinquency. This was true at various stages: reporting, charging and arresting; indictment, prosecution, conviction and imprisonment. Even after imprisonment an objector might be paroled to comply with the law.

During the 612 years of the System's operation 6,086 C. O.'s were convicted of violation. This was more than a third of the 15,758 registrant convictions. However, 4,411 or more than two-thirds of the objectors were Jehovah's Witnesses. As would be expected most of the convictions were made at the height of the war when calls for induction were large: 1,086 in fiscal year 1942-43 and 1,826 in 1943–44.

Of the total C. O. convictions 3,722 were for failing to report for induction and 1,624 for refusing to report for assignment to the civilian work program. Practically all of the convictions including problem

. 

CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION 

cases of order and discipline at Civilian Public Service Camps carried prison sentences and some also carried fines. The median sentence was between 2 and 3 years though again there was a very marked tendency for longer sentences during the peak of war activities. 

In comparison with the estimated total of 50,000 registrants classified as conscientious objectors, 6,000 convictions is a substantial proportion. As the experience of the System progressed, however, the value of educational and persuasive measures in reducing violation became increasingly evident and their successful application grew. 

More intensive effort in this regard might have made even greater inroads upon the problem of delinquency among conscientious objectors.

XIV 

COURT DECISIONS INVOLVING CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION 

The problem of service or duty for conscientious objectors during a national emergency like that of World War II, could not be posed for so comprehensive a solution as in the Selective Service Act of 1940, without creating significant court litigation. The general proposition in the United States during the 1940-47 period was for all liable, selected persons to serve. However, consideration of the Nation's history on religious tolerance and of the pacifist backgrounds for certain churches caused the Congress to make the individual's faith a condition upon which duty should be predicated. The basic law implemented by the general regulations of the System allowed registrants whose beliefs were opposed to war and armed forces, to file claims for noncombatant service in the Army and Navy or for assignment to work of national importance in a Civilian Public Service 

Camp. 

The educational and persuasive efforts of Selective Service in classification and other matters through its local and appeal boards, Presidential Appeal Board and State and National Headquarters were not always enough to convince the objector of the fairness, justice, and impartialness of this new attempt to help him fulfill his obligation. 

The same was sometimes true with respect to the Justice Department's investigation and hearing of his case. In consequence, the Federal courts being additionally charged with handling law violation, delinquency, or enforcement had to continue his education. If they likewise failed to persuade him to accept combatant, noncombatant, or civilian duty, there was no course left but to convict him of a criminal offense and sentence him to prison.

Major Legal Opinions on Objectors 

The major decisions of the Federal courts in the cases of conscientious objectors were, therefore, an essential part of the 1940-47 experience of Selective Service in this field. The present discussion does not review all of the opinions delivered by the courts regarding objectors. A number of cases were still pending at the expiration of the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940, 737977°-50-vol. 1—19 271

as amended, and when this monograph was completed. However, most of the major types of decisions are included. Jehovah's 

Witnesses cases are for the most part excluded because the principal claim of this group was for the completely exempt status of the minister. A considerable number of Jehovah's Witnesses made the auxiliary claim of conscientious objection, though, and the important decisions in these instances are covered.¹

A Decision on the Objector Provisions of 1917 

Before presenting the important court opinions on objection for the 1940 Act, one ruling should be mentioned which was made during World War I on the constitutionality of the conscientious objector provisions of the Selective Service law of 1917. At that time the argument was advanced "that the act of May 18, 1917 (40 Stat. 76), exempting ministers of religion and theological students from the draft, and exempting from strict military service members of sects whose tenets exclude the moral right to engage in war," was repugnant to the first amendment to the Constitution, as establishing or interfering with religion. "However, the argument was held too unsound to require more than a mere statement." 2

The "Substantial Evidence" Rule for the 1940 Law The question of finality in the determinations of Selective Service local and appeal boards under the 1940 law was subject to interpretation. This arose in connection with that part of section 10 (a) (2) of the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940, as amended, which read as follows: 

Such local boards, under rules and regulations prescribed by the President, shall have power within their respective jurisdictions to hear and determine, subject to the right of appeal to the appeal boards herein authorized all questions or claims with respect to inclusion for, or exemption or deferment from, training and service under this act of all individuals within the jurisdiction of such local boards. The decisions of such local boards shall be final except where an appeal is authorized and is taken in accordance with such rules and regulations as the President may prescribe. Appeal boards within the Selective 

Service System shall be composed of civilians who are citizens of the United States. The decision of such appeal boards shall be final in cases before them on appeal unless modified or changed by the President as provided in the last sentence of section 5 (1) of this act.

With respect to the question of finality, Judge Charles E. Clark, of the Circuit Court of Appeals, Second Circuit, used the following language to state the "substantial evidence" rule in an opinion on the case of Isaac Trainin: 

1 Special Monograph No8. 6 and 14, "Industrial Deferment" and "Enforcement of the

Selective Service Law," Selective Service System (Washington: 1947 and 1950), like wise discuss Jehovah's Witnesses and ministerial cases. 

2 Arver v. United States (245 U. S. 366).

* * * (2, 3) Undoubtedly the statutory provision that decisions of the selective service boards shall be final narrowly limits the scope of judicial examination of board actions; but it is clear that Congress through use of such words cannot deny any registrant the constitutional protections of due process of law. 

Thus it is error reviewable by the courts when it appears that the proceedings conducted by such boards "have been without or in excess of their jurisdiction, or have been so manifestly unfair as to prevent a fair investigation, or that there has been a manifest abuse of the discretion with which they are invested under the act." * * But generalities of this nature, themselves pregnant with ambiguities, do not greatly assist to decision in particular cases, or specifically delimit judicial power to review evidence before the boards. On this latter point many cases, without sharp consideration of the issues, merely state the now usual rule of review applied to many administrative agencies, namely, that review of the facts is limited to ascertaining whether there is "substantial evidence" to support the findings of the agencies. * There seems, however, considerable tendency to state a more limited rule than this, such as that examination is only to determine whether there is any evidence at all to support the findings of the local boards. * * These different formulas represent at most only slight differences of degree of restriction of judicial review; indeed, it may be concluded that the exact formula is not of the greatest importance, since under all the degree of finality accorded actions of local boards during both wars has been very great. In this circuit, however, we seem practically committed to the test of whether the local board had any evidence before it to sustain its result; indeed, in United 

States ex rel. Brandon v. Downer, 2 Cir., 139 F. 2d 761, 765, we practically said as much."

This ruling of the Second Circuit Court of Appeals was made on August 15, 1944, and that of the citation contained therein on July 7 of that year. The case covered by the August 15 opinion was one involving a IV-D or ministerial classification, but the decision had equal implications for conscientious objector and other registrants. 

The July 7 ruling cited was concerned with conscientious objection based on moral grounds. The import of the August 15 decision was that in questions of finality on determinations of the System about all the courts could do was to ascertain whether such actions had been based upon "substantial evidence." 

The same question reached the U. S. Supreme Court in Estep v. 

United States, 327 U. S. 114, 66 S. Ct. 423, 2-4-46, when the Court said, "The decisions of the local boards made in conformity with the regulations are final even though they may be erroneous. The question of jurisdiction of the local board is reached only if there is no basis in fact for the classification which it gave the registrant." This narrowed the "substantial evidence" rule to "basis in fact." 

Determination of Entitlement to Objector Exemption 

The question of when a registrant met the requirements of the statute as a conscientious objector was often difficult to decide. An * United States v. Cain, 144 F. 2d 944.

example of such a case which reached the Federal courts at a relatively early date (February 8, 1943) was that of Mathias Kauten."

This became a rather celebrated case, because interested people read divergent views into the opinion as handed down by Judge Augustus Hand. The registrant had been brought up in the Catholic faith, but at the time was by his own admission an atheist or at least an agnostic. 

He believed organized religion to be detrimental and a hindrance to science. This objector claimed philosophical and political opposition to World War II alone and not to all war or wars, and his conviction by a lower court was therefore upheld. Pertinent parts of the decision follow:

The only error suggested is the adoption by the latter of the report of the hearing commissioner whose conclusions are appended in the margin. No question is raised about the facts which he and the appeal board found, but only whether the statute was properly interpreted as excluding from the exemption of section 5 (g) a person having such beliefs as the defendant expressed. (6-8) We hold that Mr. Hardy's interpretation was well founded. In order to avail himself of his privilege a registrant must establish that his objection to participation in war is due to "religious training and belief." It must ex vi termini be a general scruple against "participation in war in any form" and not merely an objection to participation in this particular war. Moreover, the conviction that war is a futile means of righting wrongs or of protecting the state, that it is not worth the sacrifice, that it is waged for base ends, or is otherwise indefensible is not necessarily a ground of opposition based on "religious training and belief." Though the registrant may have been entirely sincere in the ideas he expressed, his objections to reporting for induction were based on philosophical and political considerations applicable to this war rather than on “religious training and belief." They, therefore, were properly overruled, but not because he lacked membership of any sect or organization whose religious convictions were against war. Such a status was necessary to obtain exemption under the act of 1917, but the provisions of the present statute are more generous for they take into account the characteristics of a skeptical generation and make the existence of a conscientious scruple against war in any form, rather than allegiance to a definite religious group or creed, the basis of exemption. We are not convinced by anything in the record that the registrant did not report for induction because of a compelling voice of conscience, which we should regard as a religious impulse, but his declarations and reasoning seem to indicate that he was moved by convictions, however sincere, of quite a different character. (9) In the early days of the draft, many thousands of the American people distrusted our foreign policy. If men holding such views had been ipso facto classed as conscientious objectors, the military effort might well have been seriously hampered. In granting such exemption, we think Congress intended to satisfy the consciences of the very limited class we have described and [not to give exemption to the great number of persons who might object to a particular war on philosophical or political grounds. 

It is unnecessary to attempt a definition of religion; the content of the term is found in the history of the human race and is incapable of compression into a few words. Religious belief arises from a sense of the inadequacy of [Religious 

United States v. Kauten, 133 F. 2d 703.

COURT DECISIONS INVOLVING CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION >>> 

275 reason as a means of relating the individual to his fellow-men and to his universe -a sense common to men in the most primitive and in the most highly civilized societies. It accepts the aid of logic but refuses to be limited by it. 

It is a belief finding expression in a conscience which categorically requires the believer to disregard elementary self-interest and to accept martyrdom in preference to transgressing its tenets. A religious obligation forbade Socrates, even in order to escape condemnation, to entreat his judges to acquit him because he believed that it was their sworn duty to decide questions without favor to anyone and only according to law. Such an obligation impelled Martin Luther to nail his theses on the door of the church at Wittenberg and, when he was summoned before Emperor Charles and the Diet at Worms, steadfastly to hold his ground and to utter the often quoted words: "I neither can nor will recant anything, since it is neither right nor safe to act against conscience. Here I stand. I cannot do other. God help me. Amen." Recognition of this obligation moved the Greek poet Menander to write almost twenty-four hundred years ago: "Conscience is a god to all mortals;" impelled Socrates to obey the voice of his "Daimon" and led Wadsworth to characterize "Duty" as the "Stern 

Daughter of the Voice of God." (10) There is a distinction between a course of reasoning resulting in a conviction that a particular war is inexpedient or disastrous and a conscientious objection to participation in any war under any circumstances. The latter, and not the former, may be the basis of exemption under the act. The former is usually a political objection, while the latter, we think, may justly be regarded as a response of the individual to an inward mentor, call it conscience or God, that is for many persons at the present time the equivalent of what has always been thought a religious impulse.) (11) Even if the board might have found that the registrant's objections to reporting for induction were based "on religious training and belief," rather than on personal predilection or political and social philosophy respecting the folly and futility of war, yet the record contained substantial indications that the objections were not because of "religious training and belief" in the sense those words are used in the statute, and the weight of the evidence was a matter for the appeal board. (12) For the foregoing reasons we find no error in the decision of the trial court and the judgment of conviction is accordingly affirmed." 

This opinion was considered by some as evidence in support of a liberalized conscientious objection viewpoint, of a broad basis for it later of helping this and not just the narrow limits of "religious training and belief," opposition based on any grounds as long as it was objection to all waron or wars. But it was difficult for others to accept this interpretation specific without question. They held that parts (9) and (10) were, after all issue according to the latter, gratuitous dicta, included after the decision of the case was clearly outlined in parts (6) and (8). But the first contenders believed these parts not to have been dicta but necessary to the decision. Another fact which tended to confuse the issue was that the case was reviewed in an appellate court and in part 11 it was pointed out that "the weight of evidence was a matter for the appeal board" and that "the record contained substantial indications" that the appeal board decision was proper.
