A Ruling Against Social Belief as a Basis 

The refusal of the Supreme Court of the United States on December 23, 1946, to grant certiorari, that is, review, in the case of Herman

Berman added considerable interest to the lower court decisions in the case and particularly to the opinion written by Judge Harold M. 

Stephens. Registrant Berman refused to accept induction into the armed forces after being given a valid order to do so by his local board. He was thereupon reported as a delinquent and tried, convicted and sentenced in the District Court of the United States for the Southern District of California, Central Division. Upon appeal to the United States Circuit Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, the district court judgment and the sentence upon the judgment after conviction was affirmed by this circuit court. The refusal of the 

Supreme Court to review the case left the judgment and sentence standing and was interpreted as a measure of approval by this high court of the opinions or decisions of the lower courts in this case. At least this ultimate action left the registrant without relief. In handing down the district court ruling Judge Stephens said, in part: [It is our opinion that the expression "by reason of religious training and belief" is plain language, and was written into the statute for the specific purpose of distinguishing between a conscientious social belief, or a sincere devotion to a high moralistic philosophy, and one based upon an individual's belief in his responsibility to an authority higher and beyond any worldly one.] 

The first expression contained in section 1 of the first amendment to the Constitution of the United States is as follows: "Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof; * 

It would be quite ridiculous to argue that the use of the word "religion" could have been understood by the authors of this part of our national charter or by those having to do with its adoption as meaning to be inclusive of morals or of devotion to human welfare or of policy of government. Congress has and does make laws respecting the establishment of all of these subjects. We are not saying that man's comprehension of religions is static and remains today the same as a short hundred-and-fifty-odd years ago in the area of our constitution making. Undoubtedly, the human mind is less limited by the literal word meanings of creeds and has been given clearer insight as to realities by man's excursions into nature's wonderland. And it is true that scientific discoveries have greatly influenced the trend of philosophic thought. [Manifestations, now understood through scientific law, were once attributed to the direct interposition of deity. Nature and God seem so close to oneness that some thinkers blend them inseparably.

Yet all discoveries of science and the deepest reach of minds do not fill a life or satisfy the soul hunger to understand the daily joys and sadnesses and disappointments of life or to understand the ultimate purpose of creation. 

Faith in a Supreme Power above and beyond the law of all creation mollifies our fears and satisfies our longings. It is not possible to still the innate human desire against going beyond the physical revelations of life. The area of our • Herman Berman v. United States of America, 156 F. 2d 377.

COURT DECISIONS INVOLVING CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION » 277 

logical equations comes to an end, but we do not assign all beyond as a great vacancy. Faith "which passeth all understanding" carries on. The intellectually satisfying meditations of Marcus Aurelius do not suffice for the boy in the fox hole, under fire. His philosophy is not called upon in that agonizing hour. 

He goes direct to his God to bolster his flagging strength and courage. 

There are many eminent lawyers and others in Congress with wide knowledge and we cannot assume that they were ignorant of expressions in the Constitution and in opinions of our own Supreme Court when treating of the subject of religion. We have already referred to the word "religion" as used in the Constitution; in United States v. Machintosh, 283 U. S. 605, at 633, Mr. Justice Hughes in his dissent, Holmes, Stone, and Brandeis concurring (the dissent was on another point), said: “The essence of religion is belief in a relation to God involving duties superior to those arising from any human relation." See United 

States v. Schwimmer, 279 U. S. 644. The committee in writing the present law was not venturing anything new in limiting exemptions of conscientious objectors on a religious basis. That has been done in every draft law ever enacted in the United States. There are those who have a philosophy of life, and who live up to it. There is evidence that this is so in regard to appellant. However, no matter how pure and admirable his standard may be, and no matter how devotedly he adheres to it, his philosophy and morals and social policy without the concept of deity cannot be said to be religion. It is said in State v. Amana Society, 109 N. W. 894, 888: "Surely a scheme of life designed to obviate such results (man's inhumanity to man), and by removing temptations, and all the inducements of ambition and avarice, to nurture the virtues of unselfishness, patience, love, and service, ought not to be denounced as not pertaining to religion when its devotee regards it as an essential tenet of their religious faith. 

Whether or not the triers of fact thought appellant's objections to war were conscientious is not decisive of this case. Even if the evidence should compel the finding that he was conscientious, and we do not suggest that it does, he could not succeed in his appeal. There is not a shred of evidence in the case to the effect that appellant relates his way of life or his objections to war to any religious training or belief. That Congress, when preparing the Selective Training、 and Service Act, was not thinking of philosophical views and good deeds and deep beliefs in social actions as different exemplifications of deity, is demonstrated by congressional hearings. At one time in the course of its composition, the Burke-Wadsworth Bill, which through progressive steps grew into the act, applied the exemption only to members of religious sects whose principles were opposed to war on conscientious grounds. The exemption was changed so as to include individual conscientious objectors without regard to membership in a religious organization, but did not eliminate the religious element for it incorporated in section 5 (g) of the act, the expression "by reason of religious training and belief." At a hearing after this expression was written into the bill, many organizations supported the Civil Liberties Union proposal (p. 152, House hearings) that conscientious objection without regard to any religious requirement should be brought within the terms of the exemption. The proposal was not adopted.

Religion is defined in Funk & Wagnall's New Standard Dictionary as follows: 

"religion * * * 1. A belief in an invisible superhuman power (or powers), conceived of after the analogy of the human spirit, on which (for whom) he thinks himself in some degree responsible, together with the feelings and prac-

tices which naturally flow from such a belief.

" It is defined in Webster's New 

International Dictionary, 2d ed., as follows: "religion * * 串 ​1. The service and adoration of God or a god as expressed in forms of worship, in obedience to divine commands, esp. as found in accepted sacred writings or as declared by recognized teachers and in the pursuit of a way of life regarded as incumbent on true believers; as ministers of religion * * ** 6. An apprehension, awareness, of conviction of the existence of a supreme being, or more widely, of supernatural powers or influences controlling one's own, humanity's, or nature's destiny; also, such an apprehension, etc., accompanied by or arousing reverence, love, gratitude, the will to obey specif., the awakening of religious belief, convictions, etc., as in conversion; as, one without religion; man only is capable of religion to get religion. In the Encyclopedia of Social Sciences, vol. 13, p. 229, under the title "Religion" by Alfred Bertholet, it is said: "Thus it is possible to arrive at a preliminary definition of religion as the complex of man's interrelations with the superhuman powers. Such a definition implies the fundamental truth that religion, as defined by C. A. Bernoulli in Theologie and Wissenschaft (Basel 1933), is 'not an autonomous activity of man or a unilateral but involves a process of vital and reciprocal interplay' between the human and the supernatural." 

We have not referred specifically to the requirement that before one comes within the exemption provided in the act, he must be opposed to war not only by reason of his religious belief but by reason of religious training. The record is as silent on religious training as the basis of appellant's claimed conscientious objections, as it is on a religious belief as the basis of his conscientious objections. 

Whatever may be said as to appellant's conscientiousness in his objections to war aside from the religious phase of the subject, the evidence in this case conclusively supports the finding that appellant's objections to war do not come within the purview of the exemption claimed by him. We may add with propriety that to sustain appellant's thesis, we should, in effect, be deciding that the exemption from military service written into the statute runs to all who sincerely entertain conscientious objections to participation in war. Should we come to that conclusion, the phrase "by reason of religious training and belief" would have no practical effect whatever. As we have indicated, we think the latter phrase must be regarded as a definite limitation on the scope of the exemption and cannot be deprived of its effectiveness by specious reasoning that something which to its user is more acceptable than some other thing is therefore the same thing. There is evidence to support the conclusion that appellant was sincere in the belief which he professed, but it is clear that such belief was based entirely upon a philosophical, social, or political policy and does not entitle him to exemption from military duty: We find no error.' 

This opinion was delivered by Judge Stephens in the district court on June 29, 1946, and served among other things to support the decision of United States v. Kauten (133 F.2d 703) which has already been discussed. It said in summary that although the registrant was sincere and conscientious in being opposed to war, his objection was based on "philosophical, social, or political policy" rather than "religious training and belief" and therefore he was not entitled to exemption from military duty under the Selective Service Act. The point was made that the Constitution said Congress could "make no law 

'Loc. cit.

COURT DECISIONS INVOLVING CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION » 279 

regarding an established religion, or prohibit the free exercise thereof" and that neither the Constitution, nor the Congress as it passed the 1940 conscription law, defined religion as including morals or devotion to human welfare or policy of government. Social belief, high moralistic philosophy, a philosophy of life involving high standards, philosophy, morals, social policy-none of them constituted a basis for conscientious objection under the act. A way of life, philosophical views, good deeds, or deep beliefs in social actions were not exemplifications of deity as envisaged by the Congress in such connection. The court recalled that, if other than a religious basis had been in mind, the Congress in passing the law would not have failed to give consideration to the proposal of the Civil Liberties Union which conceived of objection on any and all grounds as being valid for exemption purposes. 

Decision Allowing Defendant to Attack Classification

Not many Selective Service cases involving conscientious objection reached the Supreme Court of the United States. In all of its decisions on such cases, however, this high court leaned to a liberal interpretation of the right of a defendant to challenge the "finality" of his classification contrary to any strict construction of the meaning of section 10 (a) (2) of the act. The essence of the opinion of the 

Supreme Court appeared in a footnote to a decision rendered December 23, 1946 which read:

Provided that he has exhausted his administrative remedies, the registrant who has not been actually inducted into the armed forces may in defense to a criminal prosecution attack a board's order as arbitrary and illegal.

This opinion was not so crystallized until late in the operation of the System and its effect was perhaps negligible. In addition, it did not indicate how much influence such an attack would have on the outcome of a criminal prosecution. But the large proportion of conscientious objector convictions and the small number of cases decided in their favor indicates that, as a rule, the courts found relatively few registrants to be in fact conscientious objectors whose claims had not been given proper and sufficient consideration by Selective Service. 

A Registrant's Right to Seek Court Redress 

The question of ministerial claims was at issue in most of the Supreme Court decisions that are of interest for this monograph on conscientious objection. However, there were some in which claims of conscientious objection were important enough that extensive citation of the opinion is desirable. For example, these statements were made in the case of Estep v. United States: 

8 Gibson v. United States, 67 S. Ct. 301.

< 

Congress entrusted the administration of the Selective Service System to civilian agencies, not to the military. It authorized the President to create and establish a Selective Service System and to establish civilian local boards and appeal boards to administer it (sec. 10 (a) (2)). The Selective Service System was designed to "provide for the classification of registrants and of persons who volunteer for induction under this act on the basis of availability for training and service." (Id.) Congress specified certain restricted classes for deferment or exemption from service, including in the latter sec. 5. The President was authorized to provide for the deferment of other classes by rules and regulations (sec. 5 (e)). And the local boards "under rules and regulations prescribed by the President" were granted the "power within their respective jurisdictions to hear and determine, subject to the right of appeal to the appeal boards herein authorized, all questions or claims with respect to inclusion for, or exemption or deferment from, training and service under this act of all individuals within the jurisdiction of such local boards" (sec. 10 (a) (2)). The act makes no provision in terms for judicial review of the actions of the local boards or the appeal boards. For sec. 10 (a) (2) states that the "decisions of such local boards shall be final except where an appeal is authorized in accordance with such rules and regulations as the President may prescribe." 

By the terms of the act Congress enlisted the aid of the Federal courts only for enforcement purposes. Section 11 makes criminal a willful failure to perform any duty required of a registrant by the act or the rules or regulations made under it. An order to report for induction is such a duty; and it includes the duty to submit to induction. Billings v. Truesdell, supra, page 557. Section 11 confers 

Jurisdiction on the district courts to try one charged with such offense. But section 11 is silent when it comes to the defenses, if any, which may be interposed. 

Thus we start with a statute which makes no provision for judicial review of the actions of the local boards or the appeal agencies. That alone, of course, is not decisive. For the silence of Congress as to judicial review is not necessarily to be construed as a denial of the power of the Federal courts to grant relief in the exercise of the general jurisdiction which Congress has conferred upon them. School of Magnetic Healing v. McAnnulty, 187 U. S. 94; Gegiow v. Uhl, 239 U. S. 276. Apart from constitutional requirements, the question whether judicial review will be provided where Congress is silent depends on the whole setting of the particular statute and the scheme of regulation which is adopted. 

Switchmen's Union v. Mediation Board, 320 U. S. 297, 301. And except when the Constitution requires it, judicial review of administrative action may be granted or withheld as Congress chooses.

The authority of the local boards whose orders are the basis of these criminal prosecutions is circumscribed both by the act and by the regulations. Their authority to hear and determine all questions of deferment or exemption is, as stated in section 10 (a) (2), limited to action "within their respective jurisdictions." It is only orders "within their respective jurisdictions" that are made final. It would seem, therefore, that if a Pennsylvania board ordered a citizen and resident of Oregon to report for induction, the defense that it acted beyond its jurisdiction could be interposed in a prosecution under section 11. That case would be comparable to Tung v. United States, 142 F. 2d 919, where the local board ordered a registrant to report for induction without allowing him the appeal to which he was entitled under the regulations. Since section 10 (a) (2) makes the decisions of the local boards final "except where an appeal is authorized" under the regulations, the defense was allowed in the criminal trial. 

Any other case where a local board acts so contrary to its granted authority as to exceed its jurisdiction does not stand on a different footing. By section

COURT DECISIONS INVOLVING CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION » 281 

10 (a) (2) the local boards in hearing and determining claims for deferment or exemption must act "under rules and regulations prescribed by the President." 

Those rules limit, as well as define, their jurisdiction. One of those regulations forbids the local boards from basing their classification of a registrant on a discrimination "for or against him because of his race, creed, or color, or because of his membership or activity in any labor, political, religious, or other organization" (623.1). Another provides, in accordance with the mandate contained in section 5 (c) (1) of the act, for the deferment of Governors of States and Members of Congress while they hold their offices (622.42). Another provides that the local board "shall reopen and consider anew the classification of a registrant" on the written request of the State Director or the Director and upon receipt of the request "shall immediately cancel" any order to report for induction or for work of national importance (626.2-1). If a local board ordered a Member of Congress to report for induction, or if it classified a registrant as available for military service, because he was a Jew, or a German, or a Negro, it would act in defiance of the law. If a local board refused to reopen on the written request of the State Director a registrant's classification and refused to cancel its order to report for induction, it would be acting in the teeth of the regulations. In all such cases its action would be lawless and beyond its jurisdiction. 

We cannot read section 11 as requiring the courts to inflict punishment on registrants for violating whatever orders the local boards might issue. We cannot believe that Congress intended that criminal sanctions were to be applied to orders issued by local boards no matter how flagrantly they violated the rules and regulations which define their jurisdiction. We are dealing here with a question of personal liberty. A registrant who violates the act commits a felony. 

A felon customarily suffers the loss of substantial rights. Section 11, being silent on the matter, leaves the question of available defenses in doubt. But we are loathe to resolve those doubts against the accused. We cannot readily infer that Congress departed so far from the traditional concepts of a fair trial when it made the actions of the local boards "final" as to provide that a citizen of this country should go to jail for not obeying an unlawful order of an administrative agency. We are loathe to believe that Congress reduced criminal trials under the act to proceedings so barren of the customary safeguards which the law has designed for the protection of the accused. The provision making the decisions of the local boards "final" means to us that Congress chose not to give administrative action under this act the customary scope of judicial review which obtains under other statutes. It means that the courts are not to weigh the evidence to determine whether the classification made by the local boards was justified. The decisions of the local boards made in conformity with the regulations are final even though they may be erroneous. The question of jurisdiction of the local board is reached only if there is no basis in fact for the classification which it gave the registrant. See Goff v. United States, 135 F. 2d 

610, 612.

Falbo v. United States, supra, does not preclude such a defense in the present cases. In the Falbo case the defendant challenged the order of his local board before he had exhausted his administrative remedies. Here these registrants had pursued their administrative remedies to the end. All had been done which could be done. Submission to induction would be satisfaction of the orders of the local boards, not a further step to obtain relief from them. 

If section 11 were not construed to permit the accused to defend on the ground that his local board acted beyond its jurisdiction, a curious result would follow. 

The remedy of habeas corpus extends to a case where a person "is in custody in

violation of the Constitution or of a law of the United States" (Rev.

Stat., sec. 753, 28 U. S. C. sec. 453). It has been assumed that habeas corpus is available only after a registrant has been inducted into the armed services. But if we now hold that a registrant could not defend at his trial on the ground that the local board had no jurisdiction in the premises, it would seem that the way would then be open to him to challenge the jurisdiction of the local board after conviction by habeas corpus. The court would then be sending men to jail today when it was apparent that they would have to be released tomorrow.

We do not suggest that because Congress has provided one judicial remedy another should be implied. We may assume that where only one judicial remedy is provided, it normally would be deemed exclusive. But the fact that habeas corpus after conviction is available in these cases gives added support to our reading of section 11. It supports a rejection of a construction of the act that requires the courts to march up the hill when it is apparent from the beginning that they will have to march down again. 

We express no opinion on the merits of the defenses which were tendered. 

Since the petitioners were denied the opportunity to show that their local boards exceeded their jurisdiction, a new trial must be had in each case." 

This decision was handed down by the Supreme Court on February 4, 1946. It held, in brief, that while Congress (1) entrusted the administration of the Selective Service System to civilian agencies, (2) provided that among these agencies the determination of the local board would be final though subject to appeal, (3) did not provide for judicial review of local and appeal board actions and (4) enlisted the aid of the Federal Courts for enforcement onlynevertheless the act of 1940, though silent on the subject, did not preclude an objector or other registrant from seeking defense against illegal determinations of the boards, nor did the Constitution. On the other hand, the 1940 law and regulations thereunder limited the action of the boards to "their respective jurisdictions" and forbade a local board from basing classification on "discrimination." Thus the Federal courts could review the determination of a board to see that it had a "basis in fact" because Congress did not intend a registrant to be subject to illegal orders from the board based on nonjurisdiction or discrimination. This was further borne out by the fact that a registrant inducted into the armed forces could, under certain circumstances, obtain release through habeas corpus proceedings and thereby secure relief from illegal determinations of the boards. Such an approach was of far-reaching importance to the conscientious objector though it came late in the operation of the 

System's program.

Civilian Status of Class IV-E Registrants in C. P. S. Camps 

The status of the Class IV-E objector assigned to the civilian work program was reviewed at some length by a Supreme Court opinion 

'Estep v. United States, 327 U. S. 114.

COURT DECISIONS INVOLVING CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION >> 

283 handed down in the cases of Gibson v. United States and Dodez v. 

Same. The decisions in these cases which were decided together in one opinion, held that conscientious objectors assigned to Civilian Public Service Camps for work of national importance at a time when a change in Selective Service Regulations had removed any chance for them to secure rejection at camp, were not required to report to the camp in order to complete the administrative process, and were, therefore, not foreclosed from making any defense open to them in their criminal trial for violating the act. While the Court indicated that the remedy of "habeas corpus" might not be available in such cases "since the only compulsion laid upon such a person by the act or otherwise is the force of the legal command plus the provision for criminal penalty in case of disobedience," the Court did say "We need not decide this question, however, and we express no opinion upon it." 

Unlike the man "actually inducted," the person classified IV-E remains a civilian; his duties are not military in character; he is not subject to military discipline or authority; and for violation of duties or orders he cannot be tried by court martial or military tribunal. On the contrary the Selective Service 

Act expressly provides the same civil penalties and mode of trial for violating duties arising when he enters the camp as for those arising before that time. 

There is therefore no such profound change in rights, duties and status as occurs when one crosses the line between civil and military jurisdiction by being "actually inducted" under the rule of Billings v. Truesdell, supra. It was this change and the consequences it entailed together with the statute's command that no one should be tried by military or naval court martial in any case arising under the act until he had been actually inducted, which we there held to require placing the line precisely, not only for exhausting administrative remedies under the Falbo rule, but also for marking the point of actual induction at which the registrant's right ends to choose between going forward into the service and incurring the civil liability for breach of that duty. 

The person classified as conscientious objector is never confronted with that choice. He is relieved by the act from any duty to perform military service. 

He is not threatened with induction. He is in fact farther removed from military status or jurisdiction after he is finally assigned to civilian public service of national importance, and for this reason is rejected for military service, than he was before that time. His choice is not between going into service and taking the civil penalty laid for violating that duty. It is between performing civilian service under civilian authority and incurring the civil penalty for refusing to do so. 

Moreover, in the case of one entering the armed forces, the loss of civil rights, including those of recourse to the civil courts other than by way of habeas corpus, results altogether by virtue of the change from civilian to military status. The reasons underlying those rulings do not apply in the case of one who does not undergo that change, remains at all times a civilian, subject only to civilian duties and to civil penalties for violating them. There is not the same necessity or compulsion in such a case for bringing about forfeiture of civilian rights, including remedies for questioning the validity of the order the registrant is charged with violating. The compulsion arises from the necessity for preventing interruption of military processes by intrusion of the civil courts beyond the essential minimum of keeping open the habeas corpus chan-

nel to show that the military authority has exceeded its jurisdiction in dealing with the individual. It is on this foundation that the forfeiture of other civil remedies is held to take place. 

But there is no such necessity, or therefore any such foundation for forfeiture, in the case of one classified as a conscientious objector and assigned for work of national importance. Serious as are the consequences of his refusal to perform that work, dealing with such breaches of duty by the civil courts does not involve, in the remotest sense, interruption or interference by civilian authority with military processes or jurisdiction. Entirely wanting therefore is any such foundation for forfeiture of civil rights as exists in the case of one inducted into the armed services. Without such a foundation the analogy dissolves and with it the asserted forfeiture. 

This becomes even more clear when it is recalled that one basis for the forfeiture, which the Government has maintained, is that habeas corpus is available for the person classified IV-E and wrongfully denied classification and exemption as a minister of religion. This remedy, it was asserted originally, is adequate and exclusive, and therefore should be held to foreclose resort to other forms of relief.

But here again the asserted analogy fails. It has been clearly established that the remedy by way of habeas corpus is open to the wrongfully inducted member of the armed forces to secure his release. But at the argument it was conceded that neither the camp director nor other officials of the Selective Service System are authorized to use force to arrest or restrain one who refuses to remain in camp. And this, it was also admitted, would make doubtful the availability of relief by way of habeas corpus. Indeed it might well be urged that the remedy is not available for one charged with violation of any duty, whether failure to report to the camp, to remain there, or to perform other obligations, since the only compulsion laid upon such a person by the act or otherwise is the force of the legal command plus the provision for criminal penalty in case of disobedience.

We need not decide this question, however, and we express no opinion upon it. For it is enough to destroy the analogy the Government seeks to draw that the remedy by habeas corpus is an uncertain one. Should it be found unavailable and at the same time we should rule that petitioner's defense could not be made in the criminal proceeding, he would be left entirely without remedy, a result consistent neither with our decision in the cases of Estep and Smith, supra, nor with the statute. No more, we think, is it consistent with the act or those rulings to foreclose the right of defense upon the basis of uncertainty whether the habeas corpus remedy might be had.

Finally, Congress has provided expressly for enforcing the duty to report to the camp for work and duties arising thereafter through the criminal proceedings and penalties prescribed by sec. 11. In its view these were adequate for the purpose. Nothing in the section or the statute, in the light of our prior decisions, can be taken to indicate that Congress intended persons charged with violating such duties to be deprived of their rights of defense on the ground of invalid classification, either absolutely should habeas corpus prove unavailable or contingently depending upon how the doubt concerning that remedy's availability might be resolved. The Government concedes that Congress intended some remedy to be available. We know of no way by which this can be assured, in such a case as Gibson's, otherwise than by permitting the defense to be raised in the criminal trial.

The analogy failing, for both of the reasons we have stated, by which it is sought to confine the remedy to habeas corpus, we think the defense has been

1 left open for presentation in this case and should have been allowed. Estep v.

A Court Opinion on C.P.S. Camp Assignment 

Separate court proceedings were taken by the United States against 

Igal Roodenko, Donald West Rockwell, James Glenn Hutchison, and

Everett A. White for violation of the Selective Training and Serv ice Act as Civilian Public Service Camp assignees. The United 

States District Court for the District of Colorado wherein their cases were first heard, rendered adverse judgments to the four registrants. 

All of the defendants thereupon appealed the judgments and the appeal was consolidated in the Circuit Court of Appeal, Tenth Circuit." Practically all of the common objections to the performance of work of national importance in Civilian Public Service Camps were raised in this consolidated appeal. The opinion handed down for the Circuit Court by Judge Walter A. Huxman explains very logically the reasons these objections were rejected by that Court and the judgments of the District Court were severally affirmed. 

In these cases there seems to have been no dispute regarding the proper classification of the registrants as conscientious objectors to war in any form and to any service in the armed forces. They were assigned to work of national importance by the Director of Selective Service and placed in a Civilian Public Service Camp in Colorado. Each was convicted of refusing to work and to perform the duties assigned by the director of the camp, which was the issue. The essence of the challenge in the appeal was set forth as follows by Judge Huxman on December 22, 1944: 

The appeal challenges the constitutionality of that part of section 5 (g) of the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940 which relates to those who by reason of religious training and belief are opposed to participation in war in any form. 

It is claimed that this portion of the act is unconstitutional because (1) it deprives such persons as are covered thereby of the free exercise of religion, contrary to the first amendment to the United States Constitution; (2) it deprives them of liberty and property without due process of law, and takes their private property without just compensation, contrary to the fifth amendment; and (3) it subjects them to involuntary servitude not as punishment for crime, contrary to the thirteenth amendment.

It is further urged that Executive Order No. 8675 of February 6, 1941, Selec tive Service System Order No. 111, Mancos Project, Colo., and Selective Service 

System Regulations, Part 692-Rules for Government Operated Camps, are void

because: (a) They are in excess of any power which Congress had to delegate and are in excess of the power delegated by the act; (b) the order, rules, and regulations violate the United States Constitution; and (c) they subject assignees to such camps to military direction in violation of the act." 

Constitutionality of Assignment to Civilian Work He disposed thus of the question of the unconstitutionality of the act as set forth in the first of the two paragraphs above quoted: (1) There is no constitutional right of exemption from service in our armed forces on account of religious training or conscientious scruples against participation in war, or for any other reason. This principle is too well settled to need any extended discussion or the citation of a great number of cases. There are none holding to the contrary. (2, 3) While assignment No. 1 asserts a constitutional right of exemption from military service, Roodenko apparently does not make this asserted ground the basis of his appeal. He states in his brief that "So far as this case is concerned, it may be admitted that appellant had no constitutional exemption and that, had Congress seen fit so to do, it might have refused any exemption whatsoever on the ground of conscience or religious objection." He then argues that the act of 

1940 was limited in its scope to raising and training armed forces, and that it does not purpose to be an exercise of the general war powers of Congress. The argument is made that when Congress limited the act to raising and training soldiers and sailors for our armed services and thereunder granted appellant an exemption from such service, Congress could not make that exemption conditional by requiring appellant to render service in works of national importance in civilian public service camps. We cannot agree that the act is, or was intended by 

Congress to be, so narrowly limited in its operation. In 1940, when this act was before Congress, the world was aflame. War was all about us. All charged with the safety of our country felt that there was great danger that the scourge of war would not pass us by. Under these conditions Congress recognized the existence of a grave emergency. The act itself declares the existence of such an emergency which made necessary the passage of this legislation. Congress had in mind more than the limited objective appellant would ascribe to it in the passage of this act. It sought to completely and adequately prepare our country for defense by marshaling the manpower of the nation and by raising, equipping, and supporting armies for the defense of our land. This is the interpretation which the Supreme Court has placed upon the scope and purpose of this act. 

It is not correct to say that appellant and those who believe as he does are exempt from the operation of the act. They are subject to draft the same as one who has no scruples against serving his country in the armed forces, the only difference being that under the provisions of the act they are excused from military service. The act specifically provides that they may be drafted or "called up," if one prefers that term, to serve their country in work considered of national importance under civiilan direction. (4) If Congress, as we have held, has the power to compel conscientious objectors to serve in the military forces, they cannot be heard to complain that they are relieved from such service on condition that they nevertheless recognize their obligation of citizenship and respond to call and serve their country in nonmilitary work of national importance, under civilian authority. Congress could have required Roodenko to serve in the armed forces. Having no constitutional right of exemption from such service, he certainly can have no constitu-

Legal Authorization for C.P.S. Camps 

Judge Huxman went on to discuss the issues raised with respect to the setting up of Civilian Public Service Camps and their general operation. The language which he used in this regard was as follows: (6) The contention that the act does not authorize the President to set up Civilian Public Service Camps for conscientious objectors is without merit. The act specifically provides that they shall be assigned to work of national importance under civilian direction. This contemplates an organization perfected for this purpose. It was not necessary for the act to define in detail the organization which was to be created. It was sufficient to designate the framework within which it was to be confined. This it did when it designated a civilian organization devoted to work of national purposes. 

(7) Section 310 (a) (1) of the act (50 U. S. C. A. appendix) directs the 

President to make all necessary rules and regulations to carry out the act. This includes the provision for an organization to which conscientious objectors are to be assigned. The yardstick is laid down in the act. It remains only to consider whether the President remained within it. 

(8) By Executive Order 8675, the President directed the Director of Selective 

Service to set up these organizations within the framework of the act, and directed him to adopt necessary rules and regulations for the same. It further directed that he should determine the agencies that should provide the civilian control and that he should have general supervision and control over such work. Pursuant to this authority, by Order No. 111, the Director declared the

Colorado project to which Roodenko was assigned to be a work of national importance. The project was a water storage and irrigation project. It was placed under the technical direction of the Bureau of Reclamation of the Department of the Interior. The Bureau of Reclamation was made responsible for the housing, feeding, clothing, discipline, and health of those assigned to it. Supervision of the project was under the Selective Service System through the Camp 

Operations Division of the National Selective Service Headquarters. 

From this brief analysis of the orders creating this agency, it is apparent that they contemplate civilian control. The particular project was placed under the control of a branch of the Department of the Interior. There are presently 

108 of these projects in operation, with 7,601 conscientious objectors assigned to them. Of these, 105 are sponsored and operated by private religious organizations, such as Brethren Service Committee, Mennonite Central Committee, Association of Catholic Conscientious Objectors, and others. Only 3 are sponsored directly by the Government without the aid of religious groups. All of them are governed by the same rules and regulations set up pursuant to Executive Order 8675. 

It is argued that the military character of these establishments is shown by the fact that the act itself makes the Chief of Finance of the United States Army the fiscal disbursing and accounting agent of the Director of Selective Service, 13 Ibid. 737977°-50-vol. 1—20

that the head of the Selective Service System is a major general in the Army, and that the head of the Camp Operations Division is an Army colonel and signs his directives as "Colonel, Field Artillery." The fact that the organization is headed by an Army officer does not make it a part of the Army. There are innumerable instances where Army or Navy officers have been assigned to civilian work. In Southern Pac. Co. v. United States, 285 U. S. 240, 52 S. Ct. 324, 76 L. Ed. 

736, it was held that Army officers who were assigned to rivers and harbors work were engaged in nonmilitary work. Neither the Army nor the Navy has any control over these assignees. They are not subject to court martial or punishment by the Army or Navy for infractions of any of the rules of the organization or for the commission of any offense against either the laws of the State in which they are located or against the laws of the Nation. For all such offenses they are subject to prosecution in the civil courts and not in the military courts. 

They may not be court martialed or disciplined by the Army because they are not subject to nor a part of the armed services." 

The "National Importance" of Camp Work 

There remained one point which had been stressed by the appeal, that the work done in the particular camp, the Mancos unit in Colorado, was not "of national importance." This, the court held, the defendant could not challenge. The opinion was: (9, 10) And, finally, it is contended that Order No. 111, setting up this project, is void because the project is not of national importance. It is contended that it is a local reclamation water storage and irrigation project of no national importance, having no connection with the war effort. The proper maintenance of agriculture, civilian business, transportation, sanitation, health, and many other civilian activities are as essential to the successful prosecution of the war and as much a part of the war effort as the production of munitions of war and the arming and equipping of the military forces. The act places the determination of what projects are of national importance with the President. 

Roodenko has no standing to challenge the exercise of this discretion by the President.15

Additional minor questions which had been raised, were disposed of briefly as follows: 

Other incidental questions are raised, such as the one attacking the rules and regulations governing the conduct of the assignees to the project in question. 

They are not of sufficient importance to justify a detailed discussion thereof. 

Suffice it to say that we have given them careful consideration and find them without merit. It is our conclusion that neither the act, Executive Order No. 

8675, Selective Service Order No. 111, nor the rules and regulations governing the camp violate any of Roodenko's constitutional rights or immunities.10 

Sum and Substance 

In such fashion, then, the Federal courts continued the educational, persuasive, and other enforcement activities of Selective Service and the Department of Justice with respect to conscientious objector registrants. Their efforts covered for this type of registrant such funda- 

14 Ibid. 

15 Ibid. 

10 Ibid.

COURT DECISIONS INVOLVING CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION » 

289 mentals as (1) local and appeal board classification, (2) induction into the armed forces, (3) assignment to the civilian work program, (4) compliance with the living and working procedures of the Civilian Public Service Camps and (5) other phases of the System's operation.

Among other things the decisions of the courts held that when it came to a question of finality in Selective Service determinations, the role of judicial review amounted to little more than ascertaining whether such actions were based on "substantial evidence." The courts held further in considering specific "substantial evidence" that a claim for conscientious objection on philosophical, political, social or any other basis than "religious training and belief" as stated in the 

1940 Act, was not valid.

Court opinions of significance also dealt with the right of the objector to seek defense against the System's classifications or other determinations when he deemed them illegal, just as the System could prosecute him for an offense when it felt such had been committed. 

In addition, they held that a Class IV-E registrant assigned to work of national importance was still in civilian status and should probably not seek release from such assignment through habeas corpus proceedings as could an objector or other registrant inducted into the armed forces and thus having military status. The C. P. S. Camp assignee should request defense through regular civil court procedure. 

Other important rulings were (1) that assignment to the civilian work program was constitutional, (2) that Civilian Public Service Camps were legal, and (3) that the projects carried on by such camps constituted "work of national importance under civilian direction" as provided for by the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940. 

Thus the new phase of service for conscientious objectors—the civilian work program-came in for much court attention. Being entirely new as a legal provision it would perhaps be expected to arouse more litigation than the provision for noncombatant duty with the armed forces, that is, than the induction of the Class I-A-O objector. What is more, it might be expected also to involve more court proceedings than the induction of a Class I-A registrant who claimed objection but whose claim was not found valid. At any rate, the Federal courts in the 1940-47 program of Selective Service contributed heavily to explaining and interpreting the new concept of civilian work just as they did other phases of the System's activities with reference to conscientious objection.

XV 

THE SEPARATION OF C.O.'s FROM C. P. S. CAMPS 

The separation of conscientious objectors from service under the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940 has already been mentioned. 

However, most of this attention was given to the release of objectors from noncombatant duty with the armed forces. In this connection, it was pointed out that noncombatant inductees of the Army and Navy were discharged upon exactly the same basis as registrants in combatant service.

Generally speaking Selective Service, the National Service Board for Religious Objectors and the agencies of the Federal Government, technically interested in the work projects of the Civilian Public Service Camps, had a feeling that objectors assigned to work of national importance should be separated upon a basis comparable to that of registrants in combatant and noncombatant service. But such procedure for the discharge of Class IV-E men in camps was not always feasible as will be seen from the following discussion. 

The One-Year Period of First Camp Assignments 

Conscientious objectors who were sent to Civilian Public Service Camps "in lieu of induction" were occasionally called "inductees." 

However, the process by which they were ordered to camp was officially known as "assignment" and they were usually termed "assignees." As assignees to work of national importance they were expected to serve the same length of time as registrants who were inducted into the armed forces. In this connection the originally enacted section 3 (b) of the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940 read as follows: 

Each man inducted under the provisions of subsection (a) shall serve for a training and service period of twelve consecutive months, unless sooner discharged, except that whenever the Congress has declared that the national interest is imperiled, such 12-month period may be extended by the President to such time as may be necessary in the interests of national defense. 

The duty of the first assignees to the civilian work program, then, was for a one-year period like that of the early inductees into the armed forces. 291

Extension of the Period to 18 Months 

This length-of-service section of the 1940 law was effected, however, by a provision of the Service Extension Act of 1941, approved August 18, 1941, which declared that the national interest was imperiled and provided "that extension of the periods of active military service, or training and service, in the case of any person subject to the provisions of this section, shall not, without his consent exceed 

18 months in the aggregate." Accordingly President Franklin D.

Roosevelt issued a proclamation on August 21 in which it was ordered: 1 1. The periods of training and service of all persons inducted for training and service under the provisions of the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940, as amended, who are now, or who may hereafter be, in such training and service are hereby extended for a period of 18 months, unless such persons are sooner discharged."

Thus the period of service for both the camp assignee and the armed forces inductee became 18 months instead of 12 as originally established.

A Further Change to "Duration and Six Months" 

Other laws approved after Pearl Harbor on December 13 and 20, 1941, provided that registrants inducted under the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940, might have their periods of service or training and service extended by the President. He could extend their terms of duty for such additional time as he felt might be necessary in the interest of national defense. Such periods of extension, however, should end not less than 6 months after the termination of the war unless the men involved should voluntarily extend their own terms of service. Both assignees and inductees were therefore on duty for the duration of the war and 6 months thereafter under these new provisions.'

Return to 18 Months After VE- and VJ-Days 

Section 3 (b) of the Selective Service Act was again amended on June 29, 1946, and this was its final form. The final change provided that inductees who completed a period of training and service under the 1940 Act, of 18 months or more (excluding time served while pursuing a course of instruction in a university, college, or other similar institution of learning) should, on or after October 1, 1946, upon their request, be relieved from their period of training and service.*

293 Here and in the previous connections cited, Selective Service attempted to follow exactly the same general procedure as the armed forces with respect to the separation of objectors who had served for the legally specified length of time in C. P. S. Camps. The intent of 

National Headquarters in such regard was expressed in a memorandum by its General Counsel, October 21, 1941, in which he made the following observation:

Though section 5 (g), dealing with a conscientious objector, very generally provides that "he shall, in lieu of such induction, be assigned to work of national importance under civilian direction;" nevertheless, in dealing with conscientious objectors, National Headquarters has, in all cases wherever consistently possible, clearly followed the specific rules applicable to persons inducted into the land forces.

Although registrants inducted into the armed forces during the last months in which the System operated were legally subject to 18 months' service, the expiration of the 1940 law on March 31, 1947, left Selective Service without authority to continue the C. P. S. Camps. 

Accordingly, the last of the objector assignees were given their certificates of release in advance of that date. This action was somewhat anticipatory as regards that of the armed forces, but the War Department, which had stopped inductions October 15, 1946, subsequently announced the release of all remaining inductees effective on or about 

June 30, 1947.

Release of Assignees 28 Years of Age and Over 

In the summer of 1941 public opinion became fairly well crystallized in the United States to the effect that it was inadvisable to train older registrants for service with the armed forces. Consequently, an amendment to the Act of 1940 was enacted on August 16, 1941. It limited future inductions to men of the ages 21 through 27. It likewise provided that a registrant 28 years of age and over, who had already been inducted, could be released from active duty upon his own request, if he had attained the 28th anniversary of his birth prior to induction and on or prior to July 1, 1941. The amendment provided specifically: 

That the Secretary of War shall, as soon as practicable and when not in conflict with the interests of national defense, release from active training and service under section 3 (b) of this act, and transfer to a reserve component of the land forces under the provisions of section 3 (c) of this act, regardless of his period of training and service, any person who has heretofore been inducted into the land forces under this act, who requests such release, and who had attained the twenty-eighth anniversary of the day of his birth on or prior to July 1, 1941, and prior to such induction." 

Public Law 206, 77th Cong., 1st Sess. (Washington: 1941).

Proceeding to execute this provision, the System gave the National Service Board for Religious Objectors instructions, on August 21, 1941, regarding the form in which assignees to the civilian work program meeting these general qualifications, might make application for discharge. As a result, in October and November of that year 97 assignees to C. P. S. Camps were issued Interim Certificates of Release (DSS Form 46). While these certificates were technically of an interim nature and the 97 registrant objectors to whom they were issued were subject to recall as "C. P. S. Reservists," none of them were ever recalled as such. Instead, the Selective Service local boards reclassified them in Class IV-H or IV-EH and later into deferred or exempt classifications. However, after the age limit for liability was raised to 44 years following the declaration of war, 52 of these men were subsequently reclassified IV-E and again returned to camp through the issuance of DSS Forms 48, 49, and 50.

The Separation of Objectors Aged 38 and Over 

Beginning in December 1942, the Army gave discharges to men 

38 years of age and over.

This was done at first because older men were found prone to develop disabilities in training; later, however, the provision for separating older men was made more lenient, though restricted to those who planned to enter employment in essential industry, including agriculture." Selective Service made similar arrangements for assignees who were 38 and over by the issuance of 

Administrative Directive No. 14 on May 6, 1943. This directive pro vided for transferring to a Civilian Public Service Reserve the objectors who had attained that age on February 28, 1943, and who made application on or before June 1, 1943.8 There was not much activity in this regard, however, until demobilization. 

It will be noted from Table No. 16 that the first 17 of these furloughs to the C. P. S. Reserve were granted in May and June 1943. 

Within the next 6 months 33 more registrants were given similar transfers. Thereafter, only a scattered few of this kind of separation occurred until February 1946. In connection with the general demobilization plan in effect at that time a special procedure for furloughing men to the Reserve was adopted. Under this special arrangement a camp assignee might be furloughed for a particular purpose when he was within approximately 6 months of qualifying for final discharge. Principal among these purposes was work in the preparation of foreign relief supplies in this country and as a cattle-boat attendant for the relief shipment of livestock to European countries.

Release of Assignees 40 Years of Age and Older 

On June 14, 1945, the separation of registrants in C. P. S. Camps who had attained 40 years of age was authorized, provided their services had been satisfactory. This was done through Administrative Directive No. 25. Applications for discharge under this provision were to be accompanied by statements indicating when the assignees could be spared from the project. The application was subject to approval by National Headquarters and after it was approved, a complete final type physical examination was required.10 This type of examination also became a requirement for all men subsequently released under the general demobilization plan. 

The release of 40-year olds affected but a small group of objectors, since only about 20 men of this age were still left in camps at the time of its initiation. Half of these were promptly discharged. The remainder were separated in October of 1945 having been held temporarily until replacements could be trained for the key positions they occupied.

Its function in this capacity was to pass upon the cases of physical disability referred for such consideration by Headquarters. The advisory board was to send to National Headquarters a report of examination and make a recommendation as to the disposition of each case referred to it.

Part Played by Medical Advisory Boards 

With the increase in assignees and in camp units the general regulations of Selective Service were amended on February 20, 1943, to include in the duties of medical advisory boards the examining and reporting of assignees performing work of national importance, as follows: 

603.31. Composition, appointments, and duties.—(b) Upon proper request the medical advisory board shall examine and submit a report on the physical and mental fitness for service of a registrant who has been rejected for or separated from either military service or work of national importance under civilian direction. Upon request of the Director of Selective Service, the medical advisory board shall examine and submit a report on the physical and mental fitness of any assignee who is performing work of national importance and, if requested, shall recommend for or against the discharge of such assignee based upon his physical or mental condition." 

Before referring a physical disability case to the medical advisory board, the camp director first arranged for the camp physician to make an examination of the assignee, prepare a diagnosis and submit a request to the National Headquarters of the System through the National Service Board for Religious Objectors. The materials accompanied the Director's own request that the registrant be referred to a medical advisory board. If the Service Board concurred in the findings of the physician, the communications were forwarded to National Headquarters with a recommendation that the assignee be examined by the advisory board.

Following the receipt of the request at National Headquarters, it was referred to the Medical Division for review and recommendation as to a medical advisory board examination. If the Medical Division recommended the examination, the necessary correspondence was sent to the State Director where the camp was located, asking that the chairman of the most conveniently located advisory board arrange with the camp director for the appearance of the assignee for examination by the proper specialist of the board. Whenever transportation by commercial carrier was necessary and available, the camp director provided Government transportation requests to the registrant for travel purposes together with meal and lodging tickets for the period of his absence from camp.

Following the examination, the report on it together with the recommendation of the medical advisory board, was forwarded through the State Director to National Headquarters where it was reviewed in the Medical Division. A variety of recommendations came from the advisory boards, such as, discharge, correct disability by medical or surgical treatment, place assignee on light duties, reassign 

11 Selective Service Regulations, 2d edition, 2d printing (Washington: 1948), Amend. 

No. 129.

THE SEPARATION OF C. O.'s FROM C. P. S. CAMPS » 299 

to different work in same camp or unit, transfer to another location, retain in camp on full-time work of national importance. 

In general, the recommendations of the medical advisory boards were concurred in by the Medical Division and the information they submitted was furnished to the camp directors through the National Service Board for Religious Objectors. It should be pointed out, however, that in numerous cases where medical or surgical treatment was recommended by an advisory board and offered to the assignee, he refused to submit to corrective treatment because of religious scruples. 

As has already been indicated some sects to which objectors belonged did not believe in doctors or medicine of any kind. Practically all of such cases were disposed of through separation. This was found to be the most logical solution. These assignees could perform no useful work and were liabilities to the camp administration and the Government.

In a considerable number of cases where the medical advisory boards recommended discharge, the Medical Division of National Headquarters did not concur, because other evidence on record indicated that there was malingering or activity on the part of the particular objectors to exaggerate their symptoms and complaints in an effort to obtain release. Under such circumstances, camp directors were informed that it was the opinion of the Medical Division that the registrants were not suffering from any physical or mental disability for which discharge was justified. 

In other instances, there were histories of long-standing disabilities existing prior to assignment. If this condition was considered disqualifying as of the time of assignment, the objector was discharged from camp without examination by a medical advisory board. In some cases assignees were found to be suffering from disabilities which existed at the time of assignment but were not then considered disqualifying. At a later date these disabilities appeared on a newly developed list of defects for rejecting registrants from service with the armed forces. However, since the Army was not discharging men with like disabilities, assignees with these defects were required to remain in camp and were given duties commensurate with their abilities.12

Release Because of Previous Service 

Mention has been made of the first separation from a Civilian Public Service Camp. It occurred July 13, 1941, and was on physical grounds. The second release was five days later on July 18. The reason for this discharge was that the objector had previously served for more than 32 years in the Navy. His separation came about by

Dependency Separations 

A total of 290 objectors were separated from C. P. S. Camps on dependency grounds. A larger proportion of releases due to dependency hardship were necessary from the civilian work program than from the armed forces. In this connection it will be recalled that assignees received neither pay for their services nor dependency allowances and allotments for their families. Although the objector's religious group attempted to contribute to the needs of his family where undue hardships existed, this did not always rectify the situation. The qualifications for the camp discharge of registrants on account of undue hardship were perhaps only slightly more liberal than those of the armed forces, but in view of the situation with reference to earnings there were proportionately more cases which came up for consideration on these grounds. 

More than half of the dependency hardship separations were granted during the time the Special Separation Board for Camps was handling cases in an advisory capacity; release was made upon the recommendation of the Board. An examination of the statistics on the activities of the Board discloses that a proportionately larger number of applications for dependency discharge were granted than for other reasons 

(Table No. 18, et seq.). 

Objectors Released for Occupational Reasons 

As many as 184 assignees were separated from camp for occupational reasons. In certain instances it appeared advisable to release registrants to return to their previous occupations, that is, mostly to the same positions or jobs held before assignment. Ordinarily, such action was not taken until after the case had been reconsidered by the 

18 Public Law 87, 77th Cong., 1st Sess. (Washington: 1941).

THE SEPARATION OF C. O.'s FROM C. P. S. CAMPS » 301 

local board concerned and after a study of the board's comments and recommendations by the Camp Operations Division. 

New information was submitted by the objector in some instances and the local board in effect gave an unofficial reconsideration to the case. Quite often expert opinion was sought by the board, such as, from the county agent in agricultural cases. In a good many of such instances the assignee applied for discharge on the grounds of changes in the home situation, such as illness, disability, or death of an essential farm worker.

It should be added that the greater majority of occupational discharges were for agricultural purposes. However, there were isolated instances where registrants in C. P. S. Camps were allowed through separation to go back to copper and coal mining and other occupations. All releases of this kind were "for the convenience of the Government" and "in the national interest." 

Separation to Join the Armed Forces 

Shortly after the release of the first and second assignees from civilian work three additional objectors were discharged for the purpose of entering the armed forces. Separations of this nature surprisingly enough continued throughout the 1940-47 operations of Selective Service. Such fact is a tribute to the educational and persuasive efforts of the System, the National Service Board, the technical agencies and the Department of Justice.

A total of 905 registrants, or between 7 and 8 percent of the objectors who were assigned to C. P. S. Camps, were later reclassified by local boards at their own request into classes available for armed service, or went directly into the Army or Navy through volunteering. During most of the World War II operation a request made by an assignee for reclassification was referred to his local board along with permission to reclassify him as available for induction. The registrant would then be sent to an induction station in the regular manner. In such cases requests for immediate induction were often made by the objectors. As a means of expediting the procedure, some assignees simply walked out of camp, went to a recruiting station and enlisted. 

During the time when the Army and the Navy were relying on Selective Service for all their men and were not accepting volunteers, it was necessary that the objector in camp who wished to join the armed forces be reclassified and forwarded to the induction station. 

Then too, if an assignee requested a noncombatant status in the Army or Navy, it was necessary to process him through his local board in order to insure such status. It is true, however, that during this period the Army did upon occasion accept objector volunteers from C. P. S. Camps for the Medical Corps and that the Navy accepted them

<CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION 

for assignment to hospitals. It is believed, though, that no volunteers so enlisted and assigned received authoritative guarantees against later reassignment to combatant types of duty. 

It was the usual custom, during times when the armed forces were recruiting, to give the assignee who stated in writing that he was no longer a conscientious objector, an emergency furlough from a camp for the purpose of enlisting. He was also given a letter of permission to enlist, signed by the Director of Selective Service, with the suggestion that he take this with him to the recruiting station. 

Complete statistics are not available but those at hand indicate that about two-thirds of the registrants leaving work of national importance for armed service asked for noncombatant duty. The other third went into service without reservation. In general the men simply stated in writing that they were no longer conscientious objectors or that they were no longer opposed to noncombatant duty in the armed forces. Sometimes they offered additional information. 

Some said that their assignment to an objector camp was through misunderstanding; others indicated that they felt out of place in camp, were not conscientious objectors at heart, or did not like the idea of working without pay.

Release Through Death 

Thirty registrants died while assigned to objector camps. The causes of death were varied. Some met death while "on project work." Others died from accident or sickness while "in camp" and a few while at home on furlough. The information available shows the causes of death to have been: Infection arising from carbuncle, automobile accident on furlough, drowning (discharge had already been recommended because of psychoneurosis severe, with anxiety and hysteria; coroner's verdict was "suicide"), machinery accident on job, cerebral embolus following appendectomy (sickness developed on job), drowned while searching for lost Coast Guard airplane, poliomyelitis contracted on job as laboratory technician, brain abscess (on duty at time of sickness), drowned on recreation trip (5 cases), peritonitis following appendectomy (on duty), accidentally electrocuted while changing fuse on transformer pole, lymphosarcoma of anterior mediastinum with aplastic anemia (contracted while on project in Puerto Rico), accidental death on railroad track while on liberty from camp, pneumonia while home on furlough, burns caused by explosion in bunk house used for side camp (2 cases), automobile accident en route to duty station, automobile accident on furlough, killed by falling tree on project while driving bulldozer, drowned while aiding farmers to get cattle out of storm, head injury from falling tree on project, brain tumor while on absent-sick status, injured by rolling log
