on project, bicycle accident on recreation trip, death following operation by home physician pursuant to diagnosis of gall bladder pathology and killed by falling snag on project. 

Desertions and Other Delinquency Separations 

A total of 523 assignees were separated from C. P. S. Camps as delinquents including those reported to the Department of Justice at the time of the expiration of the Selective Service Act in 1947. When an objector deserted his assignment or failed to comply with the requirements in camp, he was, as has been seen, subject to criminal prosecution by the Federal courts in accordance with the punitive provisions of the act. Whether the man merely walked out of camp as a deserter, refused to return to his assignment after an authorized furlough, left camp on an order to transfer to another camp and failed to report to the new unit, or refused to perform assigned duties, he was reported for prosecution to the United States attorney having jurisdiction over the area in which the offense was committed or directly to the Department of Justice.

In cases of this type, the date of reporting the assignee for prosecution might have been considered the time when the System lost practical control over him. However, in instances of work refusal, the objectors usually remained in camp physically until they were arrested and removed by authority of the Justice Department. 

The Camp Operations Division ordinarily continued to carry all delinquent assignees on its records until such time as the question of violation was resolved through court action or through action of the Department of Justice indicating that there would be no further prosecution. A conviction in the district court was considered sufficient reason to drop the man from the Civilian Public Service Camp rolls even though an appeal was noted. 

When the registrant was charged with a violation and after trial found not guilty, or when his case was dismissed in court, or when the Justice Department or the United States attorney concerned with the case refused to prosecute, the assignee was also considered to have been separated from work of national importance. In actuality, at such time the National Headquarters of Selective Service lost complete control over the objector. An exception to this rule existed in cases where the man had been charged with a violation of camp procedure and where the finding of not guilty or the dismissal of the case or the refusal to prosecute had the effect of requiring the man to return to the unit.

Discharge for Miscellaneous Reasons 

The reasons for separation in 44 cases were listed as miscellaneous. 

These included 10 who could justifiably have been exempted as min- 737977°-50-vol. 1-21

isters of religion, four who were found to have been otherwise erroneously assigned, and four who were released for administrative reasons. 

The reasons for the remaining discharges of this miscellaneous category are varied and not readily described. Demobilization

In the closing months of 1945 a demobilization program was put into operation for both inductees and assignees. The one for conscientious objectors operated month by month into December 1946. 

While in a sense not separated under the terms of the demobilization program, the assignees released because of legislative changes in the basic act were treated statistically as demobilized men. Using this approach, a total of 8,408 or 70 percent of all separations from Civilian Public Service Camps were the result of demobilization. Ninety-four of these discharges were before Pearl Harbor and by reason of being 28 years of age and over but the others were demobilized after 

November 1945. 

Proposed Legislation for Demobilizing Objectors 

14 On May 26, 1945, a plan for the partial demobilization of conscientious objectors assigned to the civilian work program was announced by Selective Service. It was based on a point system of service similar to that of the armed forces, but nevertheless its announcement created considerable public interest and the opposition of various groups. The Committee on Military Affairs of the House of Representatives became especially concerned and a member of that committee, Mr. Winstead introduced the following bill which was known as H. R. 3597, Seventy-ninth Congress, First session: 

A BILL To make the point system in effect with respect to discharge or release from the Army applicable to the release of conscientious objectors from the work to which they have been assigned. 

Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled, That in determining from time to time the order in which men assigned to work of national importance under civilian direction pursuant to section 5 (g) of the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940, as amended, shall be released from such work, the same point system, the same point values, and the same minimum number of points to establish eligibility for discharge or release, as are applicable with respect to the discharge of men from, and the release of men from active duty in, the Army, shall apply.

H. R. 3597 did not receive much support, however, so after considerable discussion in committee at which the System was represented, Mr. Winstead introduced a new bill on July 12, 1945, known as H. R. 3772, Seventy-ninth Congress, First session, and reading as follows: 

14 Appendix D, Item No. 48.

THE SEPARATION OF C. O.'s FROM C. P. S. CAMPS >>> 305 

A BILL To prevent a point system for the release of conscientious objectors performing assigned work under civilian direction pursuant to section 5 (g) of the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940, as amended, from being put into effect.

Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled, That no point system shall be applied in the release of men assigned to work of national importance under civilian direction pursuant to section 5 (g) of the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940, as amended: Provided, That nothing herein shall prevent the release of such men because of undue hardship. 

This second bill was recommended favorably for passage by the House Committee on Military Affairs in a unanimous vote. Such action was covered by Report No. 904 submitted from the Committee on Military Affairs by Mr. Winstead. On the same day as its introduction the bill was referred to the Committee of the Whole House on the State of the Union and ordered to be printed. The report which Mr. Winstead had submitted read:

The Committee on Military Affairs, to whom was referred the bill (H. R. 3772) to prevent a point system for the release of conscientious objectors performing assigned work under civilian direction pursuant to section 5 (g) of the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940, as amended, from being put into effect, having considered the same report favorably thereon without amendment and recommend that the bill do pass. 

The bill directs that no point system shall be established for the release of men assigned to work of national importance under civilian direction pursuant to section 5 (g) of the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940, as amended, which contains the provisions relating to the deferment of conscientious objectors. The bill does not affect releases for undue hardship. 

Under recent regulations issued by the Selective Service System, conscientious objectors were to be released under a point system similar in principle to the plan for partial demobilization of the Army, but differing in important details from, and being in some respects more liberal than, that plan. Under the Selective Service System regulations, 1 credit for each month of service in a civilian public-service camp, 12 credits for each child under 18, and 3 credits for a wife were allowed conscientious objectors. Completion of 1 full year in a civilian public-service camp prior to May 12, 1945, is a prerequisite for application and release and, although no minimum number of credits necessary for release has been established by the regulations, it has been stated that conscientious objectors possessing the highest number of credits will be released and that the first discharges under the plan would occur during August 1945. 

It is the opinion of the committee that conscientious objectors performing assigned civilian work should not be permitted release to resume normal life while the armed forces are still engaged in combat with the enemy and members of such forces are denied release. To provide for release of such conscientious objectors under the point system would adversely affect morale in the armed forces.

Shortly thereafter the Congress recessed and further action was not taken on the bill. However, Selective Service had no disposition to continue with its original plan for placing into effect a point system of discharge for Class IV-E registrants in Civilian Public

Service Camps. The sentiment as pressed in the House Committee on 

Military Affairs was that action would probably be taken by the Congress to prevent the use of such a plan if it was put into effect. 

A Final Plan Requiring No Legislation 

In the meantime, Japan surrendered. Following VJ-Day, members of the System's National Headquarters' staff met with a group of Congressmen to discuss further the matter of the separation of conscientious objectors from camp duty. At this conference it was informally agreed that further action would not be taken on the Winstead bill. 

It was likewise agreed that plans for the demobilization of objector assignees would be carried forward without the use of a point system and in such manner that these registrants would not be discharged more rapidly or under more favorable circumstances than those in the armed forces. An agreement was likewise made that the principal basis for release would be the length of objector service in camp. 

Circular Letters on the Demobilization Program 

The general plan of the System's program for demobilizing Class IV-E objectors was brought to the attention of the various Civilian Public Service Camps through the issuance of a series of Circular 

Letters entitled "To All Camps and Institutions Using Conscientious 

Objectors." These were sent out on the following dates: October 18 and 25, November 9 and 19, December 3 and 20, 1945; January 4 and 

23, February 25, March 25, April 25, May 24, June 24, July 1, and 

November 5, 1946.15

For the most part month-to-month policies were established for different categories of assignees according to age, marital status, and length of service. In a number of cases factors were combined in the establishing of a category. For instance, the first circular contained the information that, as of November 1, 1945, application might be made for discharge by registrants who had completed four years of service and were married. The previous bulletin had made assignees who were 35 years of age and who had been on camp duty for a period of two years eligible for discharge on October 20.

Categories Set Up For Release 

The following summary sets forth the pertinent changes in these directives. In interpreting this compilation it should be remembered that once a standard of discharge was set up there was an attempt to maintain it until the end of demobilization though it might be subject to some liberalization in the meantime. The first directive stated that 35 year old assignees with 24 months of camp service would be eligible for discharge. This rule held true not only until the issuance

A Separation Board for the Discharge of Objectors 

On May 19, 1945, the Director of Selective Service created the Separation Board for Conscientious Objectors for the purpose of recommending procedures and policies regarding the discharge of men from C. P. S. Camps and to consider and make recommendations

on individual applications for release.

The directive in this connection was Operations Order No. 39, and it read: 

Under and by virtue of the authority vested in me by the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940, as amended, I hereby order: 

1. There is created in National Headquarters a board of three officers to be designated by the Director; one to be known as legal member; one to be known as medical member; and one to be known as administrative member. The board shall be known as The Separation Board for Conscientious Objectors, and its function shall be to consider and recommend to the Director of Selective Service procedures and policies concerning the discharge of conscientious objectors from work of national importance and make recommendations thereon to the Director of Selective Service. The Assistant Director, Camp Operations, may appoint a recorder for said board who shall be assigned to Camp Operations and who shall not be a member of said board or possess voting privileges thereon. 

About a year later a new order was issued changing the size of the Board from three to five officers. This order deleted the first sentence of the original directive and substituted for it the following: "There is created in National Headquarters a board of not less than three nor more than five officers to be designated by the Director of Selective 

Service." 17

The personnel as well as the membership of the Separation Board, changed from time to time.18 It began considering cases in June 1945 and officially handled 630 cases between that time and March 31, 1947. 

Cases were referred to the Board by Col. Lewis F. Kosch, the Assistant Director of Selective Service in charge of the Camp Operations Division and the Board in turn made advisory recommendations to him. It should be stated also that in many instances the Assistant 

Director acted upon discharge matters without formal reference to the Separation Board, the principal function of the Board being to give advice in questionable cases.

Application Procedure for Release 

As a rule, the applications for separation were mailed to the Camp Operations Division directly by the assignee or through the National Service Board for Religious Objectors. In most cases the materials presented to National Headquarters were forwarded through the appropriate State Director of Selective Service to the registrant's own local board with a request for investigation regarding the claims made by the objector and for comment or recommendation by either the board or the State Director. In general, when cases were returned to the local board of the assignee the following type of letter to the State 

Director was used:

Forwarded herewith is information concerning the application of the abovenamed assignee for discharge from work of national importance on the grounds of unusual hardship or on the grounds that such discharge is in the national health, safety, or interest.

In granting discharges for hardship, we attempt to parallel the procedure of the armed forces, taking into consideration the additional fact that the assignees receive no pay or family allowances from the Government. 

It is requested that this particular case be referred to the concerned local board with instructions to have some city, county, or State welfare agency, the Red Cross, or other similar organization complete an independent investigation of the situation. It is further requested that when the investigation has been completed the original copy of the welfare report be returned to us, through your Headquarters. In this connection, any comment and recommendation which the concerned local board cares to make will also be appreciated. 

The Cover Sheet of this individual is forwarded to you herewith in order that both you and the local board may be informed regarding the background material of the case. It should be returned to this Headquarters with your report. It will be appreciated if you will expedite action in this case."

Most of the cases which came before the Separation Board were those in which it was claimed that the assignment of the objector registrant to work of national importance in a Civilian Public Service Camp was resulting in extreme hardship and privation to a wife, child or parent with whom he had maintained a bona fide family relationship in their home. The second largest number of cases came under the general heading of national health, safety, and interest. In addition there

THE SEPARATION OF C. O.'s FROM C. P. S. CAMPS » 

» 311 During most of the time the Separation Board was functioning, the general demobilization program for the conscientious objectors of the C. P. S. Camps was in effect. As a result a considerable number of assignees whom the Board voted to retain in camp, were discharged shortly thereafter under the demobilization plan. In fact, the situation whereby the applicant would soon be eligible for regular discharge was often an important factor in the retention action of the Board. 

Conspectus 

With the advent of VE- and VJ-Days, demobilization got under way for Selective Service registrants who were assigned to civilian work of national importance as well as for those who had been inducted into the armed forces. The original plan of the System for demobilizing the conscientious objectors in Civilian Public Service Camps was to apply a point-scoring procedure similar to that set up for Army and Navy personnel. There was public and congressional opposition to the arrangement, however, on the grounds that it unduly favored the camp assignee. Selective Service indicated that this was not the case since objectors in camps did not receive the same allowances, allotments, pay, and other benefits of like nature as did individuals of the armed services. Nevertheless, the plan had to be revised. 

The change made length of service alone the principal factor in separation from camp duty and tended to ignore the factors of children under 18 and wives.

Prior to demobilization the release of Class IV-E registrants from the work-of-national-importance program was conducted on very much the same basis as discharge from the Army and Navy: over-age, physical disability, previous service in the armed forces, dependency hardship, occupational need, death, desertion, delinquency, and miscellaneous. It should be noted especially in this connection that a total of 905 or from 7 to 8 percent of all objectors in C. P. S. Camps were separated because of their desire to join the Army or Navy for noncombatant or combatant duty. 

Regarding physical disability as a cause of release, the camp physician, the camp director, the National Service Board for Religious Objectors, the Camp Operations and Medical Divisions of National Headquarters and the medical advisory boards of the System all participated. Dependency hardship as a reason for discharge came under the purview of the camp director, the National Service Board, the 

Camp Operations Division, a Special Separation Board of National 

Headquarters, the State Headquarters and the local board.

<CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION 

Most camp assignees, 70 percent to be exact, were separated in connection with demobilization and since C. P. S. Camps were not authorized to operate after the expiration of the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940 on March 31, 1947, all registrants in such units were released by that date. Thus came to a close the first national experience of the United States in a civilian work program for conscientious objectors.

XVI 

A STATISTICAL REVIEW OF CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTORS 

Statistics have already been presented on some phases of Selective Service operations in the field of conscientious objection during World War II. Information of this type has appeared in the discussions of (1) pacifist church denominations, (2) the American history of objection, (3) registrants who performed noncombatant service, (4) those who did work of national importance, (5) the System's classification of objectors, (6) Civilian Public Service Camps and their accomplishments in work of national importance, (7) camp assignees and other objectors who were law violators, and (8) the separation of registrants from the civilian work program. A brief review of these statistics and the presentation of additional data along this line should therefore be attempted.

Total Registrants Claiming Objection 

Separate statistics were not compiled on the total number of registrants who claimed to be conscientious objectors. It is probable, however, that between 70,000 and 75,000 made such claims either as objectors to combatant service or to any duty with the armed forces. This estimate is based on the rosters kept by the local boards as required in section 5 (g) of the Act:

Each person whose claim for exemption from combatant training and service because of conscientious objections is sustained shall be listed by the local board on a register of conscientious objectors.

Section 623.62 of the general Selective Service Regulations implemented this provision as follows: 

623.62. Register of conscientious objectors.-The local board shall list on a register of conscientious objectors each registrant whose claim for special classification as a conscientious objector has been sustained, either by the local board or upon appeal. The register of conscientious objectors shall show separately those registrants who have been classified as available for noncombatant military service (Class I-A-O) and those who have been classified as available for work of national importance under civilian direction only (Class IV-E). No special form is provided for this register.¹

The local board roster total does not include those who claimed to be objectors but whose claims were disallowed and whose boards therefore placed them in Class I-A. Nor does it contain registrants whose claims were never considered because they were at all times found to be exempt or deferred from service on legal, dependency or occupa tional grounds and classified IV (other than IV-E), III, or II. The number of such objectors can only be estimated roughly. In proceeding to do this there are a number of factors involved, such as the types of registrants who might make valid claims for exemption or deferment on the grounds of objection and the percentages of all registrants who at no time were classified as available for service. After considering these and other factors, it is estimated that at least 20,000 registrants 18-44 years of age claimed to be conscientious objectors who at no time were placed in Classes I-A-O and IV-E. These added to the 52,354 registrants so classified indicates that there were between 70,000 and 75,000 of the ages liable for service who filed claims of conscientious objection. For example, attention is invited to the figures for the neighboring States of Indiana and Michigan. In Indiana there were 2,500 Class 

IV-E registrants as compared with 1,722 of Class I-A-O. For Michi gan the reverse was true, that State having 1,338 in I-A-O and 789 in IV-E. Local Boards With No Objectors 

As noted the Director's February 1947 letter also requested the number of local boards with no Class I-A-O and IV-E objector registrants on their rosters. More than 1,200 boards were reported as at no time having any registrants so classified. This indicated that there were many places in the United States where the conscientious objector issue was not a problem during World War II. Although the question of conscientious objection claims, is not entirely ruled out by such data, it is safe to conclude that these boards at the most had very few claimants. A STATISTICAL REVIEW OF CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTORS » 321 The Close Following of Doctrine by Christadelphians 

It would appear from Table No. 25 that the members of the Christadelphian Church followed more closely than any other denomination the doctrine of their denomination as it related to conscientious objection and refusal to enter the armed forces. For this denomination, there was complete additional information to show that only 10 registrants of this church entered the armed forces and 4 others served prison sentences rather than perform such duty.

The Mennonites 

The Mennonite bodies not only furnished Civilian Public Service Camps with the largest number of objector assignees but they also furnished the largest proportion of these Class IV-E registrants as related to their membership, of any church among the larger denominations. However, if these statistics are read to indicate that four assignees out of each 100 members went to camp, the question arises as to what happened to the remainder who were liable for service; speaking in round numbers there was during World War II one man in the armed services for each 10 people in the country. The Mennonite central committee provided part of the answer. The following statement was made in a letter to the National Headquarters of Selective Service under date of January 18, 1947:

Of all the Mennonite young men who were drafted prior to December 1, 1944, 39.6 percent took regular military service, 14.5 percent took noncombatant work, and 45.9 percent were assigned to C. P. S. Camps. These figures are based on a survey which was made as of the above-mentioned date. 

The Friends 

The Friends rank next in Table No. 25. Information regarding the numbers of this faith who served in the armed forces is not available. 

At one time a report was circulated that there were twice as many Friends in the armed forces as in C. P. S. Camps, but this statement could not be verified statistically.

The Brethren 

A valuable classification survey was made by Merlin C. Shull, of the Ministry to Servicemen of the Church of the Brethren, in March 1945. The results of the survey were provided to Selective Service through the Brethren Service Committee. It listed the members of the church and the friends of the church (cases where a man was the son of a church member) who were in the armed services. Only 

51.2 percent of the local churches of the denomination furnished reports to the survey, but the totals reported were increased to 100 percent to obtain a complete estimate. Table No. 26 presents the resulting estimates, which are believed to be generally reliable.

Numbers 21, 481 1, 382 1, 365 24, 228 These figures indicate a fairly high ratio of servicemen in the Brethren Church, somewhat higher than the one in 10 for the total population of the United States which was referred to above. Of course, ratios are relative indexes and many factors could cause variances. For instance, there is a considerable difference between church memberships in the matter of sex ratios. In the Christadelphian 

Church the ratio of males to females was 65.3, while in the different branches of the Brethren group it ranged from 54.5 to 80.3 with the latter figure given for the Church of the Brethren, which had about 85 percent of the members. Another factor of importance was the percentage of young people affiliating with the denomination who were not necessarily members. Then, too, the membership figures available were for 1936. 

Writing in April 1945, Dr. Rufus D. Bowman, president of Bethany 

Biblical Seminary, tells of a questionnaire survey which he conducted among a sampling of one-fifth of the member churches of the Church of the Brethren. He based the following comments on the answers which 161 churches gave to the question, "What are the reasons Brethren boys have given for going into Army service?":

According to the replies from local churches giving the statements from the young men themselves, duty to country, social pressure, the economic problem, inadequate peace teaching, the feeling that the war was forced upon them, indifference to the church and lack of sympathy with the conscientious objector position were the primary reasons why Brethren boys went into the Army. A study of the replies indicates that lack of vital peace teaching should be given a larger place than is indicated by the schedules. It could hardly be expected that the Army boys would mention inadequate peace teaching as the reason for their accepting military service. However, if the Brethren had carried on a thorough peace-education program in the local churches, it is probable that more young men would have withstood social pressures and the influence of propaganda. The reports show that propaganda, the economic problem, and the influence of friends and community have been stronger in motivating action than the program of the church."

Furthermore, there were enough members of the group in prison as Selective Service violators that the number actually in C. P. S. Camps did not accurately represent the thinking of the entire body.

Churches of Christ 

The Churches of Christ are of particular interest in regard to conscientious objectors in view of the doctrinal position taken by this group as reported to the Bureau of the Census in 1936. A special study of the position of this denomination was made with the assistance of some of the leaders within the church. The following paragraphs are quoted from a letter received at National Headquarters, Selective Service, from Dr. George S. Benson, president of Harding 

College, Searcy, Ark., and written under date of April 18, 1947:

The Churches of Christ maintain strict congregational independence. We have no national headquarters. We have no creed other than the Bible and consequently, there is no single person or single group of persons who can speak for the Churches of Christ as a whole. 

As might be expected under this condition, the Churches of Christ are not in agreement with regard to military service. We have some congregations that refuse to participate in war at all.

In my opinion however, the larger number of our congregations believe that Christians should be subject to all requirements on the part of their Government and consequently, should obey the orders of the Government with regard to anything that they do not consider from the Bible to be wrong within itself. 

Consequently, most of our young men responded when they were called to arms but requested noncombatant service. Some went into quartermaster service, some into medical service, some into communications. In fact, they were willing to accept anything except actually taking up arms and attempting to take life. 

Then we have a considerable group of churches that advocate no conscientious objections at all and whose young men accordingly accept combatant service without objection.

By way of summarizing what I have said above, the vast majority of our brethren fall in three groups: first, a small group that objects to any type of military service, even objecting to wearing of the uniform; second, a larger group who believe in accepting any orders from the Government so long as the task within itself does not require taking of life and who accordingly accepted any kind of noncombatant service; third, a small group of churches that offer no conscientious objections at all to military service.

Throughout World War II, I believe our Government did a marvelous job in respecting the conscience of young men and I know our brethren in the Churches of Christ were so impressed. Our young men who requested noncombatant service and succeeded in convincing the officers that they were sincere in it, were readily given such service. This often times did not mean less dangerous service at all nor were they asking to escape from danger. They were only asking to refrain from taking life which they believed out of harmony with the doctrine of the New Testament.

The Assemblies of God 

A similar question existed concerning the stand of the Assemblies of God, as quoted by the Bureau of the Census in its 1936 Census of Religious Bodies. This church was reported as taking a pacifist position, but only 23 of its members and affiliates appeared in C. P. S. 

Camps as assignees. Based on a 1936 membership of 148,053 this would indicate a ratio figure of 0.1 per 1,000 members, which was extremely low for any group taking a nonresistance position. The following statement made by Rev. J. Roswell Flower, General Secre tary of the General Council, under date of April 28, 1947, helps to explain the low ratio, however. 

The statement which appeared in the publication of the United States Department of Commerce, Religious Bodies 1936, on page 71 of volume II, part I, is founded on an article which appears in the bylaws of the general council of the Assemblies of God. We are enclosing a page taken from the bylaws containing this statement.

By way of explanation, the Assemblies of God were organized in the year 1914 just before the beginning of the first World War, and the statement on military service was adopted at that time. The local assemblies which became part of the general council were few in number at that time, and few of the members of the Assemblies of God took the conscientious objector position. 

In the year 1940 the denomination had grown to approximately 5,000 churches with an enrolled membership of approximately 200,000. These churches are independent, sovereign entities which have agreed to cooperate in the general body much on a similar basis to that of the Baptist denomination. The bylaws on military service is not binding on any of the local churches although it was not rescinded and remained in force all during the years of World War II. 

Your records are correct in that there were only about 22 who claimed to be members of the Assemblies of God who took the extreme conscientious objector position and were consigned to civilian public service. We had the responsibility of raising support for these men and did so. 

We have no means of knowing the number of members or sons of members of Assemblies of God serving in the armed forces. None of those members of the eight churches here in Springfield, Mo., asked for noncombatant service, but we do know that a number of members in other parts of the country did ask for noncombatant service and were so classified. 

When the United States entered the war and Selective Service was authorized, many inquiries for advice poured in to this office. The universal advice given to our young men was that instead of taking the extreme conscientious objector position that it was better for them to ask for noncombatant service. I will send you copies of the letters mailed to many of these inquirers. 

Our records show that we had no difficulty to obtain proper classification for those who did ask for noncombatant service. For the most part, the local 

Selective Service boards were considerate of the applicant and gave the proper classification without question.

The following statement is taken from one of the letters referred to by Reverend Flower: 

We would like for you to consider carefully the matter, and should you feel that you could serve the Government in noncombatant service, we would suggest

A STATISTICAL REVIEW OF CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTORS » 325 

that you get in touch with your draft board and inform them that you are willing to accept such service. They might even permit you to volunteer in the service which you might choose.

The Molokans and the Church of God The Molokans constituted another church with definite conscientious objector leanings. However, during World War II Selective Service was told by a high ranking official of the church that only one in 20 of its registrants had asked for civilian work when called for service. 

This statement agreed well with the church membership ratio of 7.5 

C. P. S. assignees per 1,000, based on an estimated membership of 10, 000. It makes this church rank next after the Christadelphian, Mennonite, Friends, and Brethren.

The Church of God among the larger avowed pacifist churches was even lower in position, with a rate of 1.2 per 1,000. It ranked in last position among this group of churches. 

The Cooperativeness of the Adventists 

The Seventh-Day Adventist Church, avowedly noncombatant, was very cooperative in that regard. Only 23 of its members were assignees to camps, giving it a rate of 0.2 per 1,000, similar to that of the 

Assemblies of God.

Small Ratios of Many Churches Whereas figures of from 124 to 845 assignees from denominations without nonresistance doctrines, appear large in Table No. 24, they do not seem so large when considered in relation to their memberships (Table No. 25). A figure of 845 for the Methodist means that only 

0.1 out of each 1,000 in the membership of this group served as an assignee in a Civilian Public Service Camp. All of this information for the large religious groups indicates the extreme willingness of the rank and file of American denominations to support the national effort in a time of emergency.

Church Affiliations of Assignees Separated as Delinquents 

Another topic of importance in connection with the church affiliation of conscientious objectors is the difference between these groups as to the number of delinquency separations from Civilian Public Service Camps. The largest number of such discharges was among 

Jehovah's Witnesses, a total of 151, followed by 71 men of no religious affiliation and 70 who were Methodists (Table No. 27). The Friends, Molokans, and Brethren were also among the first 10 in total delinquency releases from camps, along with such very large denominational groups as Presbyterians, Baptists, and Catholics. Denominations not listed in Table No. 27 had less than 10 separations of this kind.

The largest percentage of camp delinquents was in the Theosophist group where four out of 11 acquired such status. The Molokans were second, with 22 out of 75 becoming delinquent. In third place were the 

Jehovah's Witnesses, with 151 out of 532 dropped for delinquency.

Most of the remainder of the groups listed were, as already noted, small in size.

However, it is perhaps significant that 11 churches having more than 10 men in objector camps had no delinquents whatsoever. These were the Assembly of God, Evangelical, Evangelical Association,

First Century Gospel, Holiness, International Bible Students, Latter
