In addition, it is noted that the three principal "peace churches" ranked very low in camp delinquency. The Friends, with 42 delinquents out of a total of 902, had a percentage of 4.6. The Brethren, with 16 delinquents out of 1,468, had 1.1 percent. The Mennonites had a most remarkable record in that only four of their 4,610 men became delinquent, for a percentage of 0.09. These data suggest that members of the principal "peace churches" were generally more willing to cooperate in camp activities than those of other groups with less doctrinal opposition to war. Possibly this was due to the definite

A STATISTICAL REVIEW OF CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTORS » 

327 acceptance by "peace group" leaders of the civilian work program as a satisfactory war service arrangement for C. O.'s and a stronger tendency for registrants of these churches to act according to the will of their leaders.

Summary and Recommendation 

To summarize, it is estimated that between 70,000 and 75,000 militarily liable registrants, aged 18 through 44 years, filed claims of conscientious objection during the 62 years of Selective Service operations during World War II. Of these an estimated 20,000 were never classified I-A-O (available for noncombatant duty) or IV-E (available for civilian work) by the System; they were found exempt or deferable for other reasons and placed in Class IV other than IV-E 

(legal), III (dependency) or II (occupational). An additional 

13,780 were put in I-A-O or IV-E but most of them were reclassified as not available before being processed for induction or assignment. 

A few may have been placed in I-A (available for combatant service). 

Reports also showed that 11,950 Class IV-E's were assigned to Civilian Public Service Camps for work of national importance and that 1,624 more so assigned refused to go to these camps and were convicted in the Federal courts as law violators in this regard. As many as 25,000 however, were estimated to have been inducted for noncombatant service.

Among the States, California and Pennsylvania had the largest number of objectors in Classes I-A-O and IV-E, around 5,500 each, though Indiana and Ohio each had more than 4,000. As to proportion of registrants so classified, however, Kansas easily ranked first and Indiana and Washington readily second and third. In the relationship of I-A-O's to IV-E's Washington stood first among selected States and Nevada and Kentucky close to it, while Ohio was lowest along with New Hampshire; these data apparently show the influence of the pacifist churches. As many as 1,262 local boards reported no

Class I-A-O and IV-E registrants; in this connection Georgia had the highest percentage, 82, and other Southern States likewise stood well. Delaware and the District of Columbia had no boards without such classes and the proportion was also low in the Northeastern and Pacific States.

When it came to the church affiliations of Class IV-E objectors assigned to C. P. S. Camps, the Mennonite denomination had by far the largest number, 4,610. The Brethren came second with 1,468 and the

Society of Friends third with 902. Ten other denominations supplied more than 100 each. Ratios of camp assignees to church membership, however, show the Christadelphians highest with 5 assignees per 100 members although objectors in camps affiliated with this denomination numbered but 136. The ratio of 4 per 100 among Mennonites

placed them second and indicated that they, as well as the Christadelphians, followed their pacifist doctrines closely during the emergency of 1940-47. The Friends' ratio along this line was about 1 per 100 and the Brethren's a little less than one. 

Camp delinquency and church denominations are likewise significant. There were a total of 151 Jehovah's Witnesses separated or dropped from C. P. S. Camps for refusal to obey orders and for other camp delinquencies. This was the largest number of such releases and amounted to 28 percent of the 532 members of this sect on the work-ofnational-importance program. The Theosophists had 36 percent so discharged and the Molokans 29.

All of the conscientious-objector statistics of this chapter and previous ones are of considerable interest and importance. They did not entirely cover the informational, operating, or educational needs of that phase of the Selective Service program, however. Like the reemployment or veteran's assistance activity, another new phase of the System's 1940 effort, the tendency as regards conscientious objection was to attempt operation on a minimum of data. It is therefore recommended that in future work of this nature more comprehensive records and reports be instituted at the beginning. The resulting statistics will contribute materially to both the internal tasks and the external relationships of the churches, the technical agencies and the Department of Justice, as well as to Selective Service operations.

XVII 

CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION- PAST, PRESENT AND FUTURE 

This monograph has dealt with the role played in the various national emergencies of the United States by citizens who were conscientious objectors to war and the armed forces. It has covered the subject briefly for the past and at length for the present, that is, for the Selective Service operations of 1940-47 in connection with World War II. The next step is to review this experience as concisely as possible and to indicate what lessons are found therein for future activities of the System.

The point should probably be made first of all that opposition to violence and resistance in the United States may be said to stem from the beginning of its history. The right of the individual to act in accordance with his conscience was recognized from the first as one of the principles upon which the country was founded. For more than 

200 years this precept developed until it crystallized in the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940 with the most comprehensive provisions of national scope yet enacted for the conscientious objector. 

Objection From Colonial Times to the Civil War 

The right of the objector to exemption from armed service as expressed in the 1940 law, was embodied in some of the earliest legislation of the colonies. Later William Penn, in 1701, declared by way of a charter for Pennsylvania that no person should be compelled to perform any act contrary to his "religious persuasion." In 1775 the 

Continental Congress passed a resolution calling upon all to respect the rights of nonresisters. Following the Declaration of Independence, individual States provided through their constitutions for the exemption of religious objectors from bearing arms. While all of this legislation exempting those opposed to violence, was not necessarily restricted to members of specific religious groups, it was nevertheless directed mainly to members of the historic peace churches: Friends, Brethren, Mennonites with creeds forbidding participation in war.

These three religious organizations, incidentally, had the largest numbers of objectors in Civilian Public Service Camps during World 

War II. 

329

<CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION 

Parallel with this recognition of the principle for objector exemption there existed the philosophy that in return for exemption an alternative form of service should be demanded. In 1757 for instance, the Quakers passed an act in the Pennsylvania colony containing rather broad provisions for noncombatant service by granting exemption to nonresisters who would assist in time of emergency by such acts as extinguishing fires; caring for the wounded, the women and children; and acting as messengers. Thus hospital service, which in 

World War II was one of the main duties in the armed forces to which noncombatant objectors were assigned, was established as one of the early forms of service required of the objector. In the Revolution, the payment of a fine or commutation fee was substituted for armed duty. 

This principle of alternative service has remained a basic part of successive legislation in the field, although the form of service required has changed.

National Programs During the Civil War 

The Civil War marked the first national legislation with special provisions for the conscientious objector. The Federal Draft Act of 

February 24, 1864, recognized the rights of members of religious denominations "conscientiously opposed to the bearing of arms and who are prohibited from doing so by the rules and articles of faith and practice." In lieu of military service the citizen opposed to war and armed forces was given four alternatives: hospital service, care of the freedmen, securing a substitute, or payment of a commutation fee. 

Also the Confederate Congress on October 11, 1862, had passed a law providing for the exemption of Friends, Dunkards, Nazarenes, and Mennonites. In addition, noncombatant service was broadened by the 

Confederacy to include those engaged in "the production of grain and provisions for the army and the families of soldiers," a precursor of the agricultural activities to which objectors were assigned in both World War I and II. It should be noted that not until the Civil War was church membership per se generally a prerequisite. 

The New Approach of World War I 

The First World War brought distinct changes in the approach to the problem of conscientious objection. Under the Selective Service law of 1917, all militarily liable men if selected for duty were subject to induction into the armed forces. No relief from service was possible through the payment of commutation fees or obtaining substitutes. 

Only if the objector could prove after registering with the local board that he was a member of a well-recognized religious organization whose creed forbade participation in war in any form was he exempted from combatant duty; he was still inducted into the armed forces, however, and then assigned to noncombatant service.

CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION-PAST, PRESENT, AND FUTURE >> 

331 On March 16, 1918, an act was passed allowing the furlough without pay and allowances of enlisted men from the Army. This was applied to broaden the duty available to objectors by furloughing noncombatants to agriculture and for service in the Friends' Reconstruction Unit in France. Recommendations for such assignments were made by a board of inquiry which visited Army camps for the purpose of querying registrants averse to any service with the armed forces on the sincerity of their claims. Objectors subsequently assigned to these projects remained under the control of the military, however, despite the fact they were engaged in civilian projects, and all on such assignments who violated the 1917 law were liable for trial by court martial.

The Liberalizations of World War II 

It is a significant commentary on American democracy that in a period of concentration camps, slave labor and other features of totalitarianism elsewhere in the world, an extremely small minority group of registrants who claimed conscientious objection, were protected by legislation in World War II that liberalized in four important respects the provisions of World War I. First, the Selective Training and 

Service Act of 1940 broadened the basis of exemption to include all persons who "by reason of religious training and belief" were conscientiously opposed to war in any form. The law thus embraced members of all churches, not merely those whose creed specifically forbade participation in war. But the enactment went still further by stipulating that recognition should also be given to the claims of nonchurch members provided they had a religious basis. Claims to conscientious objection on social, political, philosophical or other grounds were not valid, however, an interpretation upheld by the Federal courts in the United States v. Kauten and Berman v. United 

States of America cases.

Secondly, the act introduced special appeal consideration for the objector registrant by providing for investigation, hearing and recommendation on his appeal by the Department of Justice. 

Civilian Work of National Importance 

The third important advance toward a more adequate objector program was the recognition given those who could not conscientiously perform any service under the control of the armed forces. For this group, work of national importance under civilian direction was provided by the law and upon being given a special classification, Class IV-E, such objectors were assigned to such work. Almost 12,000 of these registrants participated in this program. 

A fourth liberalization of World War II legislation was that work of national importance should at all times be under civilian control.

. CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION 

Thus the assignee to such work was never under the direction of the armed forces. Furthermore, if he was indicted for violation of the 

1940 Act he was given a civil trial by a Federal court. 

Noncombatant Service Within the Armed Forces For the registrant who was against combatant service only, the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940 provided noncombatant duty within the armed forces. In this respect the act followed closely the 1917 law. All noncombatant assignments were restricted by the 

Army and Navy to medical and hospital activities although the President had previously determined that only duty which involved the bearing and use of arms and training in these regards was outside of the definition for noncombatant. An estimated 25,000 claimants were placed in Class I-A-O by the System as being available for noncombatant service and were inducted into the armed forces for such duty. The peace churches as well as Selective Service were active in working with the Congress on the objector provisions of the law and although they allowed greater opportunity than ever before for the cooperation of the registrant opposed to war, they were not the subject of any amendment during the entire emergency of 1940–47.

Classifying the Conscientious Objector 

The registration, classification, and other processing of the conscientious objector as to exemption or deferment from or selection for noncombatant service in the armed forces or for work of national importance under civilian direction, did not differ essentially from that of other Selective Service registrants. General regulations for the System covered this, while special ones dealt only with the work program for objectors. All militarily liable males, including objectors, were required to register with the System and to prepare a 

Questionnaire (DSS Form 40) for classification purposes. All must serve if selected but within the confines of their beliefs. The registrant opposed to war indicated this on his Form 40 and was then provided a Special Form for Conscientious Objector (DSS Form 47) on which to submit information substantiating his claim. 

In classifying any registrant the Selective Service local board first considered him for exemption in Class IV (over-age, official, alien, minister, unfit) and next for deferment in III (dependency) and then in II (occupational) without reference to his claim, if he was an objector. In the event of ineligibility for any of these classes, he was held to be selected and available for service, and if he was an objector, attention was then given to his claim which in effect requested either noncombatant service or civilian work. His claim being found valid, he was next placed in Class I-A-O, available for noncombatant duty, or IV-E, available for work assignment, to await his call for service.

CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION-PAST, PRESENT, AND FUTURE » 333 

The validity of his claim depended heavily upon information regarding his past and present conduct.

From that point on, the processing of the I-A-O registrant was the same as that for the I-A man available for combatant service. 

As regards the IV-E objector when his order number was reached, he received an Order to Report-Preinduction Physical Examination 

(DSS Form 215) like all registrants, followed by a Certificate of Fitness (DSS Form 218) indicating he was physically, mentally, morally, emotionally, and educationally acceptable for duty. A Conscientious Objector Report (DSS Form 48) was then mailed from the local board via the State Director of the System to National Headquarters. The latter, working with a National Service Board for 

Religious Objectors, prepared an Assignment to Work of National Importance (DSS Form 49) for forwarding through State Headquarters to the local board which then issued an Order to Report for 

Work of National Importance (DSS Form 50). 

Principles of Classification 

In case the objector's claim was not considered valid by his local board and he was placed in Class I-A when he had asked for I-A-O or IV-E or he was put in I-A-O when he desired IV-E, he had recourse like all other registrants to the board of appeal and the Presidential Appeal Board. Almost 90 percent of the objectors classified in Classes 

I-A-O and IV-E did not seek appeal, however, thus accepting the System's determination. The Selective Service Act contained special provisions so that when a C. O. filed an appeal the appeal board would refer the case to the Department of Justice for investigation by the Federal Bureau of Investigation, hearing by an officer appointed specifically for this purpose, and recommendation by the United States attorney as a result of the investigation and hearing. 

In over three-fourths of such cases, the boards of appeal carried out the Justice Department's recommendation, although they were required only to give consideration to it. The Department tended to be more liberal than the appeal boards and the appeal boards more so than the local boards. The Department of Justice, for instance, recommended that 64.6 percent of the objectors who made appeals, be sustained in their claims to exemption from combatant duty and that 49.2 percent be sustained in their claims to exemption from all armed service.

If the board of appeal failed to sustain the claim of the conscientious objector, the claimant might still appeal his case to the Presidential Appeal Board, provided one or more members of the appeal board had dissented from his local board classification. His case might also be appealed by action of the State Director or Director of

the System. Despite the fact, that this Board was composed of military personnel, only 12 percent of the 712 objector cases appealed to it were classified for combatant duty, an indication of an even greater liberality on the part of the Presidential Appeal Board. 

Establishing the Civilian Work Program 

In World War II the principle which had existed for many years that conscientious objectors owed some form of alternate service in return for exemption from the armed forces found concrete expression in an effective program of work of national importance under civilian direction. For the first time in American history, a wellorganized plan was established at the beginning of an emergency which would enable the objector to make a consistent contribution to the national health, safety, and interest. The importance of this contribution to the country's welfare is evidenced by the nature of the activities in which the registrant engaged: forest protection and preservation; public park maintenance; soil conservation; land reclamation; dam construction; wildlife preservation; crop production and harvesting; dairy-herd testing; mental hospital and trainingschool service; diet, nutrition, climate, malaria and hookworm experiments; health and medical activities; surveying and mapping; and compiling and plotting weather data. 

Civilian Public Service Camps 

This work program for registrants who were opposed to any service with the armed forces, was operated by means of Civilian Public Service Camps which had both regular and special projects as noted above. 

The general administration of these camps was vested in the Director of Selective Service. Technically, however, the work of camps having mainly the regular type of project, was under the direction of an agency of the Federal Government participating in the program: 

United States Forest Service, Soil Conservation Service, National Parks Service, Bureau of Reclamation, Farm Security Administration, Fish and Wildlife Service, and General Land Office. Special project units were under the Department of Agriculture, Coast and Geodetic Survey, Weather Bureau, Office of Scientific Research and Development, Office of the Surgeon General of the Army, United 

States Public Health Service, Puerto Rico Reconstruction Admin istration, Veterans' Administration, and various State mental hospitals and training schools. 

At first the demand for camp assignees on regular and special projects was not great but eventually it far exceeded the supply. In the fall of 1946, for instance, when the units were at their greatest strength, more men were assigned to State hospitals and schools

CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION—PAST, PRESENT, AND FUTURE » 335 

F than to any single agency. A total of 5,931,632 man-days of work were performed from May 1941 through March 1947 by Class IV-E objectors in C. P. S. Camps on both types of projects. Thus a civilian work program which began basically as a regular manual-labor activity, became more and more unique and specialized, saving the Federal and State Governments several millions of dollars in personnel costs, fulfilling the service obligations of registrants with beliefs against armed force and contributing importantly to the national effort during an emergency.

As mentioned above, the camps were all administered by Selective Service. Of the 151 units established, 8 were under Government supervision, 120 under the historic peace churches and the remaining 23 under other religious organizations. Both Government-operated and church-operated camps had a director and most camp staffs also included a physician, nurse, dietitian, safety assistant, and other administrative personnel. In the former, the camp director and his staff were appointed by the technical agency; in the latter, by the National 

Service Board for Religious Objectors, a voluntary association of religious organizations which acted as spokesman for the churches and the conscientious objectors. These latter camps whose activities outside of working hours were all handled by the church group, likewise had a project superintendent designated by the technical agency to supervise the work program. 

Administering the Camps To obtain, equip, and administer the camps, the System set up at National Headquarters a Camp Operations Division. Many of the camps were founded on former Civilian Conservation Corps sites and their work was in general a continuation and an expansion along special lines of projects originated by the CCC. 

The operation of the C. P. S. Camp was predicated in large part on that of the CCC. Like all other Federal employees, the Class IV-E registrant on camp assignment worked an 8-hour day. Medical care was provided. Sanitation standards were set by the United States 

Public Health Service. Recreation was furnished, as well as religious services at the camp. Furlough privileges were the same as those of enlisted and inducted men in the armed forces. There were small allowances which varied with the type of project. Assignees on regular projects who were provided with living accommodations, food, clothing, and other essentials, received $5 a month. A more flexible and liberal arrangement was found necessary for special projects. Assignees at mental hospitals and training schools, for instance, worked and lived under the same conditions as regular em- 737977°-50—vol. 1- -28

• CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION 

ployees. Some objectors on such work drew as much as $15 from monthly allowances, the remainder being deposited in the United 

States Treasury; others received a per diem allowance.

The administration of the camps was beset from the first with problems of order and discipline as regards individual assignees. 

Most all of the objectors on civilian work performed this duty satisfactorily; but although they had been shown every consideration during the classification process of Selective Service, their life at camp created economic hardships for the families of many. In addition, there was a handful of registrants who accepted camp assignments, though opposed even to this service, rather than have the courage of their convictions and face a prison sentence. The latter were extremely uncooperative in the work activities of the units; some passively so, others actively. United States attorneys upon frequent occasions were slow to prosecute them after they were reported as law violators and delinquents and this encouraged their noncooperativeness and caused others to join them on a more or less organized-resistance basis. Before the movement was finally ended by court action as regards the leaders, it came near to damaging materially the reputation of the work program which most of the objectors, the churches, the technical agencies and the System were interested in making successful as a first attempt at a comprehensive solution of service for registrants opposed to war. 

Violations of the Act

For the first time in United States history, the enforcement of a Federal conscription law was made the sole responsibility of civil authorities. By virtue of the Selective Training and Service Act of 

1940 no registrant could be tried by court martial unless he had actually been inducted into the armed forces. Of the 16,000 registrants convicted as law violators during the System's 1940-47 operation, over 6,000 were conscientious objectors, two-thirds of these being Jehovah's Witnesses. The large number from this sect was accounted for by their refusal to request or accept I-A-O or IV-E classifications as objectors and their insistence upon deferment as ministers. More than 5,000 of the objector convictions were for failure to report for armed forces induction or for assignment to civilian work. Other violations of the law included failure to register, to return the Questionnaire, or to report for physical examination; refusal to comply with orders in C. P. S. Camps; and counselling or aiding evasion. 

Inasmuch as the purpose of the law was to increase and train the armed forces, the dominating philosophy of enforcement was that delinquent registrants should be educated and persuaded to comply with with the law rather than penalized for violating it. Every effort of 1 1

CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION-PAST, PRESENT, AND FUTURE » 337 

Selective Service and the Department of Justice was therefore turned in this direction. Even after having been adjudged guilty in the 

Federal courts a delinquent could offer to comply and the charges against him were very likely to be withdrawn. Further there were provisions in the general regulations of the System which allowed violators serving prison sentences to seek parole for assignment to work of national importance. 

Court Decisions

Court decisions sustained the basic principles upon which the C. O. provisions of the 1940 Act were based. The United States v. Cain case held that the only role the Federal courts could play in the finality of Selective Service local and appeal board actions was to see that they were based on "substantial evidence." The United States v. Kauten and Herman Berman v. United States cases ruled that a valid conscientious objector claim to exemption must be based solely on "religious training and belief” and not on philosophical, political, social, or other grounds; whereas Gibson v. United States established the right of the delinquent objector to request defense from the 1940 law in the courts and decided that registrant assignees to C. P. S. 

Camps were civilians and should seek redress from their IV-E classifications and assignments through the civil courts rather than by habeas corpus. In Roodenko, Rockwell, Hutchison, and White v.

United States it was held that assignments to camps were constitutional, that the camps were legally authorized, and that camp projects constituted work of national importance. 

Separations From the Civilian Work Program 

Under the original provisions of the Selective Service Act registrants assigned to work of national importance were required to serve 12 months, the same length of time as those inducted into the armed forces, before being eligible for discharge. By succeeding amendments, the period of service was extended, first to 18 months, then for the duration of the war plus 6 months and finally to 18 months again. 

A demobilization program for both inducted and assigned registrants was put into effect the latter part of 1945. As regards combatant and noncombatant inductees, their releases were upon identical bases. The separation procedures for assignees then and earlier followed the same general pattern as those for members of the armed forces. Congressional and public opposition during demobilization restricted them somewhat, however, but in any event no conscientious objector was discharged from work of national importance before a man in like category was separated from the armed forces. 

Releases from Civilian Public Service Camps made prior to demobilization were as follows: physical disability, 1,566; dependency

CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION 

hardship, 290 cases; and occupational, largely agricultural, 184; 905, or between 7 and 8 percent, left the work program to enter at their own request, the armed forces; 30 died while on civilian work assignments; and 523 were discharged by reason of desertion or delinquency. 

This left a total of 8,408 or 70 percent for discharge through demobilization.

To recommend procedures and policies on releases and make rec ommendations on individual applications, a Special Separation Board was set up at National Headquarters, May 19, 1945; 630 cases, involving pleas of extreme hardship, the national health, safety and interest, and physical disability were acted upon by this Board. 

Statistical Data 

Although the problem of conscientious objection may have appeared quite widespread, there were nevertheless 1,262 local boards of the System with no registrants ever classified as objectors in I-A-0 or IV-E. Southern States had proportionately more of such boards than other areas. Among assignees to C. P. S. Camps members of the 

Christadelphian and Mennonite churches had higher percentages in comparison with their memberships. As to camp delinquents the proportions in relationship to denomination, were much the higher for Theosophists, Molokans, and Jehovah's Witnesses in that order. Since the C. O. program was a developing activity for the System during the 62-year period of its existence, the coverage of statistics for this part of the operation was not too complete. 

Lessons from Conscientious Objection Experience 

The Selective Service program for conscientious objectors during World War II was generally regarded as a satisfactory operation. 

The claims of more than 50,000 objectors, either for noncombatant service in the armed forces or work of national importance under civilian direction, were considered by the System. Assignees to both regular and special projects in Civilian Public Service Camps performed duties essential to the country's welfare. Despite the general success of the program, however, certain major problems arose during its operation. To bear upon the solution of these problems in future mobilization efforts, the following suggestions are therefore made: 

1. The basic principle-service for every liable, selected registrant but such duty within the dictates of conscience-was tested comprehensively both in theory and practice during the emergency of 1940-47.

As a result future Selective Service legislation should again include conscientious-objector provisions for both noncombatant service in military and naval organizations and civilian duty in work of national importance.

CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION—PAST, PRESENT, AND FUTURE » 339 Improved Status for Objectors in Civilian Work 

2. Although the armed forces over and above giving observance to belief averse to war, allowed the objector in noncombatant service exactly the same status as the registrant on combatant duty, this was not specified by the 1940 law as would perhaps have been advisable. 

In addition, there would probably be advantages to the System and the Federal Government in trying to utilize the objector whose faith precludes any duty with the Army and Navy if future conscription acts provided him with somewhat more rights and privileges than he had in World War II. The assignee to the civilian-work program and his family make certain sacrifices during a period of national emergency, and serious attention should at least be given to providing him with some pay and his family with some allowance or allotment. 

Better Classification Procedures 

3. Expanding the fundamental Selective Service legislation in this regard would require suitable implementation of both the general regulations for the System as regards classification and other procedures and the special ones for the work program. First of all there is some likelihood that the number of registrants claiming objection to any service in the armed forces, would increase under a liberalized program of this nature. This kind of a development would require more effective methods within Selective Service and the Department of Justice for determining the validity of such claims. On the other hand, their consideration as well as that for law violations or delinquencies must be thorough and painstaking as in the past, even if it involves activity by State and National Headquarters of the System and the Federal Bureau of Investigation in the Justice Department. 

Regarding the exemption, deferment or selection of conscientious objectors, any new enactment should provide for the special assistance of appeal boards by the Justice Department in matters of hearing, investigation and recommendation on selected registrants averse to war who appeal their local board classifications. The general regulations should perhaps provide for a somewhat more specific classification of objectors; for instance, if Class I-A is used to designate selection for combatant service, I-C for this type of duty within the armed forces, and I-D for discharge from that kind of service, it might be found advisable to use classifications like I-A-O, I-C-O and I-D-O in similar capacities for the registrant of the noncombatant category and I-A-E, I-C-E and I-D-E for the objector concerned with civilian work.

Improved Camp Discipline 

4. With the assignee to work of national importance having somewhat greater rights and privileges, he might attain a greater appre-

340. 

< 

ciation of his classification and other processing by the System and his assignment to a Civilian Public Service Camp. The result would probably be fewer problems of order and discipline in camp. However, for the handful of objectors who would still refuse to work and obey related orders, there should be adequate provisions in the act or otherwise for immediate and continued detention by the authority in charge of the camp until the malefactor has complied with the orders or has been removed from the unit. This would tend to avoid damage to the morale of the camp and to the reputation of the program. 

5. The camp organization either in centralized or decentralized units is perhaps the best arrangement for carrying on a civilian work program which involves registrants opposed to war and military or naval components. A camp probably needs to be operated throughout by that agency of the Federal or a State government concerned with the work project or projects being carried on there. The camp director should be an employee of this agency and in full control of the unit. 

Selective Service would procure personnel for the camp just as it does for the armed forces, and have a representative on its staff along with one from the national church organization if such existed. In a case of delinquency and detention as a result of such delinquency, the director should review the case thoroughly with his Selective Service, church, medical, legal, and other staff, and have the power thereafter to reissue the order which has been disobeyed, and/or refer the case (1) to a regional or Presidential board for action, (2) the United

States attorney for prosecution, or (3) to the System for reclassification and induction into the armed forces. 

6. In adjudging the validity of a registrant's claim of conscientious objection, the history of his past and present conduct will continue to be of basic importance. And when an objector interested in civilian work is selected for service, he should have a physical examination well in advance of such assignment, the same as a registrant selected for duty with the armed forces. In addition, it ought to be the same kind of an examination as that given to the other type of registrant. This would tend to reduce camp delinquency resulting from unfitness and to make for greater efficiency at the unit. 

Law Violation and Delinquency 

7. The objector who violates a Selective Service law by failing to register, return his Questionnaire or report for physical examination; by refusing to report at the work camp or obey orders there; or by counseling or aiding evasion at that unit or elsewhere, needs to be subject to prompt prosecution when reported to the United States attorney. Placing the responsibility of enforcement, as regards objectors and others, upon civil authority, such as the System and the 1

CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION-PAST, PRESENT, AND FUTURE » 341 

1 Department of Justice, is advisable but in such event the Federal courts must give priority to the delinquencies which are referred to them; lack of expeditious handling creates problems of morale and encourages further disobedience. 

8. The courts ought not only to act expeditiously in cases where the registrant is accused of an offense against the enactment, but in those where the objector believes Selective Service has made an illegal determination in his regard. Further, objector and other registrants should be encouraged to seek redress in court just as they are encouraged to seek appeal within the System.

Educational Activities 

9. Such court interpretation of the basic legislation is in itself an educational and persuasive process with regard to objector and other violators. Since a conscription act is to procure manpower for service, the delinquent at his request should generally be allowed to comply with the law during court proceedings, or even after imprisonment upon parole for such purpose. This procedure would also be followed by Selective Service during the period before he is reported to the United States attorney as a violator. Compliance with the law, and not penalty for its violation, is the desirable policy and much time could profitably be devoted to the development and use of such approach to reduce delinquency. 

10. As a part of this educational and persuasive task and also as an aid to operational phases of the program for conscientious objectors, consideration might well be given to the early establishment and application of comprehensive statistical and other records and reports on the activities of the System in the field. A special activity like that relating to objection, as well as a regular one, needs information upon which to base its various tasks. To illustrate, comparative figures by church denomination on the number of registrants claiming objection; being selected for service; having valid claims; classified I-A-O, IV-E or otherwise; inducted or assigned; becoming delinquent; and separated would be of significance not only to Selective Service, but to the objectors themselves, to their churches and to the technical agencies concerned with the work projects. 

Regular and Special Projects 

11. Speaking of projects, a civilian work program for objectors should preferably be composed of a wide variety of regular projects, manual in nature, and also of special ones, skilled and professional. 

The qualifications for camp assignees to become eligible for the different types of projects need to be adequate to insure both quantity and quality of work performance and there should be ample opportunity

for progressive activity-to-activity transfer. Since such transfers increase the personal contribution of the camp assignee to the national effort, there would seem to be advantages in having added responsibilities accompanied by some up-grading at least with respect to pay and perhaps in connection with allowances. 

12. In advance of new legislation and regulations of a comprehensive nature for conscientious objectors, extensive study and planning of program activities might prove beneficial in connection with later operations. Attention of this nature would probably be of greatest value with reference to the civilian work program. The subject of camp organization and administration is of particular importance here. 

In addition, the national significance of various regular and special civilian projects, even those located overseas, should be given consideration. If it is important that each objector to any service in the armed forces perform a work duty in lieu of induction, it is equally pertinent that such service be applied to the greatest advantage in a time of emergency. In the vast majority of cases the camp assignee will perform his duty satisfactorily and such effort, like that of the inductee, should be directed where most essential to the country.
